metadata.title: Code Optimization (Compiler)
metadata.definition: A compiler phase that attempts to improve the performance (e.g., speed, memory usage, power consumption) of the generated target code without altering its external observable behavior. It often operates on an intermediate representation, applying various transformations to make the code more efficient.

metadata.title: Common Subexpression Elimination
metadata.definition: A compiler optimization technique that identifies and removes redundant computations of expressions whose values have already been computed and are still available within the current scope. It replaces subsequent occurrences of such expressions with a reference to the previously computed value.

metadata.title: Loop Invariant Code Motion
metadata.definition: A compiler optimization that identifies expressions within a loop that compute the same value on every iteration and moves them to execute before the loop begins. This reduces redundant computations inside the loop, significantly improving execution speed.

metadata.title: Dead Code Elimination
metadata.definition: A compiler optimization that removes code which does not affect the program's observable output or state. This includes code that is unreachable, or computations whose results are never used by any subsequent operations.

metadata.title: Constant Folding (Compiler)
metadata.definition: A compiler optimization that evaluates expressions involving only constant operands at compile time, replacing the entire expression with its computed constant value. This reduces runtime computation and can expose opportunities for further optimizations.

metadata.title: Function Inlining
metadata.definition: A compiler optimization technique where a function call is replaced by the body of the called function directly at the call site. This eliminates the overhead associated with a function call (e.g., stack frame setup, argument passing) but can potentially increase code size.

metadata.title: Linker (Programming)
metadata.definition: A system program that takes one or more object files (generated by a compiler) and combines them into a single executable program, a library, or another object file. Its primary tasks include resolving references to external symbols and arranging code and data sections in the final output.

metadata.title: Loader (Operating System)
metadata.definition: An essential component of an operating system responsible for taking an executable program from disk and placing it into main memory, preparing it for execution. This involves allocating memory, copying program instructions and data segments, and setting up the CPU's registers and stack.

metadata.title: Dynamic Linking
metadata.definition: A linking process where references to library routines are resolved at runtime, either when the program is loaded or during its execution. This approach allows multiple programs to share a single copy of a library's code in memory, saving disk space and RAM, and enables easier library updates.

metadata.title: Static Linking
metadata.definition: A linking process where all necessary library code is copied directly into the executable file at compile/link time. This results in larger, self-contained executables that do not depend on external libraries at runtime, simplifying deployment but potentially increasing disk and memory footprint.

metadata.title: Source Code
metadata.definition: High-level programming language instructions written by a human programmer that are understandable and modifiable. It serves as the primary input to a compiler or interpreter for translation into executable forms.

metadata.title: Object Code
metadata.definition: The machine code output generated by a compiler for a single source file, often contained in an object file, which is not yet a complete executable program. It typically contains unresolved references to symbols (functions, variables) defined in other object files or libraries.

metadata.title: Binary Code
metadata.definition: The lowest-level representation of computer instructions and data, consisting solely of sequences of binary digits (0s and 1s). It is the native language of a computer's processor and is directly executable without further translation.

metadata.title: Compiler Bootstrapping
metadata.definition: The complex process of writing a compiler for a programming language using that very same language. This typically requires an initial, simpler compiler (often written in a different language or a subset of the target language) to compile the full compiler's source code, after which the compiler can then compile itself.

metadata.title: Foreign Function Interface (FFI)
metadata.definition: A mechanism that enables a program written in one programming language to call functions or use data types defined and compiled in another language. FFIs bridge different runtime environments and calling conventions, allowing interoperability between disparate language ecosystems.

metadata.title: Binary Compatibility
metadata.definition: The ability of a new version of a software component (like a library or operating system) to work correctly with existing compiled programs without requiring those programs to be recompiled. This implies that the new version's Application Binary Interface (ABI) remains consistent with the older version's.

metadata.title: Application Programming Interface (API)
metadata.definition: A set of clearly defined methods of communication between various software components, typically describing the data structures, routines, remote calls, and protocols a developer can use to interact with a library, operating system, or web service. It defines a contract for how to request services from the software component.

metadata.title: Application Binary Interface (ABI)
metadata.definition: A low-level interface that defines how compiled code interacts with other compiled code and the operating system. It specifies details such as calling conventions, data structure layout, register usage, exception handling mechanisms, and system call mechanisms, ensuring that different compiler-generated code modules can interoperate.

metadata.title: Applicative Functor
metadata.definition: An Applicative Functor is a concept in functional programming that extends Functors by providing a way to apply a function wrapped in a context to a value also wrapped in a context. It introduces the `pure` function to lift a value into a context and an 'apply' operator (often `<*>`) to combine contextual computations.

metadata.title: Strict Evaluation
metadata.definition: Strict evaluation, also known as eager evaluation, is an evaluation strategy where all arguments to a function are fully computed and evaluated before the function itself is applied. This means that expressions are evaluated as soon as they are bound to a variable or passed as an argument, regardless of whether their values are ultimately used within the function body.

metadata.title: Stream (Functional Programming)
metadata.definition: In functional programming, a stream is a potentially infinite sequence of data elements, often characterized by lazy evaluation, where elements are computed only when they are needed. This allows for the representation and processing of large or unending data sets without requiring all elements to be stored in memory simultaneously.

metadata.title: List Comprehension
metadata.definition: List comprehension is a syntactic construct available in many programming languages for creating new lists (or other iterable sequences) based on existing ones. It provides a concise and readable way to apply transformations and filter elements from a source iterable.

metadata.title: Higher-Order Component (HOC)
metadata.definition: A Higher-Order Component (HOC) is an advanced technique in component-based UI frameworks (like React) where a function takes a component as an input and returns a new component with enhanced functionality. HOCs are used for reusing component logic, abstracting common concerns, and manipulating props or state.

metadata.title: Type Class
metadata.definition: A type class is a feature in some programming languages (notably Haskell) that enables ad-hoc polymorphism by defining an interface or a set of operations that specific types must implement. It allows functions to be written generically for any type that is an 'instance' of a particular type class, providing a form of constrained polymorphism.

metadata.title: Orthogonality (Language Design)
metadata.definition: Orthogonality in language design refers to the principle that a small set of primitive constructs can be combined in a relatively small number of ways to form the language's features, with each combination having a clear, predictable meaning. It implies that language features are independent and do not interact in unexpected or arbitrary ways, contributing to simplicity and consistency.

metadata.title: Readability (Language Design)
metadata.definition: Readability is a language design principle concerning how easy it is for a human programmer to understand and interpret source code, especially code written by someone else. Factors contributing to readability include clear syntax, meaningful keywords, consistent structure, and features that prevent obscure or ambiguous constructs.

metadata.title: Writability (Language Design)
metadata.definition: Writability in language design refers to the ease and speed with which a programmer can write code in a particular language to achieve desired functionality. It encompasses factors like conciseness, availability of powerful abstractions, syntactic sugar, and the ability to express complex ideas with minimal code, thereby improving programmer productivity.

metadata.title: Reliability (Language Design)
metadata.definition: Reliability in programming language design concerns the extent to which a language helps prevent errors and ensures that programs behave as intended, both during compilation and at runtime. This is achieved through features like strong type systems, robust exception handling, memory safety mechanisms, and thorough error checking.

metadata.title: Cost of Use (Language Design)
metadata.definition: Cost of use, in language design, refers to the total overhead associated with employing a particular programming language throughout its lifecycle, encompassing various practical aspects. This includes development time, execution speed, memory consumption, required tooling, and the cost of training and retaining developers proficient in the language.

metadata.title: Expressiveness (Language Design)
metadata.definition: Expressiveness in language design measures how easily and concisely a language allows programmers to represent complex ideas, algorithms, and abstractions. A highly expressive language often enables writing less code to achieve more functionality, typically through powerful built-in constructs and sophisticated abstraction mechanisms.

metadata.title: Simplicity (Language Design)
metadata.definition: Simplicity, as a language design principle, advocates for a small number of basic constructs and features, with minimal exceptions, special cases, or redundant ways to achieve the same task. A simple language is generally easier to learn, understand, implement, and maintain, reducing the cognitive load on developers.

metadata.title: Safety (Language Design)
metadata.definition: Safety in programming language design refers to the degree to which a language prevents invalid operations or unintended program behaviors, thereby contributing to program correctness and integrity. This often involves robust mechanisms for type checking, memory management, and error handling to reduce the likelihood of bugs and security vulnerabilities.

metadata.title: Turing Completeness
metadata.definition: Turing completeness is a property of a computational system (such as a programming language or an abstract machine) indicating that it can simulate any arbitrary Turing machine. A Turing-complete system is theoretically capable of performing any computation that a computer can perform, given enough time and memory.

metadata.title: Type Theory
metadata.definition: Type theory is a branch of mathematical logic, computer science, and philosophy that studies formal systems involving types, particularly as they apply to programming languages. It provides a rigorous framework for designing, analyzing, and proving properties about type systems, ensuring program correctness, safety, and consistent behavior.

metadata.title: Programming Language Specification
metadata.definition: A programming language specification is a formal or informal document that precisely defines the syntax, semantics, and often the standard library of a programming language. It serves as the definitive reference for language implementers (e.g., compiler or interpreter writers) and users, ensuring consistency across different implementations and understanding of language behavior.

metadata.title: Dependent Type
metadata.definition: A dependent type is a type whose definition depends on a value, meaning that types can embed information known only at runtime or derived from program logic. This allows for incredibly expressive and precise type systems, enabling the compiler or type checker to prove complex properties about programs, extending well beyond traditional static typing.

metadata.title: Linear Type
metadata.definition: A linear type is a feature in a type system that ensures a resource or value typed as 'linear' is used exactly once: it must be consumed and neither discarded nor duplicated. This property is primarily used to manage unique resources safely, prevent unwanted side effects from uncontrolled aliasing, and enable more precise control over memory or I/O operations.

metadata.title: Gradual Typing
metadata.definition: Gradual typing is a type system that allows a programming language to support both static and dynamic typing within the same codebase, enabling a smooth transition between flexible prototyping and robust, type-checked code. It typically allows dynamically typed code to interact with statically typed code through runtime type checks at their boundaries.

metadata.title: Isomorphism (Type Theory)
metadata.definition: In type theory, two types A and B are isomorphic if there exist two functions, f: A → B and g: B → A, such that composing them in either direction yields the identity function (g(f(x)) = x and f(g(y)) = y). This signifies that the types are structurally equivalent and can be converted into each other without any loss of information.

metadata.title: Dependency Management
metadata.definition: Dependency management is the process of identifying, acquiring, configuring, and updating external libraries, frameworks, or modules (dependencies) that a software project relies on. It ensures that all necessary components are available in the correct versions for the project to build, run, and function correctly.

metadata.title: Read-Eval-Print Loop (REPL)
metadata.definition: A REPL is an interactive programming environment that repeatedly reads a single user input, evaluates it, prints the result, and then loops to await the next input. It provides immediate feedback, making it a valuable tool for experimentation, learning, debugging, and rapid prototyping.

metadata.title: Debugger
metadata.definition: A debugger is a software tool used to test and debug target programs by monitoring their execution, allowing developers to set breakpoints, step through code line by line, inspect variable values, and examine memory states. It is essential for identifying and resolving logical errors (bugs) within an application.

metadata.title: Profiler (Programming)
metadata.definition: A profiler is a software tool that analyzes the performance characteristics of a program, measuring resource usage such as execution time, memory consumption, CPU cycles, and function call frequencies. Its primary goal is to help developers identify performance bottlenecks and areas for optimization within an application.

metadata.title: Static Analysis Tool
metadata.definition: A static analysis tool examines source code or compiled code without executing it, to detect potential bugs, security vulnerabilities, and deviations from coding standards. It helps improve code quality, reliability, and security early in the development lifecycle by identifying issues before runtime.

metadata.title: Linter
metadata.definition: A linter is a type of static analysis tool specifically designed to flag programmatic errors, bugs, stylistic errors, and suspicious constructs in source code. Linters enforce coding conventions and best practices, thereby improving code readability, maintainability, and consistency across a project or team.

metadata.title: Data Link Layer
metadata.definition: The second layer of the OSI model, responsible for node-to-node data transfer, handling framing, physical addressing (MAC addresses), error detection, and flow control. It ensures reliable transmission of data frames across a physical link.

metadata.title: Session Layer
metadata.definition: The fifth layer of the OSI model, responsible for establishing, managing, and terminating communication sessions between applications. It provides services like synchronization, dialog control, and checkpointing to manage the flow of data.

metadata.title: Presentation Layer
metadata.definition: The sixth layer of the OSI model, responsible for data translation, encryption, and compression, ensuring that data is presented in a readable format for the application layer. It acts as a data translator for the network.

metadata.title: Network Access Layer
metadata.definition: The lowest layer in the TCP/IP model, combining the functionalities of the OSI model's Physical and Data Link layers. It handles all the physical aspects of data transmission, including hardware addressing, physical cabling, and error detection on the local network segment.

metadata.title: Internet Layer
metadata.definition: The second layer of the TCP/IP model, corresponding to the OSI Network layer. It is responsible for logical addressing (IP addresses), routing data packets across different networks, and determining the best path for data delivery.

metadata.title: Bandwidth (Networking)
metadata.definition: The maximum rate at which data can be transferred over a network connection, typically measured in bits per second (bps). It represents the capacity of a communication channel.

metadata.title: Throughput
metadata.definition: The actual rate at which data is successfully transmitted over a communication channel per unit of time, often measured in bits per second (bps). Unlike bandwidth, throughput reflects the real-world performance affected by factors like latency, packet loss, and network congestion.

metadata.title: Latency (Networking)
metadata.definition: The time delay from when a data packet is sent from a source to when it is received at its destination. It is often measured in milliseconds (ms) and is a critical factor in real-time application performance.

metadata.title: Jitter
metadata.definition: The variation in latency of successive data packets on a network. It is an undesirable phenomenon that can cause issues like audio dropouts or video freezing, especially in real-time communication applications.

metadata.title: Packet Loss
metadata.definition: Occurs when one or more data packets travelling across a computer network fail to reach their destination. It results in missing information and often necessitates retransmission, increasing latency and reducing effective throughput.

metadata.title: Bit Rate
metadata.definition: The number of bits, or binary digits, that are conveyed or processed per unit of time. It is a fundamental measure of digital data transfer speed, typically expressed in bits per second (bps).

metadata.title: Baud Rate
metadata.definition: The number of signal changes (symbols) per second that occur on a transmission medium. Each symbol can represent one or more bits, so baud rate is not always equal to bit rate, but it measures the rate of modulation.

metadata.title: Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)
metadata.definition: A measure that compares the level of a desired signal to the level of background noise. A higher SNR indicates a clearer signal with less interference, which allows for higher data transmission rates and fewer errors.

metadata.title: Shannon-Hartley Theorem
metadata.definition: A fundamental theorem in information theory that specifies the maximum rate (channel capacity) at which information can be transmitted over a communication channel with a specified bandwidth in the presence of noise. It states that capacity C = B log2(1 + S/N), where B is bandwidth, S is signal power, and N is noise power.

metadata.title: Nyquist-Shannon Sampling Theorem
metadata.definition: A theorem stating that to perfectly reconstruct a continuous-time signal from its samples, the sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency component of the signal (the Nyquist rate). It's crucial for digital audio and video.

metadata.title: Guided Media
metadata.definition: Physical communication pathways where electromagnetic waves are guided along a solid medium, such as cables. This type of media offers predictable performance and high security compared to unguided media.

metadata.title: Unguided Media
metadata.definition: Communication pathways that transmit electromagnetic waves through the air or space without a physical conductor. Also known as wireless communication, it relies on broadcast signals and offers flexibility but can be prone to interference.

metadata.title: Twisted Pair Cable
metadata.definition: A type of guided media consisting of pairs of insulated copper wires twisted together to reduce electromagnetic interference (EMI) from external sources and crosstalk between adjacent pairs. It is widely used in Ethernet networks and telephone lines.

metadata.title: Coaxial Cable
metadata.definition: A type of guided media featuring a central conductor surrounded by an insulating layer, which is then encased by a metallic shield and an outer insulating jacket. This design provides excellent protection against external interference and supports higher bandwidth over longer distances than twisted pair for certain applications.

metadata.title: Fiber Optic Cable
metadata.definition: A type of guided media that transmits data as pulses of light through thin strands of glass or plastic fiber. It offers significantly higher bandwidth, longer transmission distances, and immunity to electromagnetic interference compared to copper cables.

metadata.title: Turbo Codes
metadata.definition: A class of high-performance forward error correction (FEC) codes noted for their ability to achieve near the Shannon limit. They use parallel concatenated convolutional codes (PCCCs) with an interleaver and iterative decoding to recover data sent over noisy channels.

metadata.title: Low-Density Parity-Check (LDPC) Codes
metadata.definition: A class of highly efficient linear block codes with a sparse parity-check matrix, known for their excellent performance approaching the Shannon limit. They are decoded using iterative belief propagation algorithms, providing high throughput and low error rates.

metadata.title: Viterbi Algorithm
metadata.definition: A dynamic programming algorithm for finding the most likely sequence of hidden states – the Viterbi path – that results in a sequence of observed events. It is widely used for decoding convolutional codes and in applications involving Hidden Markov Models (HMMs).

metadata.title: Framing (Data Link Layer)
metadata.definition: The process of encapsulating network layer datagrams into frames, adding a header and a trailer to define the beginning and end of the data unit. This allows the receiver to properly delineate the data and perform error checking.

metadata.title: Flow Control (Data Link Layer)
metadata.definition: A mechanism at the Data Link Layer to ensure that a sender does not overwhelm a receiver with data by regulating the rate at which data is transmitted. It prevents buffer overflow at the receiving end, ensuring reliable communication between directly connected nodes.

metadata.title: Error Control (Data Link Layer)
metadata.definition: Mechanisms employed at the Data Link Layer to detect and often correct errors that may occur during data transmission over an unreliable physical medium. This ensures reliable data delivery between adjacent network nodes.

metadata.title: Media Access Control (MAC)
metadata.definition: A sublayer of the Data Link Layer responsible for controlling how multiple devices share a common transmission medium. It handles physical addressing (MAC addresses), channel access methods, and often frame error detection for local network communication.

metadata.title: Logical Link Control (LLC)
metadata.definition: A sublayer of the Data Link Layer (IEEE 802.2) that provides the interface between the Media Access Control (MAC) sublayer and the network layer. It handles multiplexing of network layer protocols over the MAC layer and can provide optional flow and error control services.

metadata.title: Ethernet Frame Format
metadata.definition: The specific structure and fields of a data unit (frame) used for transmitting information over an Ethernet network. It includes fields for preamble, start-of-frame delimiter, destination MAC address, source MAC address, EtherType/Length, data payload, and Frame Check Sequence (FCS).

metadata.title: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (CSMA/CD)
metadata.definition: A media access control method used in early Ethernet networks and half-duplex connections where a device first listens (carrier sense) to see if the medium is free before transmitting. If a collision is detected during transmission, the device stops, waits a random backoff time, and retries the transmission.

metadata.title: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance (CSMA/CA)
metadata.definition: A media access control method primarily used in wireless networks (e.g., Wi-Fi) where devices attempt to avoid collisions before they occur. It involves mechanisms like 'listen before talk' (carrier sense), explicit acknowledgements (ACKs), and sometimes Request-To-Send/Clear-To-Send (RTS/CTS) to reserve the medium.

metadata.title: Collision Domain
metadata.definition: A network segment where data packets can 'collide' with one another if two or more devices attempt to transmit simultaneously. Devices within the same collision domain compete for shared network bandwidth, and the entire domain is effectively operating in half-duplex mode.

metadata.title: Broadcast Domain
metadata.definition: A logical network segment in which all connected devices can receive broadcast frames originating from any other device within the same segment. Routers typically delineate broadcast domains, preventing broadcasts from propagating further into other networks.

metadata.title: Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN)
metadata.definition: A logical grouping of network devices that allows them to communicate as if they were on the same physical LAN, regardless of their actual physical location. VLANs are used to segment broadcast domains, improve security, and enhance network management within a switched environment.

metadata.title: VLAN Tagging (802.1Q)
metadata.definition: An IEEE standard (802.1Q) that specifies a system for inserting a 4-byte tag into an Ethernet frame to identify the Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) to which the frame belongs. This allows multiple VLANs to share a single physical network link, known as a trunk link, while maintaining logical separation.

metadata.title: VLAN Trunking Protocol (VTP)
metadata.definition: A Cisco proprietary messaging protocol that manages the addition, deletion, and renaming of VLANs across a switched network. VTP propagates VLAN configuration changes from a central VTP server to all VTP clients within the same VTP domain, simplifying network administration and ensuring consistency.

metadata.title: Spanning Tree Protocol (STP)
metadata.definition: An IEEE 802.1D network protocol that prevents loop formation in a switched Ethernet network by selectively blocking redundant paths. It ensures a single, loop-free logical path between all network devices, preventing broadcast storms, MAC table instability, and multiple frame copies.

metadata.title: Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol (RSTP)
metadata.definition: An evolution of STP (IEEE 802.1w) that significantly improves convergence time in switched networks compared to its predecessor. RSTP achieves faster convergence by introducing new port roles and states, and by actively negotiating rather than passively listening for topology changes, making networks more resilient to failures.

metadata.title: Link Aggregation Group (LAG)
metadata.definition: A technology that bundles multiple physical network links (e.g., Ethernet interfaces) into a single logical link to increase bandwidth, provide redundancy, and balance traffic load. This logical link appears as one to the network layer, enhancing network performance and availability.

metadata.title: EtherChannel
metadata.definition: Cisco's proprietary implementation of Link Aggregation Group (LAG), allowing multiple Fast Ethernet or Gigabit Ethernet links to be bundled together. It provides increased bandwidth and link redundancy between Cisco switches, routers, and servers, simplifying configuration and management.

metadata.title: Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP)
metadata.definition: A protocol that controls the bundling of multiple physical network links into a single logical link, providing increased bandwidth and redundancy. It allows network devices to negotiate and manage the aggregation of links automatically, defined by IEEE 802.3ad.

metadata.title: Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
metadata.definition: A vendor-neutral Layer 2 protocol used by network devices to advertise their identity, capabilities, and neighbors on a local area network (LAN). It helps in network topology discovery and troubleshooting, defined by IEEE 802.1AB.

metadata.title: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP)
metadata.definition: A Cisco-proprietary Layer 2 protocol that runs on Cisco devices to discover directly connected Cisco equipment. It allows devices to share information about their device type, IOS version, capabilities, and connected ports, aiding in network management and troubleshooting.

metadata.title: Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP)
metadata.definition: A data link layer (Layer 2) protocol used to establish a direct connection between two nodes. It provides connection authentication, transmission encryption, and data compression, commonly used for dial-up connections and DSL.

metadata.title: Point-to-Point Protocol over Ethernet (PPPoE)
metadata.definition: A network protocol that encapsulates PPP frames inside Ethernet frames. It is primarily used to provide point-to-point connections over an Ethernet network, commonly by ISPs to deliver DSL and fiber optic services.

metadata.title: High-Level Data Link Control (HDLC)
metadata.definition: A bit-oriented code-transparent synchronous data link layer protocol developed by ISO. It provides error-free transmission of data frames over point-to-point or multi-point links and is a fundamental building block for many other protocols.

metadata.title: Frame Relay
metadata.definition: A standardized wide area network (WAN) technology that provides data communication services for interconnected devices by packaging data into frames. It operates at the data link layer and offers connection-oriented, packet-switching communication over a shared network infrastructure.

metadata.title: Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM)
metadata.definition: A connection-oriented, cell-based switching technology designed for high-speed transmission of voice, video, and data traffic. It uses small, fixed-size cells (53 bytes) to achieve efficient multiplexing and quality of service (QoS) guarantees, primarily used in backbone networks.

metadata.title: Token Ring
metadata.definition: A local area network (LAN) technology where all devices are connected in a physical ring topology and communicate using a special frame called a "token." Only the device holding the token can transmit data, preventing collisions and ensuring deterministic access.

metadata.title: Fiber Distributed Data Interface (FDDI)
metadata.definition: A high-speed token-passing local area network (LAN) technology, typically operating over fiber optic cable, designed to provide a 100 Mbps backbone for large networks. It uses a dual-ring topology for redundancy and fault tolerance.

metadata.title: Network Interface Card (NIC)
metadata.definition: A hardware component that connects a computer or other network device to a network, allowing it to communicate with other devices. It processes network data at the physical and data link layers, converting digital data into electrical signals or light pulses for transmission.

metadata.title: Hub (Networking)
metadata.definition: A basic networking device that connects multiple Ethernet devices together, acting as a multi-port repeater. It broadcasts all incoming data packets to every connected port, operating at the physical layer (Layer 1) and creating a single collision domain.

metadata.title: Switch (Networking)
metadata.definition: A networking device that connects devices on a local area network (LAN) and intelligently forwards data frames to specific destination devices based on their MAC addresses. It operates at the data link layer (Layer 2) and creates separate collision domains for each port.

metadata.title: Bridge (Networking)
metadata.definition: A data link layer (Layer 2) device that connects two separate network segments and selectively forwards frames between them based on MAC addresses. It learns MAC addresses to filter traffic and reduce collisions, effectively creating multiple collision domains.

metadata.title: Repeater (Networking)
metadata.definition: A physical layer (Layer 1) device that regenerates and retransmits network signals to extend the reach of a network segment. It amplifies or reshapes the signal to overcome attenuation and maintain signal integrity over longer distances.

metadata.title: Modem
metadata.definition: A device that modulates an analog carrier signal to encode digital information and demodulates such a carrier signal to decode transmitted information. It enables digital data to be transmitted over analog transmission lines, such as telephone lines, coaxial cables, or fiber optics.

metadata.title: Wireless Access Point (WAP)
metadata.definition: A networking device that allows Wi-Fi enabled devices to connect to a wired network. It acts as a central hub for wireless clients, converting wireless signals into wired Ethernet signals and vice versa, often supporting various security protocols.

metadata.title: IPv4 Header
metadata.definition: The section of an IPv4 packet that contains control information necessary for routing the packet across an IP network. Key fields include Source/Destination IP Addresses, Time to Live (TTL), Protocol, Header Length, and Checksum.

metadata.title: IPv6 Header
metadata.definition: The control information portion of an IPv6 packet, designed to be simpler and more efficient than its IPv4 counterpart, while supporting larger address spaces. It includes fields such as Source/Destination IPv6 Addresses, Traffic Class, Flow Label, Payload Length, and Next Header.

metadata.title: Classful Addressing (IPv4)
metadata.definition: An outdated IPv4 addressing scheme where IP addresses were divided into predefined classes (A, B, C, D, E) based on the first few bits of the address, explicitly defining the network and host portions. This system led to inefficient address allocation and is superseded by Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR).

metadata.title: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR)
metadata.definition: CIDR is a method for allocating IP addresses and routing Internet Protocol packets more efficiently than with the original classful addressing system. It uses a variable-length subnet mask to specify the prefix length, allowing for arbitrary-sized address blocks and reducing routing table sizes.

metadata.title: Subnet Mask
metadata.definition: A subnet mask is a 32-bit number used in conjunction with an IP address to determine the network portion and the host portion of the address. It indicates which bits of an IP address belong to the network identifier and which bits belong to the host identifier.

metadata.title: Private IP Address
metadata.definition: Private IP addresses are specific ranges of IP addresses reserved for use in private networks, such as local area networks (LANs), and are not routable on the public internet. They allow organizations to use the same address ranges internally without conflict and conserve public IP addresses.

metadata.title: Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN)
metadata.definition: CGN is a large-scale NAT implementation used by Internet Service Providers (ISPs) to allow multiple customers to share a single public IPv4 address. It addresses IPv4 address exhaustion by mapping many private customer IP addresses to a smaller pool of public addresses, often resulting in customers being behind 'double NAT'.

metadata.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP)
metadata.definition: DHCP is a network management protocol used on Internet Protocol (IP) networks for dynamically assigning IP addresses and other communication parameters to devices connected to the network. It automates the configuration process for new and existing hosts, simplifying network administration.

metadata.title: DHCP Discover
metadata.definition: DHCP Discover is the first message in the DHCP DORA process, broadcast by a client that is searching for a DHCP server on the network. The client sends this message to identify any available DHCP servers that can offer an IP address.

metadata.title: DHCP Offer
metadata.definition: A DHCP Offer is a response from a DHCP server to a DHCP Discover message, proposing an available IP address and other configuration parameters to the client. The server also temporarily reserves the offered IP address for the client.

metadata.title: DHCP Request
metadata.definition: A DHCP Request is a message sent by a DHCP client to either formally accept a specific DHCP server's offer (if multiple offers were received) or to renew an existing IP address lease. It's the client's explicit confirmation of the desired IP configuration.

metadata.title: DHCP ACK
metadata.definition: A DHCP ACK (Acknowledgment) is a DHCP server's final message, confirming the IP address lease and all configuration parameters to the client. This message signals the successful completion of the DHCP DORA process, and the client can now use the assigned IP address.

metadata.title: DHCP NAK
metadata.definition: A DHCP NAK (Negative Acknowledgment) is a DHCP server's message sent to a client if its DHCP Request is invalid or cannot be fulfilled. This might occur if the requested IP address is no longer available, is outside the server's scope, or belongs to a different network.

metadata.title: DHCP Relay Agent
metadata.definition: A DHCP Relay Agent is a network device, typically a router, that forwards DHCP messages between clients and servers located on different IP subnets. It allows a single DHCP server to serve clients across multiple broadcast domains, preventing the need for a DHCP server on every subnet.

metadata.title: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)
metadata.definition: ARP is a protocol used by the Internet Protocol (IP) for mapping an IP address to a physical machine address, such as an Ethernet MAC address, on a local area network. ARP is essential for local network communication between devices, allowing them to send data frames to each other.

metadata.title: ARP Request
metadata.definition: An ARP Request is a broadcast message sent by a device on a local network to discover the MAC address associated with a specific IP address. The message is sent to all devices on the segment, asking the owner of the target IP to reply with its MAC address.

metadata.title: ARP Reply
metadata.definition: An ARP Reply is a unicast message sent by a device in response to an ARP Request, providing its own MAC address to the requesting device. This allows the requester to update its ARP cache with the IP-to-MAC mapping and send subsequent IP packets to the correct physical address.

metadata.title: Proxy ARP
metadata.definition: Proxy ARP is a technique where a router or host responds to ARP requests for IP addresses that are not on its local network segment, effectively acting as a proxy for the actual owner of the IP. It helps devices on a segment reach devices on another segment without needing to know about routing or having a default gateway configured.

metadata.title: Gratuitous ARP
metadata.definition: Gratuitous ARP is an ARP request or reply that is not prompted by an ARP request, typically sent by a device to announce its presence and IP-to-MAC mapping on the network. It is used for detecting duplicate IP addresses, updating other devices' ARP caches after an interface comes online, or when an IP address changes.

metadata.title: Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP)
metadata.definition: ICMP is a network layer protocol used for sending error messages and operational information, such as whether a host is reachable or if a service is unavailable. It is fundamental for network diagnostics and reporting problems with IP packet delivery, though it does not carry application data.

metadata.title: ICMP Echo Request
metadata.definition: An ICMP Echo Request is an ICMP message sent by a source host to a destination host to test connectivity and measure the round-trip time between them. This message is the primary mechanism utilized by the `ping` utility.

metadata.title: ICMP Echo Reply
metadata.definition: An ICMP Echo Reply is an ICMP message sent by a destination host in response to an ICMP Echo Request, indicating that the destination is reachable and functioning. It completes the round-trip measurement for connectivity tests and is crucial for `ping` to report success.

metadata.title: ICMP Redirect
metadata.definition: An ICMP Redirect is an ICMP message sent by a router to a host, informing the host that it should use a different router (a more optimal one) for future traffic to a specific destination network. It helps optimize host routing tables by guiding hosts to the most efficient gateway on their segment.

metadata.title: Routing (Networking)
metadata.definition: Routing is the process of selecting the optimal path across one or more networks for data packets to travel from their source to their destination. It involves routers making decisions based on routing tables to forward traffic to the next hop.

metadata.title: Forwarding (Networking)
metadata.definition: Forwarding is the actual process of moving a packet from an incoming interface of a network device (like a router or switch) to an outgoing interface. This decision is based on the information derived from the routing (control plane) process and stored in the forwarding information base (FIB).

metadata.title: Routing Table
metadata.definition: A routing table is a data table stored in a router or a networked computer that lists all known network destinations, the associated next-hop addresses, and the outgoing interfaces required to reach those destinations. Routers use this table to make forwarding decisions for incoming packets.

metadata.title: Static Routing
metadata.definition: Static routing is a method of routing where network administrators manually configure and maintain routes in a router's routing table. These routes remain fixed unless manually changed, offering simplicity and security for small, stable networks.

metadata.title: Dynamic Routing
metadata.definition: Dynamic routing is a method that uses routing protocols to automatically discover, maintain, and update routing tables in response to network topology changes. Routers exchange routing information with each other to adapt to network failures or additions.

metadata.title: Distance-Vector Routing
metadata.definition: Distance-vector routing is a class of dynamic routing protocols where each router periodically exchanges its entire routing table with its directly connected neighbors. The best path to a destination is determined by its 'distance' (metric) and the 'vector' (next-hop router) provided by a neighbor.

metadata.title: Link-State Routing
metadata.definition: Link-state routing is a class of dynamic routing protocols where each router builds a complete topological map of the entire network. This is achieved by exchanging small 'link-state advertisements' (LSAs) with all other routers within its area, and then running Dijkstra's algorithm to calculate the shortest path to every destination.

metadata.title: Routing Information Protocol (RIP)
metadata.definition: RIP is an older, distance-vector routing protocol that uses hop count as its metric to determine the best path to a destination. It is characterized by periodic full routing table updates to neighbors and a maximum hop count of 15, limiting its scalability to smaller networks.

metadata.title: RIPv1
metadata.definition: RIPv1 is the original, classful version of the Routing Information Protocol. It does not send subnet mask information in its routing updates and therefore does not support Variable Length Subnet Masking (VLSM) or Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR).

metadata.title: RIPv2
metadata.definition: RIPv2 is an enhanced, classless version of the Routing Information Protocol that overcomes the limitations of RIPv1. It includes subnet mask information in its routing updates, enabling support for Variable Length Subnet Masking (VLSM) and Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR).

metadata.title: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
metadata.definition: OSPF is a widely used link-state routing protocol that divides a large autonomous system into hierarchical areas for improved scalability and faster convergence. It uses Dijkstra's algorithm to calculate the shortest path to all destinations based on link costs.

metadata.title: OSPFv2
metadata.definition: OSPFv2 is the version of OSPF specifically designed for routing IPv4 networks. It is the most common implementation of OSPF, supporting VLSM and CIDR, and is defined in RFC 2328.

metadata.title: OSPFv3
metadata.definition: OSPFv3 is the version of OSPF primarily designed to support IPv6 networks, although it was later enhanced to also support IPv4 through address families. It separates the addressing semantics from the routing protocol, making it more flexible.

metadata.title: OSPF Area
metadata.definition: An OSPF Area is a logical grouping of routers and their connected networks within an OSPF autonomous system. It is used to segment the network, reducing the size of the link-state database, limiting the scope of LSA flooding, and minimizing the frequency of SPF calculations, which improves scalability.

metadata.title: OSPF Link State Advertisements (LSAs)
metadata.definition: LSAs are data packets used by OSPF routers to share information about their local links and network topology with other routers within the same OSPF area. Different LSA types describe various components of the network, such as router links, network segments, or external routes.

metadata.title: OSPF Designated Router (DR)
metadata.definition: The OSPF Designated Router (DR) is a router elected on a multi-access network segment (like Ethernet) to reduce the number of adjacencies and LSA flooding. It serves as a central point for all routers on that segment to exchange link-state information, minimizing overhead.

metadata.title: OSPF Backup Designated Router (BDR)
metadata.definition: The OSPF Backup Designated Router (BDR) is a router elected on a multi-access network segment alongside the DR. Its primary role is to monitor the DR and immediately take over the DR's responsibilities if the DR fails, ensuring high availability and continuous routing operations without re-election.

metadata.title: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP)
metadata.definition: EIGRP is an advanced distance-vector routing protocol (originally Cisco proprietary, now open standard) known for its fast convergence and efficiency. It uses the Diffusing Update Algorithm (DUAL) to guarantee loop-free paths and supports unequal-cost load balancing, VLSM, and CIDR.

metadata.title: EIGRP DUAL Algorithm
metadata.definition: DUAL (Diffusing Update Algorithm) is the core algorithm used by EIGRP to calculate the shortest, loop-free paths to all destinations. It maintains a topology table that includes both successor (best) routes and feasible successor (backup) routes, allowing for extremely fast convergence in the event of a primary path failure.

metadata.title: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)
metadata.definition: BGP is the primary exterior gateway routing protocol (EGP) responsible for exchanging routing and reachability information between different autonomous systems (AS) on the Internet. It is a path-vector protocol, making routing decisions based on network policies, AS path attributes, and rulesets rather than just metrics.

metadata.title: BGP-4
metadata.definition: Border Gateway Protocol version 4 is the current standard exterior gateway protocol used for exchanging routing and reachability information among autonomous systems (AS) on the Internet. It's a path-vector protocol that makes routing decisions based on paths, network policies, and a set of rules.

metadata.title: BGP Attributes
metadata.definition: BGP attributes are parameters appended to a BGP route that provide additional information about the route, significantly influencing the BGP best path selection process. They are categorized as well-known mandatory, well-known discretionary, optional transitive, or optional non-transitive.

metadata.title: eBGP (External BGP)
metadata.definition: eBGP refers to BGP sessions established between BGP speakers located in different autonomous systems (AS). It is primarily used for exchanging routing information and establishing reachability between different organizations or ISPs across the internet.

metadata.title: iBGP (Internal BGP)
metadata.definition: iBGP refers to BGP sessions established between BGP speakers within the same autonomous system (AS). Its primary purpose is to ensure consistent routing information within an AS, often used to distribute eBGP-learned routes to all internal BGP routers.

metadata.title: BGP Peer
metadata.definition: A BGP peer (or neighbor) is a router that has established a BGP session with another router to exchange routing information. This session involves a TCP connection on port 179 and subsequent exchange of BGP messages.

metadata.title: BGP Router ID
metadata.definition: The BGP Router ID is a 32-bit value, typically an IP address, that uniquely identifies a BGP router within an autonomous system. It is used in the BGP best path selection process to break ties and prevent routing loops.

metadata.title: BGP Best Path Selection Algorithm
metadata.definition: The BGP Best Path Selection Algorithm is a deterministic process used by a BGP router to choose the single optimal path from multiple available paths to a destination prefix. It evaluates routes based on a predefined sequence of attributes, such as Weight, LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH length, Origin code, and MED.

metadata.title: BGP Communities
metadata.definition: BGP Communities are optional, transitive attributes that provide a way to group destinations and apply a common policy to them, independent of their AS. They are used for simplified route tagging and policy application across networks.

metadata.title: BGP Route Reflector
metadata.definition: A BGP Route Reflector is a mechanism used to scale iBGP deployments by reducing the need for a full mesh of iBGP sessions within an AS. It allows a BGP router to advertise iBGP-learned routes to other iBGP peers, effectively breaking the standard iBGP split-horizon rule.

metadata.title: BGP Confederation
metadata.definition: A BGP Confederation is an advanced iBGP scaling technique that divides a large autonomous system (AS) into multiple sub-autonomous systems, appearing as a single AS to the outside world. This reduces the number of iBGP sessions required by using eBGP-like peering between sub-ASes and iBGP within them.

metadata.title: Multicast Routing
metadata.definition: Multicast routing is a method of sending network traffic from a single source to multiple selected destinations simultaneously, forming a 'one-to-many' communication. It efficiently delivers data to groups of receivers that have explicitly joined a multicast group, avoiding unnecessary replication and flooding.

metadata.title: Anycast Addressing
metadata.definition: Anycast addressing is a network addressing and routing method where data is routed to the 'nearest' or 'best' available service endpoint among a group of potential receivers identified by the same IP address. It is often used for redundancy, load distribution, and improved latency.

metadata.title: Unicast Addressing
metadata.definition: Unicast addressing is a one-to-one communication method where a packet is sent from a single source to a single specific destination device on a network. It is the most common and fundamental form of data transmission used in IP networks.

metadata.title: Broadcast Addressing
metadata.definition: Broadcast addressing is a one-to-all communication method where a packet is sent from a single source to all devices on a specific network segment or subnet. Devices typically listen for their own address and the broadcast address to receive relevant messages.

metadata.title: IP Fragmentation
metadata.definition: IP fragmentation is the process of breaking down an IP packet into smaller pieces (fragments) when its size exceeds the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of a network link it needs to traverse. This allows the packet to pass through links with smaller MTUs, with reassembly occurring at the destination.

metadata.title: Time To Live (TTL)
metadata.definition: Time To Live (TTL) is an 8-bit field in the IP header that specifies the maximum number of hops an IP packet can traverse before being discarded by a router. It prevents packets from looping indefinitely on a network, consuming resources and causing congestion.

metadata.title: Path MTU Discovery
metadata.definition: Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) is a process that determines the largest Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) that can be used on the entire network path between two IP hosts without causing IP fragmentation. It typically works by sending packets with the 'Don't Fragment' (DF) bit set and reacting to 'Fragmentation Needed' ICMP messages.

metadata.title: TCP Segment Header
metadata.definition: The TCP Segment Header is a control block prepended to application data, containing essential information for reliable, ordered, and error-checked delivery of data over an IP network. Key fields include Source and Destination Ports, Sequence and Acknowledgement Numbers, Window Size, and Checksum.

metadata.title: UDP Segment Header
metadata.definition: The UDP Segment Header is a minimal control block prepended to application data, providing connectionless, unreliable, and unordered datagram service over an IP network. It contains only Source and Destination Ports, Length, and an optional Checksum, offering efficiency over reliability.

metadata.title: TCP Checksum
metadata.definition: The TCP Checksum is a 16-bit field in the TCP header used for error detection, verifying the integrity of the TCP header, TCP data, and a pseudo-header derived from the IP header. It helps ensure that no bits have been accidentally altered during transmission across the network.

metadata.title: UDP Checksum
metadata.definition: The UDP checksum is an optional (but commonly used) 16-bit field in the UDP header used for error detection, allowing the receiver to determine if any bits in the UDP datagram (header and data) have been flipped during transmission.

metadata.title: TCP Three-Way Handshake
metadata.definition: The TCP three-way handshake is a fundamental process used to establish a reliable, full-duplex TCP connection between a client and a server, involving the exchange of three segments: SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK.

metadata.title: TCP Connection Establishment
metadata.definition: TCP connection establishment is the overall process of initiating and setting up a logical end-to-end communication path between two hosts, primarily achieved through the three-way handshake, before any application data can be reliably exchanged.

metadata.title: TCP Connection Termination
metadata.definition: TCP connection termination is the process of gracefully closing an existing TCP connection, typically involving a four-way handshake (FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK) to ensure both sides have finished sending data and acknowledged receipt before tearing down the connection.

metadata.title: TCP Flow Control
metadata.definition: TCP flow control is a mechanism designed to prevent a fast sender from overwhelming a slower receiver by dynamically adjusting the sender's data transmission rate based on the receiver's available buffer space, advertised via the receive window.

metadata.title: TCP Congestion Control
metadata.definition: TCP congestion control is a set of algorithms that aim to prevent network collapse by adapting the sender's transmission rate to the current network conditions, primarily by detecting and reacting to signs of congestion like packet loss or increased round-trip times.

metadata.title: Slow Start
metadata.definition: Slow Start is a TCP congestion control algorithm phase where the congestion window (cwnd) begins at a small value and increases exponentially with each received acknowledgment, quickly probing for available network bandwidth until a congestion event occurs or a slow start threshold (ssthresh) is reached.

metadata.title: Congestion Avoidance (TCP)
metadata.definition: Congestion Avoidance is a TCP congestion control phase that follows Slow Start, where the congestion window (cwnd) increases linearly (additively) for each Round Trip Time (RTT), allowing a more conservative probe for additional bandwidth after the slow start threshold (ssthresh) has been met.

metadata.title: Fast Retransmit
metadata.definition: Fast Retransmit is a TCP congestion control enhancement that allows the sender to retransmit a lost segment without waiting for a retransmission timeout, by inferring packet loss from the receipt of three duplicate ACKs for the same unacknowledged segment.

metadata.title: Fast Recovery
metadata.definition: Fast Recovery is a TCP congestion control algorithm used in conjunction with Fast Retransmit, which, upon detecting packet loss via duplicate ACKs, reduces the congestion window by half and enters a phase of additive increase, avoiding the drastic reset of slow start while data continues to be sent.

metadata.title: TCP Retransmission
metadata.definition: TCP retransmission is the mechanism by which TCP ensures reliable data delivery by re-sending unacknowledged data segments, either after a retransmission timeout (RTO) or upon receiving multiple duplicate acknowledgments (Fast Retransmit), to recover from packet loss.

metadata.title: TCP BBR
metadata.definition: TCP BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and RTT) is a congestion control algorithm developed by Google that optimizes network throughput and minimizes latency by actively estimating the bottleneck bandwidth and round-trip time of the network path, rather than solely reacting to packet loss.

metadata.title: Multipath TCP (MPTCP)
metadata.definition: Multipath TCP (MPTCP) is an extension to TCP that enables a single TCP connection to simultaneously utilize multiple distinct network paths (e.g., Wi-Fi and cellular data), aggregating bandwidth, enhancing resilience, and improving performance.

metadata.title: Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP)
metadata.definition: Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) is a transport layer protocol that provides reliable, message-oriented data transfer with features such as multihoming, support for multiple independent data streams within a single association, and resilience against network failures.

metadata.title: Socket (Networking)
metadata.definition: A network socket is an endpoint of a bidirectional inter-process communication (IPC) flow across a computer network, defined by an IP address, a port number, and the protocol (e.g., TCP or UDP), enabling applications to send and receive data.

metadata.title: Multiplexing (Transport Layer)
metadata.definition: Multiplexing at the transport layer is the process of gathering data from multiple different application processes on a host and encapsulating it into segments, allowing these applications to share a single network connection using distinct port numbers.

metadata.title: Demultiplexing (Transport Layer)
metadata.definition: Demultiplexing at the transport layer is the process of delivering incoming data segments from the network to the correct destination application process on a host, using the port numbers within the segment header to identify the target application.

metadata.title: Reliable Data Transfer
metadata.definition: Reliable data transfer (RDT) is a service model that guarantees the delivery of data without errors, loss, or duplication, and in the correct order, despite underlying unreliable network conditions, typically achieved through mechanisms like acknowledgments, retransmissions, and sequencing.

metadata.title: Go-Back-N Protocol
metadata.definition: Go-Back-N (GBN) is a sliding window protocol for reliable data transfer where the sender maintains a window of unacknowledged packets and, upon detecting a lost packet (e.g., via timeout), retransmits that lost packet along with all subsequent packets that were already sent.

metadata.title: Selective Repeat Protocol
metadata.definition: Selective Repeat (SR) is a sliding window protocol for reliable data transfer where the sender only retransmits specific packets that are detected as lost or corrupted, and the receiver accepts and buffers out-of-order packets, sending individual acknowledgments for correctly received segments.

metadata.title: Stop-and-Wait Protocol
metadata.definition: A basic Automatic Repeat Request (ARQ) protocol where the sender transmits a single data frame and then waits for an acknowledgment (ACK) from the receiver before sending the next frame. This simple mechanism ensures reliable data transfer but is highly inefficient for links with high latency or low bandwidth.

metadata.title: Sliding Window Protocol
metadata.definition: An Automatic Repeat Request (ARQ) protocol that allows a sender to transmit multiple data frames (a 'window' of data) without waiting for an acknowledgment for each one, thereby improving throughput. It uses a sequence numbering scheme and a window size to manage outstanding frames and ensures reliable, in-order delivery.

metadata.title: Window Size (Networking)
metadata.definition: In networking, the window size refers to the maximum amount of unacknowledged data that a sender is permitted to transmit before receiving an acknowledgment from the receiver. It is a critical parameter for flow control, preventing a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver, and also plays a role in congestion control.

metadata.title: Round Trip Time (RTT)
metadata.definition: The total time it takes for a data packet to travel from a source to a destination and for an acknowledgment packet to be sent back to the source. RTT is a fundamental measure of network latency, impacting the perceived responsiveness of network applications.

metadata.title: Bandwidth-Delay Product
metadata.definition: A measure of the maximum amount of data that can be in transit on a network link at any given time, calculated by multiplying the link's bandwidth by its Round Trip Time (RTT). It represents the 'volume' of the network pipe, indicating how much data can fill the path without being acknowledged.

metadata.title: Congestion Collapse
metadata.definition: A severe degradation of network performance that occurs when network congestion becomes so extreme that effective network throughput drops drastically, often approaching zero. It is characterized by excessive packet retransmissions, increased queueing delays, and routers dropping most incoming packets.

metadata.title: Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN)
metadata.definition: A mechanism that allows network routers to signal impending congestion to end hosts by marking packets, rather than dropping them. This proactive notification enables ECN-aware senders to reduce their transmission rate before actual packet loss occurs, thus improving network efficiency and reducing retransmissions.

metadata.title: Random Early Detection (RED)
metadata.definition: An active queue management algorithm used in network routers to prevent congestion collapse by proactively dropping packets or marking them for Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) before queues become full. RED randomly drops packets based on a calculated average queue length and configured thresholds, aiming to signal congestion to senders early.

metadata.title: Weighted Random Early Detection (WRED)
metadata.definition: An enhancement to the Random Early Detection (RED) algorithm that provides differentiated congestion management based on traffic type or priority. WRED applies different RED parameters, such as minimum and maximum thresholds and drop probabilities, to different classes of traffic (e.g., distinguished by IP precedence or DSCP values), allowing higher-priority traffic to experience less packet loss during congestion.

metadata.title: Application Layer Protocol
metadata.definition: A set of rules and procedures that define how applications communicate and exchange data over a network. Operating at the highest layer of the TCP/IP or OSI model, these protocols provide high-level services directly to end-user applications, abstracting the underlying network complexities.

metadata.title: Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Model
metadata.definition: A distributed network architecture where individual participants, known as peers, act as both clients and servers to other peers, directly sharing resources and processing power without relying on a central server. This model promotes decentralization, scalability, and resilience.

metadata.title: Domain Name System (DNS)
metadata.definition: A hierarchical and distributed naming system for computers, services, or any resource connected to the Internet or a private network. DNS translates human-readable domain names (e.g., `www.example.com`) into machine-readable numerical IP addresses (e.g., `192.0.2.1`), making internet navigation user-friendly.

metadata.title: DNS Resolution
metadata.definition: The multi-step process by which a DNS client (resolver) queries various DNS servers to translate a human-readable domain name into its corresponding IP address. This typically involves an iterative or recursive series of queries starting from a root server, proceeding through Top-Level Domain (TLD) servers, and finally reaching authoritative name servers.

metadata.title: DNS Record Types
metadata.definition: Different categories of information stored in DNS zone files, each defining a specific type of resource or mapping associated with a domain name. These records are fundamental to how DNS functions, directing traffic and providing various services.

metadata.title: DNS Root Servers
metadata.definition: The absolute top-level servers in the DNS hierarchy, forming the starting point for all DNS resolution queries that cannot be answered from cache. There are 13 logical root server names, managed by various organizations, which primarily direct requests to the appropriate Top-Level Domain (TLD) servers.

metadata.title: DNS Top-Level Domain (TLD) Servers
metadata.definition: Servers in the DNS hierarchy responsible for managing all the domain names under a specific top-level domain, such as `.com`, `.org`, `.net`, or country-code TLDs like `.uk`. They don't store individual host records but respond to queries by pointing to the authoritative name servers for the specific second-level domain (e.g., `google.com`).

metadata.title: DNS Authoritative Name Servers
metadata.definition: DNS servers that hold the definitive, original DNS records for a specific domain and are the ultimate source of truth for its DNS information. When a DNS resolver needs an IP address for a domain, it eventually queries the authoritative name servers for that domain to get the final answer.

metadata.title: DNS Recursive Resolvers
metadata.definition: DNS servers that handle a client's DNS query by performing all the necessary steps to find the IP address, including querying root, TLD, and authoritative servers on behalf of the client. They then return the final answer to the client and typically cache results to speed up future identical queries.

metadata.title: DNS over HTTPS (DoH)
metadata.definition: A protocol for performing remote Domain Name System (DNS) resolution via the HTTPS protocol, encrypting DNS traffic between the client and the DoH resolver. By encapsulating DNS queries within encrypted HTTPS traffic, DoH enhances user privacy, prevents eavesdropping, and mitigates DNS manipulation.

metadata.title: DNS over TLS (DoT)
metadata.definition: A protocol for encrypting DNS queries and responses using the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol, typically over a dedicated port (853). Similar to DoH, DoT aims to enhance user privacy and prevent DNS spoofing by establishing an encrypted connection between the DNS client and the DoT server, thereby protecting DNS traffic from eavesdropping and tampering.

metadata.title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP)
metadata.definition: HTTP is an application-layer protocol for transmitting hypermedia documents, such as HTML, forming the foundation of data communication for the World Wide Web. It operates as a stateless, request-response protocol between a client and a server, typically over TCP.

metadata.title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS)
metadata.definition: HTTPS is an extension of HTTP that encrypts communication between a web browser and a website server using SSL/TLS protocols. It ensures data confidentiality, integrity, and server authentication, protecting sensitive information exchanged over the internet.

metadata.title: HTTP Methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE)
metadata.definition: HTTP methods, also known as HTTP verbs, are standardized actions used to indicate the desired operation to be performed on the target resource identified by a given URL. They define the semantics of a request, enabling clients to interact with web resources.

metadata.title: HTTP Status Codes
metadata.definition: HTTP Status Codes are three-digit numbers returned by a server in response to an HTTP client's request, indicating whether a particular HTTP request has been successfully completed, and if not, why. They are grouped into five classes: Informational (1xx), Success (2xx), Redirection (3xx), Client Error (4xx), and Server Error (5xx).

metadata.title: HTTP/2 Protocol
metadata.definition: HTTP/2 is a major revision of the HTTP network protocol designed to improve web performance by addressing limitations of HTTP/1.1. Key features include multiplexing multiple requests over a single TCP connection, header compression, and server push, making web applications faster and more robust.

metadata.title: HTTP/3 Protocol
metadata.definition: HTTP/3 is the third major version of the HTTP protocol, built atop QUIC rather than TCP, aiming to further enhance web performance and reliability, especially on unreliable networks. It addresses head-of-line blocking at the transport layer, a common issue in HTTP/2 due to TCP.

metadata.title: QUIC Protocol
metadata.definition: QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections) is a general-purpose transport layer network protocol developed by Google, designed to provide security equivalent to TLS/SSL, reduce connection and transport latency, and avoid head-of-line blocking. It runs over UDP, offering stream multiplexing and improved congestion control.

metadata.title: WebSockets Protocol
metadata.definition: The WebSockets protocol provides full-duplex communication channels over a single TCP connection, enabling real-time, bidirectional data exchange between a client and a server. Unlike HTTP's request-response model, WebSockets maintain a persistent connection, allowing either party to send data at any time.

metadata.title: File Transfer Protocol (FTP)
metadata.definition: FTP is a standard network protocol used for transferring computer files between a client and server on a computer network. It uses separate control and data connections between the client and the server, typically operating over TCP.

metadata.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP)
metadata.definition: SMTP is an application-layer protocol used for sending and distributing email messages between mail servers. It defines the mechanism for transmitting email messages from a sender to a recipient's mail server, and from a client to an outgoing mail server.

metadata.title: Post Office Protocol version 3 (POP3)
metadata.definition: POP3 is an application-layer protocol used by email clients to retrieve email from a remote mail server. It typically downloads all new messages to the local device and, by default, deletes them from the server, making it suitable for single-device access.

metadata.title: Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP)
metadata.definition: IMAP is an application-layer protocol that allows an email client to access and manage email messages directly on a remote mail server. Unlike POP3, IMAP keeps messages on the server, enabling synchronization across multiple devices and persistent server-side storage of emails.

metadata.title: Secure Shell (SSH)
metadata.definition: SSH is a cryptographic network protocol for operating network services securely over an unsecured network. It provides a secure channel over an unsecured network by using strong encryption to authenticate the communicating parties and encrypt data.

metadata.title: Telnet
metadata.definition: Telnet is an older network protocol used to provide a bidirectional interactive text-oriented communication facility using a virtual terminal connection over TCP. It transmits data, including login credentials, in plain text, making it insecure for sensitive information and largely superseded by SSH.

metadata.title: Network Time Protocol (NTP)
metadata.definition: NTP is a networking protocol for clock synchronization between computer systems over packet-switched, variable-latency data networks. It ensures accurate and synchronized timekeeping across devices, which is critical for logging, distributed systems, security, and many network operations.

metadata.title: Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
metadata.definition: SNMP is an application-layer protocol used to manage and monitor network devices, collect data, and modify device configuration across an IP network. It is a widely used protocol in network management systems to oversee network performance and diagnose problems.

metadata.title: SNMP Agent
metadata.definition: An SNMP Agent is a software component that runs on a network device (e.g., router, switch, server, printer) and collects management information about the device's state, performance, and configuration. It responds to requests from an SNMP Manager, providing access to the device's Management Information Base (MIB).

metadata.title: SNMP Manager
metadata.definition: An SNMP Manager is a software application that typically runs on a network management station and communicates with SNMP Agents to query device information, receive event notifications (traps), and configure devices. It provides a centralized interface for network administrators to oversee and control network infrastructure.

metadata.title: SNMP Trap
metadata.definition: An SNMP Trap is an unsolicited notification message sent by an SNMP Agent to an SNMP Manager to report an asynchronous event or alert, such as a critical error, a change in device status, or a threshold violation. Traps allow for immediate notification of significant events without the manager needing to poll continuously.

metadata.title: Management Information Base (MIB)
metadata.definition: A MIB is a hierarchical database structure that formally describes all the network objects that an SNMP Agent can manage on a device. It defines the specific data points, their types, and relationships, which an SNMP Manager can query or modify using unique Object Identifiers (OIDs).

metadata.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
metadata.definition: A signaling protocol used for initiating, maintaining, modifying, and terminating real-time multimedia communication sessions, such as voice and video calls over Internet Protocol (IP) networks. It operates at the application layer and is independent of the underlying transport layer.

metadata.title: Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP)
metadata.definition: A network protocol for delivering audio and video over IP networks, specifically designed for real-time applications like streaming media and video conferencing. It provides mechanisms for sequencing, timestamping, and payload type identification to handle out-of-order delivery and data loss.

metadata.title: Real-time Transport Control Protocol (RTCP)
metadata.definition: A companion protocol to RTP that provides out-of-band control information for RTP streams, enabling quality of service (QoS) monitoring and synchronization between different media streams. It periodically sends control packets to all participants in a session to report reception quality and participant information.

metadata.title: Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT)
metadata.definition: A lightweight, publish-subscribe network protocol designed for low-bandwidth, high-latency, or unreliable networks, making it ideal for Internet of Things (IoT) devices. It uses a broker-based architecture to facilitate efficient message exchange between numerous clients.

metadata.title: Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)
metadata.definition: A specialized web transfer protocol for use with constrained nodes and networks in the Internet of Things (IoT). Designed to be similar to HTTP but optimized for resource-constrained devices, it often runs over User Datagram Protocol (UDP) for efficiency.

metadata.title: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP)
metadata.definition: A proprietary protocol developed by Microsoft that provides a user with a graphical interface to connect to another computer over a network connection. It enables users to view and interact with the remote computer's desktop as if they were physically present.

metadata.title: Network File System (NFS)
metadata.definition: A distributed file system protocol that allows a user on a client computer to access files over a network as if they were stored locally. It enables transparent file sharing and remote access primarily between Unix-like operating systems and other platforms.

metadata.title: Server Message Block (SMB)
