metadata.definition: A network file sharing protocol primarily used by Microsoft Windows to provide shared access to files, printers, serial ports, and other communications between nodes on a network. It is also known as Common Internet File System (CIFS).

metadata.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)
metadata.definition: An open, vendor-neutral, industry-standard application protocol for accessing and maintaining distributed directory information services. It is commonly used for storing and retrieving user, group, and device information, often for authentication and authorization purposes.

metadata.title: Kerberos Authentication
metadata.definition: A network authentication protocol that works on the basis of 'tickets' to allow nodes communicating over a non-secure network to prove their identity to one another in a secure manner. It provides strong authentication for client/server applications by using secret-key cryptography, preventing eavesdropping and replay attacks.

metadata.title: Confidentiality (Security)
metadata.definition: The security principle that prevents unauthorized disclosure of information, ensuring that data is accessible only to those authorized to have access. It is a cornerstone of information security, often achieved through encryption, access controls, and data segregation.

metadata.title: Integrity (Security)
metadata.definition: The security principle that ensures data has not been altered or destroyed in an unauthorized or accidental manner, guaranteeing that information is accurate, complete, and trustworthy. It is often maintained using hashing, digital signatures, and version control.

metadata.title: Availability (Security)
metadata.definition: The security principle that ensures authorized users can reliably access and use systems and data when needed, focusing on preventing denial-of-service and ensuring reliable operation of IT infrastructure. It involves measures like redundancy, backup, and disaster recovery.

metadata.title: Non-repudiation
metadata.definition: A security service that provides undeniable proof of an action's origin and integrity, preventing a sender from falsely denying having sent a message or a receiver from falsely denying having received it. It is typically achieved through digital signatures and trusted third-party services.

metadata.title: Encryption
metadata.definition: The process of transforming readable information (plaintext) into an unreadable secret code (ciphertext) to conceal its content and prevent unauthorized access. It is a fundamental method for achieving data confidentiality and is reversible only with the correct key.

metadata.title: Decryption
metadata.definition: The process of converting encrypted information (ciphertext) back into its original readable form (plaintext) using a specific cryptographic key and algorithm. It is the inverse operation of encryption, allowing authorized parties to access the concealed data.

metadata.title: Symmetric-key Cryptography
metadata.definition: A cryptographic system where the same secret key is used for both encryption and decryption of data. Both the sender and receiver must possess this shared key, making secure key distribution a critical challenge.

metadata.title: Asymmetric-key Cryptography
metadata.definition: A cryptographic system that uses a pair of mathematically linked keys: a public key for encryption (or verification) and a private key for decryption (or signing). The public key can be freely distributed, while the private key must be kept secret by its owner.

metadata.title: Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
metadata.definition: A symmetric-key encryption standard adopted by the U.S. government and widely used globally, replacing DES. It is a block cipher that supports key sizes of 128, 192, and 256 bits, offering strong security and efficient performance for various applications.

metadata.title: Data Encryption Standard (DES)
metadata.definition: An older symmetric-key block cipher standard that was widely used but is now considered insecure for most applications due to its relatively small 56-bit key size. It is vulnerable to brute-force attacks and has been officially deprecated, superseded by AES.

metadata.title: Triple DES (3DES)
metadata.definition: A symmetric-key block cipher that applies the DES algorithm three times to each data block for enhanced security, using either two or three distinct DES keys. It addresses the security vulnerabilities of the original DES by increasing the effective key length.

metadata.title: RSA Cryptosystem
metadata.definition: An asymmetric (public-key) encryption algorithm widely used for secure data transmission and digital signatures, based on the computational difficulty of factoring large prime numbers. It uses a pair of keys: a public key for encryption and a private key for decryption.

metadata.title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC)
metadata.definition: A public-key cryptosystem that uses the algebraic structure of elliptic curves over finite fields to create more efficient and secure cryptographic keys compared to RSA for the same level of security. It provides strong security with shorter key lengths.

metadata.title: SHA-256 Hashing Algorithm
metadata.definition: A cryptographic hash function belonging to the SHA-2 (Secure Hash Algorithm 2) family that takes an input (message) and produces a fixed-size 256-bit (32-byte) hash value, also known as a message digest. It is designed to be a one-way function, making it computationally infeasible to reverse or find collisions.

metadata.title: MD5 Hashing Algorithm (deprecated)
metadata.definition: A widely used cryptographic hash function that produces a 128-bit (16-byte) hash value. While once popular for verifying data integrity, it is now considered cryptographically broken due to significant vulnerabilities, including the ease of finding collisions, and should not be used for security-critical applications.

metadata.title: Certificate Authority (CA)
metadata.definition: A trusted entity in a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) responsible for issuing, managing, revoking, and renewing digital certificates. CAs bind public keys to specific identities, ensuring trust in digital communications.

metadata.title: Digital Certificate
metadata.definition: An electronic document used to prove the ownership of a public key, issued by a Certificate Authority (CA). It includes the public key, information about the owner, the issuer's digital signature, and validity dates, providing authentication and facilitating secure communication.

metadata.title: Certificate Revocation List (CRL)
metadata.definition: A list maintained and published by a Certificate Authority (CA) that contains the serial numbers of digital certificates that have been revoked before their scheduled expiration date. Browsers and applications can check CRLs to determine if a certificate they are presented with is still valid.

metadata.title: Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP)
metadata.definition: An internet protocol used for obtaining the revocation status of an X.509 digital certificate in real-time. Instead of downloading an entire CRL, OCSP allows a client to send a request to an OCSP responder for the status of a specific certificate, receiving a 'good', 'revoked', or 'unknown' response.

metadata.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS)
metadata.definition: A cryptographic protocol designed to provide communication security over a computer network, widely used for encrypting communications between web applications and servers. TLS establishes a secure channel by authenticating parties, encrypting data, and ensuring data integrity between two communicating applications.

metadata.title: TLS Handshake
metadata.definition: A multi-step process that initiates a TLS connection, allowing the client and server to establish cryptographic parameters, authenticate each other (optional for client), and agree on a session key before any application data is exchanged. It involves messages like ClientHello, ServerHello, Certificate, ServerKeyExchange, ClientKeyExchange, and Finished.

metadata.title: Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) (deprecated)
metadata.definition: A cryptographic protocol that preceded TLS, designed to provide secure communication over a computer network. While its original versions are now deprecated due to known security vulnerabilities, the term "SSL" is still commonly used informally to refer to TLS, especially in the context of web security certificates.

metadata.title: IP Security (IPSec)
metadata.definition: A suite of protocols that provides cryptographic security services at the Internet Layer (Layer 3) of the TCP/IP model. IPSec ensures data confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity for IP packets, commonly used to create Virtual Private Networks (VPNs).

metadata.title: IPSec Tunnel Mode
metadata.definition: An IPSec mode where the entire original IP packet (header and payload) is encrypted and authenticated, then encapsulated within a new IP packet with a new header. This mode is typically used for connecting networks (e.g., site-to-site VPNs) or connecting remote users to a private network, as it hides the internal network topology.

metadata.title: IPSec Transport Mode
metadata.definition: An IPSec mode where only the payload of the original IP packet is encrypted and/or authenticated, while the original IP header remains intact. This mode is typically used for end-to-end communication between two hosts, offering security for the application data without hiding the source and destination IP addresses.

metadata.title: Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)
metadata.definition: An IPSec protocol that provides confidentiality (encryption), data origin authentication, data integrity, and anti-replay services for IP packets. ESP encapsulates the data to be protected, adding an ESP header and trailer, and can be used in both transport and tunnel modes.

metadata.title: Authentication Header (AH)
metadata.definition: An IPSec protocol that provides data origin authentication, data integrity, and anti-replay services for IP packets, but does NOT provide confidentiality (encryption). AH authenticates the entire IP packet, including the mutable parts of the IP header that ESP does not protect.

metadata.title: Internet Key Exchange (IKE) Protocol
metadata.definition: A protocol used in conjunction with IPSec to set up a Security Association (SA) between two peers. IKE handles the negotiation of cryptographic algorithms, exchange of keys (e.g., using Diffie-Hellman), and authentication of the peers, establishing a secure channel for subsequent IPSec communication.

metadata.title: Virtual Private Network (VPN)
metadata.definition: A technology that creates a secure, encrypted connection over a less secure network, such as the internet. VPNs allow users to send and receive data as if their computing devices were directly connected to the private network, enhancing privacy and security.

metadata.title: Site-to-Site VPN
metadata.definition: A type of Virtual Private Network (VPN) that establishes a secure, encrypted connection between two or more fixed networks, such as two branch offices of an organization. Unlike remote access VPNs, individual clients do not connect directly, but rather entire networks communicate securely through VPN gateways (e.g., routers or firewalls).

metadata.title: Remote Access VPN
metadata.definition: A type of Virtual Private Network (VPN) that allows individual users to securely connect to a private network, such as a company's internal network, from a remote location over a public internet connection. It typically involves client software on the user's device that establishes an encrypted tunnel.

metadata.title: Firewall (Networking)
metadata.definition: A network security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predefined security rules. It acts as a barrier between a trusted internal network and untrusted external networks, such as the internet, preventing unauthorized access.

metadata.title: Stateful Firewall
metadata.definition: A firewall that monitors the state of active network connections, enabling it to make decisions based on the context of traffic flow rather than just individual packets. It remembers outgoing requests and automatically permits corresponding incoming responses, significantly enhancing security and efficiency.

metadata.title: Stateless Firewall
metadata.definition: A firewall that inspects each network packet individually, without considering the context of previous packets or the overall connection state. It applies rules based solely on information contained within the packet header, making it simpler but less secure than stateful firewalls.

metadata.title: Packet Filtering Firewall
metadata.definition: A basic type of firewall that operates at the network (Layer 3) and transport (Layer 4) layers of the OSI model. It inspects individual packets and applies rules to permit or deny them based on criteria such as source/destination IP addresses, port numbers, and protocols.

metadata.title: Application Layer Gateway (Firewall)
metadata.definition: A firewall that operates at the application layer (Layer 7) of the OSI model, providing deep packet inspection and understanding specific application protocols to enforce more granular security policies. It acts as a proxy, terminating and re-establishing connections, offering enhanced security for application-specific traffic.

metadata.title: Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW)
metadata.definition: A firewall that extends traditional firewall capabilities by integrating advanced features like deep packet inspection, intrusion prevention systems (IPS), application awareness, and identity awareness. NGFWs provide more comprehensive network security and visibility beyond basic port and protocol inspection.

metadata.title: Firewall Rules
metadata.definition: A set of instructions or criteria configured within a firewall that dictate how network traffic should be handled. These rules specify whether to permit, deny, or block packets based on various attributes like source/destination IP, port, protocol, application, and user identity.

metadata.title: Intrusion Detection System (IDS)
metadata.definition: A security technology that monitors network or system activities for malicious activity or policy violations and alerts administrators when potential threats are detected. An IDS is a passive listening device that does not actively prevent the detected intrusion.

metadata.title: Intrusion Prevention System (IPS)
metadata.definition: A network security device that actively monitors network or system activities for malicious activity and immediately blocks or prevents detected threats in real-time. Unlike an IDS, an IPS operates as an inline device, taking direct action on traffic to stop intrusions.

metadata.title: Host-based IDS (HIDS)
metadata.definition: An Intrusion Detection System that runs on individual host computers or servers, monitoring system files, log files, processes, and network connections specific to that host for suspicious activities or policy violations. HIDS provides granular visibility into individual endpoint behavior.

metadata.title: Network-based IDS (NIDS)
metadata.definition: An Intrusion Detection System that monitors network traffic across an entire network segment by analyzing packet headers and payloads for signatures of known attacks or anomalous behavior. NIDS typically operates on a promiscuous interface, passively observing traffic without interfering.

metadata.title: Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) Attack
metadata.definition: A cyberattack where multiple compromised computer systems, often forming a 'botnet,' are orchestrated to flood a target server, service, or network with a massive volume of illegitimate traffic. This overwhelms the target's resources, making it unavailable to legitimate users.

metadata.title: Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) Attack
metadata.definition: A type of cyberattack where an attacker secretly intercepts and relays messages between two parties who believe they are communicating directly with each other. This allows the attacker to eavesdrop on, or alter, the communication without the knowledge of the legitimate parties.

metadata.title: Packet Sniffing
metadata.definition: The process of intercepting and logging network traffic as it passes over a digital network, often performed using specialized software or hardware tools. This technique allows for the capture and analysis of data packets, revealing information exchanged between devices.

metadata.title: Port Scanning
metadata.definition: An attack technique used to identify open ports and services running on a target network host. By sending connection requests to a range of ports, attackers can discover potential vulnerabilities that could be exploited to gain unauthorized access.

metadata.title: Malware
metadata.definition: Short for 'malicious software,' malware is any software intentionally designed to cause disruption to a computer, server, client, or network, leak private information, gain unauthorized access, or otherwise exploit, compromise, or incapacitate computer systems.

metadata.title: Phishing
metadata.definition: A type of social engineering attack where attackers attempt to trick individuals into divulging sensitive information (e.g., usernames, passwords, credit card details) or performing malicious actions (e.g., clicking dangerous links) by impersonating a trustworthy entity in electronic communication.

metadata.title: IP Spoofing
metadata.definition: The creation of Internet Protocol (IP) packets with a falsified source IP address, used to masquerade as another computer system. This technique is often employed to hide the attacker's identity, bypass security measures, or launch denial-of-service attacks by making traceback difficult.

metadata.title: MAC Spoofing
metadata.definition: The act of changing a network interface controller's (NIC) factory-assigned Media Access Control (MAC) address. This is often done to bypass MAC-based access controls, impersonate another device on a local network, or hide one's true identity to evade tracking.

metadata.title: ARP Spoofing
metadata.definition: A malicious attack where an attacker sends forged ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) messages over a local area network. This links the attacker's MAC address with the IP address of another legitimate host or router, thereby intercepting or modifying network traffic intended for the legitimate device.

metadata.title: DNS Spoofing
metadata.definition: An attack where an attacker intercepts or corrupts DNS queries and responses to redirect users to malicious websites instead of legitimate ones. This is typically achieved by associating a legitimate domain name with the attacker's IP address.

metadata.title: Session Hijacking
metadata.definition: An attack where a malicious actor takes control of a user's authenticated session with a web server or application. This usually occurs after the user has logged in, by stealing or predicting a valid session ID or token.

metadata.title: Wireless Local Area Network (WLAN)
metadata.definition: A wireless computer network that links two or more devices using wireless communication to form a local area network (LAN). WLANs typically operate within a limited area such as a home, school, or office building, enabling devices to connect without physical cables.

metadata.title: IEEE 802.11 Standards
metadata.definition: A family of technical specifications for implementing wireless local area network (WLAN) computer communication, primarily in the 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz frequency bands. These standards are commonly known as Wi-Fi and define the protocols for wireless connectivity.

metadata.title: Wi-Fi
metadata.definition: A popular wireless technology that allows devices such as computers, mobile devices, and other equipment to connect to the Internet or communicate with one another wirelessly within a particular area. It is based on the IEEE 802.11 standards for wireless local area networking.

metadata.title: Wireless Security Protocols (WEP, WPA, WPA2, WPA3)
metadata.definition: A series of security protocols designed to protect wireless networks from unauthorized access and data interception by providing authentication and encryption for data transmitted over Wi-Fi. Each iteration offers enhanced security features over its predecessors.

metadata.title: Wireless Eavesdropping
metadata.definition: The act of clandestinely listening to or intercepting private communications transmitted over wireless networks, often to gain unauthorized access to sensitive information. This can involve passively capturing data packets or actively decrypting them.

metadata.title: Evil Twin Attack
metadata.definition: A type of malicious attack where an attacker sets up a fraudulent Wi-Fi access point that mimics a legitimate one (e.g., using the same SSID). The goal is to trick users into connecting to it, allowing the attacker to intercept their traffic, steal credentials, or inject malware.

metadata.title: Rogue Access Point
metadata.definition: An unauthorized wireless access point that has been installed on a secure network without explicit permission or knowledge of the network administrator. It creates a significant security vulnerability by potentially allowing unauthorized access to the network or facilitating man-in-the-middle attacks.

metadata.title: Deauthentication Attack
metadata.definition: A type of denial-of-service (DoS) attack specifically targeting wireless networks, where an attacker sends forged deauthentication frames to one or more clients connected to a Wi-Fi access point. This forces the clients to disconnect from the network, often as a precursor to other attacks like an Evil Twin attack or Wi-Fi password cracking.

metadata.title: Bluetooth
metadata.definition: A short-range wireless technology standard used for exchanging data between fixed and mobile devices over short distances (typically up to about 30 feet or 10 meters). It operates using UHF radio waves in the ISM band from 2.402 to 2.480 GHz, enabling the creation of personal area networks (PANs).

metadata.title: Zigbee
metadata.definition: An IEEE 802.15.4-based specification for a suite of high-level communication protocols designed to create personal area networks with small, low-power digital radios. It is primarily used for home automation, industrial control, and other Internet of Things (IoT) applications where low data rates and long battery life are crucial.

metadata.title: LoRaWAN
metadata.definition: A Low Power Wide Area Network (LPWAN) specification for wireless battery-operated 'things' in a regional, national, or global network. Designed for Internet of Things (IoT) applications, LoRaWAN enables low-cost, mobile, and secure bi-directional communication over long ranges with minimal power consumption.

metadata.title: Cellular Networks (2G, 3G, 4G, 5G)
metadata.definition: Wireless communication networks that allow mobile devices to connect over a large geographical area by dividing the area into 'cells', each served by a base station. Each generation (G) represents significant advancements in data speed, capacity, and technology, evolving from basic voice to high-speed mobile broadband and IoT capabilities.

metadata.title: Base Station (Cellular)
metadata.definition: A transceiver station in a cellular network that serves as a central hub for communication within a specific geographical cell. It transmits and receives radio signals to and from mobile devices within its coverage area, connecting them to the core network.

metadata.title: Mobile Switching Center (MSC)
metadata.definition: The primary service delivery node for 2G/3G GSM/CDMA cellular networks, responsible for routing voice calls, SMS, and other services between mobile devices and to other networks (like the PSTN). It also plays a crucial role in managing mobile subscribers and their mobility.

metadata.title: Home Location Register (HLR)
metadata.definition: A central database within a cellular network that stores permanent subscriber data for all users registered within the network's home domain. This includes service subscriptions, assigned unique identifiers (like IMSI), and the current location information (via the VLR address) of each mobile subscriber.

metadata.title: Visitor Location Register (VLR)
metadata.definition: A temporary database in a cellular network that stores information about mobile subscribers who are currently located within the geographical area served by a particular Mobile Switching Center (MSC). The VLR enables local call routing, service provision, and efficient management of roaming users without constantly querying the HLR.

metadata.title: Handover (Cellular)
metadata.definition: The process in cellular networks where an ongoing call or data session is transferred from one cell to another, or from one channel to another within the same cell, without interruption as the mobile device moves. This ensures continuous service connectivity for mobile users.

metadata.title: Network Management
metadata.definition: Network Management encompasses the broad set of activities required to plan, deploy, monitor, optimize, and maintain a network infrastructure. It ensures network availability, performance, and security while efficiently utilizing resources.

metadata.title: Network Configuration Management
metadata.definition: Network Configuration Management (NCM) is a sub-discipline of network management focused on consistently managing, tracking, and auditing the configurations of network devices. It ensures devices are configured correctly, securely, and in compliance with policies.

metadata.title: Network Performance Management
metadata.definition: Network Performance Management focuses on measuring, monitoring, analyzing, and improving the quality of service provided by the network to its users and applications. It aims to identify and resolve performance degradation issues proactively.

metadata.title: Fault Management (Networking)
metadata.definition: Fault Management in networking involves the detection, isolation, diagnosis, and correction of network faults and failures. Its primary goal is to minimize network downtime and restore normal operations as quickly as possible.

metadata.title: Accounting Management (Networking)
metadata.definition: Accounting Management in networking involves tracking and measuring the usage of network resources by users or applications. This data is essential for billing, capacity planning, auditing, and enforcing usage policies.

metadata.title: Quality of Service (QoS)
metadata.definition: Quality of Service (QoS) refers to mechanisms and technologies that manage network traffic to minimize packet loss, latency, and jitter, ensuring predictable and desired performance levels for critical applications. It allows prioritizing certain types of traffic over others.

metadata.title: Differentiated Services (DiffServ)
metadata.definition: Differentiated Services (DiffServ) is a coarse-grained QoS architecture that classifies and marks network traffic at the edge of the network. Core routers then apply different 'per-hop behaviors' (PHBs) based on these markings, without requiring per-flow state.

metadata.title: Integrated Services (IntServ)
metadata.definition: Integrated Services (IntServ) is a fine-grained QoS architecture that provides end-to-end resource reservation for individual traffic flows. It uses the Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) to signal resource requirements and establish reservations along the path.

metadata.title: Traffic Shaping
metadata.definition: Traffic Shaping is a QoS mechanism that delays packets exceeding a configured rate, buffering them to smooth out traffic bursts and prevent network congestion. It aims to reduce the variability of packet arrivals and ensure traffic conforms to a specific rate.

metadata.title: Traffic Policing
metadata.definition: Traffic Policing is a QoS mechanism that enforces bandwidth limits by dropping or re-marking packets that exceed a configured rate. Unlike shaping, policing drops or downgrades non-conformant traffic immediately without buffering.

metadata.title: Queuing (Networking)
metadata.definition: Queuing in networking is the process of temporarily storing packets when an outbound interface or network resource is busy, waiting for their turn to be transmitted. Different queuing algorithms determine the order in which packets are processed.

metadata.title: Weighted Fair Queuing (WFQ)
metadata.definition: Weighted Fair Queuing (WFQ) is a flow-based queuing algorithm that provides fairness by ensuring each active traffic flow receives a proportional share of available bandwidth. It dynamically allocates bandwidth based on assigned weights or flow characteristics, preventing a single flow from monopolizing resources.

metadata.title: Class-Based Weighted Fair Queuing (CBWFQ)
metadata.definition: Class-Based Weighted Fair Queuing (CBWFQ) is an enhanced queuing mechanism that allows administrators to define custom traffic classes based on various criteria (e.g., protocol, port, IP address). Each class is then assigned a guaranteed minimum bandwidth, and excess bandwidth is shared fairly.

metadata.title: Low Latency Queuing (LLQ)
metadata.definition: Low Latency Queuing (LLQ) is a QoS queuing mechanism that combines the class-based traffic handling of CBWFQ with a strict priority queue. It guarantees minimal latency for delay-sensitive traffic by always transmitting packets from the strict priority queue before any other queues.

metadata.title: Strict Priority Queuing (SPQ)
metadata.definition: Strict Priority Queuing (SPQ) is a basic QoS queuing algorithm where packets in a higher-priority queue are always transmitted before any packets in lower-priority queues. While ensuring immediate processing for high-priority traffic, it risks starving lower-priority traffic.

metadata.title: Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS)
metadata.definition: Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) is a high-performance data-forwarding technique that directs data packets through a network using short path labels instead of complex IP address lookups. It integrates Layer 2 switching with Layer 3 routing, enabling traffic engineering and VPNs.

metadata.title: Label Distribution Protocol (LDP)
metadata.definition: Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) is a signaling protocol used in MPLS networks to distribute, map, and manage labels between Label Switching Routers (LSRs). It enables LSRs to agree on the labels used for forwarding packets along a Label Switched Path (LSP).

metadata.title: Label Switched Path (LSP)
metadata.definition: A Label Switched Path (LSP) is a pre-determined, uni-directional path through an MPLS network, established by a sequence of labels. Traffic entering the network at an Ingress Label Edge Router (LER) is tagged with a label and forwarded along the LSP to an Egress LER.

metadata.title: MPLS Label Stack
metadata.definition: An MPLS Label Stack is a mechanism where a single packet can carry multiple labels, allowing for hierarchical or nested label operations. Each label in the stack provides a layer of forwarding instruction, with the top label being processed first.

metadata.title: OpenFlow Protocol
metadata.definition: OpenFlow is a foundational protocol for Software-Defined Networking (SDN) that enables a centralized controller to directly program the forwarding plane of network devices like switches and routers. It decouples the control plane from the data plane, enhancing network flexibility and programmability.

metadata.title: SDN Controller
metadata.definition: The central control plane in a Software-Defined Networking (SDN) architecture, responsible for managing and programming network devices. It abstracts the underlying network infrastructure, providing a unified view and centralized control over network traffic forwarding.

metadata.title: SDN Northbound API
metadata.definition: An interface that allows applications and higher-level services to communicate with the SDN Controller, requesting network services or providing network policies. It enables programmatic interaction with the network from an application perspective.

metadata.title: SDN Southbound API
metadata.definition: An interface used by the SDN Controller to communicate with and program the data plane elements (e.g., switches, routers) in an SDN network. It dictates how network devices forward traffic based on policies set by the controller.

metadata.title: Network Function Virtualization (NFV)
metadata.definition: A network architecture concept that virtualizes entire classes of network node functions, moving them from dedicated hardware appliances into software running on generic servers. This allows for greater flexibility, scalability, and reduced operational costs.

metadata.title: Virtual Network Function (VNF)
metadata.definition: A software implementation of a network function that traditionally ran on proprietary, dedicated hardware. VNFs run on standard commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) servers, virtual machines, or containers.

metadata.title: NFV Orchestration
metadata.definition: The process of managing and automating the deployment, scaling, and lifecycle of Virtual Network Functions (VNFs) and NFV infrastructure resources. It ensures that network services composed of VNFs are provisioned and operate correctly.

metadata.title: Service Chaining (NFV)
metadata.definition: The process of directing network traffic through a defined sequence of network functions, often Virtual Network Functions (VNFs), to apply multiple services in a specific order. This allows for dynamic and flexible service delivery.

metadata.title: Cloud Networking
metadata.definition: The provision of network services and infrastructure within a cloud computing environment, enabling connectivity between virtual machines, containers, and other cloud resources, as well as external networks. It emphasizes on-demand, scalable, and software-defined network resources.

metadata.title: Edge Computing (Networking)
metadata.definition: A distributed computing paradigm that brings computation and data storage closer to the source of data generation, minimizing latency and bandwidth usage. In networking, it involves deploying network functions and services at the network edge, closer to end-users or IoT devices.

metadata.title: Internet of Things (IoT) Networking
metadata.definition: The network infrastructure and protocols that enable connectivity and communication among physical objects (things) embedded with sensors, software, and other technologies. It focuses on low-power, wide-area, and often heterogeneous network requirements.

metadata.title: Spine-Leaf Architecture
metadata.definition: A two-tier network topology used in data centers to create high-performance, low-latency, and highly scalable networks. Leaf switches connect to all server racks and then connect to every spine switch, which form the network backbone and interconnect all leaf switches.

metadata.title: Fabric Networking
metadata.definition: A high-speed, non-blocking, and often flattened network architecture designed for data centers, often based on a spine-leaf topology. It provides any-to-any connectivity with low latency and high bandwidth, simplifying network management and scaling.

metadata.title: VXLAN (Virtual Extensible LAN)
metadata.definition: A network virtualization technology that encapsulates Layer 2 Ethernet frames within Layer 3 UDP packets, allowing virtual networks to span across physical IP-based underlays. It provides extended scalability for virtual machines and networks in data centers.

metadata.title: NVGRE (Network Virtualization using Generic Routing Encapsulation)
metadata.definition: A network virtualization technology similar to VXLAN, which encapsulates Layer 2 Ethernet frames within Layer 3 GRE packets. It creates overlay networks to provide logical isolation and scalability for virtual machines across physical IP networks.

metadata.title: Load Balancing (Networking)
metadata.definition: The process of distributing incoming network traffic across multiple servers or resources to ensure no single server becomes a bottleneck, thereby maximizing throughput, minimizing response time, and ensuring high availability.

metadata.title: Reverse Proxy
metadata.definition: A server that sits in front of one or more web servers and intercepts client requests, forwarding them to the appropriate backend server. It can provide load balancing, SSL termination, caching, compression, and enhanced security.

metadata.title: Demilitarized Zone (DMZ)
metadata.definition: A physical or logical subnetwork that contains and exposes an organization's external-facing services to an untrusted, larger network, usually the internet, while isolating these services from the internal local area network (LAN). It acts as a buffer zone for security.

metadata.title: Intranet
metadata.definition: A private computer network used by an organization to share information, operational systems, and computing services exclusively among its employees. It uses Internet Protocol (IP) technologies but is secured from public access by firewalls.

metadata.title: Extranet
metadata.definition: A controlled private network that allows access to certain parts of an organization's intranet or information to external users, such as vendors, partners, or customers. It extends the internal network while maintaining security through authentication and authorization.

metadata.title: Queueing Theory (Networking)
metadata.definition: A mathematical study of waiting lines, or queues, used in networking to analyze and model the performance of systems where requests (e.g., data packets) arrive, wait if resources are busy, and then are served. It helps optimize resource allocation and predict network congestion.

metadata.title: Network Calculus
metadata.definition: A deterministic theory for analyzing performance bounds in communication networks, providing guarantees on metrics like delay and buffer requirements based on service curves and arrival curves. It's used to model traffic flow and network elements without probabilistic assumptions.

metadata.title: Markov Chains (Networking)
metadata.definition: A stochastic process that models a sequence of events where the probability of each event depends only on the state attained in the previous event. In networking, they are used to analyze network behavior, such as queueing systems, packet arrival processes, and protocol state transitions, under probabilistic assumptions.

metadata.title: Network Topology (Bus, Star, Ring, Mesh, Tree)
metadata.definition: The physical or logical arrangement of connected devices in a network. Common topologies include Bus (all devices share a single cable), Star (all devices connect to a central hub/switch), Ring (devices connect in a closed loop), Mesh (every device connects to every other device), and Tree (a hierarchical structure combining star and bus).

metadata.title: Message Switching
metadata.definition: A network communication method where data is stored and forwarded as complete messages from source to destination, typically across intermediate nodes. Each message is treated as a self-contained unit and may take different paths, with nodes storing the entire message before forwarding it, leading to variable delays.

metadata.title: Access Network
metadata.definition: The part of a telecommunications network that connects end-user subscribers to their immediate service provider's core network. It represents the "last mile" or "first mile" connection, enabling users to access services like the internet, voice, or video.

metadata.title: Core Network
metadata.definition: The central part of a telecommunication network that provides high-capacity, high-speed routing and switching capabilities to interconnect various access networks, other core networks, and data centers. It acts as the backbone, handling aggregated traffic and offering transport services across vast distances.

metadata.title: Local Area Network (LAN)
metadata.definition: A computer network that interconnects computers within a limited geographical area, such as a residence, school, laboratory, or office building. LANs are characterized by high data rates, low latency, and private ownership.

metadata.title: Wide Area Network (WAN)
metadata.definition: A telecommunications network that extends over a large geographical area, often spanning cities, states, or even countries. WANs are used to connect multiple LANs and other localized networks, facilitating communication and resource sharing across distant locations.

metadata.title: Metropolitan Area Network (MAN)
metadata.definition: A computer network that interconnects users with computer resources in a geographic area larger than a LAN but smaller than a WAN, typically spanning a city or a large campus. MANs are often used to connect multiple LANs within a city.

metadata.title: Personal Area Network (PAN)
metadata.definition: A computer network used for data transmission among devices, such as computers, smartphones, and personal digital assistants, for an individual user within a very short range, typically a few meters. PANs can be wired or wireless.

metadata.title: Storage Area Network (SAN)
metadata.definition: A dedicated, high-speed network that provides access to consolidated, block-level data storage. SANs allow multiple servers to access shared storage devices, making them appear as locally attached drives, thereby improving storage utilization, performance, and management.

metadata.title: Gigabit Ethernet
metadata.definition: A version of Ethernet that supports data transfer rates of 1 gigabit per second (Gbps), defined by the IEEE 802.3z and 802.3ab standards. It operates over copper twisted-pair cabling (1000BASE-T) or fiber optic cabling (1000BASE-SX/LX).

metadata.title: 10 Gigabit Ethernet
metadata.definition: A version of Ethernet that supports data transfer rates of 10 gigabits per second (Gbps), defined by the IEEE 802.3ae and 802.3an standards. It is primarily used in backbone networks, data centers, and high-performance server connections due to its significantly higher bandwidth.

metadata.title: Passive Optical Network (PON)
metadata.definition: A fiber-optic access network technology that uses a single optical fiber to serve multiple endpoints without requiring active electronic components between the central office and the subscribers. Instead, it uses passive optical splitters to distribute the signal, significantly reducing power consumption and maintenance.

metadata.title: Gigabit Passive Optical Network (GPON)
metadata.definition: A specific standard for Passive Optical Networks (PON) that provides gigabit-capable speeds, supporting asymmetric data rates typically up to 2.488 Gbps downstream and 1.244 Gbps upstream. GPON is widely deployed globally for Fiber to the Home/Building (FTTH/FTTB) broadband access.

metadata.title: Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiplexing (OFDM)
metadata.definition: A digital multi-carrier modulation method that divides a single high-rate data stream into several lower-rate streams, which are then transmitted simultaneously over multiple orthogonal sub-carrier frequencies. This technique is highly robust against frequency-selective fading and inter-symbol interference.

metadata.title: Carrier Aggregation
metadata.definition: A technology used in wireless communication, particularly in LTE-Advanced and 5G, that combines multiple component carriers (frequency bands) to increase bandwidth and improve data rates. It allows a user device to simultaneously transmit and receive data over several different frequency blocks as if they were a single, wider channel.

metadata.title: Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO)
metadata.definition: A wireless communication technology that uses multiple transmit and receive antennas to increase data capacity, improve spectral efficiency, and enhance link reliability without requiring additional bandwidth or transmit power. It achieves this through spatial multiplexing or diversity techniques.

metadata.title: Beamforming (Wireless)
metadata.definition: A signal processing technique used in smart antennas for wireless communication that directs a wireless signal towards a specific receiver or direction, rather than broadcasting it uniformly in all directions. This improves signal quality, range, and efficiency by focusing energy and reducing interference.

metadata.title: Network Segmentation
metadata.definition: The practice of dividing a computer network into smaller, isolated segments or subnets, often based on function, department, or security requirements. This enhances security by limiting the scope of breaches, improves performance by reducing traffic on individual segments, and simplifies management.

metadata.title: Zero Trust Architecture
metadata.definition: A security model where no user or device is trusted by default, regardless of whether they are inside or outside the traditional network perimeter. All access attempts must be continuously verified and authenticated before granting access to resources.

metadata.title: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM)
metadata.definition: A system that aggregates and analyzes security log data from various sources across an organization's IT infrastructure, providing real-time analysis of security alerts. It aids in compliance reporting, threat detection, and incident response.

metadata.title: Threat Intelligence (Networking)
metadata.definition: Evidence-based knowledge, including context, mechanisms, indicators, implications, and actionable advice about existing or emerging threats. In networking, this intelligence is used to inform decision-making regarding the organization's response to network-related threats.

metadata.title: Vulnerability Assessment (Networking)
metadata.definition: A systematic process of identifying and quantifying security weaknesses (vulnerabilities) in a network, its systems, applications, and configurations, typically using automated tools. It aims to provide a prioritized list of potential security risks.

metadata.title: Penetration Testing (Networking)
metadata.definition: A simulated cyberattack against a network, system, or application to check for exploitable vulnerabilities. Unlike a vulnerability assessment, it actively attempts to exploit weaknesses to demonstrate potential impact and validate security controls.

metadata.title: Security Operations Center (SOC)
metadata.definition: A centralized function within an organization employing security analysts and engineers who monitor, detect, analyze, and respond to cybersecurity incidents around the clock. The SOC team uses various tools and processes to protect organizational assets.

metadata.title: Data Loss Prevention (DLP)
metadata.definition: A set of tools and processes designed to ensure that sensitive data is not lost, misused, or accessed by unauthorized users. DLP solutions classify sensitive data and enforce policies to prevent its exfiltration or inappropriate sharing across the network.

metadata.title: Unified Threat Management (UTM)
metadata.definition: A single security appliance that combines multiple security features—such as firewall, intrusion prevention, antivirus, and content filtering—into one comprehensive solution. UTM simplifies deployment and management for small to medium-sized businesses.

metadata.title: Cloud Security
metadata.definition: The set of technologies, policies, controls, and services that protect cloud-based infrastructures, applications, and data. It involves securing cloud services (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) and ensuring compliance with regulatory requirements.

metadata.title: Digital Subscriber Line (DSL)
metadata.definition: A family of technologies that provide internet access by transmitting digital data over standard telephone lines. DSL offers higher speeds than dial-up and utilizes the higher frequencies of the line, allowing simultaneous phone calls.

metadata.title: Cable Modem (DOCSIS)
metadata.definition: A type of modem that provides bi-directional data communication via radio frequency (RF) channels on a cable television (CATV) infrastructure. It uses the Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification (DOCSIS) standard for high-speed internet access.

metadata.title: Network Probe
metadata.definition: A device or software agent deployed within a network to collect data about network traffic, performance, and security events. Probes actively monitor network activity and can capture packets, record flow data, or send alerts.

metadata.title: Packet Capture (e.g., Wireshark)
metadata.definition: The process of intercepting and logging data packets that pass across a computer network or a part of a network. Tools like Wireshark allow detailed analysis of individual packets, including headers and payload data, for troubleshooting and security analysis.

metadata.title: Flow-based monitoring (e.g., NetFlow)
metadata.definition: A method of network monitoring that collects metadata about network traffic flows (conversations) rather than capturing entire packets. Protocols like NetFlow or IPFIX summarize information such as source/destination IP, ports, protocols, and byte counts.

metadata.title: Network Automation
metadata.definition: The process of automating the configuration, management, testing, deployment, and operation of physical and virtual network devices and services. It leverages software to programmatically control network infrastructure, reducing manual effort and human error.

metadata.title: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) (Networking)
metadata.definition: The practice of managing and provisioning network infrastructure (e.g., routers, switches, firewalls, load balancers) using code and software development practices, rather than manual configuration. This allows for versioning, reproducibility, and automation of network deployments.

metadata.title: NetDevOps
metadata.definition: An approach that applies DevOps principles and practices—such as automation, collaboration, continuous integration/delivery, and Infrastructure as Code—to network operations. It aims to bridge the gap between development and networking teams for faster, more reliable network changes.

metadata.title: Container Networking
metadata.definition: The mechanisms and configurations that enable communication between containers, and between containers and the external network. It involves concepts like virtual networks, network overlays, and specific Container Network Interface (CNI) plugins.

metadata.title: Kubernetes Networking
metadata.definition: The specific networking model and implementations within a Kubernetes cluster, ensuring that Pods can communicate with each other across nodes, services can be accessed, and external traffic can reach applications. It relies on CNI plugins and abstract service concepts.

metadata.title: Service Mesh
metadata.definition: A dedicated infrastructure layer for handling service-to-service communication in microservices architectures, typically implemented as an array of network proxies. It provides features like traffic management, security, and observability without requiring changes to application code.

metadata.title: Sidecar Proxy (Service Mesh)
metadata.definition: A sidecar proxy is a deployment pattern in a service mesh where a proxy (like Envoy) runs alongside each service instance, intercepting all inbound and outbound network traffic for that service. It abstracts away network concerns such as traffic management, security, and observability from the application code.

metadata.title: Traffic Engineering (Networking)
metadata.definition: Traffic Engineering in networking involves techniques and methods to optimize the performance of an operational network by dynamically analyzing and controlling network traffic. The goal is to ensure efficient utilization of network resources, minimize congestion, and meet specific service requirements.

metadata.title: MPLS Traffic Engineering
metadata.definition: MPLS Traffic Engineering (MPLS-TE) is an advanced traffic engineering technique that leverages Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS) to explicitly route traffic through specific paths across a network. It allows network administrators to pre-determine paths based on criteria like bandwidth, latency, and administrative policies, independent of the underlying IP routing protocols.

metadata.title: Segment Routing
metadata.definition: Segment Routing (SR) is a source-routing architecture that simplifies network operations by encoding forwarding instructions as a list of segments in the packet header. It allows a source node to dictate the exact path a packet should take across a network without relying on per-hop state in intermediate nodes.

metadata.title: Carrier Ethernet
metadata.definition: Carrier Ethernet refers to Ethernet services that meet specific performance and reliability standards, making them suitable for carrier-grade Wide Area Network (WAN) deployments. It provides standardized, manageable, and highly reliable services over a metro or regional area, often used for business connectivity and mobile backhaul.

metadata.title: Voice over IP (VoIP)
metadata.definition: Voice over IP (VoIP) is a methodology and group of technologies that enable the delivery of voice communications and multimedia sessions over Internet Protocol (IP) networks. It converts analog audio signals into digital packets that are transmitted over the internet, allowing phone calls to be made without traditional telephone lines.

metadata.title: Jitter Buffer
metadata.definition: A jitter buffer (or playout buffer) is a temporary storage area used in real-time communication systems, such as VoIP or video conferencing, to compensate for variations in packet arrival times (jitter). It collects incoming packets, holds them briefly, and then releases them at a steady rate to ensure smooth playback and prevent audio/video dropouts.

metadata.title: Echo Cancellation
metadata.definition: Echo cancellation is a signal processing technique used in telecommunications to remove unwanted echoes from a communication path, particularly in voice calls. It identifies and subtracts the echo signal that originates from the speaker's own voice being picked up by their microphone after being played through the far-end speaker.

metadata.title: Forward Error Correction (FEC)
metadata.definition: Forward Error Correction (FEC) is a digital signal processing technique used for controlling errors in data transmission over unreliable or noisy communication channels without requiring a reverse channel to request retransmission. It adds redundant data (error-correcting codes) to the message, allowing the receiver to detect and correct a certain number of errors without contacting the sender.

metadata.title: Quality of Experience (QoE)
metadata.definition: Quality of Experience (QoE) is a subjective measure of a user's satisfaction with a service or application, reflecting the overall impression of the user rather than just objective technical metrics. It encompasses all aspects of the user's interaction, including factors like usability, performance, and emotional response, ultimately indicating how 'good' a service feels to the end-user.

metadata.title: IP Multicast
metadata.definition: IP Multicast is a method of sending network traffic from a single source to multiple selected receivers simultaneously, efficiently utilizing network bandwidth. Instead of sending separate copies to each receiver (unicast) or to all devices (broadcast), multicast sends one copy to a specific group address, and network routers duplicate it only when necessary to reach all group members.

metadata.title: Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP)
metadata.definition: The Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) is a communication protocol used by hosts and adjacent routers on IPv4 networks to establish and maintain IP multicast group memberships. Hosts use IGMP to inform local routers that they want to receive multicast traffic for a particular group, and routers use IGMP to discover which groups have active members on their directly attached networks.

metadata.title: Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM)
metadata.definition: Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) is a family of multicast routing protocols that provide efficient multicast routing across IP networks, independent of the underlying unicast routing protocol. PIM builds multicast distribution trees to deliver traffic from sources to receivers, leveraging information from unicast routing tables to determine reachability.

metadata.title: Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF)
metadata.definition: Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF) is a security and loop-prevention mechanism used in IP routing, primarily for multicast and unicast source validation. An RPF check ensures that an incoming packet arrived on the interface that would be used to send a unicast packet back to the source of that incoming packet, preventing spoofing and forwarding loops.

metadata.title: Network Orchestration
metadata.definition: Network Orchestration is the automated configuration, coordination, and management of network services, functions, and resources across multiple network domains or devices. It involves defining workflows and policies to provision, scale, and manage complex network infrastructures, often across physical and virtual environments, to achieve specific business goals.

metadata.title: Cloud-Native Network Functions (CNF)
metadata.definition: Cloud-Native Network Functions (CNFs) are network functions designed and implemented using cloud-native architectural principles, such as microservices, containers, and declarative APIs, running on cloud infrastructure (public, private, or hybrid). Unlike traditional VNFs, CNFs are built for agility, resilience, and scalability in a containerized environment, often orchestrated by Kubernetes.

metadata.title: Container Network Interface (CNI)
metadata.definition: The Container Network Interface (CNI) is a specification for configuring network interfaces for Linux containers, defining a common interface between container orchestration systems and network plugins. It allows different network providers to integrate seamlessly with container runtimes (like containerd or CRI-O) and orchestrators (like Kubernetes), providing a standardized way to connect containers to networks.

metadata.title: eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter)
metadata.definition: eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) is a revolutionary technology that allows programs to run in a sandboxed virtual machine inside the Linux kernel, enabling safe and efficient custom logic without modifying the kernel source code. In networking, eBPF is used for high-performance packet processing, observability, security, and traffic control, replacing or enhancing traditional kernel modules.

metadata.title: Machine Learning for Networking
metadata.definition: Machine Learning for Networking involves applying machine learning algorithms and techniques to analyze network data, predict network behavior, detect anomalies, and automate network management tasks. This approach enables intelligent decision-making to optimize network performance, enhance security, and improve operational efficiency beyond traditional rule-based systems.

metadata.title: Network Telemetry
metadata.definition: Network telemetry refers to the collection of data from network devices and infrastructure in real-time or near real-time. This data is used for monitoring network health, performance analysis, capacity planning, and troubleshooting.

metadata.title: Streaming Telemetry
metadata.definition: Streaming telemetry is a modern approach where network devices continuously push operational data to collectors using subscription-based models, often over high-performance protocols like gRPC. This contrasts with traditional pull-based methods like SNMP polling, offering real-time visibility and granular data.

metadata.title: Protocol Data Unit (PDU)
metadata.definition: A Protocol Data Unit (PDU) is a single unit of information exchanged between peer entities of a computer network, consisting of control information (headers and trailers) and user data. It represents the data unit at a specific layer of the OSI or TCP/IP model.

metadata.title: Service Data Unit (SDU)
metadata.definition: A Service Data Unit (SDU) is the data payload passed from an upper layer to a lower layer in the protocol stack for processing and encapsulation. It represents the data that a specific layer's protocol needs to transmit on behalf of the layer above it.

metadata.title: Encapsulation (Networking)
metadata.definition: Encapsulation is the process by which a protocol adds its own control information (headers and sometimes trailers) to data received from a higher layer of the protocol stack. This forms a new, larger Protocol Data Unit (PDU) before passing it down to the next lower layer.

metadata.title: Decapsulation (Networking)
metadata.definition: Decapsulation is the reverse process of encapsulation, where a protocol layer removes its specific header (and potentially trailer) from a received Protocol Data Unit (PDU). After removal, the remaining data payload is passed up to the next higher layer in the protocol stack for further processing.

metadata.title: Protocol Stack
metadata.definition: A protocol stack is a set of network protocols that work together in a hierarchical manner to enable communication between computer systems. Each layer in the stack performs a specific function, building upon the services provided by the layers below it.

metadata.title: Ethernet Virtual Private Network (EVPN)
metadata.definition: EVPN is a standards-based technology that provides Layer 2 and Layer 3 VPN services over an MPLS or IP backbone, offering multihoming, load balancing, and fast convergence. It's widely used in data centers and service provider networks for extending Ethernet segments and enabling efficient VM mobility.

metadata.title: 5G Core Network
metadata.definition: The 5G Core Network is the next-generation architecture for 5G mobile communication, characterized by its cloud-native, service-based architecture (SBA) and support for ultra-reliable low-latency, enhanced mobile broadband, and massive machine-type communications. It disaggregates control and user planes and leverages virtualization.

metadata.title: 5G New Radio (NR)
metadata.definition: 5G New Radio (NR) is the global standard for the 5G wireless air interface, designed to operate across a wide range of spectrum bands, including sub-6 GHz and millimeter wave. It offers significantly higher speeds, lower latency, and greater capacity compared to previous generations, enabling diverse 5G use cases.

metadata.title: Network Slicing (5G)
metadata.definition: Network slicing is a key 5G capability that allows the creation of multiple virtual, logically isolated networks on top of a common physical infrastructure. Each slice is custom-designed and optimized with specific resources and characteristics to meet the demands of different services, applications, or customer groups.

metadata.title: Massive MIMO (5G)
metadata.definition: Massive MIMO (Multiple-Input Multiple-Output) is a 5G antenna technology that employs a very large number of antennas (tens to hundreds) at the base station to serve multiple user devices simultaneously within the same frequency and time resources. This significantly boosts spectral efficiency, capacity, and coverage through advanced beamforming.

metadata.title: Millimeter Wave (mmWave) Communication (5G)
metadata.definition: Millimeter Wave (mmWave) communication in 5G refers to the utilization of radio frequencies in the 24 GHz to 100 GHz range. This spectrum enables extremely high bandwidth and data rates, crucial for enhanced mobile broadband, but is characterized by shorter range and susceptibility to physical obstructions.

metadata.title: Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC) (5G)
metadata.definition: URLLC is one of the three primary 5G service categories, focusing on providing extremely high reliability (e.g., 99.999%) and very low end-to-end latency (e.g., <1ms) for mission-critical applications. It addresses use cases where even tiny delays or failures can have severe consequences.

metadata.title: Enhanced Mobile Broadband (eMBB) (5G)
metadata.definition: eMBB is one of the three primary 5G service categories, designed to deliver significantly higher data rates, increased network capacity, and improved coverage compared to 4G technologies. Its main objective is to provide a superior mobile internet experience for consumers and enterprises.

metadata.title: Massive Machine Type Communications (mMTC) (5G)
metadata.definition: mMTC is one of the three primary 5G service categories, focused on enabling connectivity for an extremely large number of low-cost, low-power devices over a wide geographical area. These devices typically transmit small amounts of data infrequently, making power efficiency and scalability paramount.

metadata.title: Open Radio Access Network (Open RAN)
metadata.definition: Open RAN is an industry movement towards open, disaggregated, and virtualized radio access network (RAN) architectures. It advocates for open interfaces between RAN components (e.g., radio unit, distributed unit, centralized unit) to foster multi-vendor interoperability, innovation, and competition.

metadata.title: Virtual RAN (vRAN)
metadata.definition: Virtual RAN (vRAN) is a Radio Access Network (RAN) architecture that centralizes and virtualizes baseband processing functions, moving them from proprietary hardware appliances to software running on commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) servers. This allows for greater flexibility, scalability, and resource pooling compared to traditional RANs.

metadata.title: Cloud RAN (CRAN)
metadata.definition: Cloud RAN (CRAN) is an advanced architectural evolution of vRAN that centralizes baseband processing units (BBUs) into cloud-based data centers, connecting them to remote radio units (RRUs) via high-bandwidth fronthaul links. This centralization enables advanced coordination, dynamic resource allocation, and reduced operational costs.

metadata.title: Network Exposure Function (NEF)
metadata.definition: The Network Exposure Function (NEF) is a key functional element within the 5G Core Network's Service-Based Architecture (SBA). Its primary role is to securely expose the capabilities and events of the 5G network to authorized third-party applications and services, enabling new business models and innovative use cases.

metadata.title: Network Repository Function (NRF)
metadata.definition: A key component in the 5G Core Network architecture that acts as a central repository for network function (NF) profiles and discovery services. It enables other NFs to discover and interact with each other without hardcoded configurations, facilitating a flexible and scalable network.

metadata.title: Access and Mobility Management Function (AMF)
metadata.definition: The central control plane function in the 5G Core Network responsible for connection and mobility management, including User Equipment (UE) registration, authentication, authorization, and tracking. It handles non-access stratum (NAS) signaling between the UE and the core network.

metadata.title: Session Management Function (SMF)
metadata.definition: A 5G Core Network control plane function responsible for managing Protocol Data Unit (PDU) sessions, which are the logical connections carrying user data. This includes IP address allocation, session establishment, modification, and release, interacting with the UPF for user plane routing.

metadata.title: User Plane Function (UPF)
metadata.definition: The 5G Core Network function responsible for handling all user plane traffic, including packet routing, forwarding, inspection, and application of QoS rules. It serves as the data anchor for PDU sessions and interconnects with the data network.

metadata.title: Unified Data Management (UDM)
metadata.definition: A central 5G Core Network function that stores and manages user subscription data, authentication credentials, and access authorization policies. It provides a unified interface for other network functions (like AMF, SMF, AUSF) to access this critical subscriber information.

metadata.title: Authentication Server Function (AUSF)
metadata.definition: A 5G Core Network function dedicated to performing authentication of User Equipment (UE) and network functions, ensuring that only authorized entities can access network services. It collaborates with the UDM to retrieve authentication credentials.

metadata.title: Policy Control Function (PCF)
metadata.definition: A 5G Core Network function that provides policy rules to control network behavior, including Quality of Service (QoS), traffic routing, and charging parameters. These policies are based on subscriber profiles, network conditions, and operator-defined business rules.

metadata.title: Charging Function (CHF)
metadata.definition: A 5G Core Network function responsible for collecting charging-related events from other network functions and generating charging data records (CDRs) for billing purposes. It supports both online (real-time) and offline charging models.

metadata.title: Network Data Analytics Function (NWDAF)
metadata.definition: A 5G Core Network function designed to collect network data from various sources, perform analytics using AI/ML, and provide insights, predictions, and recommendations to other network functions. This enables optimized network operation, resource management, and automated decision-making.

metadata.title: Dynamic Spectrum Sharing (DSS)
metadata.definition: A technology that enables 4G (LTE) and 5G New Radio (NR) to operate simultaneously within the same frequency band by dynamically allocating spectrum resources between the two technologies based on real-time demand. DSS facilitates a smoother and faster transition to 5G coverage using existing spectrum assets.

metadata.title: Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN)
metadata.definition: Communication networks that utilize airborne or space-borne platforms, such as satellites, high-altitude platform stations (HAPS), or drones, to provide connectivity. NTNs are crucial for extending coverage to remote or underserved areas, supporting IoT, and enhancing network resilience.

metadata.title: Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN)
metadata.definition: A set of IEEE 802.1 standards that extend standard Ethernet to provide deterministic data delivery with guaranteed bandwidth, ultra-low latency, and high reliability. TSN is critical for real-time applications in industrial automation, automotive, and professional audio/video.

metadata.title: Deterministic Networking (DetNet)
metadata.definition: An IETF-defined architecture that provides bounded latency, low packet loss, and high reliability over Layer 2 and Layer 3 networks, enabling time-sensitive applications to operate predictably over IP networks. DetNet often leverages TSN capabilities at Layer 2 to achieve end-to-end determinism.

metadata.title: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD)
metadata.definition: A communication method that uses principles of quantum mechanics to establish a shared, secret cryptographic key between two parties. QKD's unique property is that any attempt by an eavesdropper to intercept the key is physically detectable, thereby guaranteeing the key's security.

metadata.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC)
metadata.definition: Cryptographic algorithms designed to be secure against attacks by quantum computers, which are capable of breaking many current public-key cryptosystems like RSA and ECC. PQC aims to future-proof digital communications and data security against the advent of large-scale quantum computing.

metadata.title: Software-Defined Wide Area Network (SD-WAN)
metadata.definition: An architectural approach to managing Wide Area Networks (WANs) that leverages software-defined networking (SDN) principles to abstract the underlying network hardware. It enables centralized control, intelligent traffic routing, and simplified management over multiple connection types, improving performance and reducing costs.

metadata.title: Secure Access Service Edge (SASE)
metadata.definition: A cloud-native security model that converges wide area networking (WAN) and a comprehensive set of security functions into a single, cloud-delivered service. SASE provides secure, optimized access for users and devices regardless of their location, embodying Zero Trust principles.

metadata.title: Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA)
metadata.definition: A security framework that operates on the principle 'never trust, always verify,' requiring strict identity verification and device posture assessment for every user and device attempting to access network resources. Access is granted based on the least privilege needed, irrespective of the user's location.

metadata.title: Extended Detection and Response (XDR)
metadata.definition: A unified security platform that automatically collects and correlates security data from multiple sources, including endpoints, networks, cloud environments, and email. XDR provides broader visibility, enhanced threat detection capabilities, and faster, more efficient incident response across an organization's entire attack surface.

metadata.title: Security Orchestration, Automation and Response (SOAR)
metadata.definition: A security solution that integrates disparate security tools, automates security tasks, and orchestrates incident response workflows. SOAR platforms enable security operations teams to manage and respond to threats more efficiently by standardizing processes and reducing manual effort.

metadata.title: Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB)
metadata.definition: A CASB is a security policy enforcement point placed between cloud service consumers and cloud service providers to combine and interject enterprise security policies as cloud-based resources are accessed. It extends an organization's security controls to the cloud, addressing risks like data exfiltration, malware, and compliance violations.

metadata.title: Secure Web Gateway (SWG)
metadata.definition: A Secure Web Gateway is a security solution that protects organizations from online threats and enforces internet usage policies by inspecting and filtering web traffic. It typically sits between users and the internet, offering functionalities such as URL filtering, malware detection, and application control.

metadata.title: Firewall as a Service (FWaaS)
metadata.definition: Firewall as a Service is a cloud-native network security solution that provides traditional firewall capabilities, such as traffic filtering, intrusion prevention, and advanced threat protection, delivered entirely as a cloud service. It allows organizations to deploy and manage firewall policies without needing on-premise hardware.

metadata.title: Application-Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC)
metadata.definition: An ASIC is a microchip customized for a particular use rather than for general-purpose computing. In networking, ASICs are designed to perform specific, high-volume functions like packet forwarding, routing table lookups, or cryptographic operations with extremely high speed and efficiency.

metadata.title: Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) (Networking)
metadata.definition: An FPGA is an integrated circuit designed to be configured by a customer or designer after manufacturing, allowing for flexible hardware programmability. In networking, FPGAs are used for high-speed packet processing, protocol acceleration, and adaptable network functions where ASICs might be too rigid or slow to develop.

metadata.title: SmartNIC (Smart Network Interface Card)
metadata.definition: A SmartNIC is a Network Interface Card (NIC) with integrated programmable processing capabilities, typically incorporating an FPGA or ARM CPU, which offloads network functions from the host CPU. This acceleration frees up host resources, improves performance, and enables advanced network services directly at the server's edge.

metadata.title: Programmable Data Plane
metadata.definition: The programmable data plane refers to the ability to define and dynamically modify how network devices (like switches and routers) process and forward packets. This allows network engineers to customize forwarding logic, implement new protocols, and adapt network behavior in real-time, contrasting with traditional fixed-function hardware.

metadata.title: P4 Programming Language (Networking)
metadata.definition: P4 (Programming Protocol-Independent Packet Processors) is a high-level, domain-specific programming language for programming the data plane of network devices. It allows network engineers to specify how network devices parse, process, and forward packets, enabling custom network behaviors and new protocols on programmable hardware.

metadata.title: Internet Exchange Point (IXP)
metadata.definition: An Internet Exchange Point is a physical infrastructure where Internet service providers (ISPs), content delivery networks (CDNs), and other network operators exchange Internet traffic between their networks directly. IXPs facilitate peering relationships, reducing latency and transit costs by localizing traffic exchange.

metadata.title: Peering (Networking)
metadata.definition: Peering is a voluntary and direct interconnection between two administratively separate Internet networks for the purpose of exchanging traffic between their respective users without paying a third party. This arrangement typically reduces transit costs and often improves performance and redundancy by shortening traffic paths.

metadata.title: Transit (Networking)
metadata.definition: Transit is the service where one network pays another network (typically a larger, Tier 1 or Tier 2 ISP) to carry its traffic to the entire global Internet. Unlike peering, transit provides full access to the global routing table, allowing the buying network to reach any destination on the Internet through the selling network.

metadata.title: Anycast DNS
metadata.definition: Anycast DNS is a networking technique where multiple DNS servers, located in different geographic locations, are configured with the same IP address. Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) routing then directs client DNS requests to the topologically nearest available server, improving performance, redundancy, and DDoS mitigation.

metadata.title: Zero-Touch Provisioning (ZTP)
metadata.definition: Zero-Touch Provisioning is a method that allows network devices, such as switches and routers, to automatically configure themselves upon initial power-up without requiring manual intervention. This process typically involves discovering a configuration server and downloading its operational configuration and software images.

metadata.title: Network Reliability Engineering (NRE)
metadata.definition: Network Reliability Engineering is a discipline focused on ensuring the continuous availability, performance, and operational excellence of network infrastructure and services. It applies software engineering principles, automation, and data analysis to network operations to build and maintain scalable, highly reliable networks.

metadata.title: Chaos Engineering (Networking)
