metadata.definition: A weakness or flaw in a system, design, implementation, or configuration that can be exploited by a threat actor to cause harm, gain unauthorized access, or otherwise compromise the system's security. It represents a potential entry point for an attack.

metadata.title: Exploit
metadata.definition: A piece of software, data, or sequence of commands that takes advantage of a specific vulnerability in a system or application to cause unintended or unanticipated behavior. It is the practical tool or technique used to leverage a vulnerability for malicious purposes.

metadata.title: Stack Overflow
metadata.definition: An error that occurs when a program attempts to use more memory than is available on the call stack, typically due to excessive recursion without a proper base case or large local variable allocations. This can lead to program crashes, data corruption, or, in security contexts, arbitrary code execution.

metadata.title: Return-Oriented Programming (ROP)
metadata.definition: An advanced exploit technique that bypasses non-executable memory protections (like DEP/NX bit) by chaining together small, existing instruction sequences (called 'gadgets') within the victim program's memory. These gadgets typically end with a `ret` instruction and are used to perform arbitrary operations by manipulating the call stack to control program flow.

metadata.title: Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU)
metadata.definition: A race condition vulnerability that occurs when a system checks the state of a resource (Time-of-Check) and then uses that state later (Time-of-Use), but the state of the resource changes between these two operations. An attacker can exploit this window to create an inconsistent or malicious state, leading to unauthorized access or privilege escalation.

metadata.title: Privilege Escalation
metadata.definition: The act of an attacker or malicious software gaining higher access rights or permissions than initially authorized on a computer system. This can be either vertical (to a user with more privileges, like root or administrator) or horizontal (to another user with similar privileges but different access to resources).

metadata.title: Rootkit
metadata.definition: A collection of malicious software tools designed to hide the existence of other malware or unauthorized access on a computer system. It modifies the operating system, often at a low level, to maintain persistent stealthy control and evade detection by legitimate tools.

metadata.title: Computer Virus
metadata.definition: A type of malicious software that attaches itself to legitimate programs, documents, or boot sectors and spreads from one computer to another, typically requiring user interaction (like opening an infected file) to activate. It aims to alter how a computer operates without the user's knowledge or permission.

metadata.title: Computer Worm
metadata.definition: A standalone malicious program that replicates itself and spreads across computer networks autonomously, without needing to attach to an existing program or require human interaction to propagate. Worms often exploit network vulnerabilities to infect other systems.

metadata.title: Trojan Horse
metadata.definition: A type of malicious software that disguises itself as legitimate or desirable software to trick users into installing and running it. Once executed, it performs its advertised function while secretly carrying out malicious activities in the background, without the user's knowledge.

metadata.title: Side-Channel Attack
metadata.definition: An attack that extracts sensitive information from a system by observing indirect effects of its operation rather than directly targeting the system's input or output. These unintended information leaks can include timing information, power consumption, electromagnetic emissions, acoustic emanations, or cache access patterns.

metadata.title: Rowhammer (Attack)
metadata.definition: A hardware-level side-channel attack that exploits a physical vulnerability in modern DRAM (Dynamic Random-Access Memory) chips, where repeatedly accessing (hammering) a row of memory can cause electrical interference that induces bit flips in physically adjacent, unaccessed 'victim' rows. Attackers can leverage these uncontrolled bit flips to gain unauthorized access or elevate privileges within a system.

metadata.title: Meltdown (Vulnerability)
metadata.definition: A hardware vulnerability affecting modern out-of-order execution CPUs, allowing unprivileged programs to read data from arbitrary kernel memory locations, including sensitive data. It exploits a race condition where speculative execution can leave traces in the CPU cache even if the instruction is later aborted due to privilege violations.

metadata.title: Spectre (Vulnerability)
metadata.definition: A class of hardware vulnerabilities that exploit speculative execution in modern CPUs, allowing an attacker to trick a program into accessing arbitrary memory locations and leak their contents via side channels. Unlike Meltdown, Spectre does not rely on directly accessing privileged memory but rather on influencing the CPU's branch predictor.

metadata.title: Security Sandbox
metadata.definition: A security mechanism for separating running programs, typically to execute untrusted code in a controlled environment, restricting resource access. It creates a tightly controlled set of resources for guest programs to use, preventing them from accessing or modifying system-critical resources or user data outside their designated area.

metadata.title: Trusted Computing Base (TCB)
metadata.definition: The set of all hardware, firmware, and software components of a system that are critical to its security, meaning if any component within the TCB is compromised, the security of the entire system is at risk. Its size and complexity are inversely proportional to the confidence one can have in the system's security.

metadata.title: Secure Boot
metadata.definition: A security standard developed by the UEFI Forum that helps ensure that a device boots only using software trusted by the Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM). It works by verifying the digital signatures of boot components (firmware, boot loader, OS kernel) against a database of trusted certificates stored in the system's firmware.

metadata.title: Storage Hierarchy
metadata.definition: A system architecture that organizes different types of data storage devices based on their speed, cost, and capacity, typically arranged in levels from fastest/most expensive/smallest to slowest/cheapest/largest. Data frequently accessed or requiring low latency resides in higher (faster) levels, while less frequently accessed data is moved to lower (slower) levels.

metadata.title: Hard Disk Drive (HDD)
metadata.definition: A non-volatile data storage device that stores and retrieves digital data using rapidly rotating platters coated with magnetic material. Data is read and written by magnetic heads that move across the platters.

metadata.title: Solid State Drive (SSD)
metadata.definition: A non-volatile storage device that stores data persistently on solid-state flash memory, rather than using spinning platters and read/write heads like traditional HDDs. SSDs offer significantly faster read/write speeds, lower latency, and greater durability due to the absence of moving parts.

metadata.title: Flash Memory
metadata.definition: A type of non-volatile computer memory that can be electrically erased and reprogrammed. It is a form of EEPROM (Electrically Erasable Programmable Read-Only Memory) and is widely used for storage and data transfer in portable devices and SSDs.

metadata.title: NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express)
metadata.definition: A communications interface standard and protocol specifically designed for accessing non-volatile storage media attached via the PCI Express (PCIe) bus. It allows for significantly higher throughput and lower latency compared to older protocols like SATA/AHCI by taking full advantage of the parallelism inherent in solid-state drives.

metadata.title: SATA (Serial ATA)
metadata.definition: A computer bus interface that connects host bus adapters to mass storage devices such as hard disk drives, optical drives, and solid-state drives. It replaced the older Parallel ATA (PATA) standard, offering advantages like reduced cable bulk, faster data transfer rates, and hot-swapping capabilities.

metadata.title: SCSI (Small Computer System Interface)
metadata.definition: A set of standards for physically connecting and transferring data between computers and peripheral devices. Historically, it was prevalent in servers and high-end workstations for connecting hard drives, tape drives, and other peripherals, offering more features and higher performance than consumer-grade interfaces of its era.

metadata.title: RAID Level 0 (Striping)
metadata.definition: A RAID configuration that splits (stripes) data across multiple hard drives without parity or mirroring. It offers improved performance (read/write speeds) as data can be accessed simultaneously from multiple disks, but provides no data redundancy, meaning the failure of any single drive results in complete data loss.

metadata.title: RAID Level 1 (Mirroring)
metadata.definition: A RAID configuration that duplicates (mirrors) data across two or more hard drives. It provides excellent data redundancy, as the system can continue operating if one drive fails, but its usable capacity is halved (or more, depending on the number of mirrors).

metadata.title: RAID Level 5 (Striping with Parity)
metadata.definition: A RAID configuration that stripes data blocks across multiple drives and distributes parity information among all drives. It offers a good balance of performance, capacity, and data redundancy, allowing for the failure of any single drive without data loss. Recovery is performed using the distributed parity.

metadata.title: RAID Level 6 (Striping with Dual Parity)
metadata.definition: A RAID configuration that stripes data blocks across multiple drives and distributes two independent parity blocks among all drives. This provides enhanced data redundancy, allowing for the failure of any two drives simultaneously without data loss, making it suitable for critical applications requiring higher fault tolerance.

metadata.title: RAID Level 10 (Striping and Mirroring)
metadata.definition: Also known as RAID 1+0, this configuration combines RAID 1 (mirroring) and RAID 0 (striping). Data is first mirrored in sets, and then these mirrored sets are striped together. It offers excellent performance and high data redundancy, tolerating multiple drive failures as long as no two failed drives are from the same mirrored set.

metadata.title: Block Storage
metadata.definition: A storage architecture where data is stored in fixed-size blocks, each with a unique address, independent of other blocks. It presents raw storage volumes directly to the operating system, allowing for high-performance and flexible management, often used in Storage Area Networks (SANs).

metadata.title: File Storage (NAS)
metadata.definition: A storage architecture where data is organized and accessed as files and folders, typically presented to users and applications over a network. Network Attached Storage (NAS) devices are dedicated file servers that make storage available to clients using network protocols like NFS or SMB/CIFS.

metadata.title: Disk Controller
metadata.definition: A hardware component that acts as an interface between a computer's central processing unit (CPU) and its storage devices (e.g., HDDs, SSDs). It manages data transfer, handles low-level commands, error detection and correction, and often facilitates features like RAID.

metadata.title: I/O Device
metadata.definition: A peripheral hardware component that allows a computer system to interact with the outside world, either by receiving data (input) or sending data (output). These devices are essential for user interaction and data persistence.

metadata.title: Programmed I/O
metadata.definition: A method of input/output where the CPU directly controls the I/O operations by repeatedly checking the status of an I/O device until it is ready for data transfer. This polling mechanism consumes CPU cycles, potentially reducing system efficiency.

metadata.title: Interrupt-Driven I/O
metadata.definition: An I/O method where a peripheral device, upon completion of an operation or needing service, signals the CPU via an interrupt. This allows the CPU to perform other tasks concurrently instead of continuously polling, significantly improving system efficiency.

metadata.title: Disk Seek Time
metadata.definition: The time required for the read/write heads of a hard disk drive (HDD) to move from their current position to the track containing the desired data. It is a major component of disk access time and is influenced by the physical movement of the actuator arm.

metadata.title: Disk Rotational Latency
metadata.definition: The time required for the desired sector of a hard disk platter to rotate under the read/write head once the head has reached the correct track. It is dependent on the disk's rotational speed (RPM) and averages half a full rotation.

metadata.title: Disk Transfer Rate
metadata.definition: The rate at which data can be read from or written to a storage device after the seek and rotational latency have been accounted for. It represents the speed at which actual data bits flow between the disk and the system's memory.

metadata.title: Flash Erase Block
metadata.definition: The smallest contiguous region of a Flash memory device (like an SSD) that can be erased at once. Erasing smaller units is not possible, meaning an entire block must be cleared before data can be rewritten to any page within it.

metadata.title: Wear Leveling (Flash Memory)
metadata.definition: A technique used in Flash memory controllers (e.g., in SSDs) to distribute write and erase cycles evenly across all memory blocks. This prevents specific blocks from wearing out prematurely due to repeated operations, extending the overall lifespan of the storage device.

metadata.title: Garbage Collection (Flash Memory)
metadata.definition: An automatic background process in Flash memory controllers that reclaims space occupied by 'invalid' or 'stale' data pages within erase blocks. It involves reading valid data from partially invalid blocks, writing it to new, erased blocks, and then erasing the original, now completely invalid, blocks.

metadata.title: TRIM (SSD Command)
metadata.definition: An ATA command that allows an operating system to inform an SSD controller which data blocks are no longer in use and can be internally erased. This helps the SSD's garbage collection operate more efficiently, reducing write amplification and improving long-term performance and endurance.

metadata.title: Hypervisor (Type 1)
metadata.definition: Also known as a 'bare-metal' hypervisor, it runs directly on the host hardware, controlling the hardware and managing guest operating systems. It is typically used in server virtualization for high performance and efficiency.

metadata.title: Hypervisor (Type 2)
metadata.definition: Also known as a 'hosted' hypervisor, it runs as an application on top of a conventional host operating system. It virtualizes guest operating systems, relying on the host OS for hardware access and resource management.

metadata.title: Hardware-Assisted Virtualization
metadata.definition: A technology that adds virtualization extensions to the CPU architecture (e.g., Intel VT-x, AMD-V) and chipset, enabling more efficient and secure virtualization. It provides CPU features that simplify the virtualization of privileged instructions and memory management.

metadata.title: Full Virtualization
metadata.definition: A virtualization technique where the hypervisor completely simulates enough hardware to allow an unmodified guest operating system to run in isolation. The guest OS is unaware it is virtualized, believing it has direct access to hardware.

metadata.title: Paravirtualization
metadata.definition: A virtualization technique where the guest operating system is modified or 'ported' to include special calls (hypercalls) that interact directly with the hypervisor. This cooperation between guest and hypervisor reduces the need for full hardware emulation, often leading to better performance than full virtualization without hardware assistance.

metadata.title: Container (Software)
metadata.definition: A lightweight, standalone, executable package of software that includes everything needed to run an application: code, runtime, system tools, system libraries, and settings. Containers share the host OS kernel but run in isolated user-space environments.

metadata.title: Docker (Containerization)
metadata.definition: A popular open-source platform that enables developers to build, ship, and run applications in containers. It provides tools for packaging applications and their dependencies into portable images and for running these images as isolated containers.

metadata.title: Kubernetes (Orchestration)
metadata.definition: An open-source system for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. It groups containers that make up an application into logical units for easy management and discovery, providing a robust framework for complex distributed systems.

metadata.title: Virtual Network Interface Card (vNIC)
metadata.definition: A software-defined network interface that functions like a physical NIC within a virtual machine or container. It allows the virtualized guest to connect to virtual networks, which can then bridge to physical networks, enabling communication with other VMs or the outside world.

metadata.title: Virtual CPU (vCPU)
metadata.definition: A virtualized representation of a physical CPU core, allocated by a hypervisor to a virtual machine. Multiple vCPUs can be assigned to a single VM, which then perceives them as dedicated processors, enabling it to execute instructions and perform computations.

metadata.title: Guest Operating System
metadata.definition: The operating system that runs inside a virtual machine (VM), isolated from the underlying physical hardware and the host operating system. It operates as if it were running on bare metal, but its hardware interactions are virtualized and managed by the hypervisor.

metadata.title: Host Operating System
metadata.definition: The operating system installed directly on the physical hardware, responsible for managing the hardware resources and running one or more virtual machines through a hypervisor. It provides the environment in which virtual machines and their guest operating systems operate.

metadata.title: VM Image
metadata.definition: A file or set of files that encapsulate the complete state of a virtual machine's disk, including the operating system, applications, and data, as well as configuration settings. It serves as a template for creating new VM instances.

metadata.title: VM Snapshot
metadata.definition: A saved state of a virtual machine at a specific point in time, allowing the VM to be reverted to that exact state later. It typically captures the VM's disk state, memory state, and hardware configuration.

metadata.title: Live Migration (VM)
metadata.definition: The process of moving a running virtual machine from one physical host server to another without any perceptible interruption to its services, applications, or network connections. This technique ensures continuous availability during maintenance or load balancing.

metadata.title: Cloud Computing
metadata.definition: The delivery of on-demand computing services—including servers, storage, databases, networking, software, analytics, and intelligence—over the Internet ('the cloud') with pay-as-you-go pricing. It offers flexibility, scalability, and reduced management overhead.

metadata.title: Assembly Language
metadata.definition: A low-level programming language that provides a symbolic representation of machine code instructions, using mnemonics for operations and labels for memory addresses. Each assembly instruction typically corresponds directly to a single machine instruction.

metadata.title: Machine Code
metadata.definition: The lowest-level programming language, consisting of binary instructions (opcodes and operands) that a computer's central processing unit (CPU) can directly execute. It is the native language of the processor and is specific to a particular CPU architecture.

metadata.title: Dynamic Link Library (DLL)
metadata.definition: A shared library in Windows operating systems that contains code and data that multiple programs can use simultaneously. DLLs are loaded into memory at runtime when an application needs them, promoting code reuse and reducing memory footprint.

metadata.title: Static Link Library
metadata.definition: A collection of compiled object files that are combined with an executable program by the linker at compile time. The library's code and data become an integral part of the final executable binary, making it self-contained.

metadata.title: C Programming Language
metadata.definition: A powerful, imperative, procedural programming language developed in the early 1970s, known for its efficiency, direct memory access, and high portability. It is widely used for systems programming, operating systems, and embedded systems.

metadata.title: Pointer (C Language)
metadata.definition: A variable that stores the memory address of another variable or a function, rather than storing a direct value. Pointers enable direct memory manipulation, dynamic memory allocation, and efficient implementation of data structures and function calls.

metadata.title: C Standard Library Memory Allocation (malloc/free)
metadata.definition: Functions provided by the C standard library (`<stdlib.h>`) for dynamic memory management on the heap. `malloc()` allocates a specified block of memory and returns a pointer to it, while `free()` deallocates previously allocated memory, returning it to the system.

metadata.title: POSIX System Calls
metadata.definition: Standardized interfaces provided by the operating system kernel that allow user-level applications to request services from the operating system, such as file I/O, process creation and management, and inter-process communication. They form the primary way programs interact with the OS.

metadata.title: Process Creation (fork/exec)
metadata.definition: A fundamental mechanism in Unix-like operating systems for creating new processes. `fork()` creates a child process that is an exact copy of the parent, while the `exec()` family of calls replaces the current process's image (code and data) with a new program specified by its arguments.

metadata.title: Signal Handling
metadata.definition: A mechanism in Unix-like systems for asynchronous notification to a process about an event, such as an error, a user request (e.g., Ctrl+C), or the termination of a child process. Processes can register signal handlers to intercept and respond to specific signals.

metadata.title: Environment Variable
metadata.definition: A dynamic-named value that can affect the way running processes behave in a computer. Environment variables are part of a process's environment and are commonly used to store configuration settings, paths to executables, or other system-wide or user-specific information.

metadata.title: Memory Layout of a Program
metadata.definition: The typical organization of a running program's virtual address space into distinct segments, each serving a specific purpose. These segments commonly include text (code), data (initialized global/static variables), BSS (uninitialized global/static variables), heap (dynamic allocation), and stack (local variables and function calls).

metadata.title: Profiler
metadata.definition: A software tool used to analyze the performance characteristics of a program, such as CPU usage, memory allocation, function call frequency, and execution time. Profilers help developers identify performance bottlenecks and optimize code.

metadata.title: Subset
metadata.definition: A set A is a subset of a set B, denoted A ⊆ B, if every element of A is also an element of B. This implies that A could be equal to B, or A could be a proper subset of B (meaning A is a subset of B but A ≠ B).

metadata.title: Empty Set
metadata.definition: The empty set, denoted {} or ∅, is the unique set containing no elements. It is a subset of every set, including itself.

metadata.title: Universal Set
metadata.definition: In a particular context or discussion, the universal set, denoted U, is the set of all possible elements or objects under consideration. All other sets in that specific context are subsets of the universal set.

metadata.title: Union of Sets
metadata.definition: The union of two sets A and B, denoted A ∪ B, is the set containing all elements that are in A, or in B, or in both. Elements that appear in both sets are listed only once in the union.

metadata.title: Intersection of Sets
metadata.definition: The intersection of two sets A and B, denoted A ∩ B, is the set containing all elements that are common to both A and B. Elements must be present in both sets to be included in the intersection.

metadata.title: Complement of a Set
metadata.definition: Given a universal set U and a set A ⊆ U, the complement of A (denoted A' or Aᶜ) is the set of all elements in U that are not in A. It represents everything outside of A within the bounds of the universal set.

metadata.title: Cardinality of a Set
metadata.definition: The cardinality of a set A, denoted |A| or card(A), is the number of distinct elements in the set. For finite sets, this is a non-negative integer; for infinite sets, it refers to a specific type of 'size' or transfinite number.

metadata.title: Power Set
metadata.definition: The power set of a set A, denoted P(A) or 2^A, is the set of all possible subsets of A, including the empty set and A itself. If a set A has n elements, its power set P(A) will have 2ⁿ elements.

metadata.title: Ordered Pair
metadata.definition: An ordered pair (a, b) is a collection of two elements where the order of the elements is significant. Unlike a set {a, b}, (a, b) is not generally equal to (b, a) unless a = b.

metadata.title: Relation
metadata.definition: A binary relation R from a set A to a set B is any subset of the Cartesian product A × B. If an ordered pair (a, b) is in R, we say that 'a is related to b' and often write a R b.

metadata.title: Reflexive Relation
metadata.definition: A binary relation R on a set A is reflexive if every element in A is related to itself. Formally, for every a ∈ A, the ordered pair (a, a) must belong to R.

metadata.title: Symmetric Relation
metadata.definition: A binary relation R on a set A is symmetric if, whenever an element 'a' is related to an element 'b', then 'b' is also related to 'a'. Formally, for all a, b ∈ A, if (a, b) ∈ R, then (b, a) ∈ R.

metadata.title: Transitive Relation
metadata.definition: A binary relation R on a set A is transitive if, whenever 'a' is related to 'b' and 'b' is related to 'c', then 'a' is also related to 'c'. Formally, for all a, b, c ∈ A, if (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R, then (a, c) ∈ R.

metadata.title: Equivalence Relation
metadata.definition: A binary relation R on a set A is an equivalence relation if it is simultaneously reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Equivalence relations partition a set into disjoint equivalence classes, where all elements within a class are related to each other.

metadata.title: Partial Order Relation
metadata.definition: A binary relation R on a set A is a partial order relation if it is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive. Antisymmetric means that if (a, b) ∈ R and (b, a) ∈ R, then a must equal b.

metadata.title: Total Order Relation
metadata.definition: A partial order relation R on a set A is a total order relation (or linear order) if for every pair of elements a, b ∈ A, either (a, b) ∈ R or (b, a) ∈ R. This means that every pair of elements in the set is comparable.

metadata.title: Injective Function (One-to-one)
metadata.definition: A function f: A → B is injective, or one-to-one, if every distinct element in the domain A maps to a distinct element in the codomain B. This means that if f(x₁) = f(x₂), then x₁ must be equal to x₂.

metadata.title: Surjective Function (Onto)
metadata.definition: A function f: A → B is surjective, or onto, if every element in the codomain B is the image of at least one element in the domain A. In other words, the range of the function is equal to its codomain.

metadata.title: Bijective Function (One-to-one correspondence)
metadata.definition: A function f: A → B is bijective, or a one-to-one correspondence, if it is both injective (one-to-one) and surjective (onto). A bijection establishes a perfect pairing between elements of A and B, meaning an inverse function f⁻¹: B → A always exists.

metadata.title: Composition of Functions
metadata.definition: Given two functions f: A → B and g: B → C, the composition of f and g, denoted (g ∘ f), is a new function (g ∘ f): A → C defined by (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)) for all x in A. The output of the first function becomes the input for the second function.

metadata.title: Logical Proposition
metadata.definition: A declarative statement that is either true or false, but not both. It forms the basic building block of logical reasoning and can be assigned a truth value.

metadata.title: Truth Value
metadata.definition: A designation that indicates the relationship of a proposition to truth, typically either 'True' (T or 1) or 'False' (F or 0). It quantifies the veracity of a statement.

metadata.title: Logical Connective (AND)
metadata.definition: A logical operator that produces a true result only if all its constituent propositions are true. It represents conjunction, often denoted by ∧ or '&'.

metadata.title: Logical Connective (OR)
metadata.definition: A logical operator that produces a true result if at least one of its constituent propositions is true. It represents disjunction, often denoted by ∨ or '|'.

metadata.title: Logical Connective (NOT)
metadata.definition: A logical operator that negates the truth value of a proposition, changing True to False and False to True. It represents negation, often denoted by ¬ or '~'.

metadata.title: Logical Connective (Implication)
metadata.definition: A logical operator that states 'If P, then Q', denoted by P → Q. It is false only when the antecedent (P) is true and the consequent (Q) is false; otherwise, it is true.

metadata.title: Logical Connective (Biconditional)
metadata.definition: A logical operator that states 'P if and only if Q', denoted by P ↔ Q. It is true if and only if P and Q have the same truth value (both true or both false).

metadata.title: Truth Table
metadata.definition: A mathematical table used in logic to compute the functional truth values of logical expressions for each possible assignment of truth values to their constituent propositional variables. It systematically lists all possible outcomes.

metadata.title: Tautology
metadata.definition: A logical expression or proposition that is always true, regardless of the truth values of its constituent propositional variables. Its truth table will show 'True' for every possible assignment.

metadata.title: Logical Contradiction
metadata.definition: A logical expression or proposition that is always false, regardless of the truth values of its constituent propositional variables. Its truth table will show 'False' for every possible assignment.

metadata.title: Logical Equivalence
metadata.definition: Two logical propositions or statements are logically equivalent if they always have the same truth value under all possible assignments of truth values to their propositional variables. This is often denoted by P ≡ Q or P ↔ Q being a tautology.

metadata.title: Logical Satisfiability
metadata.definition: A logical formula or set of clauses is satisfiable if there exists at least one assignment of truth values to its variables that makes the entire formula true. If no such assignment exists, the formula is unsatisfiable.

metadata.title: Logical Validity
metadata.definition: An argument is logically valid if its conclusion necessarily follows from its premises. In other words, if all the premises are true, then the conclusion must also be true, regardless of the actual truth values of the propositions.

metadata.title: Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF)
metadata.definition: A standardized representation of a logical formula that is a conjunction (AND) of one or more clauses, where each clause is a disjunction (OR) of literals. Every propositional formula can be converted into an equivalent CNF.

metadata.title: Disjunctive Normal Form (DNF)
metadata.definition: A standardized representation of a logical formula that is a disjunction (OR) of one or more conjunctive clauses (minterms). Each conjunctive clause is a conjunction (AND) of literals. Every propositional formula can be converted into an equivalent DNF.

metadata.title: Literal (Logic)
metadata.definition: In propositional logic, a literal is either an atomic proposition (like P) or the negation of an atomic proposition (like ¬P). Literals are the basic components of clauses in CNF and DNF.

metadata.title: Quantifier (Universal)
metadata.definition: A logical operator, denoted by ∀ (for all), that indicates a statement is true for every member of a specified domain or set. It asserts that a property holds universally.

metadata.title: Quantifier (Existential)
metadata.definition: A logical operator, denoted by ∃ (there exists), that indicates a statement is true for at least one member of a specified domain or set. It asserts that a property holds for some particular instance.

metadata.title: Modus Ponens
metadata.definition: A fundamental rule of inference in propositional logic stating that if a conditional statement (P → Q) is accepted as true, and its antecedent (P) is also true, then the consequent (Q) can be logically concluded to be true.

metadata.title: Modus Tollens
metadata.definition: A fundamental rule of inference in propositional logic stating that if a conditional statement (P → Q) is accepted as true, and its consequent (Q) is false, then the antecedent (P) can be logically concluded to be false.

metadata.title: Proof by Direct Proof
metadata.definition: A method of proof where the conclusion is established by logically deriving it from the premises and axioms, using definitions and previously established theorems. It proceeds from 'if P, then Q' by assuming P is true and showing that Q must logically follow.

metadata.title: Proof by Contraposition
metadata.definition: A method of proof that establishes 'if P, then Q' by proving its contrapositive statement 'if not Q, then not P.' If the contrapositive is true, then the original statement must also be true, based on logical equivalence.

metadata.title: Proof by Induction (Mathematical)
metadata.definition: A technique used to prove that a statement holds for all natural numbers, or for all members of an infinite sequence, by establishing a base case and an inductive step. The inductive step proves that if the statement holds for some arbitrary natural number k, then it must also hold for k+1.

metadata.title: Proof by Strong Induction
metadata.definition: A variant of mathematical induction where the inductive step assumes that the statement holds for all natural numbers up to an arbitrary k (i.e., for 1, 2, ..., k), rather than just for k, to prove it for k+1. This stronger assumption can simplify proofs for certain types of problems.

metadata.title: Proof by Pigeonhole Principle
metadata.definition: A principle stating that if n items are put into m containers, with n > m, then at least one container must contain more than one item. More generally, if n items are distributed into m boxes, then at least one box contains at least ⌈n/m⌉ items.

metadata.title: Permutation
metadata.definition: An arrangement of a set of items in a specific order. The order of arrangement matters, and each item is used at most once.

metadata.title: Combination
metadata.definition: A selection of items from a larger set where the order of selection does not matter. It represents the number of ways to choose k items from a set of n distinct items without regard to their arrangement.

metadata.title: Binomial Coefficient
metadata.definition: The number of ways to choose k items from a set of n distinct items, denoted as 'n choose k' or C(n, k) or (n k). It is calculated as n! / (k! * (n-k)!) and represents the coefficient of x^k in the binomial expansion of (1+x)^n.

metadata.title: Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion
metadata.definition: A counting technique used to find the number of elements in the union of multiple sets by summing the sizes of the individual sets, subtracting the sum of sizes of all pairwise intersections, adding back the sum of sizes of all three-way intersections, and so on. This process corrects for elements counted multiple times.

metadata.title: Graph (Discrete Mathematics)
metadata.definition: A mathematical structure used to model pairwise relations between objects, consisting of a set of vertices (or nodes) and a set of edges (or links) connecting pairs of vertices. Graphs can be directed or undirected, and edges can have weights.

metadata.title: Vertex (Graph Theory)
metadata.definition: A fundamental component of a graph, also known as a node, representing an entity or a point. Vertices are connected to each other by edges.

metadata.title: Edge (Graph Theory)
metadata.definition: A connection between two vertices in a graph, representing a relationship or link between the entities that the vertices represent. Edges can be directed (digraphs) or undirected.

metadata.title: Path (Graph Theory)
metadata.definition: A sequence of distinct vertices in a graph such that each vertex in the sequence is connected to the next vertex by an edge. A simple path does not repeat any vertices.

metadata.title: Cycle (Graph Theory)
metadata.definition: A path in a graph that starts and ends at the same vertex, and does not repeat any other vertices or edges. A cycle must consist of at least three vertices in a simple graph.

metadata.title: Strongly Connected Graph
metadata.definition: A directed graph in which for every pair of distinct vertices (u, v), there is a path from u to v and a path from v to u. This implies that all vertices are mutually reachable.

metadata.title: Tree (Graph Theory)
metadata.definition: An undirected graph that is connected and contains no cycles. Equivalently, a connected graph with N vertices and N-1 edges. Trees are fundamental in computer science for hierarchical structures.

metadata.title: Rooted Tree
metadata.definition: A tree in which one vertex has been designated as the root, establishing a hierarchical structure where all other vertices are descendants of the root. Edges implicitly define parent-child relationships.

metadata.title: Spanning Tree
metadata.definition: A subgraph of a connected, undirected graph that includes all the vertices of the original graph and is itself a tree. It connects all vertices with the minimum possible number of edges and without introducing any cycles.

metadata.title: Bipartite Graph
metadata.definition: A graph whose vertices can be divided into two disjoint and independent sets, U and V, such that every edge connects a vertex in U to one in V; there are no edges within U or within V.

metadata.title: Planar Graph
metadata.definition: A graph that can be drawn on a plane without any edges crossing each other. Such a drawing is called a planar embedding of the graph.

metadata.title: Eulerian Path
metadata.definition: An Eulerian path in a graph is a path that traverses every edge of the graph exactly once. If the path starts and ends at the same vertex, it is called an Eulerian circuit.

metadata.title: Hamiltonian Path
metadata.definition: A Hamiltonian path in a graph is a path that visits each vertex exactly once. If the path starts and ends at the same vertex, it is called a Hamiltonian cycle.

metadata.title: Incidence Matrix
metadata.definition: An incidence matrix is a way to represent a graph where rows correspond to vertices and columns correspond to edges. An entry (i, j) is 1 if vertex 'i' is incident to edge 'j', and 0 otherwise (or +1/-1 for directed graphs).

metadata.title: Graph Isomorphism
metadata.definition: Two graphs G1 and G2 are isomorphic if there exists a bijection (one-to-one and onto mapping) between their vertex sets such that two vertices are adjacent in G1 if and only if their corresponding vertices are adjacent in G2. Essentially, they have the same structure.

metadata.title: Divisibility
metadata.definition: For two integers 'a' and 'b', with 'a' not equal to zero, 'a' divides 'b' (denoted as a | b) if there exists an integer 'k' such that b = ak. In this case, 'a' is a divisor or factor of 'b', and 'b' is a multiple of 'a'.

metadata.title: Prime Number
metadata.definition: A prime number is a natural number greater than 1 that has no positive divisors other than 1 and itself. These are the fundamental building blocks for all other natural numbers through multiplication.

metadata.title: Composite Number
metadata.definition: A composite number is a natural number greater than 1 that is not prime, meaning it has at least one positive divisor other than 1 and itself. Every composite number can be written as a product of two or more prime numbers.

metadata.title: Least Common Multiple (LCM)
metadata.definition: The Least Common Multiple (LCM) of two or more non-zero integers is the smallest positive integer that is a multiple of all the integers. It is often used when dealing with fractions or cycles.

metadata.title: Congruence Relation
metadata.definition: For integers a, b, and a positive integer n, 'a is congruent to b modulo n' (written as a ≡ b (mod n)) means that n divides the difference (a - b). This implies that 'a' and 'b' have the same remainder when divided by 'n'.

metadata.title: Chinese Remainder Theorem
metadata.definition: The Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) provides a unique solution to a system of linear congruences if the moduli are pairwise coprime. It states that for given integers a1, ..., ak and pairwise coprime integers n1, ..., nk, there exists a unique integer x modulo N = n1*...*nk that satisfies x ≡ ai (mod ni) for all i.

metadata.title: Mathematical Group
metadata.definition: A mathematical group is a set G equipped with a binary operation * (e.g., addition, multiplication) that satisfies four specific axioms: closure, associativity, existence of an identity element, and existence of an inverse element for every member.

metadata.title: Mathematical Ring
metadata.definition: A mathematical ring is a set R equipped with two binary operations, usually called addition (+) and multiplication (*), such that R is an abelian group under addition, multiplication is associative, and multiplication distributes over addition. Unlike a field, multiplication does not necessarily have inverses for all non-zero elements, nor is it necessarily commutative.

metadata.title: Mathematical Field
metadata.definition: A mathematical field is a commutative ring where every non-zero element has a multiplicative inverse. It is an algebraic structure where addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division (except by zero) are well-defined and behave as expected.

metadata.title: Algebraic Homomorphism
metadata.definition: An algebraic homomorphism is a structure-preserving map between two algebraic structures of the same type (e.g., groups, rings, or vector spaces). It means that applying the map and then the operation is equivalent to applying the operation and then the map.

metadata.title: Algebraic Isomorphism
metadata.definition: An algebraic isomorphism is a bijective (one-to-one and onto) homomorphism between two algebraic structures of the same type. If an isomorphism exists, the two structures are considered 'algebraically identical' or structurally equivalent, differing only in the names of their elements.

metadata.title: Group Axioms
metadata.definition: The four fundamental axioms that define a mathematical group (G, *): 1) Closure: For all a, b in G, a * b is in G. 2) Associativity: For all a, b, c in G, (a * b) * c = a * (b * c). 3) Identity Element: There exists an element e in G such that for every a in G, a * e = e * a = a. 4) Inverse Element: For every a in G, there exists an element a⁻¹ in G such that a * a⁻¹ = a⁻¹ * a = e.

metadata.title: Ring Axioms
metadata.definition: The axioms defining a mathematical ring (R, +, *): 1) (R, +) is an abelian group. 2) Multiplication is associative: (a * b) * c = a * (b * c). 3) Multiplication distributes over addition: a * (b + c) = (a * b) + (a * c) and (a + b) * c = (a * c) + (b * c).

metadata.title: Field Axioms
metadata.definition: The axioms defining a mathematical field (F, +, *): 1) (F, +, *) is a commutative ring. 2) The multiplicative identity (1) is not equal to the additive identity (0). 3) Every non-zero element 'a' in F has a multiplicative inverse a⁻¹ such that a * a⁻¹ = 1. These axioms ensure all standard arithmetic operations are well-defined.

metadata.title: Scalar
metadata.definition: A scalar is a quantity that is completely described by a single numerical value, representing only magnitude. It has no associated direction in space.

metadata.title: Vector
metadata.definition: A vector is a quantity that has both magnitude and direction. It is typically represented as an arrow in geometric contexts or as an ordered list of numbers (components) in algebraic contexts.

metadata.title: Matrix
metadata.definition: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers, symbols, or expressions, arranged in rows and columns. It is a fundamental data structure in linear algebra used to represent data or linear transformations.

metadata.title: Vector Addition
metadata.definition: Vector addition is the operation of combining two or more vectors to produce a single resultant vector. This is done by adding their corresponding components.

metadata.title: Scalar Multiplication (Vector)
metadata.definition: Scalar multiplication of a vector involves multiplying each component of the vector by a single scalar value. This operation scales the magnitude of the vector while preserving its direction (or reversing it if the scalar is negative).

metadata.title: Dot Product (Scalar Product)
metadata.definition: The dot product, also known as the scalar product, is an algebraic operation that takes two equal-length sequences of numbers (usually coordinate vectors) and returns a single number. Geometrically, it is the product of the Euclidean magnitudes of the two vectors and the cosine of the angle between them, indicating how much one vector goes in the direction of the other.

metadata.title: Cross Product (Vector Product)
metadata.definition: The cross product, also known as the vector product, is a binary operation on two vectors in three-dimensional space that results in a vector perpendicular to both input vectors. Its magnitude is equal to the area of the parallelogram that the vectors span, and its direction follows the right-hand rule.

metadata.title: Matrix Addition
metadata.definition: Matrix addition is the operation of adding two matrices of the same dimensions by adding their corresponding elements. The result is a new matrix with the same dimensions.

metadata.title: Matrix Subtraction
metadata.definition: Matrix subtraction is the operation of subtracting one matrix from another of the same dimensions. This is performed by subtracting their corresponding elements to produce a new matrix with identical dimensions.

metadata.title: Matrix Multiplication
metadata.definition: Matrix multiplication is a binary operation that produces a matrix from two matrices. For two matrices A (m x n) and B (n x p), their product C (m x p) is calculated by taking the dot product of each row of A with each column of B.

metadata.title: Identity Matrix
metadata.definition: An identity matrix, denoted as 'I', is a square matrix where all the elements on the main diagonal are ones, and all other elements are zeros. It serves as the multiplicative identity in matrix algebra, meaning that multiplying any matrix by an identity matrix leaves the original matrix unchanged (A * I = I * A = A).

metadata.title: Zero Matrix (Null Matrix)
metadata.definition: A zero matrix, or null matrix, is a matrix where every element is zero. It acts as the additive identity in matrix algebra, meaning that adding a zero matrix to any other matrix of the same dimensions leaves the original matrix unchanged.

metadata.title: Transpose of a Matrix
metadata.definition: The transpose of a matrix is a new matrix formed by swapping the rows and columns of the original matrix. If the original matrix A has dimensions m x n, its transpose Aᵀ will have dimensions n x m.

metadata.title: Determinant of a Matrix
metadata.definition: The determinant is a scalar value that can be computed from the elements of a square matrix. It provides crucial information about the matrix, such as whether it is invertible (non-zero determinant) and how it scales geometric transformations (area or volume scaling factor).

metadata.title: Inverse of a Matrix
metadata.definition: For a square matrix A, its inverse, denoted A⁻¹, is another square matrix such that when multiplied by A, it yields the identity matrix (A * A⁻¹ = A⁻¹ * A = I). A matrix is invertible only if its determinant is non-zero.

metadata.title: Singular Matrix
metadata.definition: A singular matrix is a square matrix whose determinant is equal to zero. This implies that the matrix does not have an inverse, and the linear transformation it represents collapses at least one dimension, meaning it maps multiple non-zero vectors to the zero vector.

metadata.title: Non-singular Matrix
metadata.definition: A non-singular matrix, also known as an invertible matrix, is a square matrix whose determinant is non-zero. Consequently, a non-singular matrix always possesses a unique inverse, and the linear transformation it represents preserves dimensionality.

metadata.title: System of Linear Equations
metadata.definition: A system of linear equations is a collection of one or more linear equations involving the same set of variables. These systems are used to model problems where several quantities are linearly related.

metadata.title: Consistent System
metadata.definition: A consistent system of linear equations is one that has at least one solution. This means the lines or planes represented by the equations intersect at one point (unique solution) or overlap (infinitely many solutions).

metadata.title: Inconsistent System
metadata.definition: An inconsistent system of linear equations is one that has no solution. Geometrically, this occurs when the lines or planes represented by the equations are parallel and distinct, meaning they never intersect.

metadata.title: Gauss-Jordan Elimination
metadata.definition: Gauss-Jordan elimination is an algorithm used to solve systems of linear equations or to find the inverse of a matrix. It works by performing a sequence of elementary row operations (swapping rows, multiplying a row by a non-zero scalar, adding a multiple of one row to another) to transform an augmented matrix into reduced row echelon form.

metadata.title: Row Echelon Form
metadata.definition: Row Echelon Form (REF) is a specific structure for a matrix obtained through Gaussian elimination, where: 1) All non-zero rows are above any rows of all zeros. 2) The leading entry (pivot) of each non-zero row is 1. 3) Each leading entry is to the right of the leading entry in the row above it.

metadata.title: Reduced Row Echelon Form
metadata.definition: A matrix is in reduced row echelon form (RREF) if it satisfies four conditions: (1) all zero rows are at the bottom, (2) the leading entry (pivot) of each non-zero row is 1, (3) each pivot is to the right of the pivot in the row above it, and (4) each pivot is the only non-zero entry in its column. RREF is unique for any given matrix and is used to solve systems of linear equations and find matrix inverses.

metadata.title: Rank of a Matrix
metadata.definition: The rank of a matrix is the maximum number of linearly independent row vectors or column vectors in the matrix. It is also equal to the dimension of the column space (image) or row space of the matrix, and the number of pivot positions in its row echelon form.

metadata.title: Null Space (Kernel)
metadata.definition: The null space (or kernel) of a matrix A is the set of all vectors x such that Ax = 0, where 0 is the zero vector. It represents all input vectors that are mapped to the zero vector by the linear transformation associated with A, forming a subspace of the domain.

metadata.title: Column Space (Image)
metadata.definition: The column space (or image) of a matrix A is the set of all possible linear combinations of the column vectors of A. It represents the range of the linear transformation associated with A, forming a subspace of the codomain.

metadata.title: Row Space
metadata.definition: The row space of a matrix A is the set of all possible linear combinations of the row vectors of A. It is a subspace of the domain of the linear transformation associated with A, and its dimension is equal to the rank of the matrix.

metadata.title: Vector Space
metadata.definition: A vector space is a set V of objects called vectors, equipped with two operations: vector addition and scalar multiplication, which satisfy ten axioms (e.g., commutativity, associativity, existence of zero vector and additive inverse, distributive properties). These axioms ensure that vectors can be manipulated in a consistent and intuitive way.

metadata.title: Subspace (Linear Algebra)
metadata.definition: A subspace of a vector space V is a subset H of V that is itself a vector space under the operations of vector addition and scalar multiplication defined on V. For H to be a subspace, it must satisfy three conditions: (1) the zero vector of V is in H, (2) H is closed under vector addition, and (3) H is closed under scalar multiplication.

metadata.title: Linear Combination
metadata.definition: A linear combination of a set of vectors `v_1, v_2, ..., v_k` is an expression of the form `c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + ... + c_kv_k`, where `c_1, c_2, ..., c_k` are scalars. This concept is fundamental to understanding vector spaces and how vectors can be constructed from others.

metadata.title: Span of Vectors
metadata.definition: The span of a set of vectors `v_1, v_2, ..., v_k`, denoted as `span{v_1, ..., v_k}`, is the set of all possible linear combinations of those vectors. It forms the smallest subspace containing all the vectors in the set.

metadata.title: Basis (Vector Space)
metadata.definition: A basis for a vector space V is a set of linearly independent vectors that span V. Any vector in V can be uniquely expressed as a linear combination of the basis vectors, and the number of vectors in any basis for V is constant (which defines the dimension of V).

metadata.title: Dimension (Vector Space)
metadata.definition: The dimension of a vector space V, denoted `dim(V)`, is the number of vectors in any basis for V. If a vector space cannot be spanned by a finite number of vectors, it is said to be infinite-dimensional.

metadata.title: Orthonormal Basis
metadata.definition: An orthonormal basis for an inner product space is a basis whose vectors are mutually orthogonal (their inner product is zero) and each have a unit length (their norm is one). Such bases simplify calculations involving projections and coordinates.

metadata.title: Gram-Schmidt Process
metadata.definition: The Gram-Schmidt process is an algorithm for orthonormalizing a set of linearly independent vectors in an inner product space. It systematically constructs an orthogonal basis from the given set, and then normalizes each vector to unit length to produce an orthonormal basis.

metadata.title: Linear Transformation
metadata.definition: A linear transformation (or linear map) is a function between two vector spaces that preserves the operations of vector addition and scalar multiplication. Specifically, for any vectors u, v and scalar c, it satisfies `T(u+v) = T(u) + T(v)` (additivity) and `T(cu) = cT(u)` (homogeneity).

metadata.title: Matrix Representation of Linear Transformation
metadata.definition: Every linear transformation `T: V -> W` between finite-dimensional vector spaces can be represented by a unique matrix with respect to chosen bases for V and W. This matrix, when multiplied by the coordinate vector of an input in V, yields the coordinate vector of its image in W.

metadata.title: Eigenspace
metadata.definition: The eigenspace of a matrix A corresponding to an eigenvalue `λ` is the set of all eigenvectors associated with `λ`, along with the zero vector. It forms a subspace of the vector space and represents the set of all vectors that are only scaled (by `λ`) when the linear transformation A is applied.

metadata.title: Characteristic Equation
metadata.definition: The characteristic equation of a square matrix A is given by `det(A - λI) = 0`, where `λ` is a scalar variable and `I` is the identity matrix of the same dimension as A. The roots of this polynomial equation are the eigenvalues of the matrix A.

metadata.title: Diagonalization of a Matrix
metadata.definition: A square matrix A is diagonalizable if it is similar to a diagonal matrix D, meaning there exists an invertible matrix P such that `A = PDP⁻¹`. This is possible if and only if A has a complete set of linearly independent eigenvectors, which form the columns of P, and the diagonal entries of D are the corresponding eigenvalues.

metadata.title: Symmetric Matrix
metadata.definition: A square matrix A is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose, i.e., `A = Aᵀ`. This means that the element in the i-th row and j-th column is equal to the element in the j-th row and i-th column (`a_ij = a_ji`).

metadata.title: Skew-Symmetric Matrix
metadata.definition: A square matrix A is skew-symmetric (or anti-symmetric) if it is equal to the negative of its transpose, i.e., `A = -Aᵀ`. This implies that `a_ij = -a_ji` for all i and j, and consequently, the diagonal elements must all be zero.

metadata.title: Orthogonal Matrix
metadata.definition: A square matrix A is orthogonal if its columns and rows are orthogonal unit vectors (orthonormal vectors). Equivalently, its transpose is equal to its inverse, i.e., AᵀA = AAᵀ = I, where I is the identity matrix.

metadata.title: Unitary Matrix
metadata.definition: A complex square matrix U is unitary if its conjugate transpose (Hermitian transpose) is equal to its inverse, i.e., UᴴU = UUᴴ = I, where I is the identity matrix. It is the complex analogue of an orthogonal matrix, preserving the inner product.

metadata.title: Hermitian Matrix
metadata.definition: A complex square matrix A is Hermitian if it is equal to its own conjugate transpose (Hermitian transpose), i.e., A = Aᴴ. All eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix are real numbers.

metadata.title: Positive Definite Matrix
metadata.definition: A symmetric (or Hermitian for complex) matrix M is positive definite if for every non-zero column vector x, the quadratic form xᵀMx > 0. This implies all its eigenvalues are strictly positive.

metadata.title: Positive Semidefinite Matrix
metadata.definition: A symmetric (or Hermitian for complex) matrix M is positive semidefinite if for every non-zero column vector x, the quadratic form xᵀMx ≥ 0. This means all its eigenvalues are non-negative (greater than or equal to zero).

metadata.title: Linear Projection
metadata.definition: A linear transformation P from a vector space to itself such that applying the transformation twice yields the same result as applying it once, i.e., P² = P. It maps vectors onto a subspace.

metadata.title: Orthogonal Projection
metadata.definition: A linear projection P that maps a vector onto a subspace such that the difference between the original vector and its projection is orthogonal to the subspace. If P is a matrix, it satisfies P = Pᵀ and P² = P.

metadata.title: Least Squares Method
metadata.definition: A statistical method used to find the best-fitting line or curve for a set of data points by minimizing the sum of the squares of the residuals (the differences between observed and predicted values). It is widely used to estimate parameters in linear models.

metadata.title: LU Decomposition
metadata.definition: A matrix factorization that decomposes a square matrix A into the product of a lower triangular matrix L and an upper triangular matrix U, i.e., A = LU. This decomposition is highly efficient for solving systems of linear equations, calculating determinants, and inverting matrices.

metadata.title: QR Decomposition
metadata.definition: A matrix factorization that decomposes a matrix A into the product of an orthogonal matrix Q and an upper triangular matrix R, i.e., A = QR. It is commonly used for solving linear least squares problems and for eigenvalue computations.

metadata.title: Cholesky Decomposition
metadata.definition: A matrix factorization that decomposes a symmetric, positive-definite matrix A into the product of a lower triangular matrix L and its conjugate transpose Lᴴ (or transpose Lᵀ for real matrices), i.e., A = LLᴴ. It is an efficient method often used in numerical analysis.

metadata.title: Eigen Decomposition
metadata.definition: A factorization of a square matrix A into the product A = PΛP⁻¹, where P is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of A and Λ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the corresponding eigenvalues. It reveals the fundamental directions and scaling factors of the linear transformation represented by A.

metadata.title: Frobenius Norm
metadata.definition: A matrix norm defined as the square root of the sum of the absolute squares of its elements, i.e., ||A||_F = √(Σᵢⱼ |aᵢⱼ|²). It is analogous to the Euclidean (L2) norm for vectors and is often used to measure the 'size' of a matrix.

metadata.title: Vector Norm (L1)
metadata.definition: Also known as the Manhattan norm or taxi-cab norm, the L1 norm of a vector x is calculated as the sum of the absolute values of its components, i.e., ||x||₁ = Σᵢ |xᵢ|. It represents the sum of distances along each axis.

metadata.title: Vector Norm (L2, Euclidean Norm)
metadata.definition: The most common vector norm, the L2 norm of a vector x is calculated as the square root of the sum of the squares of its components, i.e., ||x||₂ = √(Σᵢ xᵢ²). It represents the standard straight-line Euclidean distance from the origin to the vector's endpoint, or the magnitude of the vector.

metadata.title: Vector Norm (L-infinity)
metadata.definition: Also known as the maximum norm or Chebyshev norm, the L-infinity norm of a vector x is defined as the maximum absolute value among its components, i.e., ||x||_∞ = maxᵢ |xᵢ|. It measures the largest deviation of any component from zero.

metadata.title: Matrix Norm
metadata.definition: A function that assigns a positive number to each matrix, satisfying properties analogous to vector norms: non-negativity, definiteness, homogeneity, and sub-multiplicativity (||AB|| ≤ ||A|| ||B||). It quantifies the 'size' or 'magnitude' of a matrix and is useful for error analysis and stability.

metadata.title: Spectral Radius
metadata.definition: For a square matrix A, the spectral radius ρ(A) is the maximum of the absolute values of its eigenvalues, i.e., ρ(A) = maxᵢ |λᵢ|. It is a crucial measure for analyzing the convergence of iterative methods and the stability of dynamical systems.

metadata.title: Inner Product Space
metadata.definition: A vector space equipped with an inner product, which is a binary operation mapping two vectors to a scalar and satisfying certain properties (conjugate symmetry, linearity in the first argument, positive-definiteness). The inner product generalizes the dot product and allows for defining concepts like angle, length, and orthogonality.

metadata.title: Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality
metadata.definition: A fundamental inequality stating that for any two vectors x and y in an inner product space, the absolute value of their inner product is less than or equal to the product of their magnitudes (norms), i.e., |<x, y>| ≤ ||x|| ||y||. Equality holds if and only if x and y are linearly dependent.

metadata.title: Limit of a Sequence
metadata.definition: The value that the terms of a sequence approach as the number of terms (index) tends to infinity. If such a value exists, the sequence is said to converge to that limit.

metadata.title: Limit of a Function
metadata.definition: The value that a function approaches as its input (independent variable) gets arbitrarily close to a certain point. It describes the behavior of the function in the vicinity of a point, regardless of the function's value at that specific point.

metadata.title: Continuity of a Function
metadata.definition: A function is continuous at a point if its limit as the input approaches that point exists, the function is defined at that point, and the limit equals the function's value at that point. Informally, a continuous function can be drawn without lifting the pen from the paper.

metadata.title: Discontinuity of a Function
metadata.definition: A function is discontinuous at a point if it is not continuous at that point. This typically occurs if the limit does not exist, the function is undefined at the point, or the limit exists but does not match the function's value at the point.

metadata.title: Derivative (Calculus)
metadata.definition: The instantaneous rate of change of a function with respect to its independent variable. Geometrically, the derivative at a point represents the slope of the tangent line to the function's graph at that point.

metadata.title: Rules of Differentiation (Product Rule)
metadata.definition: A fundamental rule in calculus for finding the derivative of a function that is the product of two or more differentiable functions. If h(x) = f(x)g(x), then its derivative is h'(x) = f'(x)g(x) + f(x)g'(x).

metadata.title: Rules of Differentiation (Quotient Rule)
metadata.definition: A formula used to find the derivative of a function that is expressed as the ratio of two differentiable functions. If h(x) = f(x)/g(x), then its derivative is h'(x) = [f'(x)g(x) - f(x)g'(x)] / [g(x)]^2, provided g(x) ≠ 0.

metadata.title: Rules of Differentiation (Chain Rule)
metadata.definition: A rule for differentiating composite functions. If h(x) = f(g(x)), then its derivative is h'(x) = f'(g(x)) * g'(x), meaning the derivative of the outer function is evaluated at the inner function, then multiplied by the derivative of the inner function.

metadata.title: Gradient (Vector Calculus)
metadata.definition: For a scalar-valued multivariable function, the gradient is a vector of its first-order partial derivatives. It points in the direction of the greatest rate of increase of the function, and its magnitude is that maximum rate of increase.

metadata.title: Directional Derivative
metadata.definition: The rate at which a multivariable function changes at a given point in a specified direction. It generalizes the concept of a partial derivative, which is simply the directional derivative along a coordinate axis.

metadata.title: Jacobian Matrix
metadata.definition: A matrix composed of all first-order partial derivatives of a vector-valued function. It represents the best linear approximation of a differentiable function between Euclidean spaces near a given point, describing local scaling, rotation, and shearing.

metadata.title: Hessian Matrix
metadata.definition: A square matrix of second-order partial derivatives of a scalar-valued multivariable function. It is used to describe the local curvature of a function and is crucial for determining if a critical point is a local maximum, minimum, or saddle point.

metadata.title: Local Maximum
metadata.definition: A point in the domain of a function where the function's value is greater than or equal to the values at all other points within some small neighborhood around it. The function locally 'peaks' at this point.

metadata.title: Local Minimum
metadata.definition: A point in the domain of a function where the function's value is less than or equal to the values at all other points within some small neighborhood around it. The function locally 'bottoms out' at this point.

metadata.title: Global Maximum
metadata.definition: The point in the domain of a function where the function's value is greater than or equal to the values at all other points across its entire domain. It represents the absolute highest value the function attains.

metadata.title: Global Minimum
metadata.definition: The point in the domain of a function where the function's value is less than or equal to the values at all other points across its entire domain. It represents the absolute lowest value the function attains.

metadata.title: Saddle Point
metadata.definition: A critical point of a function where the first derivative is zero (or gradient is zero for multivariable functions), but it is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum. At a saddle point, the function increases in some directions and decreases in others.

metadata.title: Critical Point (Calculus)
metadata.definition: A point in the domain of a function where its first derivative is either zero or undefined. Critical points are candidates for local maxima, local minima, or saddle points, and they are crucial for finding extrema of functions.

metadata.title: Inflection Point
metadata.definition: A point on the graph of a function where the curvature changes sign, meaning the function changes from being concave up to concave down, or vice versa. At an inflection point, the second derivative is typically zero or undefined.

metadata.title: Definite Integral
metadata.definition: Represents the signed area between the graph of a function and the x-axis over a specified interval [a, b]. It is formally defined as the limit of Riemann sums and can be calculated using the antiderivative of the function at the upper and lower limits.

metadata.title: Indefinite Integral (Antiderivative)
metadata.definition: The indefinite integral, or antiderivative, of a function f(x) is a function F(x) whose derivative is f(x). It represents a family of functions, F(x) + C, where C is an arbitrary constant of integration.

metadata.title: Riemann Sum
metadata.definition: A Riemann sum is a method for approximating the definite integral of a function by dividing the area under its curve into a finite number of rectangles and summing their areas. This approximation approaches the exact definite integral as the number of rectangles approaches infinity.

metadata.title: Multivariable Integral (Double, Triple)
metadata.definition: A multivariable integral extends the concept of a definite integral to functions of multiple variables, typically used to compute volumes, masses, or other quantities over multi-dimensional regions. A double integral calculates volume under a surface over a 2D region, while a triple integral calculates hypervolume or mass over a 3D region.

metadata.title: Line Integral
metadata.definition: A line integral is an integral where the function to be integrated is evaluated along a curve or path in space, rather than over a region. It is commonly used to calculate work done by a force field, fluid flow circulation, or the mass of a wire with varying density.

metadata.title: Surface Integral
metadata.definition: A surface integral is an integral of a function over a surface in three-dimensional space, generalizing double integrals to curved surfaces. It is used to compute flux through a surface, total mass/charge distributed over a surface, or the total area of a parameterized surface.

metadata.title: Maclaurin Series
metadata.definition: A Maclaurin series is a special case of a Taylor series expansion of a function f(x) about x=0, representing the function as an infinite sum of terms calculated from the function's derivatives evaluated at zero. It provides a polynomial approximation of a function near the origin.

metadata.title: Lagrange Multiplier
metadata.definition: The method of Lagrange multipliers is a strategy for finding the local maxima and minima of a function subject to equality constraints. It introduces a new scalar variable (the Lagrange multiplier) for each constraint, transforming the constrained optimization problem into an unconstrained one solvable by finding critical points of an auxiliary Lagrangian function.

metadata.title: Convex Function
metadata.definition: A function `f` is convex if, for any two points `x₁` and `x₂` in its domain, the line segment connecting `(x₁, f(x₁))` and `(x₂, f(x₂))` lies entirely above or on the graph of `f`. Mathematically, `f(tx₁ + (1-t)x₂) ≤ tf(x₁) + (1-t)f(x₂)` for all `t ∈ [0, 1]`.

metadata.title: Concave Function
metadata.definition: A function `f` is concave if, for any two points `x₁` and `x₂` in its domain, the line segment connecting `(x₁, f(x₁))` and `(x₂, f(x₂))` lies entirely below or on the graph of `f`. Equivalently, `f` is concave if `-f` is convex, meaning `f(tx₁ + (1-t)x₂) ≥ tf(x₁) + (1-t)f(x₂)` for all `t ∈ [0, 1]`.

metadata.title: Strictly Convex Function
metadata.definition: A function `f` is strictly convex if it is convex and the line segment connecting any two distinct points `(x₁, f(x₁))` and `(x₂, f(x₂))` lies strictly above the graph of `f` for all interior points of the segment. Mathematically, `f(tx₁ + (1-t)x₂) < tf(x₁) + (1-t)f(x₂)` for all `t ∈ (0, 1)` and `x₁ ≠ x₂`.

metadata.title: Convex Set
metadata.definition: A set of points is convex if, for any two points within the set, the entire line segment connecting those two points also lies entirely within the set. Geometrically, a convex set has no 'indentations' or 'holes'.

metadata.title: Convex Hull
metadata.definition: The convex hull of a given set of points or objects is the smallest convex set that contains all those points or objects. Geometrically, it can be visualized as the shape formed by a rubber band stretched tightly around all the given points.

metadata.title: Jensen's Inequality
metadata.definition: Jensen's inequality is a fundamental result in convex analysis stating that for a convex function `f`, the value of the function at the average (or expected value) of a variable is less than or equal to the average of the function's values. For a concave function, the inequality is reversed: `f(E[X]) ≥ E[f(X)]`.

metadata.title: Mean Value Theorem
metadata.definition: The Mean Value Theorem states that for a function `f(x)` that is continuous on a closed interval `[a, b]` and differentiable on the open interval `(a, b)`, there exists at least one point `c` in `(a, b)` such that the instantaneous rate of change at `c` (`f'(c)`) is equal to the average rate of change over the entire interval (`(f(b) - f(a)) / (b - a)`).

metadata.title: Rolle's Theorem
metadata.definition: Rolle's Theorem is a special case of the Mean Value Theorem, stating that if a function `f(x)` is continuous on a closed interval `[a, b]`, differentiable on the open interval `(a, b)`, and `f(a) = f(b)`, then there must exist at least one point `c` in `(a, b)` where the derivative `f'(c)` is zero.

metadata.title: L'Hôpital's Rule
metadata.definition: L'Hôpital's Rule is a powerful method used to evaluate limits of indeterminate forms, specifically `0/0` or `∞/∞`. It states that if `lim (x→c) f(x) = 0` and `lim (x→c) g(x) = 0` (or both are `±∞`), then `lim (x→c) f(x)/g(x) = lim (x→c) f'(x)/g'(x)`, provided the latter limit exists.

metadata.title: Event (Probability)
metadata.definition: In probability theory, an event is a specific set of one or more outcomes from a random experiment's sample space. It is a subset of the sample space, representing a particular result or collection of results of interest.

metadata.title: Probability Measure
metadata.definition: A probability measure is a function that assigns a probability (a real number between 0 and 1, inclusive) to each event in a sample space, satisfying three axioms: non-negativity (P(A) ≥ 0), normalization (P(S) = 1 for the sample space S), and countable additivity for disjoint events.

metadata.title: Union of Events
metadata.definition: The union of two or more events is an event that occurs if at least one of the specified events occurs. It is denoted by `A ∪ B` and represents the set of all outcomes that are in event A, or in event B, or in both.

metadata.title: Intersection of Events
metadata.definition: The intersection of two or more events is an event that occurs if all of the specified events occur simultaneously. It is denoted by `A ∩ B` and represents the set of all outcomes that are common to both event A and event B.

metadata.title: Complement of an Event
metadata.definition: The complement of an event E, denoted Eᶜ or E', is the set of all outcomes in the sample space S that are not in E. The probability of the complement of an event is 1 minus the probability of the event itself (P(Eᶜ) = 1 - P(E)).

metadata.title: Random Variable
metadata.definition: A random variable is a variable whose value is a numerical outcome of a random phenomenon or experiment. It is a function that maps outcomes from a sample space to real numbers.

metadata.title: Probability Mass Function (PMF)
metadata.definition: The Probability Mass Function (PMF) is a function that gives the probability that a discrete random variable is exactly equal to some value. It defines the probability distribution of a discrete random variable.

metadata.title: Probability Density Function (PDF)
metadata.definition: The Probability Density Function (PDF) is a function whose value at any given sample (or point) in the sample space can be interpreted as providing a relative likelihood that the value of the continuous random variable would be equal to that sample. The probability of the variable falling within a range is found by integrating the PDF over that range.

metadata.title: Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF)
metadata.definition: The Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) for a real-valued random variable X is the function F(x) = P(X ≤ x), which gives the probability that X will take a value less than or equal to x. It is defined for both discrete and continuous random variables.

metadata.title: Expected Value (Expectation)
metadata.definition: The Expected Value (or Expectation) of a random variable is the weighted average of all possible values that the variable can take. It represents the long-run average value of the variable over many repetitions of the experiment.

metadata.title: Variance (Probability)
metadata.definition: Variance measures the spread or dispersion of a random variable's values around its expected value. It is the expected value of the squared difference between the random variable and its mean (E[(X - E[X])²]).

metadata.title: Standard Deviation (Probability)
metadata.definition: The Standard Deviation is the square root of the variance, providing a measure of the typical deviation or spread of a random variable's values around its expected value. It is expressed in the same units as the random variable itself.

metadata.title: Covariance
