metadata.definition: Covariance measures the extent to which two random variables change together. A positive covariance indicates that the variables tend to move in the same direction, while a negative covariance indicates they tend to move in opposite directions.

metadata.title: Correlation Coefficient
metadata.definition: The Correlation Coefficient is a standardized measure of the linear relationship between two random variables, ranging from -1 to 1. A value of +1 indicates a perfect positive linear relationship, -1 a perfect negative linear relationship, and 0 indicates no linear relationship.

metadata.title: Poisson Distribution
metadata.definition: The Poisson Distribution is a discrete probability distribution that expresses the probability of a given number of events occurring in a fixed interval of time or space if these events occur with a known constant mean rate and independently of the time since the last event.

metadata.title: Uniform Distribution (Discrete)
metadata.definition: A Discrete Uniform Distribution is a probability distribution where a finite number of values are equally likely to be observed. Each outcome has the same probability, 1/n, where n is the total number of possible outcomes.

metadata.title: Uniform Distribution (Continuous)
metadata.definition: A Continuous Uniform Distribution describes a probability distribution where all values within a given interval [a, b] have an equal probability density. Outside this interval, the probability density is zero.

metadata.title: Normal Distribution (Gaussian)
metadata.definition: The Normal Distribution, also known as the Gaussian distribution, is a symmetric, bell-shaped continuous probability distribution characterized by its mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ). It is fundamental in statistics and naturally arises in many natural and social phenomena.

metadata.title: Standard Normal Distribution
metadata.definition: The Standard Normal Distribution is a special case of the normal distribution with a mean (μ) of 0 and a standard deviation (σ) of 1. Any normally distributed random variable can be transformed into a standard normal variable (a z-score) by subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation.

metadata.title: Gamma Distribution
metadata.definition: The Gamma Distribution is a versatile continuous probability distribution that models the waiting time until a specified number of events occur in a Poisson process. It is characterized by a shape parameter (k) and a scale parameter (θ), or an inverse scale (rate) parameter.

metadata.title: Beta Distribution
metadata.definition: The Beta Distribution is a continuous probability distribution defined on the interval [0, 1], making it ideal for modeling probabilities or proportions. It is parameterized by two positive shape parameters, α and β, which control the shape of the distribution.

metadata.title: Chi-squared Distribution
metadata.definition: The Chi-squared Distribution is a continuous probability distribution that arises in hypothesis testing, particularly when summing the squares of independent standard normal random variables. Its shape is determined by a single parameter, the degrees of freedom (df).

metadata.title: Student's t-Distribution
metadata.definition: Student's t-Distribution is a continuous probability distribution that arises when estimating the mean of a normally distributed population when the sample size is small and the population standard deviation is unknown. It has fatter tails than the normal distribution, accounting for greater uncertainty with small samples, and converges to the normal distribution as the degrees of freedom (based on sample size) increase.

metadata.title: F-Distribution
metadata.definition: The F-Distribution is a continuous probability distribution that arises as the ratio of two independent chi-squared distributions, each divided by its degrees of freedom. It is primarily used in hypothesis testing, particularly for comparing variances or comparing multiple means in Analysis of Variance (ANOVA).

metadata.title: Multinomial Distribution
metadata.definition: A generalization of the binomial distribution for multiple outcomes, describing the probabilities of counts for each of several categories in a fixed number of independent trials. Each trial results in one of `k` possible outcomes, each with a given probability.

metadata.title: Dirichlet Distribution
metadata.definition: A family of continuous multivariate probability distributions that is the conjugate prior to the multinomial distribution. It describes the probability distribution over a simplex, specifically the probabilities for `k` different outcomes that sum to one.

metadata.title: Law of Large Numbers (Weak)
metadata.definition: States that as the number of independent and identically distributed random variables increases, the sample average converges in probability to the expected value (mean) of the random variables. It guarantees that the sample mean is a reliable estimator for the true population mean over many trials.

metadata.title: Law of Large Numbers (Strong)
metadata.definition: A more robust form stating that the sample average of a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables converges almost surely to the expected value. This implies that the probability of the sample mean deviating from the true mean goes to zero as the number of samples approaches infinity.

metadata.title: Joint Probability Distribution
metadata.definition: A probability distribution that gives the probability of two or more random variables taking on specific values simultaneously. For discrete variables, it's a joint probability mass function; for continuous variables, it's a joint probability density function.

metadata.title: Marginal Probability Distribution
metadata.definition: The probability distribution of a single random variable, derived from a joint probability distribution of multiple variables by summing (discrete) or integrating (continuous) over the possible values of the other variables. It represents the probability of that single variable regardless of the values of the others.

metadata.title: Conditional Probability Distribution
metadata.definition: The probability distribution of a random variable given that another random variable has taken on a specific value. It describes how the probability of one event changes when information about another related event becomes known.

metadata.title: Independence of Random Variables
metadata.definition: Two random variables X and Y are independent if the occurrence of an event for X does not affect the probability of an event for Y, and vice-versa. Mathematically, their joint probability distribution is equal to the product of their marginal probability distributions.

metadata.title: Moment Generating Function
metadata.definition: A function that uniquely determines a probability distribution and can be used to derive all moments (like mean, variance) of a random variable. It is defined as the expected value of `e^(tX)` for a random variable X, where `t` is a real variable.

metadata.title: Characteristic Function (Probability)
metadata.definition: A complex-valued function that uniquely determines a probability distribution, similar to the Moment Generating Function but always exists. It is defined as the expected value of `e^(itX)` for a random variable X, where `i` is the imaginary unit and `t` is a real variable.

metadata.title: Chebyshev's Inequality
metadata.definition: A fundamental inequality that provides an upper bound on the probability that a random variable deviates from its mean by more than a certain amount, regardless of the distribution's shape. It requires only the mean and variance to be finite.

metadata.title: Markov Chain (Discrete-Time)
metadata.definition: A stochastic process that describes a sequence of possible events where the probability of each event depends only on the state attained in the previous event. This 'memoryless' property is known as the Markov property, meaning the future is conditionally independent of the past given the present.

metadata.title: State Space (Markov Chain)
metadata.definition: The set of all possible outcomes or configurations that a Markov chain can be in at any given time. Each element in the state space represents a distinct state of the system being modeled.

metadata.title: Transition Matrix (Markov Chain)
metadata.definition: A square matrix where each element `P_ij` represents the probability of moving from state `i` to state `j` in one time step. The rows of the transition matrix must sum to 1, as they represent the probabilities of transitioning from a given state to all other possible states.

metadata.title: Stationary Distribution (Markov Chain)
metadata.definition: A probability distribution over the states of a Markov chain that remains unchanged after one or more transitions. If the chain is in a stationary distribution, then the probability of being in any state `j` after a transition is the same as the probability of being in state `j` before the transition.

metadata.title: Ergodicity (Markov Chain)
metadata.definition: A property of a Markov chain where it is both irreducible (all states are reachable from each other) and aperiodic (no cyclic behavior). An ergodic Markov chain guarantees that it has a unique stationary distribution, and the long-run proportion of time spent in each state converges to this stationary distribution, regardless of the initial state.

metadata.title: Martingale
metadata.definition: A sequence of random variables (a stochastic process) where the conditional expected value of the next observation, given all prior observations, is equal to the current observation. In simpler terms, it's a 'fair game' where, given the current state, the expected value of the future state is the present state.

metadata.title: Descriptive Statistics
metadata.definition: The branch of statistics concerned with summarizing and organizing data in a meaningful way, often through numerical calculations and graphical representations. It aims to describe the main features of a collection of data without drawing conclusions beyond the data itself.

metadata.title: Inferential Statistics
metadata.definition: The branch of statistics that uses a sample of data to make predictions, inferences, or generalizations about a larger population from which the sample was drawn. It involves hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, and various modeling techniques to draw conclusions beyond the observed data.

metadata.title: Parameter (Statistics)
metadata.definition: A characteristic or measure that describes an entire population, such as the population mean (μ), population standard deviation (σ), or population proportion (p). Parameters are typically unknown and are estimated using sample statistics.

metadata.title: Statistic (Estimator)
metadata.definition: A statistic is a numerical summary of a sample, typically calculated from observed data. It is often used as an estimator to approximate an unknown population parameter.

metadata.title: Mean (Sample)
metadata.definition: The sample mean, also known as the arithmetic average, is a measure of central tendency calculated by summing all values in a dataset and dividing by the count of values. It is sensitive to outliers.

metadata.title: Median (Sample)
metadata.definition: The sample median is the middle value in a dataset when all values are arranged in order. If there is an even number of data points, the median is the average of the two middle values. It is robust to extreme outliers.

metadata.title: Mode (Sample)
metadata.definition: The sample mode is the value that appears most frequently in a dataset. A dataset can have one mode (unimodal), multiple modes (multimodal), or no mode if all values appear with the same frequency.

metadata.title: Range (Statistics)
metadata.definition: The range is the simplest measure of statistical dispersion, calculated as the difference between the highest and lowest values in a dataset. It indicates the total spread of the data but is highly sensitive to outliers.

metadata.title: Quartile
metadata.definition: Quartiles are values that divide a sorted dataset into four equal parts, each containing 25% of the data. Q1 is the 25th percentile, Q2 is the median (50th percentile), and Q3 is the 75th percentile.

metadata.title: Interquartile Range (IQR)
metadata.definition: The Interquartile Range (IQR) is a measure of statistical dispersion, calculated as the difference between the third quartile (Q3) and the first quartile (Q1). It represents the spread of the middle 50% of the data and is robust to outliers.

metadata.title: Variance (Sample)
metadata.definition: The sample variance measures the average of the squared differences from the mean, indicating how far each number in the set is from the average. It quantifies the spread or dispersion of data points around the mean.

metadata.title: Standard Deviation (Sample)
metadata.definition: The sample standard deviation is the square root of the sample variance. It measures the average amount of variability or dispersion around the mean, expressed in the same units as the original data, making it more interpretable than variance.

metadata.title: Coefficient of Variation
metadata.definition: The Coefficient of Variation (CV) is a standardized measure of dispersion, expressed as the ratio of the standard deviation to the mean. It is useful for comparing the relative variability between datasets with different units or vastly different means.

metadata.title: Skewness (Statistics)
metadata.definition: Skewness is a measure of the asymmetry of the probability distribution of a real-valued random variable about its mean. A distribution is positively (right) skewed if its tail is longer on the right side, and negatively (left) skewed if its tail is longer on the left side.

metadata.title: Kurtosis (Statistics)
metadata.definition: Kurtosis is a measure of the 'tailedness' of the probability distribution of a real-valued random variable, indicating the presence of outliers. High kurtosis (leptokurtic) implies more frequent extreme outliers and a sharper peak than a normal distribution, while low kurtosis (platykurtic) implies fewer extreme outliers.

metadata.title: Histogram
metadata.definition: A histogram is a graphical representation of the distribution of numerical data. It partitions the data into 'bins' (intervals) and displays the frequency or count of data points falling into each bin as adjacent bars.

metadata.title: Box Plot
metadata.definition: A box plot (or box-and-whisker plot) is a standardized way of displaying the distribution of data based on a five-number summary: minimum, first quartile (Q1), median, third quartile (Q3), and maximum. It effectively highlights central tendency, spread, and potential outliers.

metadata.title: Scatter Plot
metadata.definition: A scatter plot is a type of data visualization that displays values for typically two numerical variables for a set of data points as coordinates on a Cartesian plane. It is used to observe the relationship or correlation between the two variables.

metadata.title: Null Hypothesis
metadata.definition: The null hypothesis (H₀) is a statement of no effect, no difference, or no relationship between variables in a population. It is the default assumption in hypothesis testing that researchers attempt to disprove or find evidence against.

metadata.title: Alternative Hypothesis
metadata.definition: The alternative hypothesis (H₁) is a statement that contradicts the null hypothesis, proposing that there is a significant effect, difference, or relationship between variables. It represents what the researcher is trying to prove or find evidence in favor of.

metadata.title: Significance Level (Alpha)
metadata.definition: The significance level (α) is the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true, representing the maximum acceptable risk of making a Type I error. Commonly set at 0.05 (5%) or 0.01 (1%), it is a threshold against which the p-value is compared.

metadata.title: P-value
metadata.definition: The p-value is the probability of obtaining test results at least as extreme as the observed results, assuming that the null hypothesis is true. A small p-value (typically less than the significance level α) indicates strong evidence against the null hypothesis, leading to its rejection.

metadata.title: Type I Error
metadata.definition: A Type I error occurs when the null hypothesis is incorrectly rejected, meaning we conclude there is a significant effect or relationship when none actually exists in the population. It is also known as a 'false positive' and its probability is denoted by the significance level α.

metadata.title: Type II Error
metadata.definition: A Type II error occurs when a statistical hypothesis test fails to reject a false null hypothesis. It means concluding there is no effect or difference when one actually exists, also known as a 'false negative'.

metadata.title: Power of a Test
metadata.definition: The power of a statistical hypothesis test is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis. It represents the probability of detecting an effect or difference when one truly exists, calculated as 1 minus the Type II error rate (1 - β).

metadata.title: Z-test
metadata.definition: A Z-test is a statistical hypothesis test used to determine if there is a significant difference between a sample mean and a population mean, or between two population means, when the population standard deviation is known. It assumes the test statistic follows a standard normal (Z) distribution, typically for large sample sizes.

metadata.title: T-test (Student's t-test)
metadata.definition: A T-test is a statistical hypothesis test used to determine if there is a significant difference between the means of two groups when the population standard deviation is unknown, or for small sample sizes. It assumes the test statistic follows a Student's t-distribution.

metadata.title: Chi-squared Test (Goodness of Fit)
metadata.definition: The Chi-squared Goodness of Fit test is a non-parametric hypothesis test used to determine if an observed frequency distribution of a single categorical variable differs significantly from an expected theoretical distribution. It assesses how well a theoretical model fits the observed data.

metadata.title: Chi-squared Test (Independence)
metadata.definition: The Chi-squared Test for Independence is a non-parametric hypothesis test used to determine if there is a statistically significant association between two categorical variables in a contingency table. It assesses whether the occurrence of one variable is independent of the occurrence of the other.

metadata.title: ANOVA (Analysis of Variance)
metadata.definition: ANOVA (Analysis of Variance) is a statistical technique used to test for differences between the means of three or more independent groups. It does this by partitioning the total variability in a dataset into variance components attributable to different sources, typically comparing variance between groups to variance within groups.

metadata.title: Covariance Matrix
metadata.definition: A covariance matrix is a square matrix that describes the covariance between each pair of elements in a random vector (i.e., multiple random variables). The diagonal elements contain the variances of each variable, while the off-diagonal elements contain the covariances between pairs of variables, showing their linear relationship.

metadata.title: Correlation (Pearson)
metadata.definition: Pearson's correlation coefficient (r) is a measure of the linear relationship between two continuous variables, ranging from -1 to +1. A value of +1 indicates a perfect positive linear correlation, -1 indicates a perfect negative linear correlation, and 0 indicates no linear correlation.

metadata.title: Correlation (Spearman)
metadata.definition: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (ρ or r_s) is a non-parametric measure of the strength and direction of a monotonic relationship between two variables, based on the ranked values of the data rather than their raw values. It is useful when the relationship is not strictly linear or when data is ordinal.

metadata.title: Simple Linear Regression
metadata.definition: Simple Linear Regression is a statistical method used to model the linear relationship between a single dependent variable (response) and a single independent variable (predictor) by fitting a straight line to the observed data. The goal is to predict the value of the dependent variable based on the independent variable.

metadata.title: Multiple Linear Regression
metadata.definition: Multiple Linear Regression is a statistical method used to model the linear relationship between a single dependent variable and two or more independent variables. It extends simple linear regression by considering multiple predictors simultaneously to explain and predict the variation in the dependent variable.

metadata.title: Least Squares Regression
metadata.definition: Least Squares Regression is a method used to estimate the unknown parameters in a linear regression model by minimizing the sum of the squared differences (residuals) between the observed values and the values predicted by the model. This minimization process produces the 'best-fit' line or hyperplane that minimizes prediction error.

metadata.title: Coefficient of Determination (R-squared)
metadata.definition: The Coefficient of Determination (R-squared, R²) is a statistical measure that represents the proportion of the variance in the dependent variable that can be explained by the independent variable(s) in a regression model. It ranges from 0 to 1, where higher values indicate a better fit of the model to the data.

metadata.title: Prior Distribution
metadata.definition: In Bayesian statistics, a prior distribution is a probability distribution that represents the initial beliefs, knowledge, or uncertainty about a parameter before any new data has been observed. It quantifies the plausible values of a parameter based on previous information or subjective judgment.

metadata.title: Posterior Distribution
metadata.definition: In Bayesian statistics, the posterior distribution is the updated probability distribution of a parameter after observing new data. It is calculated by combining the prior distribution with the likelihood function (representing the evidence from the data) using Bayes' Theorem, reflecting revised beliefs about the parameter given the evidence.

metadata.title: Likelihood Function
metadata.definition: In statistics, the likelihood function is a function of the parameters of a statistical model that quantifies the probability of observing a given set of data, assuming those parameters are true. It indicates how 'likely' specific parameter values are given the observed data, often used for parameter estimation and model selection.

metadata.title: Frequentist Statistics
metadata.definition: Frequentist statistics is a branch of statistics that interprets probability as the long-run frequency of events, focusing on objective properties of statistical procedures like confidence intervals and p-values, assuming hypothetical infinite repetitions of an experiment. It draws conclusions about populations based on sample data without incorporating prior beliefs.

metadata.title: Parametric Statistics
metadata.definition: Parametric statistics is a branch of statistics that assumes data comes from a population that follows a specific probability distribution (e.g., normal distribution) and makes inferences about the parameters of that distribution. These methods typically require stronger assumptions about the data's underlying distribution.

metadata.title: Non-parametric Statistics
metadata.definition: Non-parametric statistics is a branch of statistics that does not make strong assumptions about the underlying probability distribution of the data (i.e., it is 'distribution-free'). These methods are often used when data does not meet the assumptions of parametric tests, when sample sizes are small, or when dealing with ordinal or ranked data.

metadata.title: Bootstrapping (Statistics)
metadata.definition: Bootstrapping is a resampling technique used to estimate the sampling distribution of a statistic by repeatedly drawing samples with replacement from the original observed data. It is often employed to construct confidence intervals or estimate standard errors without assuming a specific theoretical distribution for the population.

metadata.title: Permutation Test
metadata.definition: A permutation test is a non-parametric statistical hypothesis test that shuffles the labels (e.g., group assignments) of observed data points to create a null distribution for a test statistic. This null distribution is then used to calculate a p-value, determining the likelihood of observing the actual data under the null hypothesis of no effect.

metadata.title: Sampling Distribution
metadata.definition: The sampling distribution is the probability distribution of a statistic (e.g., mean, median, standard deviation) obtained from a large number of samples drawn from a specific population. It describes the range of values a statistic can take and how frequently each value occurs across different samples.

metadata.title: Standard Error
metadata.definition: The standard error is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic, typically an estimator like the sample mean. It quantifies the typical amount of variation or error expected when using a sample statistic to estimate a population parameter.

metadata.title: Bias (Estimator)
metadata.definition: Bias of an estimator is the difference between the estimator's expected value and the true value of the population parameter it's estimating. An estimator is considered unbiased if its expected value is equal to the true parameter value, meaning it does not consistently over- or under-estimate the parameter.

metadata.title: Consistency (Estimator)
metadata.definition: Consistency is a desirable property of an estimator stating that as the sample size approaches infinity, the estimator converges in probability to the true value of the parameter. In essence, a consistent estimator becomes increasingly accurate as more data is collected.

metadata.title: Efficiency (Estimator)
metadata.definition: Efficiency of an estimator refers to how 'good' it is relative to other estimators in terms of its variance; an efficient estimator achieves the lowest possible variance among a class of unbiased estimators. It quantifies the precision of an estimator.

metadata.title: Sufficiency (Statistics)
metadata.definition: Sufficiency is a property of a statistic that indicates it captures all the relevant information about the population parameter contained in the sample data. Once a sufficient statistic is known, no additional information about the parameter can be extracted from the original data.

metadata.title: Factor Analysis
metadata.definition: Factor analysis is a statistical method used to describe variability among observed, correlated variables in terms of a potentially lower number of unobserved variables called factors or latent variables. It aims to identify underlying constructs that explain the common variance in a set of measured variables.

metadata.title: Discriminant Analysis
metadata.definition: Discriminant analysis is a statistical technique used to find a linear combination of features that best separates two or more classes of objects or events. It aims to build a predictive model for classifying new observations into predefined categories based on their characteristics.

metadata.title: Odds Ratio
metadata.definition: The odds ratio is a measure of association between an exposure and an outcome, representing the ratio of the odds of the outcome occurring in the exposed group versus the odds of the outcome occurring in the unexposed group. An odds ratio of 1 suggests no association between the exposure and the outcome.

metadata.title: Generalized Linear Model (GLM)
metadata.definition: A Generalized Linear Model (GLM) is a flexible statistical framework that extends ordinary least squares regression by allowing the response variable's error distribution to be non-normal (e.g., Poisson, binomial) and by using a link function to relate the expected value of the response to a linear predictor (a linear combination of covariates).

metadata.title: Robust Statistics
metadata.definition: Robust statistics refers to a set of statistical methods designed to be less sensitive to small departures from model assumptions (e.g., normality, constant variance) or to the presence of outliers in the data. These methods provide more reliable results when data do not perfectly fit conventional parametric models.

metadata.title: Imputation (Statistics)
metadata.definition: Imputation is the process of replacing missing data with substituted values to allow for complete data analysis. Its goal is to mitigate bias and maintain statistical power that would be lost if incomplete cases were simply discarded.

metadata.title: Constraint (Optimization)
metadata.definition: In an optimization problem, a constraint is a condition that limits the possible values of decision variables. Constraints define the boundaries within which the optimal solution must lie, typically expressed as equalities or inequalities.

metadata.title: Feasible Region
metadata.definition: The feasible region is the set of all possible points (or solutions) in an optimization problem that satisfy all given constraints. Any point within this region is a valid solution, although not necessarily the optimal one.

metadata.title: Convex Optimization
metadata.definition: Convex optimization is a subfield of mathematical optimization where the objective function to be minimized is convex, and the feasible region (the set of all allowable solutions) is a convex set. A key property is that any local minimum found is also guaranteed to be a global minimum, making these problems generally easier to solve efficiently and reliably.

metadata.title: Integer Programming
metadata.definition: Integer programming is a type of mathematical optimization problem where some or all of the decision variables are restricted to be integers. This restriction arises naturally when representing discrete choices, such as whether to build a facility or select a specific number of items, and often makes the problem much harder to solve than continuous optimization.

metadata.title: Quadratic Programming
metadata.definition: Quadratic Programming (QP) refers to a type of optimization problem where the objective function is quadratic and all constraints are linear. It is a specific form of nonlinear programming that is widely applicable in various fields.

metadata.title: Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) Conditions
metadata.definition: The Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions are a set of necessary conditions for a solution in nonlinear programming to be optimal, provided certain regularity (constraint qualification) conditions are met. For convex optimization problems, these conditions are also sufficient for global optimality.

metadata.title: Gradient Descent (Batch)
metadata.definition: Batch Gradient Descent is an iterative optimization algorithm that updates parameters by moving in the direction opposite to the gradient of the objective function. Crucially, it calculates the gradient using the entire training dataset for each single parameter update.

metadata.title: Learning Rate (Optimization)
metadata.definition: The learning rate is a hyperparameter in optimization algorithms, such as Gradient Descent, that determines the step size at each iteration while moving towards a minimum of the objective function. A properly chosen learning rate is critical for efficient and effective convergence.

metadata.title: Momentum (Optimization)
metadata.definition: Momentum is an optimization technique that accelerates convergence by adding a fraction of the previous update vector to the current update vector in iterative algorithms like Gradient Descent. This helps to smooth out oscillations, speed up learning in relevant directions, and escape shallow local minima.

metadata.title: Nesterov Accelerated Gradient (NAG)
metadata.definition: Nesterov Accelerated Gradient (NAG) is an optimization algorithm that refines the concept of momentum by calculating the gradient not at the current parameter position, but at a 'look-ahead' position influenced by the current momentum. This 'look-ahead' step allows for more accurate and often faster convergence, especially in convex problems.

metadata.title: Newton's Method (Optimization)
metadata.definition: Newton's Method is a second-order optimization algorithm that uses both the first derivative (gradient) and the second derivative (Hessian matrix) of the objective function to find a minimum. It converges quadratically near the optimum but requires calculating and inverting the Hessian, which can be computationally expensive for high-dimensional problems.

metadata.title: Quasi-Newton Method
metadata.definition: Quasi-Newton methods are a class of second-order optimization algorithms that approximate the Hessian matrix (or its inverse) using only first-order gradient information. They circumvent the computational burden of explicitly computing and inverting the exact Hessian required by Newton's Method, while still achieving superlinear convergence rates.

metadata.title: BFGS Algorithm
metadata.definition: The BFGS (Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno) algorithm is a popular quasi-Newton method for unconstrained nonlinear optimization problems. It iteratively builds up an approximation of the inverse Hessian matrix using information from successive gradient evaluations, ensuring positive definiteness and often achieving superlinear convergence.

metadata.title: L-BFGS Algorithm
metadata.definition: The L-BFGS (Limited-memory BFGS) algorithm is a memory-efficient version of the BFGS algorithm designed for large-scale optimization problems. Instead of storing the full dense approximation of the inverse Hessian matrix, L-BFGS stores only a few vectors from recent iterations to implicitly represent the approximation, making it highly suitable for high-dimensional parameter spaces.

metadata.title: Lagrangian Function
metadata.definition: The Lagrangian function is a mathematical construct used in constrained optimization problems, formed by adding the objective function to a weighted sum of the constraint functions. The weights, known as Lagrange multipliers, quantify how much the optimal value changes if the constraint is relaxed.

metadata.title: Lagrangian Duality
metadata.definition: Lagrangian Duality is a powerful concept in optimization that associates a dual optimization problem with every primal constrained optimization problem, formulated using the Lagrangian function. Solving the dual problem can often be computationally easier and always provides a lower bound on the optimal value of the primal problem, with equality (strong duality) holding under certain convexity and constraint qualification conditions.

metadata.title: Dual Problem (Optimization)
metadata.definition: In optimization, the dual problem is an alternative optimization problem derived from a primal constrained optimization problem using Lagrangian duality. Its optimal value provides a lower bound for the optimal value of the primal problem, and under conditions like convexity and constraint qualifications (strong duality), their optimal values are equal.

metadata.title: Interior-Point Method
metadata.definition: Interior-Point Methods (IPMs) are a class of algorithms used to solve linear and nonlinear convex optimization problems, particularly those with inequality constraints. Unlike the Simplex method which moves along the boundary, IPMs approach the optimal solution by traversing the interior of the feasible region, often converging in a polynomial number of iterations.

metadata.title: Simplex Method (Linear Programming)
metadata.definition: The Simplex Method is a widely used algorithm for solving linear programming problems, where the objective function and all constraints are linear. It systematically searches for an optimal solution by moving from one vertex (basic feasible solution) of the feasible region polyhedron to an adjacent one, always improving or maintaining the objective function value until an optimum is found.

metadata.title: Conjugate Gradient Method
metadata.definition: The Conjugate Gradient Method is an iterative algorithm primarily used for solving systems of linear equations with a symmetric, positive-definite matrix, and for unconstrained optimization of quadratic functions. It constructs a sequence of search directions that are 'conjugate' with respect to the Hessian matrix, ensuring convergence in at most `n` steps for `n`-dimensional quadratic problems.

metadata.title: Subgradient
metadata.definition: A subgradient is a generalization of the gradient for non-differentiable convex functions. For a convex function, a subgradient at a point is any vector that defines a supporting hyperplane to the function at that point, providing a local linear underestimator.

metadata.title: Proximal Operator
metadata.definition: The proximal operator is a generalization of orthogonal projection that arises in convex optimization, particularly for non-differentiable or constrained problems. It acts as a regularized inversion, effectively smoothing out functions or enforcing constraints in an iterative optimization setting by balancing minimizing the function with staying close to a given point.

metadata.title: Regularization (L1, Lasso)
metadata.definition: L1 regularization, also known as Lasso (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator), adds a penalty equal to the absolute value of the magnitude of the coefficients to the loss function. This encourages sparsity in the model by driving some coefficients exactly to zero, effectively performing automatic feature selection and preventing overfitting.

metadata.title: Regularization (L2, Ridge)
metadata.definition: L2 regularization, also known as Ridge regularization, adds a penalty equal to the squared magnitude of the coefficients to the loss function. This technique helps prevent overfitting and reduces model complexity by shrinking coefficients towards zero, though it rarely makes them exactly zero.

metadata.title: Entropy (Information Theory)
metadata.definition: Entropy quantifies the average amount of information or uncertainty in a random variable. It measures the unpredictability of the outcome of an experiment or the information content of a message.

metadata.title: Joint Entropy
metadata.definition: Joint Entropy measures the total uncertainty or information contained in a pair (or set) of random variables. It quantifies the unpredictability of a combined outcome from multiple sources.

metadata.title: Conditional Entropy
metadata.definition: Conditional Entropy quantifies the average uncertainty remaining about one random variable, given that the value of another random variable is known. It measures the 'remaining surprise' after partial information has been revealed.

metadata.title: Cross-Entropy
metadata.definition: Cross-Entropy is a measure of the difference between two probability distributions for a given set of events. It is commonly used as a loss function in machine learning to quantify the difference between predicted probabilities and true labels.

metadata.title: Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence
metadata.definition: Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence is a non-symmetric measure of the difference between two probability distributions. It quantifies how much one probability distribution diverges from a second, reference probability distribution.

metadata.title: Mutual Information
metadata.definition: Mutual Information measures the amount of information obtained about one random variable by observing another random variable. It quantifies the dependence between two variables, indicating how much knowing one tells you about the other.

metadata.title: Self-Information
metadata.definition: Self-Information measures the information content of a single event from a random variable's possible outcomes. Events with lower probability have higher self-information, signifying they are more 'surprising' or informative.

metadata.title: Information Gain
metadata.definition: Information Gain is the reduction in entropy (or uncertainty) about a target variable due to knowing the value of another variable. It is commonly used in decision tree algorithms to select the best splitting attribute.

metadata.title: Channel Capacity
metadata.definition: Channel Capacity is the maximum rate at which information can be transmitted reliably over a communication channel with an arbitrarily small error rate. It represents a theoretical upper bound, as defined by Shannon's Channel Coding Theorem, for a given channel's noise and bandwidth.

metadata.title: Data Compression (Information Theory)
metadata.definition: Data Compression, in the context of information theory, is the process of encoding information using fewer bits than the original representation, typically by removing redundancy or exploiting statistical regularities. Information theory provides the theoretical limits and principles for effective compression.

metadata.title: Source Coding Theorem
metadata.definition: The Source Coding Theorem, also known as Shannon's noiseless coding theorem, states that it is impossible to compress data such that its average codeword length is less than its entropy. It defines the theoretical lower bound on the average number of bits needed to encode symbols from a source without loss of information.

metadata.title: Channel Coding Theorem
metadata.definition: The Channel Coding Theorem, also known as Shannon's noisy coding theorem, states that for any noisy communication channel, data can be transmitted at any rate below the channel capacity with an arbitrarily small error rate, provided sufficient coding complexity. Conversely, it asserts that reliable transmission at rates above channel capacity is impossible.

metadata.title: Floating-Point Number
metadata.definition: A floating-point number is a representation of real numbers that approximates continuous values by maintaining a fixed number of significant digits (mantissa) and scaling them using an exponent. This structure allows for a wide range of values, from very small to very large, with a trade-off in precision.

metadata.title: Floating-Point Precision
metadata.definition: Floating-Point Precision refers to the number of significant digits that a floating-point number can accurately represent. Higher precision allows for a more accurate approximation of real numbers but typically requires more memory and computational resources.

metadata.title: Numerical Error
metadata.definition: Numerical Error is the discrepancy between an exact mathematical value and its approximate value obtained from a numerical method or computation. It arises due to limitations in representing numbers (e.g., finite precision) or performing operations on a computer.

metadata.title: Round-off Error
metadata.definition: Round-off Error is a type of numerical error introduced when a real number with infinite or more digits than a computer can handle is approximated by a finite number of digits. It is an inherent characteristic of floating-point arithmetic.

metadata.title: Truncation Error
metadata.definition: Truncation Error is the error arising from approximating an infinite mathematical process (like an infinite series, integral, or derivative) with a finite one. It is inherent in the design of many numerical algorithms and is distinct from round-off error.

metadata.title: Numerical Stability
metadata.definition: Numerical Stability is a property of numerical algorithms that describes how errors in the input data or intermediate computations propagate through the algorithm. A numerically stable algorithm produces a result that is not excessively sensitive to small perturbations, meaning errors do not grow uncontrollably.

metadata.title: Condition Number (Numerical Analysis)
metadata.definition: The Condition Number in numerical analysis is a measure of how sensitive the solution of a problem is to small changes or errors in the input data. A high condition number indicates that the problem is ill-conditioned, meaning small input errors can lead to disproportionately large output errors.

metadata.title: Root-Finding Algorithm
metadata.definition: A Root-Finding Algorithm is a numerical method used to find the roots (or zeros) of a function, which are the values where the function evaluates to zero. These algorithms are fundamental for solving equations where analytical solutions are not feasible or computationally expensive.

metadata.title: Bisection Method
metadata.definition: A root-finding algorithm that repeatedly bisects an interval and then selects the subinterval in which a root must lie for further processing. It guarantees convergence if a root exists within the initial interval and the function is continuous.

metadata.title: Newton-Raphson Method
metadata.definition: An iterative root-finding algorithm that uses the tangent line to approximate the function at each step. It starts with an initial guess and refines it by moving to the x-intercept of the tangent, requiring the function's derivative.

metadata.title: Secant Method
metadata.definition: An iterative root-finding algorithm that approximates the derivative in the Newton-Raphson method using a secant line through two points instead of a tangent line. It avoids the need to compute the derivative of the function.

metadata.title: Numerical Integration
metadata.definition: The process of approximating the definite integral of a function using numerical techniques. It is employed when an analytical solution for the integral is difficult or impossible to find.

metadata.title: Trapezoidal Rule
metadata.definition: A method of numerical integration that approximates the area under a curve by dividing the integration interval into small trapezoids. It connects consecutive points on the function with straight line segments.

metadata.title: Simpson's Rule
metadata.definition: A numerical integration technique that approximates the definite integral by dividing the area under the curve into segments and approximating each segment with parabolas. It typically provides more accurate results than the Trapezoidal Rule for smooth functions.

metadata.title: Gaussian Quadrature
metadata.definition: A powerful numerical integration technique that selects optimal points (nodes) and weights within an interval to achieve high accuracy for a given number of points. It is exact for polynomials up to a certain degree, significantly outperforming simpler methods.

metadata.title: Numerical Differentiation
metadata.definition: The process of approximating the derivative of a function using numerical techniques. It is typically used when an analytical expression for the derivative is unavailable or too complex to compute, or when the function is known only through discrete data points.

metadata.title: Finite Difference Method
metadata.definition: A numerical technique for approximating derivatives by replacing them with finite differences. It is widely used to solve differential equations by discretizing the domain and approximating the derivatives at specific grid points.

metadata.title: Solving Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs)
metadata.definition: The process of finding a function that satisfies a given ordinary differential equation, which relates a function to its derivatives. Numerical methods are often employed when analytical solutions are not possible or practical.

metadata.title: Euler Method (ODE)
metadata.definition: A first-order numerical procedure for solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with a given initial value. It approximates the solution curve by a sequence of short line segments, using the tangent at the current point to predict the next point.

metadata.title: Runge-Kutta Method
metadata.definition: A family of implicit and explicit iterative methods used for the numerical solution of ordinary differential equations (ODEs). The most common is the fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4), which offers higher accuracy than the Euler method by evaluating the derivative at several points within each step.

metadata.title: Iterative Method (Linear Systems)
metadata.definition: A numerical technique for solving systems of linear equations by starting with an initial guess and generating a sequence of approximate solutions that converge to the true solution. These methods are particularly useful for large, sparse systems.

metadata.title: Jacobi Iteration Method
metadata.definition: An iterative method for solving systems of linear equations by repeatedly updating each variable using the values from the *previous* iteration for all other variables. It is often slower than Gauss-Seidel but can be easily parallelized.

metadata.title: Gauss-Seidel Method
metadata.definition: An iterative method for solving systems of linear equations that improves upon the Jacobi method by using the most recently computed values for variables in the current iteration. This often leads to faster convergence compared to Jacobi.

metadata.title: Monte Carlo Method
metadata.definition: A broad class of computational algorithms that rely on repeated random sampling to obtain numerical results. They are often used to estimate properties of a population or distribution, or to simulate the behavior of complex systems.

metadata.title: Pseudorandom Number Generator
metadata.definition: An algorithm that produces a sequence of numbers whose properties approximate the properties of sequences of random numbers. While not truly random, they are deterministic and reproducible, making them suitable for many computational tasks.

metadata.title: Inverse Transform Sampling
metadata.definition: A method for generating random samples from a given probability distribution by using its inverse cumulative distribution function (CDF). It requires an analytically invertible CDF to transform uniformly distributed random numbers into the desired distribution.

metadata.title: Rejection Sampling
metadata.definition: A technique for generating random samples from a target probability distribution by drawing samples from a simpler proposal distribution and then accepting or rejecting them based on a comparison with the target. It is useful when the inverse CDF of the target distribution is not easily computable.

metadata.title: Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)
metadata.definition: A class of algorithms for sampling from probability distributions by constructing a Markov chain that has the desired distribution as its stationary distribution. Samples are then generated by simulating the chain, often used for high-dimensional or complex distributions.

metadata.title: Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm
metadata.definition: A Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method used for sampling from probability distributions that are difficult to sample from directly, especially in high dimensions. It constructs a reversible Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the target distribution, by iteratively proposing new states and accepting or rejecting them based on a calculated probability. This allows for estimating integrals or expected values related to the target distribution.

metadata.title: Fixed-Point Iteration
metadata.definition: A numerical method for finding a fixed point of a function g, meaning a value x such that g(x) = x. It works by repeatedly applying the function, starting with an initial guess x0, generating a sequence x_{n+1} = g(x_n). This sequence converges to a fixed point if g is a contraction mapping in a neighborhood of the fixed point.

metadata.title: Sparse Matrix
metadata.definition: A matrix in which most of the elements are zero. Due to the high proportion of zero entries, sparse matrices can be stored and manipulated more efficiently by only storing the non-zero elements along with their row and column indices, rather than the entire matrix.

metadata.title: Dense Matrix
metadata.definition: A matrix in which a significant proportion of the elements are non-zero, requiring the storage of all elements explicitly. Standard array-based storage schemes are typically used for dense matrices, as their structure does not offer significant opportunities for compression or specialized storage.

metadata.title: Preconditioner (Numerical Linear Algebra)
metadata.definition: A transformation applied to a linear system Ax = b to improve the convergence rate of iterative solvers by making the system M⁻¹Ax = M⁻¹b (or similar) better conditioned. The preconditioner M is an approximation of A⁻¹ that is easy to compute and apply, such that M⁻¹A has a smaller condition number or more clustered eigenvalues.

metadata.title: Data Structure
metadata.definition: A particular way of organizing and storing data in a computer so that it can be accessed and modified efficiently. It defines the relationships between data elements and the operations that can be performed on them.

metadata.title: Omega Notation
metadata.definition: Denoted as Ω(g(n)), it provides an asymptotic lower bound on the running time of an algorithm, indicating the minimum time an algorithm takes to complete for a sufficiently large input size 'n'. It describes the best-case time complexity or a tight lower bound for all cases.

metadata.title: Theta Notation
metadata.definition: Denoted as Θ(g(n)), it provides an asymptotically tight bound on the running time of an algorithm, meaning the algorithm's performance is bounded both from above and below by g(n) for sufficiently large input size 'n'. It represents the average or exact time complexity when the upper and lower bounds are the same.

metadata.title: Best-Case Analysis
metadata.definition: An analysis of an algorithm's resource consumption (typically time) under the most favorable input conditions, which result in the minimum possible execution time. This often provides a lower bound on the algorithm's performance.

metadata.title: Recursive Step (Recursion)
metadata.definition: The part of a recursive function or algorithm that solves a smaller instance of the same problem by calling itself, progressively moving towards the base case. It defines how a larger problem is broken down into smaller, identical subproblems.

metadata.title: Randomized Algorithm
metadata.definition: An algorithm that makes some choices randomly to achieve good expected performance or to simplify the algorithm, often without sacrificing correctness. Its execution time or output might vary based on the random choices, but typically provides a high probability of correctness or efficiency.

metadata.title: Probabilistic Analysis
metadata.definition: A method of analyzing an algorithm's performance by making assumptions about the probabilistic distribution of the inputs, rather than considering worst-case scenarios. It determines the expected running time or resource usage over all possible inputs.

metadata.title: NP-Hard
metadata.definition: A class of problems that are 'at least as hard as' the hardest problems in NP (Nondeterministic Polynomial time). If a problem P is NP-hard, then any problem in NP can be reduced to P in polynomial time. NP-hard problems do not necessarily have to be in NP themselves.

metadata.title: NP-Complete
metadata.definition: A class of decision problems that are both in NP (solvable in polynomial time by a nondeterministic Turing machine) and NP-hard. These problems are considered the 'hardest' problems in NP, meaning if any NP-complete problem can be solved in polynomial time, then all problems in NP can be solved in polynomial time.

metadata.title: Reductions (Complexity Theory)
metadata.definition: A transformation of one computational problem into another. In complexity theory, a polynomial-time reduction from problem A to problem B means that if we have an efficient algorithm for B, we can use it to construct an efficient algorithm for A. This demonstrates that problem B is 'at least as hard as' problem A.

metadata.title: Approximation Algorithm
metadata.definition: An algorithm used to find an approximate solution to an optimization problem, especially when finding an exact optimal solution is NP-hard or too computationally expensive. These algorithms guarantee a solution within a certain factor of the optimal solution.

metadata.title: Online Algorithm
metadata.definition: An algorithm that processes its input piece by piece without having the entire input available from the start. It must make irrevocable decisions at each step based only on the observed input so far.

metadata.title: Offline Algorithm
metadata.definition: An algorithm that requires the entire input to be available before it can begin processing. It can examine the whole input data at any time and make decisions based on complete information.

metadata.title: Static Array
metadata.definition: A data structure that stores a fixed-size, sequential collection of elements of the same data type in contiguous memory locations. Its size is determined at compile-time and cannot be changed during runtime.

metadata.title: Sentinel Node (Linked List)
metadata.definition: A special dummy node used in a linked list (or other data structures) that does not store actual data but simplifies boundary conditions and algorithm logic. It often acts as a placeholder for the head or tail, eliminating the need to handle null pointers explicitly for empty lists or edge cases.

metadata.title: Dequeue (Double-ended Queue)
metadata.definition: A linear data structure that allows elements to be added or removed from both the front and the rear ends. It can function as both a queue (FIFO) and a stack (LIFO) depending on which ends are used for insertion and deletion.

metadata.title: Hash Table (Hash Map)
metadata.definition: A data structure that implements an associative array abstract data type, mapping keys to values using a hash function to compute an index into an array of buckets or slots. It provides average O(1) time complexity for insertion, deletion, and lookup operations.

metadata.title: Separate Chaining (Hashing)
metadata.definition: A collision resolution technique used in hash tables where each slot (or bucket) in the hash table array points to a linked list (or another data structure) containing all key-value pairs that hash to that same index. When a collision occurs, the new item is simply added to the list at the computed index.

metadata.title: Open Addressing (Hashing)
metadata.definition: A collision resolution technique in hash tables where, if a collision occurs (the hash function maps a key to an already occupied slot), the algorithm systematically probes other slots in the array until an empty slot is found. All elements are stored directly within the hash table array itself, without using external data structures like linked lists.

metadata.title: Linear Probing (Hashing)
metadata.definition: A specific type of open addressing collision resolution technique where, if a hash function produces an index that is already occupied, the algorithm searches for the next available slot by sequentially checking subsequent positions in the array (with wrap-around). It continues probing linearly until an empty slot is found for insertion or the key is found for lookup.

metadata.title: Quadratic Probing (Hashing)
metadata.definition: A collision resolution technique used in hash tables, where subsequent probes for an empty slot are done by adding successive perfect squares (1², 2², 3²...) to the original hash index. This method helps to reduce primary clustering compared to linear probing.

metadata.title: Cuckoo Hashing
metadata.definition: A form of open addressing hashing that uses multiple hash functions (typically two) and ensures constant worst-case lookup time. When a collision occurs, it 'kicks out' the existing item to its alternate location, potentially triggering a chain of displacements.

metadata.title: Robin Hood Hashing
metadata.definition: A variation of open addressing hashing that aims to reduce the variance in probe lengths. It does this by swapping an incoming element with an existing element if the new element has a 'better' (shorter) probe distance from its ideal position than the element it's trying to evict, thereby prioritizing elements that have been displaced further.

metadata.title: Tree (Data Structure)
metadata.definition: A non-linear hierarchical data structure consisting of nodes connected by edges, where each node has at most one parent and zero or more children, and there are no cycles. It models relationships in a hierarchical fashion.

metadata.title: Root Node
metadata.definition: The topmost node in a tree data structure that has no parent. Every non-empty tree has exactly one root node, serving as the starting point for traversal or operations.

metadata.title: Leaf Node
metadata.definition: A node in a tree data structure that has no children. These nodes are also known as external nodes and represent the end points of any path from the root.

metadata.title: Parent Node
metadata.definition: A node in a tree data structure that has one or more child nodes directly below it in the hierarchy. It is an immediate ancestor of its children.

metadata.title: Child Node
metadata.definition: A node in a tree data structure that has a direct connection from another node higher up in the hierarchy, known as its parent. It is an immediate descendant of its parent.

metadata.title: Sibling Nodes
metadata.definition: Nodes in a tree data structure that share the same parent node. They are at the same level in the tree and branch off from the same immediate ancestor.

metadata.title: Subtree
metadata.definition: A portion of a tree that is itself a tree, rooted at any node within the original tree. It includes the chosen node and all of its descendants.

metadata.title: Tree Traversal
metadata.definition: The process of visiting each node in a tree data structure exactly once in a systematic way. Common traversal methods include in-order, pre-order, post-order, and level-order, each yielding nodes in a different sequence.

metadata.title: Level-order Traversal
metadata.definition: A tree traversal method that visits nodes level by level, starting from the root and moving from left to right at each level. It is typically implemented using a queue to manage the order of nodes to visit.

metadata.title: Self-Balancing BST
metadata.definition: A type of binary search tree that automatically adjusts its structure (e.g., through rotations) to maintain a relatively balanced height. This ensures logarithmic time complexity for search, insertion, and deletion operations even in the worst case, preventing degeneration into a linked list.

metadata.title: Heap (Binary Heap)
metadata.definition: A specialized tree-based data structure that satisfies the heap property: for a max-heap, the value of each node is greater than or equal to its children's values, and for a min-heap, it's less than or equal. It is typically implemented as an array, representing a complete binary tree.

metadata.title: Heapify Operation
metadata.definition: A process of restoring the heap property in a binary heap. If a node violates the heap property, typically after an insertion or deletion, the node is swapped with its largest/smallest child (depending on max/min heap) until the property is satisfied or it becomes a leaf node.

metadata.title: Build Heap Operation
metadata.definition: The process of converting an arbitrary array of elements into a valid binary heap. This is typically done by iteratively calling the `heapify` operation on all non-leaf nodes, starting from the last non-leaf node and working upwards to the root.

metadata.title: Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree)
metadata.definition: A data structure that can efficiently update elements and calculate prefix sums in an array, both in O(log N) time. It achieves this by representing numbers as sums of powers of two, allowing updates and queries to propagate up/down a tree-like implicit structure built on an array.

metadata.title: KD-Tree
metadata.definition: A space-partitioning data structure for organizing points in a k-dimensional space. It recursively partitions the space into two half-spaces by splitting along one dimension at each level, alternating the splitting dimension cyclically.

metadata.title: Quadtree
metadata.definition: A tree data structure in which each internal node has exactly four children. Quadtrees are primarily used to partition a two-dimensional space by recursively subdividing it into four quadrants or regions, based on some criteria.

metadata.title: Octree
metadata.definition: A tree data structure in which each internal node has exactly eight children. Octrees are used to partition a three-dimensional space by recursively subdividing it into eight octants or regions, based on some criteria.

metadata.title: Vertex (Node)
metadata.definition: In graph theory, a vertex (or node) is a fundamental unit used to represent entities or points in a graph, serving as endpoints for edges.

metadata.title: Edge
metadata.definition: In graph theory, an edge is a connection between two vertices, representing a relationship or pathway between them. Edges can be directed or undirected, and may have associated weights.

metadata.title: Cycle (Graph)
metadata.definition: A cycle in a graph is a path that starts and ends at the same vertex, where no vertex (except the start/end vertex) and no edge are repeated. Cycles are fundamental in understanding graph connectivity and properties.

metadata.title: Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)
metadata.definition: A Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) is a directed graph that contains no directed cycles. This means it's impossible to start at any vertex and follow a sequence of directed edges back to the same vertex.

metadata.title: Strongly Connected Components (SCC)
metadata.definition: In a directed graph, a Strongly Connected Component (SCC) is a maximal subgraph such that for every pair of vertices u and v within the subgraph, there is a path from u to v and a path from v to u. Identifying SCCs helps in understanding the structure and reachability within directed graphs.

metadata.title: Bridge (Graph Theory)
metadata.definition: In an undirected graph, a bridge (or cut-edge) is an edge whose removal increases the number of connected components in the graph. Bridges represent critical connections that, if broken, disconnect parts of the graph.

metadata.title: Articulation Point (Graph Theory)
metadata.definition: In an undirected graph, an articulation point (or cut-vertex) is a vertex whose removal (along with all incident edges) increases the number of connected components in the graph. Articulation points are critical nodes that, if removed, disconnect parts of the graph.

metadata.title: Hopcroft-Karp Algorithm (Bipartite Matching)
metadata.definition: The Hopcroft-Karp algorithm is an efficient algorithm used to find a maximum cardinality matching in a bipartite graph. It achieves a time complexity of O(E√V) by repeatedly finding augmenting paths using Breadth-First Search (BFS) and Depth-First Search (DFS).

metadata.title: Comparison Sort
metadata.definition: A comparison sort is a type of sorting algorithm that only relies on comparisons between elements to determine their relative order. This category includes common algorithms like Merge Sort, Quick Sort, and Heap Sort.

metadata.title: Non-Comparison Sort
metadata.definition: A non-comparison sort is a sorting algorithm that does not use comparisons between elements to determine their order. Instead, these algorithms rely on specific properties of the input data, such as digit values or frequency counts, to sort elements more efficiently than comparison sorts for certain data distributions.

metadata.title: In-Place Sort
metadata.definition: An in-place sort is a sorting algorithm that transforms the input data using only a small, constant amount of auxiliary memory space, typically O(1) beyond the input array itself. This means it modifies the original array directly without creating a significantly larger copy.

metadata.title: Manacher's Algorithm
metadata.definition: Manacher's Algorithm is an efficient string processing algorithm that finds the longest palindromic substring within a given string in linear time, O(N). It cleverly exploits symmetry and pre-processes the string to handle even and odd length palindromes uniformly, avoiding redundant computations.

metadata.title: Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find)
metadata.definition: Disjoint Set Union (DSU), also known as Union-Find, is a data structure that maintains a collection of disjoint (non-overlapping) sets. It supports two primary operations: `find` (determining which set an element belongs to) and `union` (merging two sets into one).

metadata.title: Path Compression (DSU)
metadata.definition: Path Compression is an optimization technique used in the Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find) data structure to flatten the tree structure during a `find` operation. When `find(i)` is called, it makes every node on the path from `i` to the root point directly to the root, significantly reducing the height of the tree and improving future operation times.

metadata.title: Union by Rank (DSU)
metadata.definition: Union by Rank is an optimization technique used in the Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find) data structure to maintain a balanced tree structure during a `union` operation. It always attaches the root of the smaller 'ranked' tree to the root of the larger 'ranked' tree, where rank is an upper bound on the height of the tree.

metadata.title: Union by Size (DSU)
metadata.definition: Union by Size is an optimization technique used in the Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find) data structure to maintain a balanced tree structure during a `union` operation. It always attaches the root of the smaller set (fewer elements) to the root of the larger set, ensuring that tree depth grows slowly.

metadata.title: Primality Test
metadata.definition: A primality test is an algorithm used to determine whether a given natural number is prime (i.e., has exactly two distinct positive divisors: 1 and itself). These tests are essential in cryptography and number theory.

metadata.title: Modular Exponentiation
metadata.definition: Modular exponentiation is a type of exponentiation performed over a modulus, finding the remainder when an integer `b` (base) raised to the power `e` (exponent) is divided by a positive integer `m` (modulus). It is crucial in public-key cryptography algorithms like RSA.

metadata.title: Convolution (FFT)
metadata.definition: In the context of Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), convolution is a mathematical operation on two sequences (e.g., polynomials or arrays) that results in a third sequence, representing how the shape of one is modified by the other. FFT provides an efficient O(N log N) algorithm to compute discrete convolutions by transforming sequences to the frequency domain, multiplying them point-wise, and then inverse transforming back.

metadata.title: Graham Scan (Convex Hull)
metadata.definition: Graham Scan is an algorithm for finding the convex hull of a finite set of points in the plane. It works by first finding the point with the lowest y-coordinate, then sorting the other points by the angle they make with the lowest point, and finally using a stack to build the hull by checking for left turns.

metadata.title: Jarvis March (Convex Hull)
metadata.definition: Jarvis March, also known as the Gift Wrapping algorithm, is a computational geometry algorithm that finds the smallest convex polygon enclosing a set of points in a plane. It works by iteratively finding the point that forms the smallest angle with the current hull edge, starting from the lowest point.

metadata.title: Closest Pair of Points
metadata.definition: The Closest Pair of Points problem is a fundamental problem in computational geometry that involves finding two points in a given set of n points that have the smallest Euclidean distance between them. It is commonly solved using a divide-and-conquer approach with a time complexity of O(N log N).

metadata.title: Sweapline Algorithm
metadata.definition: A sweapline algorithm is a powerful technique in computational geometry where a conceptual 'sweep line' (or plane in 3D) moves across the geometric objects, processing events at critical points. This transforms static geometric problems into dynamic problems, often simplifying their solution.

metadata.title: Reservoir Sampling
metadata.definition: Reservoir Sampling is a family of randomized algorithms for choosing k samples from a list of n items, where n is a very large or unknown number, such that each item has an equal probability of being chosen. It's particularly useful when items can only be seen once, as in streaming data.

metadata.title: Knapsack Problem (0/1)
metadata.definition: The 0/1 Knapsack Problem is a classic optimization problem where a thief must choose a subset of items, each with a specific weight and value, to put into a knapsack with a limited weight capacity. Each item can either be taken entirely (1) or not at all (0), with the goal of maximizing the total value.

metadata.title: Knapsack Problem (Unbounded)
metadata.definition: The Unbounded Knapsack Problem (also known as the unbounded or infinite knapsack problem) is a variant where each item can be selected multiple times, if desired, to maximize total value without exceeding a given weight capacity. It is typically solved using dynamic programming.

metadata.title: Knapsack Problem (Fractional)
metadata.definition: The Fractional Knapsack Problem allows for taking fractions of items to maximize total value within a weight capacity. Unlike the 0/1 or Unbounded versions, it can be solved efficiently using a greedy algorithm by prioritizing items with the highest value-to-weight ratio.

metadata.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS)
metadata.definition: The Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) problem involves finding the subsequence of a given sequence in which the subsequence's elements are in strictly increasing order, and the subsequence is as long as possible. It can be solved using dynamic programming in O(N log N) time.

metadata.title: Kadane's Algorithm (Max Subarray Sum)
metadata.definition: Kadane's Algorithm is a dynamic programming algorithm used to find the maximum sum of a contiguous subarray within a one-dimensional array of numbers. It efficiently solves the problem in O(N) time by maintaining the maximum sum found so far and the maximum sum ending at the current position.

metadata.title: Bit Manipulation
metadata.definition: Bit manipulation refers to the act of programmatically operating on individual bits or groups of bits within a binary representation of data. It involves using bitwise operators to set, clear, toggle, or test specific bits, often for optimization, space efficiency, or low-level control.

metadata.title: Prefix Sum Array
metadata.definition: A Prefix Sum Array (also known as a cumulative sum array) is an auxiliary data structure where each element `P[i]` stores the sum of all elements from the beginning of the original array up to index `i`. This enables efficient O(1) calculation of the sum of any subarray.

metadata.title: Difference Array
metadata.definition: A Difference Array is an auxiliary array where `D[i]` stores the difference between `A[i]` and `A[i-1]` (with `D[0] = A[0]`), allowing for range updates to the original array `A` in O(1) time. The original array can then be reconstructed by taking prefix sums of the difference array.

metadata.title: Huffman Coding
metadata.definition: Huffman Coding is a greedy algorithm for lossless data compression that builds a prefix-free binary code for a set of characters based on their frequencies of occurrence. It assigns shorter codes to more frequent characters and longer codes to less frequent ones, minimizing the total encoded length.

metadata.title: Lempel-Ziv-Welch (LZW) Compression
metadata.definition: LZW compression is a universal lossless data compression algorithm that replaces repeating sequences of data (strings) with fixed-length codes. It builds a dictionary of these sequences dynamically from the input data, making it adaptive and effective for various data types.

metadata.title: Run-Length Encoding (RLE)
metadata.definition: Run-Length Encoding (RLE) is a simple, lossless data compression technique that reduces the size of a data stream by replacing consecutive occurrences of the same data value ('runs') with a single instance of the value and a count. It is most effective for data with long sequences of identical values.

metadata.title: Garbage Collection Algorithm
metadata.definition: A Garbage Collection (GC) algorithm is an automatic memory management process that frees up memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable or used by a program. Its primary goals are to prevent memory leaks, reduce programmer burden, and improve memory efficiency.

metadata.title: Mark and Sweep (GC)
metadata.definition: Mark and Sweep is a foundational garbage collection algorithm that operates in two phases: first, it 'marks' all objects in memory that are reachable from a set of root references. Second, it 'sweeps' through the entire memory heap, reclaiming all unmarked (unreachable) objects as free space.

metadata.title: Memory Pool
metadata.definition: A memory pool is a memory management technique where a block of pre-allocated contiguous memory is set aside to fulfill allocation requests for objects of a specific type or size. This approach reduces allocation/deallocation overhead and external fragmentation, improving performance.

metadata.title: Cache-Oblivious Algorithm
metadata.definition: A cache-oblivious algorithm is designed to perform well on a hierarchical memory system without needing to know the specific parameters of the cache (e.g., cache size or block size). It achieves good cache performance by exploiting locality through recursive decomposition of problems.

metadata.title: Parallel Algorithm
metadata.definition: A parallel algorithm is an algorithm designed to break down a problem into smaller, independent subproblems that can be executed simultaneously on multiple processing units. The goal is to significantly reduce the total execution time compared to a sequential approach, especially for large datasets or complex computations.

metadata.title: Distributed Algorithm
metadata.definition: An algorithm designed to run on a network of independent processors, where each processor has its own local memory and communicates by message passing, often aiming for fault tolerance, scalability, and concurrency.

metadata.title: Merkle Tree
metadata.definition: A hash tree where every leaf node is labeled with the cryptographic hash of a data block, and every non-leaf node is labeled with the cryptographic hash of its children's labels, allowing efficient and secure verification of data integrity and consistency.

metadata.title: R-Tree (Spatial Indexing)
