metadata.definition: A vulnerability category where an application relies on third-party libraries, frameworks, or other software components (e.g., operating system, web server) that have publicly disclosed security flaws. This exposes the application to attacks that target these known weaknesses, even if the custom application code is secure.

metadata.title: Insufficient Logging and Monitoring
metadata.definition: A vulnerability or weakness where a system lacks adequate logging of security-relevant events, or fails to actively monitor and alert on suspicious activities. This significantly hinders an organization's ability to detect, investigate, and respond to security incidents effectively, allowing attackers to remain undetected for extended periods.

metadata.title: XML External Entities (XXE) Vulnerability
metadata.definition: A server-side vulnerability that occurs when an XML parser processes untrusted XML input containing a reference to an external entity, without proper configuration or sanitization. This can allow an attacker to read local files, execute system commands, perform server-side request forgery (SSRF), or launch denial-of-service attacks.

metadata.title: Web Application Firewall (WAF)
metadata.definition: A security solution that filters, monitors, and blocks HTTP traffic to and from a web application, protecting it from various web-based attacks such as XSS, SQL injection, and DDoS attacks. A WAF operates at Layer 7 of the OSI model, applying a set of rules to detect and mitigate malicious traffic before it reaches the application.

metadata.title: Secure Coding Principles
metadata.definition: A set of guidelines and best practices for writing software code that minimizes security vulnerabilities, making applications more resilient to attacks, and ensuring confidentiality, integrity, and availability. These principles should be integrated throughout the entire Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC).

metadata.title: Input Validation
metadata.definition: The process of ensuring that data received from external sources, especially user input, conforms to expected formats, types, ranges, and patterns before it is processed, stored, or used in an application. Proper input validation is a fundamental security control that prevents many common vulnerabilities like injection attacks, buffer overflows, and Cross-Site Scripting.

metadata.title: Output Encoding
metadata.definition: A security measure that transforms untrusted input into a safe format before displaying it, preventing the browser from misinterpreting user-supplied data as executable code or markup. It neutralizes potentially malicious characters, ensuring they are rendered as literal text rather than active elements.

metadata.title: Session Management
metadata.definition: The process of securely handling and maintaining the state of a user's interaction with a web application over multiple requests. It involves identifying authenticated users, controlling their access to resources, and ensuring session integrity and confidentiality.

metadata.title: OAuth
metadata.definition: An open standard for authorization that allows a user to grant a third-party application limited access to their resources on another service without sharing their credentials. It defines a secure delegated access mechanism, separating the roles of the resource owner, client, and authorization server.

metadata.title: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language)
metadata.definition: An XML-based standard for exchanging authentication and authorization data between security domains, primarily used for web-based single sign-on (SSO). It allows a user to authenticate once at an identity provider (IdP) and gain access to multiple service providers (SPs) without re-authenticating.

metadata.title: OpenID Connect
metadata.definition: An identity layer built on top of the OAuth 2.0 framework, providing a simple identity verification layer that allows clients to verify the identity of the end-user based on authentication performed by an Authorization Server. It obtains basic profile information about the end-user in an interoperable REST-like manner, using JSON Web Tokens (JWTs).

metadata.title: Discretionary Access Control (DAC)
metadata.definition: An access control model where the owner of a resource or a designated administrator can grant or revoke access permissions to other users or groups at their discretion. It is the most common access control model found in operating systems and applications, offering flexibility in permission management.

metadata.title: Mandatory Access Control (MAC)
metadata.definition: An access control model where the operating system or a central authority enforces access policies based on security labels assigned to both subjects (users/processes) and objects (files/resources). Access decisions are not at the discretion of the owner, but rather based on predefined security classifications and clearances, often used in high-security environments.

metadata.title: API Security
metadata.definition: The practice of protecting Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) from unauthorized access, misuse, and cyberattacks. It involves implementing measures to authenticate and authorize API consumers, validate input, encrypt data in transit, and monitor API usage for suspicious activity.

metadata.title: REST API Security
metadata.definition: Focuses on securing Representational State Transfer (REST) architectural style APIs, which are widely used for web services. It encompasses specific security considerations like statelessness, resource-based authorization, proper use of HTTP methods, and protection against common web vulnerabilities in a RESTful context.

metadata.title: GraphQL Security
metadata.definition: Addresses the unique security challenges presented by GraphQL APIs, which differ from traditional REST APIs due to their single endpoint and flexible query capabilities. Key concerns include preventing overly complex or deeply nested queries, controlling data exposure, and managing authentication and authorization within a flexible schema.

metadata.title: Software Supply Chain Security
metadata.definition: The practice of securing all stages and components involved in developing, building, and delivering software, from initial code creation to deployment and ongoing maintenance. It addresses risks introduced by third-party libraries, open-source components, build tools, and distribution channels.

metadata.title: Static Application Security Testing (SAST)
metadata.definition: A white-box testing methodology that analyzes an application's source code, bytecode, or binary code without executing it, to identify security vulnerabilities. SAST tools help developers find security flaws early in the Secure Software Development Life Cycle (SSDLC).

metadata.title: Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST)
metadata.definition: A black-box testing methodology that scans a running application from the outside, simulating attack scenarios to identify security vulnerabilities that are detectable at runtime. DAST tools interact with the application through its front-end interfaces (e.g., HTTP/S requests) to find issues like misconfigurations or runtime flaws.

metadata.title: Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST)
metadata.definition: A hybrid application security testing approach that combines elements of both SAST and DAST by analyzing application code from within while the application is running. IAST agents are deployed within the application's runtime environment to observe execution flow and identify vulnerabilities with high accuracy and context.

metadata.title: Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP)
metadata.definition: A security technology that integrates into a running application or application runtime environment and actively defends against real-time cyberattacks. RASP monitors application execution, detects malicious input or behavior, and can prevent attacks by terminating suspicious processes or sanitizing input without human intervention.

metadata.title: Container Security
metadata.definition: The practice of securing the entire lifecycle of containerized applications, from image creation and storage to deployment and runtime. It involves protecting container images from vulnerabilities, securing the container runtime environment, isolating containers, and managing access to container orchestrators.

metadata.title: Serverless Security
metadata.definition: Addresses the unique security considerations for serverless architectures, focusing on protecting function code, managing access to cloud provider resources, securing event triggers, and monitoring for malicious activity. It encompasses the shared responsibility model inherent in cloud serverless platforms.

metadata.title: Microservices Security
metadata.definition: The set of practices for securing applications built using a microservices architecture, which involves protecting individual services, securing inter-service communication, managing API gateways, and ensuring consistent authentication and authorization across distributed components. It addresses the increased attack surface and complexity inherent in distributed systems.

metadata.title: Secure Software Development Life Cycle (SSDLC)
metadata.definition: The integration of security activities and considerations into every phase of the traditional Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), from requirements gathering and design to testing, deployment, and maintenance. Its goal is to build security in from the start, reducing vulnerabilities and the cost of fixing them.

metadata.title: Threat Modeling
metadata.definition: A structured process for identifying potential security threats, vulnerabilities, and countermeasure requirements for a system or application. It involves analyzing system design, identifying assets, potential attackers, and attack vectors, and evaluating the impact of potential attacks.

metadata.title: STRIDE Threat Model
metadata.definition: A framework for classifying and understanding security threats to applications or systems, categorizing them into Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, and Elevation of Privilege. It's often used during the design phase of software development to identify potential vulnerabilities.

metadata.title: DREAD Threat Model
metadata.definition: A framework used to rate and prioritize identified security threats based on five categories: Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, and Discoverability. It helps security teams decide which threats to address first by quantifying their potential impact and likelihood.

metadata.title: Code Review (Security)
metadata.definition: A systematic examination of source code by one or more people to identify security vulnerabilities, design flaws, and adherence to security best practices. It's a proactive measure often performed manually or with automated tools during the software development lifecycle.

metadata.title: Penetration Testing
metadata.definition: A simulated cyberattack against a computer system, network, or web application to find exploitable security vulnerabilities. It mimics real-world attack scenarios to evaluate the effectiveness of an organization's security controls and response capabilities.

metadata.title: Ethical Hacking
metadata.definition: The practice of intentionally attempting to bypass or exploit the security of computer systems, networks, or applications with the explicit permission of the owner. It aims to identify vulnerabilities that malicious hackers could exploit, thereby improving security defenses.

metadata.title: Vulnerability Scanning
metadata.definition: An automated process of identifying known security weaknesses or misconfigurations in computer systems, networks, or applications. It compares system configurations and software versions against a database of known vulnerabilities to generate a report.

metadata.title: Fuzz Testing
metadata.definition: An automated software testing technique that involves injecting malformed, unexpected, or random data (fuzz) into an application's inputs to discover software bugs, security vulnerabilities, or crashes. It's particularly effective at finding robust input validation issues.

metadata.title: Buffer Overflow Vulnerability
metadata.definition: A software defect that occurs when a program attempts to write more data into a fixed-size buffer than it can hold, overwriting adjacent memory locations. This can lead to program crashes, data corruption, or the execution of arbitrary malicious code.

metadata.title: Race Condition Vulnerability
metadata.definition: A flaw that occurs when the output of a concurrent program depends on the sequence or timing of uncontrollable events, such as the interleaving of threads or processes. In a security context, this can allow an attacker to exploit a window of vulnerability to gain unauthorized access or manipulate system state.

metadata.title: Clickjacking
metadata.definition: A malicious technique where an attacker overlays a transparent or opaque layer over a legitimate webpage, tricking a user into clicking on hidden elements of the underlying page. This can lead to unintended actions like authorizing transactions, changing settings, or downloading malware.

metadata.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
metadata.definition: An attack that tricks a web browser into sending an authenticated request to a vulnerable web application, which the user is currently logged into. The attacker crafts a malicious request (e.g., a money transfer) and embeds it on a site they control, relying on the victim's browser automatically sending session cookies.

metadata.title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
metadata.definition: An attack where an attacker induces a server-side application to make HTTP requests to an arbitrary domain of the attacker's choosing. This allows attackers to access internal network resources, query metadata services, or even launch other attacks from the compromised server's perspective.

metadata.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR)
metadata.definition: A vulnerability where an application exposes a direct reference to an internal implementation object, such as a file, directory, or database record, allowing an attacker to manipulate or access unauthorized objects by simply changing a parameter value. This bypasses authorization checks.

metadata.title: User Account Management
metadata.definition: The processes and policies involved in creating, maintaining, and deleting user accounts within a system or organization, ensuring appropriate access levels and security controls. It encompasses authentication, authorization, provisioning, and deprovisioning to protect sensitive resources.

metadata.title: Operating System Hardening
metadata.definition: The process of securing an operating system configuration by reducing its attack surface, disabling unnecessary services, removing unneeded software, applying security patches, and configuring security features. The goal is to minimize vulnerabilities and enhance the OS's overall resilience against attacks.

metadata.title: Patch Management
metadata.definition: The systematic process of acquiring, testing, and applying software updates and security patches to computer systems and applications. Its primary goal is to remediate known vulnerabilities, improve system stability, and ensure compliance with security policies.

metadata.title: Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux)
metadata.definition: A security architecture for Linux systems that provides mandatory access control (MAC) capabilities, allowing administrators to define granular permissions beyond traditional discretionary access control (DAC). It enforces policies that dictate which processes can access which files, devices, or network ports.

metadata.title: AppArmor
metadata.definition: A Linux security module that provides mandatory access control (MAC) capabilities by confining programs to a limited set of resources. It uses profiles to restrict a program's capabilities, such as file access, network access, or inter-process communication, based on the program's path.

metadata.title: File System Permissions
metadata.definition: Access control attributes assigned to files and directories within a file system, determining who can read, write, or execute them. These permissions are a fundamental operating system security mechanism to control access to data and programs.

metadata.title: Operating System Logging
metadata.definition: The process of recording events and activities that occur within an operating system, such as user logins, process starts, file access, and security-related incidents. These logs are crucial for monitoring, auditing, forensic analysis, and detecting security breaches.

metadata.title: Antivirus Software
metadata.definition: Antivirus software is a type of security program designed to detect, prevent, and remove malicious software, primarily focusing on viruses, from computer systems. It commonly employs signature-based detection, behavioral analysis, and heuristic methods to identify threats.

metadata.title: Anti-Malware Software
metadata.definition: Anti-malware software is a broader category of security software that defends against a wide range of malicious programs, including viruses, ransomware, spyware, adware, and trojans. It encompasses antivirus functionalities but extends protection through advanced techniques like heuristic analysis, behavioral monitoring, and sandbox execution.

metadata.title: Host-based Firewall
metadata.definition: A host-based firewall is a software application that runs on an individual computer or device, controlling network traffic entering and exiting that specific host. It enforces security policies by filtering data packets based on predefined rules, thus protecting the local system from unauthorized network access.

metadata.title: Memory Forensics
metadata.definition: Memory forensics is the process of analyzing the volatile memory (RAM) of a computer system to identify artifacts related to an incident, such as running processes, open network connections, loaded kernel modules, and cryptographic keys. This technique is crucial for understanding the state of a system at a specific point in time, especially in live system analysis or post-mortem investigations.

metadata.title: System Call Interception
metadata.definition: System call interception is a security technique where calls made by user-mode applications to the operating system kernel are monitored, logged, or modified. This allows for controlling or observing process behavior, enforcing security policies, detecting malicious activity, or even modifying system behavior at a low level.

metadata.title: Process Isolation
metadata.definition: Process isolation is a security principle and mechanism that ensures processes running on a system operate independently of each other, preventing one process from accessing or interfering with the memory, resources, or execution of another without explicit permission. This containment limits the potential impact or 'blast radius' of a compromised process.

metadata.title: Kernel Security
metadata.definition: Kernel security refers to the measures and mechanisms implemented within the operating system kernel to protect its integrity, prevent unauthorized access to system resources, and ensure the secure execution of processes. This includes enforcing memory protection, managing access control, validating code integrity, and safeguarding critical system functions against exploitation.

metadata.title: Trusted Platform Module (TPM)
metadata.definition: A Trusted Platform Module (TPM) is a secure cryptoprocessor designed to secure hardware by integrating cryptographic keys into devices, primarily for authenticating the platform. It provides hardware-based security functions such as secure boot, cryptographic operations, platform integrity measurement, and storage of sensitive data like encryption keys.

metadata.title: Secure Enclave
metadata.definition: A Secure Enclave is a hardware-based secure subsystem within a System-on-Chip (SoC) that provides a separate, isolated execution environment for processing sensitive data, even if the main processor or operating system is compromised. It ensures the confidentiality and integrity of code and data running within its protected memory regions.

metadata.title: Trusted Execution Environment (TEE)
metadata.definition: A Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) is a secure area inside a main processor that guarantees code and data loaded inside it are protected with respect to confidentiality and integrity. It provides a level of security above the richness of the OS but below the fully fledged isolation of a hypervisor, typically by leveraging hardware features to isolate a small trusted OS and its applications.

metadata.title: Intel SGX
metadata.definition: Intel Software Guard Extensions (SGX) is a set of security features built into some Intel CPUs that allows user-level code to allocate private regions of memory, called enclaves, that are protected from other processes, including the OS, hypervisor, and even BIOS. It aims to protect selected code and data from disclosure or modification, even on a compromised platform.

metadata.title: ARM TrustZone
metadata.definition: ARM TrustZone is a security extension for ARM processors that creates two separate execution environments, a 'Secure World' and a 'Normal World', sharing the same processor core. The Secure World hosts a small trusted OS and applications, providing a hardware-isolated environment for critical computations and data, while the Normal World runs the main operating system.

metadata.title: Shared Responsibility Model (Cloud)
metadata.definition: The Shared Responsibility Model is a framework that delineates the security responsibilities between a cloud service provider (CSP) and its customers. The CSP is generally responsible for the security *of* the cloud (infrastructure, physical facilities, etc.), while the customer is responsible for security *in* the cloud (data, applications, network configuration, etc.), with the exact division varying by service model (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS).

metadata.title: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) Security
metadata.definition: IaaS security refers to the specific security considerations and practices for protecting the virtualized computing infrastructure provided by a cloud service provider, where customers provision and manage virtual machines, storage, and networking components. Under the shared responsibility model, customers are largely responsible for securing operating systems, applications, network configurations, and data within their provisioned resources.

metadata.title: Platform as a Service (PaaS) Security
metadata.definition: PaaS security addresses the security considerations for cloud environments where customers deploy their applications onto a platform managed by the cloud provider, who handles underlying infrastructure, operating systems, and middleware. Customer security responsibilities typically focus on the security of their application code, data, and user access, while the provider manages the platform's underlying security.

metadata.title: Software as a Service (SaaS) Security
metadata.definition: SaaS security involves the security considerations for cloud services where customers access fully managed applications over the internet, with the cloud provider responsible for all aspects of the application, infrastructure, and platform. Customer security responsibilities are primarily limited to data management, user access control, and proper configuration of the application's security settings.

metadata.title: Public Cloud Security
metadata.definition: Public Cloud Security refers to the security measures and practices implemented to protect data, applications, and infrastructure within public cloud environments, which are owned and operated by a third-party cloud service provider and shared among multiple tenants. It involves balancing the CSP's shared responsibility with the customer's specific configurations and controls to maintain a strong security posture.

metadata.title: Private Cloud Security
metadata.definition: Private Cloud Security encompasses the security measures applied to cloud infrastructure dedicated exclusively to a single organization, whether hosted on-premises or by a third-party provider. The organization maintains full control and responsibility for securing all layers of the cloud environment, from physical infrastructure to virtualized components, applications, and data.

metadata.title: Hybrid Cloud Security
metadata.definition: Hybrid Cloud Security is the comprehensive strategy for securing environments that combine public cloud, private cloud, and/or on-premises infrastructure, allowing data and applications to move between them. It focuses on ensuring consistent security policies, unified identity management, robust network connectivity, and consistent data protection across these disparate environments.

metadata.title: Cloud Identity and Access Management (IAM)
metadata.definition: Cloud Identity and Access Management (IAM) is a foundational cloud security service that enables organizations to securely manage and control who can access cloud resources, what actions they can perform, and under what conditions. It typically involves managing users, groups, roles, and policies to enforce the principle of least privilege, ensuring entities only have the necessary permissions.

metadata.title: Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM)
metadata.definition: Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) continuously monitors cloud environments for misconfigurations, compliance violations, and security risks, providing visibility and automated remediation recommendations. It ensures cloud resources adhere to security best practices and regulatory requirements across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS.

metadata.title: Cloud Workload Protection Platform (CWPP)
metadata.definition: A Cloud Workload Protection Platform (CWPP) provides unified visibility and threat protection for workloads across hybrid and multi-cloud environments, including virtual machines, containers, and serverless functions. It focuses on securing the runtime environment of applications, often using agents or direct integrations to detect and prevent threats.

metadata.title: Data Sovereignty
metadata.definition: Data sovereignty is the concept that digital data is subject to the laws and regulations of the country in which it is stored. It implies that data stored in a particular nation's jurisdiction is exclusively governed by that nation's legal framework, even if accessed from elsewhere.

metadata.title: Cloud Data Encryption
metadata.definition: Cloud data encryption is the process of transforming data stored or transmitted in cloud environments into an unreadable format to protect its confidentiality. This typically includes encryption at rest for stored data and encryption in transit for data moving across networks.

metadata.title: Cloud Native Security
metadata.definition: Cloud native security refers to securing applications and infrastructure built and deployed using cloud-native architectures and technologies, such as containers, microservices, serverless functions, and Kubernetes. It emphasizes security integrated throughout the development lifecycle, automation, and continuous monitoring, leveraging the cloud's inherent capabilities.

metadata.title: Container Registry Security
metadata.definition: Container registry security involves protecting the integrity and confidentiality of container images stored in a registry, as well as controlling access to these images. Key aspects include scanning images for vulnerabilities, signing images to ensure authenticity, and managing permissions for image push/pull operations.

metadata.title: Kubernetes Security
metadata.definition: Kubernetes security encompasses a range of practices and controls designed to protect Kubernetes clusters, their components, and the applications running within them from unauthorized access, misconfigurations, and vulnerabilities. This includes securing the control plane, worker nodes, network policies, and application deployments within the cluster.

metadata.title: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Security
metadata.definition: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) security involves integrating security best practices and automated checks into the management of infrastructure defined as code, such as Terraform, CloudFormation, or Ansible. It aims to prevent misconfigurations and enforce security policies early in the development lifecycle by analyzing IaC templates before deployment.

metadata.title: DevSecOps (Cloud)
metadata.definition: DevSecOps (Cloud) integrates security practices and tooling throughout the entire cloud-native software development lifecycle, from initial design and development to deployment and operation. It emphasizes automation, collaboration, and shifting security left to proactively identify and mitigate vulnerabilities and misconfigurations in cloud environments and applications.

metadata.title: Cloud Governance
metadata.definition: Cloud governance is the set of policies, processes, and tools used to manage and control cloud resources, services, and operations to ensure alignment with organizational goals, regulatory requirements, and security policies. It provides a comprehensive framework for managing risk, cost, compliance, and security in cloud environments.

metadata.title: Data Encryption in Use
metadata.definition: Data encryption in use protects data while it is being actively processed or computed by an application or system. This is traditionally the most challenging state of data to protect, as the data must often be unencrypted for computation, but new techniques like homomorphic encryption or confidential computing aim to address this.

metadata.title: Data Minimization
metadata.definition: Data minimization is the principle of collecting, processing, and storing only the absolute minimum amount of personal data necessary to achieve a specified purpose. It reduces the scope of potential data breaches and enhances privacy by limiting the exposure of sensitive information.

metadata.title: Data Retention Policy
metadata.definition: A data retention policy is a formal organizational document that specifies how long different types of data must be kept and how they should be securely disposed of once their retention period expires. It ensures compliance with legal, regulatory, and business requirements while managing storage costs and data privacy risks.

metadata.title: Data Classification
metadata.definition: Data classification is the process of categorizing data based on its sensitivity, value, and regulatory requirements, assigning appropriate labels (e.g., Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted). This process helps organizations implement consistent security controls, access policies, and retention schedules tailored to each data type.

metadata.title: General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)
metadata.definition: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is a comprehensive data privacy and security law enacted by the European Union that imposes strict rules on how personal data of individuals within the EU is collected, processed, and stored. It grants individuals significant rights over their data and mandates robust protection measures and accountability for organizations.

metadata.title: California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA)
metadata.definition: The California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) is a state-level privacy law in California that grants consumers specific rights regarding their personal information collected by businesses. It provides rights such as the right to know what data is collected, the right to request deletion, and the right to opt-out of the sale of personal information.

metadata.title: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA)
metadata.definition: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) is a U.S. federal law that establishes national standards to protect sensitive patient health information (PHI) from being disclosed without the patient's consent or knowledge. It mandates administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for covered entities and their business associates.

metadata.title: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS)
metadata.definition: The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) is a global information security standard for organizations that handle branded credit cards from the major card schemes. It aims to reduce credit card fraud by mandating strict requirements for the protection of cardholder data throughout its lifecycle, including storage, processing, and transmission.

metadata.title: Secure Data Destruction
metadata.definition: Secure data destruction is the process of permanently and irretrievably eliminating data from storage media to prevent unauthorized recovery and access. This goes beyond simple deletion, employing methods like overwriting, degaussing, or physical destruction to ensure data cannot be reconstructed.

metadata.title: Digital Rights Management (DRM)
metadata.definition: Digital Rights Management (DRM) is a set of technologies and techniques used to control access to and usage of copyrighted digital content and devices. Its primary purpose is to prevent unauthorized distribution, modification, or copying of digital media, software, and intellectual property.

metadata.title: Watermarking (Digital)
metadata.definition: Digital watermarking involves embedding hidden information, often copyright or ownership details, directly into a digital medium such as an image, audio, or video file. This embedded data is robust to common transformations and undetectable without a specific decoder, primarily used for copyright protection, source tracking, and tamper detection.

metadata.title: Steganography
metadata.definition: Steganography is the practice of concealing a message within another message or a physical object, in such a way that the presence or contents of the hidden message are not readily apparent. Its goal is to achieve covert communication by making the secret message indistinguishable from ordinary data.

metadata.title: Authentication Factor
metadata.definition: An authentication factor is a distinct category of information or characteristic used to verify an individual's identity during an authentication process. These factors typically fall into three main types: something you know (knowledge), something you have (possession), or something you are (inherence).

metadata.title: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
metadata.definition: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) is a security system that requires users to provide two or more distinct authentication factors from different categories to verify their identity. By combining knowledge, possession, or inherence factors, MFA significantly enhances security, making it much harder for unauthorized users to gain access.

metadata.title: Two-Factor Authentication (2FA)
metadata.definition: Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) is a specific type of Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) that requires exactly two distinct authentication factors to verify a user's identity. It commonly combines a knowledge factor, like a password, with a possession factor, such as a smartphone or security token, to provide enhanced security.

metadata.title: Single Sign-On (SSO)
metadata.definition: Single Sign-On (SSO) is an authentication scheme that enables a user to log in with a single set of credentials to multiple independent software systems within a given session. SSO streamlines the user experience by eliminating the need to re-enter credentials for each application and simplifies identity management for administrators.

metadata.title: Biometric Authentication
metadata.definition: Biometric authentication is a security process that verifies a user's identity by analyzing unique biological or behavioral characteristics. This method relies on 'something you are' to provide a highly secure and often convenient way to authenticate users, reducing reliance on passwords.

metadata.title: Password Authentication
metadata.definition: Password authentication is a widely used method where a user proves their identity by providing a secret string of characters (password) that only they should know. This process relies on the 'something you know' authentication factor, comparing the entered password against a stored, usually hashed, version.

metadata.title: Certificate-based Authentication
metadata.definition: Certificate-based authentication is an authentication method where a user or device proves their identity by presenting a digital certificate, which is cryptographically signed by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA). This method leverages asymmetric cryptography to establish trust and verify authenticity, often as a strong alternative to traditional passwords.

metadata.title: SAML Protocol
metadata.definition: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is an XML-based open standard for exchanging authentication and authorization data between an identity provider (IdP) and a service provider (SP). It is primarily used to enable web-based Single Sign-On (SSO) in federated identity environments, allowing users to authenticate once and access multiple services.

metadata.title: OAuth Protocol
metadata.definition: OAuth (Open Authorization) is an open standard for access delegation, widely used as a way for users to grant third-party websites or applications access to their information on other websites without sharing their passwords. It primarily focuses on authorization, allowing limited access to protected resources rather than authenticating the user's identity directly.

metadata.title: OpenID Connect Protocol
metadata.definition: OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an authentication layer built on top of the OAuth 2.0 framework, enabling clients to verify the identity of the end-user based on authentication performed by an authorization server. It provides a simple, identity layer that allows clients to obtain basic profile information about the end-user, often used for Single Sign-On (SSO).

metadata.title: FIDO Universal 2nd Factor (U2F)
metadata.definition: FIDO U2F is an open authentication standard that strengthens and simplifies two-factor authentication (2FA) using specialized USB, NFC, or Bluetooth security devices. It allows users to securely log into online services with a physical key by simply tapping or pressing it, providing strong phishing-resistant authentication based on public-key cryptography.

metadata.title: WebAuthn (Web Authentication)
metadata.definition: WebAuthn is a web standard, developed by the W3C and FIDO Alliance, that allows web applications to implement strong, secure, and passwordless authentication using public-key cryptography. It works across different platforms and with various authenticators, including built-in biometrics (like fingerprint readers) and FIDO security keys, directly within the web browser.

metadata.title: Password Policy
metadata.definition: A password policy is a set of rules and guidelines implemented by an organization or system that dictates the requirements for creating and managing user passwords. Effective password policies aim to enhance security by enforcing strong, unique, and regularly updated passwords to minimize the risk of unauthorized access.

metadata.title: Password Manager
metadata.definition: A password manager is a software application that helps users generate, store, and manage their passwords securely in an encrypted vault. It promotes strong password hygiene by allowing users to create complex, unique passwords for every online account and securely retrieve them when needed, often via browser extensions or desktop applications.

metadata.title: Identity Governance and Administration (IGA)
metadata.definition: Identity Governance and Administration (IGA) is a comprehensive framework that manages digital identities and access rights across an organization's IT landscape. IGA solutions streamline identity lifecycle management, automate access provisioning, enforce policy, and facilitate access certification to ensure compliance, reduce risk, and improve operational efficiency.

metadata.title: Privileged Access Management (PAM)
metadata.definition: Privileged Access Management (PAM) is a security strategy and set of technologies designed to manage, control, and monitor highly sensitive accounts and access rights within an IT environment. PAM focuses on accounts with elevated permissions, such as administrator or root accounts, to prevent insider threats, mitigate the impact of external attacks, and achieve regulatory compliance.

metadata.title: Active Directory Security
metadata.definition: Active Directory (AD) Security encompasses the practices, configurations, and tools used to protect Microsoft Active Directory from unauthorized access, compromise, and abuse. Securing AD is critical because it serves as the primary identity store and authentication service for most Windows-based enterprise networks, controlling access to critical resources and applications.

metadata.title: Identity Federation
metadata.definition: Identity Federation is a system or agreement that allows a user's digital identity and attributes to be shared across multiple, independent security domains or organizations. This enables seamless Single Sign-On (SSO) and simplified access to resources hosted by different services, establishing trust relationships between identity providers and service providers without redundant credential management.

metadata.title: Identity Provisioning
metadata.definition: Identity provisioning is the process of creating, updating, and managing user identities and their access rights across various systems and applications within an organization. It ensures that users are granted the appropriate permissions required to perform their roles.

metadata.title: Identity Deprovisioning
metadata.definition: Identity deprovisioning is the systematic process of revoking and removing a user's access rights and accounts across all organizational systems when their role changes, they leave the organization, or their access is no longer required. This critical security measure prevents unauthorized access by former personnel or those whose privileges have changed.

metadata.title: Credential Stuffing
metadata.definition: Credential stuffing is a cyberattack where threat actors use lists of stolen usernames and passwords (often obtained from data breaches) to gain unauthorized access to other unrelated online services. It exploits the common practice of users reusing the same credentials across multiple websites.

metadata.title: Brute Force Attack (Passwords)
metadata.definition: A brute force attack is a trial-and-error method used by attackers to guess credentials, cryptographic keys, or encrypted data by systematically trying every possible combination of characters. These attacks are typically automated and can be very time-consuming but effective against weak or short passwords.

metadata.title: Dictionary Attack (Passwords)
metadata.definition: A dictionary attack is a type of brute force attack that attempts to guess a password by trying a pre-compiled list of common words, phrases, and previously compromised passwords. This method exploits the human tendency to choose easily memorable and weak passwords.

metadata.title: Rainbow Table Attack (Passwords)
metadata.definition: A rainbow table attack is an attack technique used to crack hashed passwords more efficiently than a traditional brute-force attack by employing precomputed tables of hashes for a large number of potential passwords. It sacrifices storage space for computation time, enabling rapid reversal of hashes to their original plaintext passwords without having to recompute each hash individually.

metadata.title: Threat Intelligence Platform (TIP)
metadata.definition: A Threat Intelligence Platform (TIP) is a software solution that aggregates, processes, and disseminates threat intelligence from various internal and external sources, helping organizations manage, analyze, and act upon relevant security information. TIPs enhance an organization's ability to detect, prevent, and respond to cyber threats more effectively by providing actionable context.

metadata.title: Incident Response Plan
metadata.definition: An Incident Response Plan (IRP) is a documented set of procedures and guidelines an organization follows to prepare for, detect, contain, eradicate, recover from, and analyze cybersecurity incidents. Its primary purpose is to minimize damage, reduce recovery time, and prevent future occurrences through systematic and coordinated action.

metadata.title: Incident Identification
metadata.definition: Incident identification is the initial phase of incident response, involving the detection of anomalous or malicious activity and determining whether it constitutes a security incident requiring a formal response. This phase often relies on security monitoring tools, alert systems, and user reports to flag potential threats.

metadata.title: Incident Containment
metadata.definition: Incident containment is the phase of incident response focused on limiting the scope and impact of a security incident to prevent further damage, unauthorized access, or spread of the attack. This often involves isolating affected systems, networks, or accounts.

metadata.title: Incident Eradication
metadata.definition: Incident eradication is the phase of incident response focused on removing the root cause of the incident and any remnants of the attack from affected systems and networks. This includes cleaning malware, patching exploited vulnerabilities, removing unauthorized accounts, and strengthening security controls to prevent re-infection.

metadata.title: Incident Recovery
metadata.definition: Incident recovery is the phase of incident response focused on restoring affected systems and services to normal operation, verifying their integrity, and closely monitoring them for signs of re-infection or residual compromise. This often involves restoring from clean backups, implementing stronger security measures, and extensive testing.

metadata.title: Post-Incident Analysis
metadata.definition: Post-incident analysis, also known as 'lessons learned,' is the final phase of incident response, involving a detailed review of the entire incident to understand what happened, why it happened, and how to prevent similar incidents in the future. This phase is crucial for continuous improvement of security posture and incident response capabilities.

metadata.title: Digital Forensics
metadata.definition: Digital forensics is the scientific process of identifying, preserving, collecting, analyzing, and presenting digital evidence in a legally admissible manner to investigate cybercrimes, security incidents, or policy violations. It involves specialized techniques and tools to extract meaningful information from digital devices and systems.

metadata.title: Disk Forensics
metadata.definition: Disk forensics is a specialized branch of digital forensics focused on the acquisition, preservation, and analysis of data stored on computer hard drives, solid-state drives, and other storage media. Its goal is to uncover hidden, deleted, or otherwise unobservable information relevant to an investigation without altering the original evidence.

metadata.title: Mobile Device Forensics
metadata.definition: Mobile device forensics is a specialized branch of digital forensics dedicated to the extraction, preservation, and analysis of data from mobile devices like smartphones and tablets. It addresses unique technical challenges posed by device encryption, diverse operating systems (iOS, Android), and proprietary hardware.

metadata.title: Cloud Forensics
metadata.definition: Cloud forensics is a specialized branch of digital forensics concerned with the investigation of incidents and the acquisition of digital evidence within cloud computing environments. It addresses unique challenges related to data locality, multi-tenancy, elasticity, legal jurisdiction, and the ephemeral nature of cloud resources.

metadata.title: Chain of Custody (Forensics)
metadata.definition: The Chain of Custody in forensics refers to a documented, unbroken chronological record of the possession, handling, transfer, analysis, and disposition of physical or electronic evidence. Maintaining a strict chain of custody is crucial to ensure the integrity, authenticity, and legal admissibility of evidence in legal proceedings.

metadata.title: Forensic Imaging
metadata.definition: Forensic imaging is the process of creating an exact, bit-for-bit duplicate of a digital storage medium (like a hard drive, USB drive, or memory card) in a forensically sound manner. This ensures that the original evidence remains unaltered while analysis and investigation are performed on the duplicate copy.

metadata.title: Log Analysis
metadata.definition: Log analysis is the process of systematically reviewing and interpreting computer-generated records (logs) of events that occur within an operating system, application, or network device. It is a critical activity for security monitoring, incident detection, troubleshooting, performance analysis, and forensic investigations.

metadata.title: Indicators of Attack (IoA)
metadata.definition: Indicators of Attack (IoAs) are forensic artifacts or patterns of behavior that reveal an ongoing malicious attempt to compromise a system or network, focusing on the attacker's tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) rather than just known bad files or IPs. Unlike Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) which are reactive, IoAs are proactive signals that indicate an attack is in progress, allowing for early detection and intervention. They are typically behavioral and context-rich, providing insights into the attacker's objectives and methods.

metadata.title: Adversary Emulation
metadata.definition: Adversary emulation is a cybersecurity testing methodology that simulates the actions of a specific, known threat actor or group by replicating their tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). This approach aims to provide a realistic assessment of an organization's security posture and its ability to detect, prevent, and respond to sophisticated real-world attacks. It goes beyond generic vulnerability scanning or penetration testing by focusing on how a specific adversary would operate.

metadata.title: Incident Playbook
metadata.definition: An incident playbook is a documented, step-by-step guide outlining predefined procedures and actions to be taken by an organization in response to specific types of cybersecurity incidents. It standardizes the incident response process, ensuring consistent and efficient handling of security events by providing clear roles, responsibilities, communication protocols, and technical steps. Playbooks help minimize damage, reduce recovery time, and improve overall incident management maturity.

metadata.title: Digital Forensics Readiness
metadata.definition: Digital forensics readiness refers to the proactive measures taken by an organization to ensure that digital evidence can be efficiently and effectively collected, preserved, analyzed, and presented in a legally admissible manner, should a cybersecurity incident occur. It involves planning, establishing policies, configuring systems, and training personnel to facilitate potential future forensic investigations. By being ready, organizations can accelerate incident response and improve the chances of successful prosecution or recovery.

metadata.title: Spyware
metadata.definition: Spyware is a type of malicious software designed to secretly gather information about a person or organization and relay it to an unauthorized third party, without the user's knowledge or consent. It typically monitors user activities, collects personal data, and can install additional harmful software. The collected information can include browsing history, personal files, credentials, and keystrokes.

metadata.title: Adware
metadata.definition: Adware is software that automatically displays or downloads unwanted advertisements, often in the form of pop-ups, banners, or redirecting browser traffic to specific websites. While some adware may be benign, many forms are considered malicious as they can track user browsing habits, slow down system performance, and sometimes act as a conduit for installing other malware. It typically arrives bundled with legitimate software or via drive-by downloads.

metadata.title: Botnet
metadata.definition: A botnet is a network of compromised computer systems, often referred to as 'bots' or 'zombies,' that are controlled by a single attacker or 'bot-herder' without the knowledge of their owners. These compromised devices, which can include PCs, servers, and IoT devices, are typically used to perform coordinated malicious tasks on a large scale, such as launching Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks, sending spam, or distributing malware. The bot-herder uses a command-and-control (C2) server to direct the botnet.

metadata.title: Keylogger
metadata.definition: A keylogger is a type of surveillance technology used to record every keystroke made on a specific computer or mobile device. These can be implemented as hardware devices, software programs, or even within web browsers, operating covertly to capture sensitive information like usernames, passwords, credit card numbers, and other personal data. Keyloggers are often used by attackers to steal credentials or spy on users.

metadata.title: Backdoor
metadata.definition: A backdoor is a covert method of bypassing normal authentication or encryption to gain unauthorized, remote access to a computer system, application, or network. It is often created intentionally by developers for maintenance purposes but can also be inserted maliciously by attackers or malware to maintain persistent access. Backdoors allow attackers to control or access a system without being detected by standard security protocols.

metadata.title: Fileless Malware
metadata.definition: Fileless malware is a sophisticated type of malicious software that operates entirely in computer memory, without writing any files to disk, making it extremely difficult to detect by traditional signature-based antivirus solutions. Instead, it leverages legitimate system tools, built-in operating system processes, and memory-resident techniques to execute its payload and persist across reboots. This technique significantly reduces the attack's footprint and improves stealth.

metadata.title: Exploit Kit
metadata.definition: An exploit kit is a software package designed to automate the process of exploiting known vulnerabilities in client-side software, typically web browsers and their plugins (like Adobe Flash, Java, or Acrobat Reader). Attackers use exploit kits by driving traffic to malicious web pages hosting the kit, which then probes the visitor's system for vulnerable software. If a vulnerability is found, the kit delivers a payload, often malware, to compromise the system without user interaction.

metadata.title: Zero-Day Exploit
metadata.definition: A zero-day exploit is a cyberattack that takes advantage of a software vulnerability that is unknown to the software vendor or public, meaning there is no existing patch or workaround available. The term 'zero-day' refers to the fact that the vendor has had zero days to fix the vulnerability once it's discovered and exploited. These exploits are highly prized by attackers due to their effectiveness and difficulty of detection, often used in targeted attacks by sophisticated adversaries.

metadata.title: Denial of Service (DoS)
metadata.definition: A Denial of Service (DoS) attack is a cyberattack designed to make a machine or network resource unavailable to its intended users by temporarily or indefinitely disrupting services of a host connected to the Internet. DoS attacks typically overwhelm the target with a flood of traffic or requests, or by exploiting a vulnerability that causes the system to crash. The goal is to deny legitimate users access to information or services.

metadata.title: Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS)
metadata.definition: A Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack is a more powerful and complex form of DoS attack that uses multiple compromised computer systems as sources of attack traffic. These 'botnet' devices simultaneously target a single victim, overwhelming the target's network, server, or application with a massive flood of legitimate-looking requests or malicious data. DDoS attacks are harder to mitigate due to their distributed nature and high volume, making it difficult to distinguish malicious traffic from legitimate user requests.

metadata.title: Social Engineering
metadata.definition: Social engineering is a manipulation technique that exploits human psychology and trust to trick individuals into divulging confidential information or performing actions that benefit an attacker. It relies on psychological tactics rather than technical hacking, leveraging deception, persuasion, and impersonation to bypass security measures. Common motives include gaining unauthorized access, stealing data, or financial fraud.

metadata.title: Spear Phishing
metadata.definition: Spear phishing is a highly targeted form of phishing attack where an attacker sends a fraudulent email or electronic message to a specific individual, organization, or business, often appearing to be from a trusted sender. Unlike generic phishing, spear phishing messages are meticulously crafted using specific information about the target, gleaned from public or stolen sources, to make the communication seem legitimate and increase the likelihood of success. The goal is typically to steal sensitive data, deploy malware, or gain unauthorized access.

metadata.title: Whaling (Phishing)
metadata.definition: Whaling is a highly specific type of spear phishing attack that targets high-profile individuals within an organization, such as senior executives, CEOs, or high-level managers. The attackers often pose as a superior or another trusted authority to trick the victim into performing critical actions like authorizing large financial transfers, revealing sensitive company information, or granting access to critical systems. Due to the victim's position, the potential impact of a successful whaling attack can be severe.

metadata.title: Vishing
metadata.definition: Vishing, a portmanteau of 'voice' and 'phishing,' is a form of social engineering attack that uses voice communication, typically over the phone, to trick individuals into revealing personal information or performing actions. Attackers often impersonate trusted entities like banks, government agencies, or tech support to gain the victim's trust and manipulate them. The goal is usually to steal credentials, financial data, or induce monetary transfers.

metadata.title: Smishing
metadata.definition: Smishing, a portmanteau of 'SMS' and 'phishing,' is a social engineering attack that uses text messages (SMS) to trick victims into clicking malicious links, downloading malware, or divulging sensitive personal information. Attackers typically send messages that appear to be from legitimate sources like banks, delivery services, or government agencies, often creating a sense of urgency or offering an enticing reward to prompt immediate action. The goal is usually to steal credentials, financial information, or install malicious software.

metadata.title: Baiting (Social Engineering)
metadata.definition: Baiting is a social engineering technique where an attacker offers something enticing, a 'bait,' to lure a victim into compromising their security or disclosing information. The bait often appeals to curiosity or greed and typically involves physical media infected with malware or a deceptive online offer. Once the victim takes the bait, their system may be compromised, or their credentials stolen.

metadata.title: Pretexting
metadata.definition: Pretexting is a form of social engineering where an attacker creates a fabricated scenario or false identity (a 'pretext') to manipulate a victim into divulging sensitive information or performing an action beneficial to the attacker. The attacker uses this deception to build trust and bypass security protocols.

metadata.title: Tailgating
metadata.definition: Tailgating, also known as piggybacking, is a physical security breach where an unauthorized individual gains access to a restricted area by closely following an authorized person through a controlled entry point, often without the authorized person's explicit consent or knowledge.

metadata.title: Shoulder Surfing
metadata.definition: Shoulder surfing is the act of obtaining sensitive information by visually observing a victim's private actions, such as their screen, keyboard, or physical documents, often from an advantageous position in public or semi-public spaces.

metadata.title: Watering Hole Attack
metadata.definition: A watering hole attack is a type of cyberattack where an attacker identifies and infects a website frequently visited by a specific target group, such as employees of a particular company or members of an industry, with the goal of compromising members of that group when they visit the site.

metadata.title: Man-in-the-Middle Attack (MITM)
metadata.definition: A Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attack is a form of cyberattack where an attacker secretly intercepts, relays, and potentially alters communication between two parties who believe they are communicating directly. The attacker positions themselves in the communication path, gaining full control over the information exchanged.

metadata.title: Man-in-the-Browser Attack (MITB)
metadata.definition: A Man-in-the-Browser (MITB) attack is a type of Man-in-the-Middle attack specifically targeting a web browser, typically through a Trojan horse or malicious browser extension. The malware infects the browser, allowing the attacker to intercept, modify, or insert data directly within the victim's browser session before it is sent to the web server or displayed to the user.

metadata.title: Supply Chain Attack
metadata.definition: A supply chain attack is a cyberattack that targets less secure elements in an organization's supply chain to gain unauthorized access to the main target. This typically involves tampering with legitimate software, hardware, or third-party services before they reach the end user, introducing vulnerabilities or backdoors.

metadata.title: Insider Threat
metadata.definition: An insider threat is a security risk that originates from within the targeted organization, typically from current or former employees, contractors, or business partners who have legitimate access to systems, data, or physical premises. These threats can be malicious (intentional harm) or unintentional (negligence or error).

metadata.title: Covert Channels (Timing)
metadata.definition: A timing covert channel is a communication path that transmits information by modulating the time at which events occur, or the order of events, in a system where such communication is not intended. Information is encoded in the temporal characteristics of system operations, such as delays or execution times.

metadata.title: Covert Channels (Storage)
metadata.definition: A storage covert channel is a communication path that transmits information by directly or indirectly writing to and reading from a shared storage location or resource, where the existence of this communication is unintended by the system's security policy. Data is encoded by modifying attributes or contents of shared storage elements.

metadata.title: Side-Channel Attack (Power Analysis)
metadata.definition: A power analysis side-channel attack exploits information leaked through the fluctuating power consumption of an electronic device, particularly during cryptographic operations. By measuring and analyzing these power traces, an attacker can infer sensitive data like secret keys or internal states of an algorithm.

metadata.title: Side-Channel Attack (Electromagnetic Analysis)
metadata.definition: An electromagnetic analysis side-channel attack exploits information leaked through unintended electromagnetic (EM) radiation emitted by electronic devices during their operation. By capturing and analyzing these EM emissions, attackers can infer sensitive data, often targeting cryptographic operations or displaying screen content.

metadata.title: Side-Channel Attack (Cache Timing)
metadata.definition: A cache timing side-channel attack infers sensitive information by observing the timing differences in memory access patterns due to the behavior of processor caches during program execution. Attackers can deduce details about secret data or operations based on whether memory accesses result in cache hits or misses.

metadata.title: Memory Corruption
metadata.definition: Memory corruption is a class of software bugs where a program inadvertently writes to or reads from an unintended memory location, often leading to unpredictable behavior, program crashes, or critical security vulnerabilities. These vulnerabilities can be exploited for privilege escalation, data leakage, or arbitrary code execution.

metadata.title: Privilege Escalation Techniques
metadata.definition: Privilege escalation techniques are methods used by an attacker to gain elevated access rights or permissions than they initially possessed on a computer system or network. This typically involves moving from a standard user account to an administrator, system, or root account to achieve greater control.

metadata.title: Malware Analysis (Static)
metadata.definition: Static malware analysis is the process of examining malicious software without executing it, focusing on its inherent properties, code structure, and metadata. This involves dissecting the binary to understand its functionality, capabilities, and indicators of compromise (IOCs).

metadata.title: Malware Analysis (Dynamic)
metadata.definition: Dynamic malware analysis is the process of executing malicious software in a controlled and isolated environment, such as a sandbox, to observe its real-time behavior. This method records and analyzes its interactions with the operating system, network communications, file system changes, and process activities.

metadata.title: Sandboxing (Malware)
metadata.definition: Sandboxing for malware is a security mechanism that isolates suspicious or untrusted code within a tightly controlled environment, restricting its access to host system resources. This prevents the malware from causing harm, while allowing security analysts to observe and analyze its behavior safely.

metadata.title: Reverse Engineering (Malware)
metadata.definition: Reverse engineering of malware is the systematic process of deconstructing and analyzing malicious software to understand its design, functionality, vulnerabilities, and how it operates. This often involves a combination of static and dynamic analysis techniques to uncover its true purpose and capabilities.

metadata.title: Honeypot
metadata.definition: A honeypot is a security mechanism, typically a decoy computer system, network, or data, designed to attract, trap, and collect information about attackers and their methods. It mimics legitimate systems to entice cybercriminals, diverting them from actual production systems and allowing for observation of their tactics.

metadata.title: Honeynet
metadata.definition: A Honeynet is a network of honeypots designed to simulate a real production network, enticing attackers to interact with it. Its primary purpose is to observe attacker behavior, gather intelligence on new threats, and develop better defensive strategies without risking actual critical systems.

metadata.title: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA)
metadata.definition: The Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) is a United States federal law that prohibits unauthorized access to protected computer systems. It primarily criminalizes activities such as accessing a computer without authorization, exceeding authorized access, and causing damage to computers or data.

metadata.title: Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA)
metadata.definition: The Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) is a United States copyright law that implements two 1996 World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) treaties. It criminalizes production and dissemination of technology, devices, or services intended to circumvent measures that control access to copyrighted works, and also heightens penalties for copyright infringement on the Internet.

metadata.title: Cybersecurity Ethics
metadata.definition: Cybersecurity Ethics refers to the moral principles and values that guide the professional conduct and decision-making of individuals and organizations in the cybersecurity domain. It addresses responsible behavior concerning data privacy, system integrity, legal compliance, and the societal impact of cybersecurity activities.

metadata.title: Responsible Disclosure
metadata.definition: Responsible Disclosure is a widely accepted practice where a security researcher privately notifies a vendor or organization about a discovered vulnerability, allowing them a reasonable amount of time to patch the issue before the vulnerability is publicly revealed. This minimizes risk to users while ensuring the flaw is addressed.

metadata.title: Bug Bounty Program
metadata.definition: A Bug Bounty Program is a formal initiative offered by many organizations that invites independent security researchers to discover and report software vulnerabilities in exchange for recognition and monetary rewards. It incentivizes responsible disclosure and leverages a broad community of ethical hackers to enhance product security.

metadata.title: Information Sharing and Analysis Organization (ISAO)
metadata.definition: An Information Sharing and Analysis Organization (ISAO) is a trusted entity that facilitates the sharing of cyber threat indicators, defensive measures, and best practices among its members, typically within a specific sector or community. ISAO's promote collaborative defense by enabling timely exchange of actionable intelligence.

metadata.title: Cyber Insurance
metadata.definition: Cyber Insurance is a specialized insurance policy designed to protect businesses and individuals from financial losses and liabilities resulting from cyber incidents such as data breaches, cyberattacks, and system disruptions. It typically covers costs related to incident response, legal fees, regulatory fines, and business interruption.

metadata.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework
metadata.definition: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) is a voluntary guidance document developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to help organizations manage and reduce cybersecurity risks. It provides a common language and systematic approach, organized into five core functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover.

metadata.title: ISO/IEC 27001
metadata.definition: ISO/IEC 27001 is an international standard that provides requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining, and continually improving an Information Security Management System (ISMS). Achieving certification demonstrates that an organization has put in place a robust system to manage information security risks and protect sensitive data.

metadata.title: NIST SP 800-53
metadata.definition: NIST SP 800-53, 'Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations', is a comprehensive catalog of security and privacy controls developed by NIST for U.S. federal information systems. It provides a baseline of controls for various impact levels and guidance on selecting, implementing, and assessing them to protect organizational operations and assets.

metadata.title: ISO/IEC 22301 (BCM)
metadata.definition: ISO/IEC 22301 is an international standard that specifies requirements for a Business Continuity Management System (BCMS) to protect an organization from disruptive incidents. It helps organizations prepare for, respond to, and recover from potential threats, ensuring the continuity of critical business functions.

metadata.title: COBIT (Security)
metadata.definition: COBIT (Control Objectives for Information and Related Technologies) is a framework for enterprise IT governance and management, which includes significant guidance on information security. While comprehensive, its security aspects focus on aligning IT security with business goals, managing security risks, and ensuring compliance through a structured approach to control objectives.

metadata.title: ITIL (Security)
metadata.definition: ITIL (Information Technology Infrastructure Library) is a widely adopted framework for IT Service Management (ITSM), which incorporates security as an integral part of its service lifecycle processes. Within ITIL, security practices ensure the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of IT services throughout their design, transition, operation, and continual improvement.

metadata.title: CIS Benchmarks
metadata.definition: CIS Benchmarks are a set of globally recognized best practices for securely configuring systems, software, and networks. Developed by the Center for Internet Security (CIS), these benchmarks provide prescriptive, consensus-based configuration guides to harden IT systems against cyber threats.

metadata.title: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE)
metadata.definition: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) is a dictionary of publicly known cybersecurity vulnerabilities and exposures. Each CVE entry is assigned a unique identifier (CVE ID), description, and references, serving as a standardized way to identify, define, and catalog specific security flaws.

metadata.title: Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE)
metadata.definition: Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) is a community-developed list of common software and hardware weakness types that can lead to security vulnerabilities. It categorizes these weaknesses to provide a common language and baseline for identifying, mitigating, and preventing flaws during design, development, and testing phases.

metadata.title: Structured Threat Information eXpression (STIX)
metadata.definition: Structured Threat Information eXpression (STIX) is a standardized, structured language for sharing cyber threat intelligence in a machine-readable format. It defines various threat components (e.g., indicators, attack patterns, threat actors) and their relationships, enabling automated analysis and exchange of threat data.

metadata.title: Trusted Automated eXchange of Indicator Information (TAXII)
metadata.definition: Trusted Automated eXchange of Indicator Information (TAXII) is a standardized protocol for exchanging cyber threat information, primarily STIX-formatted data, between trusted parties. It defines services and message exchanges to enable automated sharing of threat intelligence, allowing organizations to subscribe to and publish threat feeds securely.

metadata.title: Common Attack Pattern Enumeration and Classification (CAPEC)
metadata.definition: Common Attack Pattern Enumeration and Classification (CAPEC) is a publicly available, community-developed list of common attack patterns used by attackers to exploit weaknesses in systems. It provides a comprehensive dictionary of attack methodologies, offering insights into how vulnerabilities are exploited, which aids in threat modeling and defensive planning.

metadata.title: Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA)
metadata.definition: A structured process for identifying and assessing the privacy risks associated with new or revised projects, systems, or processes that involve the processing of personal information. Its goal is to mitigate privacy risks and ensure compliance with privacy laws and regulations.

metadata.title: Data Protection Officer (DPO)
metadata.definition: An individual appointed by an organization to oversee its data protection strategy and implementation, ensuring compliance with data protection laws like GDPR. The DPO acts as an independent advisor and point of contact for supervisory authorities and data subjects.

metadata.title: GDPR Data Subject Rights
metadata.definition: A set of fundamental rights granted to individuals (data subjects) under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) regarding the processing of their personal data. These rights empower individuals to control their data and ensure transparency and accountability from data controllers.

metadata.title: Recovery Point Objective (RPO)
metadata.definition: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured in time, that an organization can tolerate following a disaster or disruption. RPO dictates how frequently data must be backed up or replicated to ensure that data loss does not exceed this threshold.

metadata.title: Recovery Time Objective (RTO)
metadata.definition: The maximum acceptable duration of time following a disaster or disruption within which a business process or system must be restored to its operational state. RTO determines how quickly systems need to be recovered to minimize business interruption.

metadata.title: Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD)
metadata.definition: The absolute maximum length of time a business function or information system can be inoperable without causing severe, irreparable damage to the organization. MTD is a critical metric used to determine appropriate recovery strategies and allocate resources for business continuity and disaster recovery.

metadata.title: Security Metrics
metadata.definition: Quantifiable measures used to assess the effectiveness of an organization's security program, track progress over time, and identify areas for improvement. These metrics provide data-driven insights into security posture, risks, and compliance.

metadata.title: Threat Intelligence Feed
metadata.definition: A continuous stream of data providing actionable information about current and emerging threats, vulnerabilities, and attack methodologies. These feeds help organizations proactively identify, prevent, and respond to cyberattacks.

metadata.title: Open Source Threat Intelligence (OSINT)
metadata.definition: Threat intelligence gathered from publicly available sources, such as news articles, social media, public databases, security blogs, and government reports. OSINT helps security professionals understand adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and identify potential risks without proprietary tools or data.

metadata.title: Internet of Things (IoT) Security
metadata.definition: The measures and practices designed to protect Internet of Things devices, their networks, and the data they generate from unauthorized access, compromise, or manipulation. IoT security addresses unique challenges due to device diversity, limited resources, and widespread deployment.

metadata.title: Operational Technology (OT) Security
metadata.definition: The cybersecurity discipline focused on protecting hardware and software that monitors and controls physical processes, devices, and infrastructure, typically found in industrial, manufacturing, and critical infrastructure environments. OT security prioritizes safety, availability, and integrity over confidentiality due to the physical impact of attacks.
