It typically involves at least two modes: user mode, for user applications with restricted privileges, and kernel mode (or supervisor mode), for the OS kernel with full hardware access and unrestricted privileges.

metadata.title: Protection Rings
metadata.definition: Protection rings are a hierarchical privilege level system used by hardware to protect system resources and prevent unauthorized access by software. The rings determine which operations a program is allowed to perform, with lower ring numbers typically indicating higher privileges.

metadata.title: Privileged Instructions
metadata.definition: Privileged instructions are CPU instructions that can only be executed by the operating system kernel or other highly privileged software when operating in a privileged mode (e.g., kernel mode). Their execution in user mode would result in a protection fault.

metadata.title: Non-privileged Instructions
metadata.definition: Non-privileged instructions are CPU instructions that can be executed by any program, including user-level applications, without requiring special permissions or operating in a privileged mode.

metadata.title: System Boot Process
metadata.definition: The system boot process is the sequence of operations performed by a computer from the moment it is powered on until the operating system is fully loaded and ready for user interaction.

metadata.title: BIOS (Basic Input/Output System)
metadata.definition: BIOS is legacy firmware stored on a motherboard's non-volatile memory, responsible for performing basic hardware initialization during the boot process and providing basic runtime services for the operating system.

metadata.title: UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface)
metadata.definition: UEFI is a modern firmware interface that replaces BIOS, offering advanced features like secure boot, support for larger disk partitions (GPT), network capabilities, and a more flexible pre-boot environment.

metadata.title: Firmware
metadata.definition: Firmware is a specific class of computer software that provides low-level control for a device's specific hardware, often embedded directly into hardware components or non-volatile memory.

metadata.title: Init System
metadata.definition: An init system is the first process started by the kernel (Process ID 1) in a Unix-like operating system, responsible for initializing the rest of the operating system services and managing them throughout the system's runtime.

metadata.title: systemd (Linux Init System)
metadata.definition: systemd is a modern, backward-compatible init system and service manager for Linux operating systems, designed to aggressively parallelize services, start them on demand, and manage their dependencies.

metadata.title: Service Manager
metadata.definition: A service manager is a component of an operating system responsible for starting, stopping, and managing system services (often called daemons) and other background processes.

metadata.title: Process Definition
metadata.definition: A process is an instance of a computer program that is being executed, comprising the program code, its current activity (program counter, registers), and its associated resources such as memory, open files, and I/O devices.

metadata.title: Process State
metadata.definition: Process state refers to the current condition or phase a process is in during its lifecycle, as perceived by the operating system's scheduler.

metadata.title: Process Creation
metadata.definition: Process creation is the act of bringing a new process into existence, typically initiated by an existing process (the parent) or by the operating system itself.

metadata.title: Process Termination
metadata.definition: Process termination is the act of ending a process's execution and releasing all its allocated resources, such as memory and open files, back to the operating system.

metadata.title: Zombie Process
metadata.definition: A zombie process is a process that has completed its execution but still has an entry in the process table because its parent process has not yet read its exit status.

metadata.title: Orphan Process
metadata.definition: An orphan process is a process whose parent process has terminated without waiting for its child processes to finish their execution.

metadata.title: Fork System Call
metadata.definition: The `fork()` system call creates a new process (the child process) by duplicating the calling process (the parent process), with both processes continuing execution from the point of the `fork()` call, but with distinct memory spaces.

metadata.title: Exec System Call
metadata.definition: The `exec()` system call (or family of calls like `execve`, `execl`) replaces the current process's memory space and program with a new program specified by its arguments, without creating a new process ID.

metadata.title: Wait System Call
metadata.definition: The `wait()` system call causes the calling parent process to pause its execution until one of its child processes terminates, allowing the parent to retrieve the child's exit status and prevent it from becoming a zombie.

metadata.title: Exit System Call
metadata.definition: The `exit()` system call is used to explicitly terminate the calling process, releasing its allocated resources back to the operating system and returning an exit status code to its parent process.

metadata.title: Thread Definition
metadata.definition: A thread is the smallest unit of processing that can be scheduled by an operating system, representing a single sequence of execution within a process. Threads within the same process share the same memory space, code, and resources but have their own program counter, stack, and register set. This allows for concurrent execution paths within a single application.

metadata.title: User-Level Threads
metadata.definition: User-level threads (ULTs) are managed entirely by the user-level thread library without kernel involvement. The kernel is unaware of the existence of ULTs and sees only the process as a single thread of control. This makes thread creation and management fast, but if one ULT blocks, the entire process blocks.

metadata.title: Kernel-Level Threads
metadata.definition: Kernel-level threads (KLTs) are managed and scheduled directly by the operating system kernel. The kernel maintains context information for each thread and handles thread creation, scheduling, and synchronization. This allows multiple threads within the same process to run concurrently on different CPUs and ensures that if one thread blocks, other threads in the same process can continue executing.

metadata.title: Many-to-One Thread Model
metadata.definition: The Many-to-One model maps many user-level threads to a single kernel-level thread. Thread management is handled by the user-level thread library. While efficient for thread creation and context switching within the application, a major drawback is that if one user-level thread performs a blocking system call, the entire process, including all other user threads, will block.

metadata.title: One-to-One Thread Model
metadata.definition: The One-to-One model maps each user-level thread directly to a kernel-level thread. This provides more concurrency as it allows multiple threads to run in parallel on multiprocessor systems and prevents one thread from blocking the entire process with a blocking system call. However, this model has more overhead in terms of creating and managing threads compared to user-level models.

metadata.title: Many-to-Many Thread Model
metadata.definition: The Many-to-Many model multiplexes many user-level threads onto a smaller or equal number of kernel-level threads. This model aims to combine the benefits of both User-Level and Kernel-Level threads, allowing for efficient creation of user threads while enabling true concurrency and avoiding the blocking problem. The operating system dynamically adjusts the number of kernel threads based on application needs.

metadata.title: Thread Creation
metadata.definition: Thread creation is the process of generating a new independent path of execution within an existing process. This involves allocating a new thread ID, program counter, register set, and a stack, and then making the new thread ready for scheduling by the operating system. Threads can be created explicitly by an application or implicitly by a runtime system.

metadata.title: Thread Termination
metadata.definition: Thread termination is the process by which a thread completes its execution and is removed from the system. A thread can terminate either implicitly by returning from its starting function or explicitly by calling a termination routine. Upon termination, resources allocated specifically to the thread, such as its stack, are reclaimed by the system.

metadata.title: Thread Synchronization
metadata.definition: Thread synchronization refers to the coordination of multiple threads to ensure proper execution ordering and consistent access to shared resources. It is essential to prevent data corruption and race conditions that can arise when threads concurrently modify shared data or depend on specific execution sequences. Mechanisms like locks, semaphores, and condition variables are used for this purpose.

metadata.title: Mutual Exclusion (Synchronization)
metadata.definition: Mutual exclusion is a synchronization property that ensures that only one thread or process can access a shared resource or critical section at any given time. This mechanism prevents race conditions and data inconsistency by serializing access to protected data structures or code segments. It is a fundamental requirement for correct concurrent programming.

metadata.title: Semaphores
metadata.definition: A semaphore is a signaling mechanism used for thread synchronization that maintains an integer value. It provides two atomic operations: `wait` (also known as `P` or `down`), which decrements the semaphore value and blocks if it's zero; and `signal` (also known as `V` or `up`), which increments the value and potentially unblocks a waiting thread. Semaphores can be counting (for resource management) or binary (acting as a mutex).

metadata.title: Mutex Lock
metadata.definition: A mutex (short for mutual exclusion) lock is a synchronization primitive that grants exclusive access to a shared resource to only one thread at a time. A thread acquires the lock before entering a critical section and releases it upon exiting, ensuring that no other thread can access the protected resource concurrently. If another thread tries to acquire an already locked mutex, it will block until the lock is released.

metadata.title: Deadlock Definition
metadata.definition: Deadlock is a situation in a multiprocessing system where two or more competing actions are perpetually waiting for each other to finish, such that none ever complete. It typically occurs when multiple threads or processes each hold resources and request resources held by others, forming a circular chain of dependencies.

metadata.title: Mutual Exclusion (Deadlock Condition)
metadata.definition: Mutual exclusion, as a condition for deadlock, states that at least one resource must be held in a non-sharable mode; that is, only one process at a time can use the resource. If another process requests that resource, the requesting process must be delayed until the resource has been released. This condition is inherent for resources that cannot be simultaneously shared.

metadata.title: Hold and Wait (Deadlock Condition)
metadata.definition: Hold and Wait, as a condition for deadlock, states that a process must be holding at least one resource and simultaneously waiting to acquire additional resources that are currently being held by other processes. This creates a scenario where processes are reluctant to release resources they already possess while waiting for others.

metadata.title: No Preemption (Deadlock Condition)
metadata.definition: No Preemption, as a condition for deadlock, states that resources cannot be forcibly taken away from a process that is holding them. A resource can only be released voluntarily by the process that is holding it, after that process has completed its task with that resource. This means that once a resource is allocated, it remains with the process until explicitly released.

metadata.title: Circular Wait (Deadlock Condition)
metadata.definition: Circular Wait, as a condition for deadlock, states that a set of processes {P0, P1, ..., Pn} must exist such that P0 is waiting for a resource held by P1, P1 is waiting for a resource held by P2, ..., Pn-1 is waiting for a resource held by Pn, and Pn is waiting for a resource held by P0. This forms a closed chain of resource dependencies.

metadata.title: Starvation (Synchronization)
metadata.definition: Starvation is a problem in concurrent systems where a process or thread is perpetually denied access to a resource or CPU time, even though the resource periodically becomes available. This often happens due to unfair scheduling policies or biased resource allocation, where other processes are always chosen over the "starving" one. Unlike deadlock, the system is not necessarily stuck, but one or more specific entities never make progress.

metadata.title: Pipes (IPC)
metadata.definition: Pipes are a form of inter-process communication (IPC) that allow unidirectional data flow between two related processes, typically a parent and child process. Data written to one end of the pipe is buffered by the operating system and can be read from the other end. They are a simple and effective mechanism for processes to exchange small amounts of data.

metadata.title: Named Pipes (FIFOs)
metadata.definition: Named pipes, also known as FIFOs (First-In, First-Out), are a type of inter-process communication (IPC) mechanism that allow two or more unrelated processes to communicate by reading and writing to a special file on the filesystem. Unlike regular pipes, named pipes have a directory entry, persist until explicitly deleted, and enable communication between processes that do not share a common ancestor.

metadata.title: Message Queues (IPC)
metadata.definition: A list of messages stored within the kernel, allowing processes to send and receive data asynchronously. Each message has a type, and processes can selectively read messages based on type, facilitating structured communication between unrelated processes.

metadata.title: Sockets (IPC)
metadata.definition: An endpoint for sending and receiving data across a network or between processes on the same machine. Sockets enable bidirectional communication, supporting various protocols like TCP and UDP, and are fundamental for network programming.

metadata.title: Signals (IPC)
metadata.definition: A limited form of inter-process communication used to notify a process of an event. Signals are asynchronous notifications sent to a process, interrupting its normal flow of execution to handle specific events like termination requests or errors.

metadata.title: SIGKILL Signal
metadata.definition: A unblockable and uncatchable signal that forcefully terminates a process immediately. It is considered the most severe signal because the target process cannot ignore it or perform any cleanup actions before exiting.

metadata.title: SIGTERM Signal
metadata.definition: A standard signal used to request a process to terminate gracefully. Unlike SIGKILL, SIGTERM can be caught, ignored, or handled by a process, allowing it to perform cleanup tasks like saving data or closing files before exiting.

metadata.title: Process Group
metadata.definition: A collection of one or more related processes, typically created by the same job, that can be managed together by the operating system. All processes in a group share a common process group ID (PGID) and can receive signals as a unit.

metadata.title: Session Leader
metadata.definition: The process that creates a new session, typically a shell or login process. The session leader serves as the anchor for a collection of process groups, and its termination often triggers the termination of all associated processes in the session (orphaning them).

metadata.title: Process Scheduling
metadata.definition: The activity of the operating system to manage and allocate the CPU time among competing processes. It determines which process runs when, for how long, and in what order, aiming to optimize system performance metrics like throughput, response time, and fairness.

metadata.title: Scheduler (OS Component)
metadata.definition: The operating system component responsible for selecting which ready process should be executed by the CPU next. It implements various scheduling algorithms to efficiently manage CPU resources, deciding when to switch processes and which one to run.

metadata.title: Long-Term Scheduler
metadata.definition: Also known as the job scheduler, it selects processes from the job pool and loads them into memory for execution. It controls the degree of multiprogramming by deciding which new jobs are admitted into the system, aiming to achieve a good mix of I/O-bound and CPU-bound processes.

metadata.title: Short-Term Scheduler (CPU Scheduler)
metadata.definition: Responsible for selecting one of the processes that are in the ready queue to be executed by the CPU next. It executes very frequently (milliseconds), making fine-grained decisions about which process gets the CPU next, aiming for rapid context switching and low latency.

metadata.title: Medium-Term Scheduler (Swapper)
metadata.definition: Primarily responsible for swapping processes out of memory and onto disk (and vice-versa) to reduce the degree of multiprogramming or free up memory. It improves system performance by temporarily removing processes from active contention for the CPU when memory is scarce.

metadata.title: Dispatcher (OS Component)
metadata.definition: The module that gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler. Its functions include context switching, switching to user mode, and jumping to the proper location in the user program to restart execution.

metadata.title: Non-Preemptive Scheduling
metadata.definition: A scheduling approach where, once a process starts executing, it continues to run until it voluntarily yields the CPU, blocks for an I/O operation, or terminates. The currently running process cannot be interrupted by the scheduler for another higher-priority or time-sliced process.

metadata.title: Shortest Job Next (SJN) Scheduling
metadata.definition: A non-preemptive scheduling algorithm that selects the process with the smallest estimated execution time (CPU burst) to run next. It minimizes the average waiting time for a given set of processes, but requires accurate prediction of future CPU burst times.

metadata.title: Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) Scheduling
metadata.definition: A preemptive version of Shortest Job Next (SJN), where the scheduler always selects the process with the shortest remaining execution time. If a new process arrives with a shorter remaining time than the currently executing process, the current process is preempted.

metadata.title: Round Robin (RR) Scheduling
metadata.definition: A preemptive scheduling algorithm designed for time-sharing systems, where each process is given a small unit of CPU time, called a time quantum or time slice, in a cyclic order. Once the quantum expires, the process is preempted and added to the end of the ready queue.

metadata.title: Multi-level Queue Scheduling
metadata.definition: A scheduling approach that partitions the ready queue into several separate queues, each with its own scheduling algorithm. Processes are permanently assigned to a specific queue based on characteristics like process type (e.g., foreground, background, real-time).

metadata.title: Multi-level Feedback Queue Scheduling
metadata.definition: A more flexible version of multi-level queue scheduling that allows processes to move between queues based on their behavior or age. It typically uses multiple queues with different time quanta and priority levels, promoting I/O-bound and interactive processes while demoting CPU-bound ones.

metadata.title: CPU Utilization (Scheduling Metric)
metadata.definition: A scheduling metric that measures the percentage of time the CPU is busy executing processes. High CPU utilization indicates that the CPU is being effectively used, but it must be balanced with other metrics like response time to avoid system sluggishness.

metadata.title: Throughput (Scheduling Metric)
metadata.definition: The total number of processes or tasks completed per unit of time by the CPU scheduler. It measures the rate at which the system successfully finishes work.

metadata.title: Turnaround Time (Scheduling Metric)
metadata.definition: The total time elapsed from the submission of a process until its completion. This includes time spent waiting in the ready queue, executing on the CPU, and performing I/O operations.

metadata.title: Waiting Time (Scheduling Metric)
metadata.definition: The total amount of time a process spends waiting in the ready queue for the CPU to become available. This metric excludes time spent executing or performing I/O.

metadata.title: Response Time (Scheduling Metric)
metadata.definition: The time interval from when a request is submitted until the first response is produced. It is a critical metric for interactive systems, indicating the perceived responsiveness to a user.

metadata.title: Affinity Scheduling
metadata.definition: A scheduling technique where a process or thread, once assigned to a specific CPU core, is preferentially scheduled on that same core in subsequent executions. This strategy leverages CPU cache locality to improve performance by reducing cache misses.

metadata.title: Load Balancing (Scheduling)
metadata.definition: The process of distributing workload evenly across multiple processing units (CPUs, cores, or machines) to maximize resource utilization, minimize response times, and prevent any single unit from becoming a bottleneck.

metadata.title: Thread Pools
metadata.definition: A collection of pre-instantiated, idle threads that are available to execute a queue of incoming tasks. This design avoids the overhead of creating and destroying threads for each new task, thereby improving performance and resource management.

metadata.title: Work-stealing (Scheduling)
metadata.definition: A dynamic load-balancing technique where an idle processor (the 'stealer') actively seeks and 'steals' tasks from the task queue of an overburdened processor (the 'victim'). This helps to efficiently distribute work in parallel computing environments.

metadata.title: Symmetric Multi-Processing (SMP)
metadata.definition: An architecture where two or more identical processors are connected to a single shared main memory and controlled by a single operating system. All processors can execute any task and share resources symmetrically.

metadata.title: Hyperthreading (Simultaneous Multi-threading)
metadata.definition: A technology that enables a single physical CPU core to execute multiple independent threads concurrently by duplicating architectural state (e.g., registers) while sharing most of the core's execution resources. This makes a single physical core appear as multiple logical processors to the operating system.

metadata.title: CPU Caching (OS Perspective)
metadata.definition: From an OS perspective, CPU caching involves the operating system's efforts to utilize and manage CPU caches (L1, L2, L3) effectively by strategically placing data and instructions in memory. While hardware physically manages the cache, the OS's memory management, scheduling, and process layout decisions significantly impact cache performance by influencing cache hit rates.

metadata.title: Cache Coherence Protocol
metadata.definition: A mechanism that ensures data consistency across all processor caches and main memory in a multi-processor system. It defines a set of rules and states for cache lines to guarantee that all processors have a unified and up-to-date view of shared memory.

metadata.title: MESI Protocol
metadata.definition: A widely adopted write-invalidate cache coherence protocol that defines four states for each cache line: Modified (M), Exclusive (E), Shared (S), and Invalid (I). These states dictate how a cache line can be read, written, or shared among multiple processor caches to maintain data consistency in a multi-processor system.

metadata.title: Address Binding
metadata.definition: The process of mapping logical addresses, generated by the CPU, to corresponding physical addresses in main memory. This binding can occur at compile time, load time, or execution time, with execution-time binding offering the most flexibility for dynamic memory management.

metadata.title: Relocation Register
metadata.definition: A hardware register, also known as a base register, that stores the starting physical address of a process's assigned memory partition. Every logical address generated by the CPU is added to the value in the relocation register to produce the actual physical address, providing memory protection and address translation.

metadata.title: Limit Register
metadata.definition: A hardware register that specifies the size or the maximum valid logical address range for a process. Any logical address generated by the CPU must be less than the value in the limit register; otherwise, a memory access violation (trap) is generated, enforcing memory protection boundaries.

metadata.title: Contiguous Memory Allocation
metadata.definition: A memory management scheme where each process is allocated a single, unbroken block of main memory. While simple to implement, this approach can suffer from external fragmentation, where available memory is scattered in small, unusable chunks.

metadata.title: First-Fit Memory Allocation
metadata.definition: A dynamic memory allocation algorithm that allocates the first available memory block (hole) from the beginning of the free list that is large enough to satisfy a process's request. It is simple and relatively fast but can lead to internal and external fragmentation.

metadata.title: Best-Fit Memory Allocation
metadata.definition: A dynamic memory allocation algorithm that searches the entire list of free memory blocks (holes) and allocates the smallest hole that is large enough to satisfy a process's request. This strategy aims to minimize the amount of wasted space (external fragmentation) left after allocation.

metadata.title: Worst-Fit Memory Allocation
metadata.definition: A dynamic memory allocation algorithm that searches the entire list of free memory blocks (holes) and allocates the largest available hole to satisfy a process's request. The goal is to leave a remaining large enough hole that might be useful for future, potentially larger, requests.

metadata.title: Non-Contiguous Memory Allocation
metadata.definition: A memory allocation scheme where a process's logical address space is mapped to physical memory that is not necessarily contiguous, allowing a process to be spread across different, non-adjacent physical memory blocks. This approach efficiently utilizes physical memory by avoiding external fragmentation and allowing larger logical address spaces than available contiguous physical memory.

metadata.title: Hierarchical Paging
metadata.definition: A paging technique used to manage very large logical address spaces by breaking the page table itself into smaller, more manageable page tables, typically forming a multi-level structure (e.g., two-level paging). This reduces the memory required for the page table by only allocating parts of the inner page tables that are actively in use.

metadata.title: Hashed Page Table
metadata.definition: A page table structure designed for address spaces larger than 32 bits, particularly sparse ones, where a hash function maps virtual page numbers to entries in a hash table. This method significantly reduces the memory overhead compared to traditional linear page tables by only storing entries for active virtual pages.

metadata.title: Inverted Page Table
metadata.definition: A page table structure that maintains a single entry for each physical memory frame, rather than an entry for each virtual page for each process. Each entry stores the virtual page number and process ID that currently occupies that physical frame.

metadata.title: Shared Pages
metadata.definition: Physical memory pages that are mapped into the address spaces of multiple distinct processes, allowing them to access the same code or data. This technique reduces overall memory usage and facilitates efficient inter-process communication.

metadata.title: Copy-on-Write (COW)
metadata.definition: A resource management optimization technique where resources (e.g., memory pages) are initially shared between processes until one of them attempts to modify the resource. At that point, a private copy of the modified resource is created for the modifying process, while others continue to share the original.

metadata.title: Segmentation
metadata.definition: A memory management scheme that divides a process's logical address space into logically meaningful, variable-sized units called segments. Each segment corresponds to a specific program component, such as code, data, or stack, offering modularity and enhanced protection.

metadata.title: Segment Table
metadata.definition: A table used in segmentation to map logical segment addresses to physical memory addresses, containing an entry for each segment owned by a process. Each entry typically specifies the segment's base address in physical memory and its limit (size), along with protection information.

metadata.title: Segment Table Entry (STE)
metadata.definition: An individual entry within a Segment Table, which describes a single memory segment. It typically includes the physical base address where the segment begins, its length or limit (size), and protection bits indicating allowed access types (e.g., read, write, execute).

metadata.title: Page Fault Rate
metadata.definition: The frequency or percentage of memory accesses that result in a page fault, indicating how often a requested virtual page is not found in physical memory and must be retrieved from secondary storage. A high page fault rate can significantly degrade system performance due to increased disk I/O.

metadata.title: Effective Access Time (EAT)
metadata.definition: The average time taken to access a memory location, calculated by considering the probabilities and access times of different memory levels, such as main memory and secondary storage in a paged virtual memory system. It quantifies the performance impact of page faults.

metadata.title: Working Set Model
metadata.definition: A memory management model that attempts to keep in physical memory the set of pages that a process is actively using, defined as the set of pages referenced by a process during a specific time window (the working-set window). The goal is to prevent thrashing by ensuring processes have enough memory for their current needs.

metadata.title: Optimal Page Replacement (OPT)
metadata.definition: A theoretical page replacement algorithm that replaces the page that will not be used for the longest period of time in the future. Although impossible to implement in practice because it requires future knowledge, it serves as a benchmark to evaluate the efficiency of other page replacement algorithms.

metadata.title: First-In, First-Out (FIFO) Page Replacement
metadata.definition: A page replacement algorithm that evicts the page that has been in physical memory for the longest time, treating pages like a simple queue. It is easy to implement but often suffers from poor performance because it ignores the actual usage frequency or recency of pages.

metadata.title: Least Recently Used (LRU) Page Replacement
metadata.definition: A page replacement algorithm that replaces the page that has not been accessed for the longest period of time, based on the principle of locality that pages used recently are likely to be used again soon. LRU generally performs well but is complex to implement efficiently, often requiring hardware support.

metadata.title: Clock Page Replacement Algorithm
metadata.definition: A practical approximation of LRU that uses a reference bit for each page frame, arranged in a circular list. When a page needs replacement, the algorithm scans the list, clearing reference bits until it finds a page with a cleared bit, which it then replaces.

metadata.title: Second Chance Page Replacement
metadata.definition: An improvement over FIFO that gives a page a 'second chance' before being replaced; if the page at the head of the FIFO queue has its reference bit set, the bit is cleared, and the page is moved to the tail of the queue, effectively postponing its replacement. This is conceptually identical to the Clock algorithm.

metadata.title: Belady's Anomaly
metadata.definition: A counter-intuitive phenomenon observed in some page replacement algorithms (most notably FIFO) where increasing the number of available physical memory frames can, under certain specific page reference strings, lead to an increase in the number of page faults. This indicates that more memory doesn't always guarantee better performance.

metadata.title: Frame Allocation
metadata.definition: The process by which the operating system decides how many physical memory frames to allocate to each running process and how to distribute those frames among the processes. This decision impacts overall system performance and the potential for thrashing.

metadata.title: Global Page Replacement
metadata.definition: A page replacement policy where any page in physical memory can be selected for replacement, regardless of which process currently owns it. The replacement decision is made based on the system-wide set of resident pages, aiming to optimize overall system throughput.

metadata.title: Local Page Replacement
metadata.definition: A page replacement strategy where each process is allocated a fixed or variable number of memory frames, and it can only replace pages within its own allocated set of frames. This prevents a process from stealing frames from other processes and potentially impacting their performance unfairly.

metadata.title: Memory-Mapped Files
metadata.definition: A technique that maps a file directly into a process's virtual address space, allowing the file's content to be accessed as if it were an in-memory array. This bypasses traditional read/write system calls, enabling faster I/O and shared memory functionality.

metadata.title: Prepaging
metadata.definition: A page replacement strategy where the operating system attempts to predict which pages a process will need next and loads them into memory before they are explicitly referenced. This proactive approach aims to reduce the number of page faults and improve application performance.

metadata.title: Executable Space Protection (NX bit, DEP)
metadata.definition: A security feature that marks certain memory regions (like the stack or heap) as non-executable, preventing code from being run from these data segments. This mitigates various types of exploits, such as buffer overflows, that attempt to inject and execute malicious code.

metadata.title: Stack Overflow Protection
metadata.definition: Mechanisms designed to detect and prevent stack overflows, which occur when a program writes beyond the allocated bounds of the call stack. These protections help guard against program crashes and security vulnerabilities that can arise from stack-based buffer overflows.

metadata.title: Heap Overflow Protection
metadata.definition: Techniques used to detect and mitigate heap overflows, which happen when a program writes beyond the boundary of a dynamically allocated buffer on the heap. These protections are crucial for preventing data corruption, crashes, and security exploits targeting heap-allocated memory.

metadata.title: Buddy System Memory Allocation
metadata.definition: A memory allocation algorithm that divides memory into blocks whose sizes are powers of two. When a request for memory is made, the smallest available block large enough to satisfy the request is found; if it's too large, it's recursively split into two 'buddies' until an appropriately sized block is formed.

metadata.title: Memory Tagging (ARM MTE)
metadata.definition: A hardware-assisted memory safety feature, exemplified by ARM Memory Tagging Extension (MTE), that assigns a small, cryptographically strong tag to both memory allocations and corresponding pointers. It detects memory errors like spatial (buffer overflows) and temporal (use-after-free) violations by comparing pointer tags with memory tags upon access.

metadata.title: File Definition
metadata.definition: A file is a named collection of related information, typically stored on non-volatile storage, that an operating system treats as a single logical unit. It serves as the basic unit for persistent data storage and retrieval.

metadata.title: File Attributes
metadata.definition: Metadata associated with a file that describes its characteristics and properties, stored separately from the file's actual data content. These attributes are used by the operating system and applications to manage and access files.

metadata.title: File Operations
metadata.definition: The set of system calls and functionalities provided by the operating system for processes to interact with files. These operations allow applications to create, delete, manipulate, and access the content of files.

metadata.title: File Types
metadata.definition: Categories of files distinguished by their structure, content, and intended use, which helps the operating system and applications determine how to interpret and interact with them. File types can be identified by extensions, magic numbers, or internal metadata.

metadata.title: Directory Definition
metadata.definition: A special type of file that serves as a container or index, organizing the file system hierarchy by mapping human-readable names to the locations of other files and subdirectories. Directories are crucial for navigating and structuring persistent storage.

metadata.title: Directory Operations
metadata.definition: The set of system calls and functions provided by the operating system for managing directories. These operations allow users and programs to create, delete, rename, list the contents of, and navigate through the hierarchical file system structure.

metadata.title: Tree-Structured Directory
metadata.definition: A hierarchical directory structure where all files and directories are organized in a tree-like fashion, starting from a single root directory. In this model, every file and subdirectory (except the root) has exactly one parent directory, ensuring a clear and intuitive organization.

metadata.title: Acyclic-Graph Directory
metadata.definition: A directory structure that extends the tree-structured model by allowing files or subdirectories to have multiple parent directories through the use of links (e.g., hard links or symbolic links), forming a directed acyclic graph. This enables sharing of files and directories without creating cycles.

metadata.title: File System Structure
metadata.definition: The overall organization and layout of data on secondary storage, defining how files and directories are stored, managed, and accessed. This includes the logical structure visible to users and applications, as well as the physical layout of metadata and data blocks on the disk.

metadata.title: Boot Control Block (Volume Boot Record)
metadata.definition: A critical sector or block on a storage device (e.g., disk partition) that contains bootstrap code and information necessary to load an operating system. It is the first block of a partitioned volume and is read by the system's firmware during the boot process.

metadata.title: Volume Control Block (Superblock)
metadata.definition: A data structure found at a fixed and well-known location on a file system volume (e.g., a disk partition) that contains essential metadata about the entire file system. It describes the file system's overall properties, such as its type, size, block counts, and pointers to free block and inode lists.

metadata.title: File Control Block (Inode)
metadata.definition: A data structure maintained by the operating system that stores all metadata about a specific file or directory, excluding its actual name and data content. It contains crucial information such as file type, permissions, owner, timestamps, and pointers to the disk blocks where the file's data is physically stored.

metadata.title: Contiguous Allocation (File)
metadata.definition: Contiguous allocation stores each file as a single contiguous block of disk addresses, meaning all its data blocks are physically adjacent on the disk. This method offers excellent read performance for sequential access but suffers from external fragmentation and difficulty in file growth.

metadata.title: Linked Allocation (File)
metadata.definition: Linked allocation stores a file as a linked list of disk blocks, where each block contains a pointer to the next block in the file. This method eliminates external fragmentation and allows dynamic file growth but suffers from poor random access performance and potential reliability issues if a pointer is corrupted.

metadata.title: Indexed Allocation (File)
metadata.definition: Indexed allocation stores all pointers to a file's data blocks in a single, dedicated index block (or multiple blocks for large files). This method provides direct access to any block, supports dynamic file growth, and avoids external fragmentation, making it the most common allocation scheme for modern file systems.

metadata.title: Block Size (File System)
metadata.definition: Block size refers to the fixed-size unit of data that a file system reads from or writes to the disk. Choosing an appropriate block size impacts disk space utilization (internal fragmentation), I/O performance, and the maximum file system size.

metadata.title: Disk Space Allocation
metadata.definition: Disk space allocation is the process by which an operating system determines where on a storage device a file's data blocks are physically stored. The primary goal is to efficiently utilize available disk space while providing acceptable file access performance.

metadata.title: Free Space Management
metadata.definition: Free space management is the operating system's mechanism for keeping track of which disk blocks are available for allocation to new files or for extending existing ones. Effective free space management is crucial for preventing data loss and ensuring efficient disk utilization.

metadata.title: Bit Vector (Free Space)
metadata.definition: A bit vector, also known as a bitmap, is a simple and efficient data structure used for free space management where each bit in the vector corresponds to a disk block. A bit value of '0' typically indicates a free block, and '1' indicates an allocated block, or vice-versa.

metadata.title: Linked List (Free Space)
metadata.definition: A linked list method for free space management maintains a list of all free disk blocks, where each free block contains a pointer to the next free block. While simple, traversing the list to find a suitable block can be slow, especially on large disks with scattered free space.

metadata.title: FCFS Disk Scheduling
metadata.definition: FCFS (First-Come, First-Served) disk scheduling processes disk I/O requests in the order they arrive in the queue. It is fair to all requests and simple to implement but often results in inefficient disk arm movement, leading to poor average seek time and throughput.

metadata.title: SSTF Disk Scheduling
metadata.definition: SSTF (Shortest Seek Time First) disk scheduling services the request that is closest to the current head position. This algorithm minimizes the total seek time and improves throughput but can lead to starvation for requests far from the current head, as the head might repeatedly service closer requests.

metadata.title: SCAN Disk Scheduling (Elevator)
metadata.definition: SCAN disk scheduling, also known as the elevator algorithm, moves the disk arm in one direction, servicing all requests in its path, until it reaches the end of the disk. It then reverses direction and services requests while moving back, effectively preventing starvation compared to SSTF.

metadata.title: C-SCAN Disk Scheduling
metadata.definition: C-SCAN (Circular SCAN) disk scheduling is a variation of SCAN where the disk arm moves in only one direction (e.g., inwards), servicing requests, and upon reaching the end, it immediately jumps back to the beginning of the disk without servicing any requests on the return trip. This provides more uniform wait times by reducing the variance in seek times.

metadata.title: LOOK Disk Scheduling
metadata.definition: LOOK disk scheduling is a refinement of the SCAN algorithm where the disk arm only moves as far as the last request in the current direction before reversing. Instead of going all the way to the end of the disk, it 'looks' for pending requests and only travels to the outermost pending request, reducing unnecessary arm movement.

metadata.title: Rotational Latency
metadata.definition: Rotational latency is the time it takes for the desired sector of a disk track to rotate under the read/write head after the head has been positioned over the correct track. It is a significant component of disk access time and is inversely proportional to the disk's rotational speed (RPM).

metadata.title: Seek Time
metadata.definition: Seek time is the time it takes for the read/write head of a hard disk drive to move from its current position to the track containing the desired data. It is the dominant factor in disk access time for hard drives and heavily influenced by disk scheduling algorithms.

metadata.title: Transfer Time
metadata.definition: Transfer time is the actual time required to move data between the disk's surface and the disk controller, once the read/write head is positioned over the correct sector. It depends on the amount of data being transferred and the disk's data transfer rate.

metadata.title: Disk Formatting
metadata.definition: Disk formatting is the process of preparing a data storage device for initial use, which typically involves two main parts: low-level formatting (creating tracks, sectors, and control structures) and high-level formatting (creating a file system structure and sometimes a boot sector).

metadata.title: Bad Blocks
metadata.definition: Bad blocks are sectors on a hard disk drive that are permanently damaged and can no longer reliably store data. Modern disk drives typically manage bad blocks by remapping them to spare sectors, preventing data loss, though an increasing number of bad blocks can indicate imminent drive failure.

metadata.title: RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks)
metadata.definition: RAID is a data storage virtualization technology that combines multiple physical disk drives into a single logical unit to improve performance, provide data redundancy, or both. Different RAID levels offer varying trade-offs between cost, reliability, and performance.

metadata.title: RAID Level 5 (Striping with Distributed Parity)
metadata.definition: RAID Level 5 stripes data across multiple disk drives and distributes parity information among all drives in the array. This setup provides fault tolerance against a single drive failure and offers good read performance, making it a popular choice for many servers.

metadata.title: File System Journaling
metadata.definition: File system journaling is a technique used by file systems to ensure data consistency and quick recovery after a system crash or power failure by first writing metadata changes to a special log (journal) before committing them to the main file system structures.

metadata.title: Log-Structured File System (LFS)
metadata.definition: A Log-Structured File System (LFS) treats the disk as a continuous log, writing all changes (data and metadata) sequentially to the end of the log to optimize for write performance, especially for small, random writes.

metadata.title: SMB/CIFS (Server Message Block / Common Internet File System)
metadata.definition: SMB (Server Message Block), historically known as CIFS (Common Internet File System), is a network file sharing protocol that allows client applications to read, write, and manage files on remote servers, as well as perform inter-process communication.

metadata.title: HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System)
metadata.definition: HDFS is a distributed file system designed to run on commodity hardware, providing high-throughput access to application data and excellent fault tolerance, making it suitable for very large datasets and big data applications like Apache Hadoop.

metadata.title: ZFS (Zettabyte File System)
metadata.definition: ZFS is a combined file system and logical volume manager known for its massive scalability, data integrity features (checksumming, self-healing), snapshotting, and integrated data protection capabilities like RAID-Z.

metadata.title: Btrfs (B-tree file system)
metadata.definition: Btrfs is a modern Linux copy-on-write (CoW) file system that aims to implement advanced features like snapshots, checksums, integrated volume management, and self-healing capabilities, leveraging B-trees for all data and metadata structures.

metadata.title: EXT4 File System
metadata.definition: EXT4 (Fourth Extended File System) is a widely used journaling file system for Linux, offering improved performance, reliability, and capacity over its predecessors (EXT2/EXT3) through features like extents, larger file system support, and faster fsck.

metadata.title: NTFS File System
metadata.definition: NTFS (New Technology File System) is the primary file system for Microsoft Windows operating systems, known for its security features, journaling, support for large files and partitions, and capabilities like file compression and encryption.

metadata.title: Inode (File System)
metadata.definition: An inode (index node) is a data structure in Unix-like file systems that stores all metadata about a file or directory, such as ownership, permissions, timestamps, and pointers to the disk blocks containing the actual data, but not its name or directory path.

metadata.title: Directory Entry
metadata.definition: A directory entry is a structure within a directory that maps a human-readable file or directory name to its corresponding inode number (or other file identifier) on the file system, acting as a pointer to the file's metadata and data.

metadata.title: Symbolic Link (Symlink)
metadata.definition: A symbolic link, or soft link, is a special type of file that contains a text string which is interpreted as a path to another file or directory, acting as an indirect pointer or alias to its target.

metadata.title: Hard Link
metadata.definition: A hard link is a directory entry that directly points to an existing inode, meaning multiple hard links can exist for the same file data and metadata on disk, and all links are equally valid ways to access the file.

metadata.title: Unix Permissions (rwx)
metadata.definition: Unix permissions define access rights for files and directories using read (r), write (w), and execute (x) attributes, applicable to three distinct categories: the file owner, the group owner, and all other users.

metadata.title: Set-UID bit
metadata.definition: The Set-UID (Set User ID) bit is a special permission bit on executable files in Unix-like systems; when set, it causes the program to run with the privileges of the file's owner, rather than the privileges of the user executing it.

metadata.title: Set-GID bit
metadata.definition: The Set-GID (Set Group ID) bit is a special permission bit with dual functions in Unix-like systems: for executable files, it runs the program with the file's group privileges; for directories, new files and subdirectories created within it automatically inherit the parent directory's group ownership.

metadata.title: Sticky Bit
metadata.definition: The Sticky Bit is a special permission primarily used on directories in Unix-like systems; when set, it ensures that only the owner of a file (or the directory's owner, or root) can delete or rename files within that directory, even if other users have write permissions to the directory.

metadata.title: I/O Hardware
metadata.definition: I/O Hardware refers to the physical components of a computer system that facilitate input and output operations, enabling the system to interact with external devices and the user.

metadata.title: Device Controller
metadata.definition: A device controller is an electronic circuit board or chip that acts as an interface between the CPU and an I/O device, managing the device's specific operations, buffering data, and translating commands between the generic CPU interface and the device's specific protocols.

metadata.title: I/O Port
metadata.definition: An I/O port is a specific memory address or register accessible by the CPU, used for sending commands to and receiving status or data from an I/O device controller, forming a communication channel between the CPU and the device.

metadata.title: Programmed I/O (PIO)
metadata.definition: Programmed I/O (PIO) is a method of I/O where the CPU directly controls all aspects of an I/O operation by repeatedly checking the status of an I/O device through its controller registers (polling) and moving data to or from the device one word or byte at a time.

metadata.title: DMA Controller
metadata.definition: A hardware component that enables I/O devices to transfer data directly to and from main memory without requiring constant CPU intervention. This mechanism significantly offloads the CPU and improves system performance for data-intensive operations.

metadata.title: Interrupt Handler
metadata.definition: A special software routine, part of the operating system kernel, that is executed by the CPU in response to an interrupt signal. Its purpose is to process the event that caused the interrupt, such as I/O completion or a timer expiration, and then return control.

metadata.title: Interrupt Vector
metadata.definition: A table in memory, maintained by the operating system, that stores the starting addresses of interrupt handlers. When an interrupt occurs, the CPU uses the unique interrupt number as an index into this vector to locate and execute the corresponding handler.

metadata.title: Polling (I/O)
metadata.definition: A method of I/O where the CPU repeatedly checks the status of an I/O device to determine if it is ready for data transfer or if an operation has completed. This approach consumes significant CPU cycles as the CPU constantly busy-waits for device readiness.

metadata.title: Caching (I/O)
metadata.definition: The technique of storing copies of frequently accessed I/O data in a smaller, faster storage area (cache), typically located in main memory, to reduce access latency and improve overall system performance. When data is requested, the system first checks the cache.

metadata.title: Device Drivers
metadata.definition: Software modules that facilitate communication between the operating system and specific hardware devices. They translate abstract OS requests into device-specific commands and handle device responses, abstracting away hardware complexities.

metadata.title: Block Devices
metadata.definition: I/O devices that store and transfer data in fixed-size blocks, allowing for random access to any block. They are typically used for persistent storage where data is organized into filesystems.

metadata.title: Character Devices
metadata.definition: I/O devices that transfer data one character (byte) at a time, often without buffering, and are typically accessed sequentially. They are generally used for stream-oriented input/output.

metadata.title: Network Devices (I/O)
metadata.definition: Hardware components that facilitate a computer's connection to a network, enabling the sending and receiving of data packets. The operating system interacts with these devices through specific device drivers.

metadata.title: I/O Protection
metadata.definition: Mechanisms implemented by the operating system and hardware to prevent user-mode programs from directly accessing I/O devices. This ensures system stability, integrity, and security by routing all I/O requests through the trusted kernel via system calls.

metadata.title: Asynchronous I/O
metadata.definition: An I/O operation that initiates a data transfer and immediately returns control to the calling process, allowing it to continue execution while the I/O operation proceeds in the background. The process is notified later, typically via a callback or event, when the I/O completes.

metadata.title: Synchronous I/O
metadata.definition: An I/O operation where the calling process is suspended and must wait until the data transfer is fully completed before it can resume execution. The program flow is halted at the point of the I/O call.

metadata.title: Blocking I/O
metadata.definition: A characteristic of an I/O operation where the calling process is paused and enters a waiting state until the I/O request has finished. This means the process cannot perform any other computations or tasks while waiting for the I/O to complete.

metadata.title: Non-blocking I/O
metadata.definition: A characteristic of an I/O operation where a process requesting I/O receives an immediate return, even if the data transfer is not yet complete. If the operation cannot finish right away, it returns an error code (e.g., `EAGAIN` or `EWOULDBLOCK`) rather than suspending the process.

metadata.title: Zero-Copy I/O
metadata.definition: A technique designed to reduce CPU overhead and memory bandwidth consumption by transferring data between an I/O device and user-space memory without redundant copying into intermediate kernel buffers. Data moves directly from source to destination.

metadata.title: Direct I/O
metadata.definition: A method where applications access storage devices directly, bypassing the operating system's buffer cache in RAM. This is typically used by applications that manage their own caching, require strict control over data consistency, or perform large sequential I/O operations.

metadata.title: io_uring (Linux Asynchronous I/O)
metadata.definition: A modern, highly efficient asynchronous I/O interface introduced in the Linux kernel, designed to allow user-space applications to submit and complete multiple I/O requests with minimal overhead. It supports a wide range of I/O operations, including both buffered and direct I/O.

metadata.title: User-Space I/O Libraries
metadata.definition: Software libraries that provide a programming interface for applications to perform I/O operations, typically wrapping underlying operating system system calls. These libraries often offer higher-level abstractions, buffering, and convenience functions to simplify I/O programming.

metadata.title: RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access)
metadata.definition: A technology that allows a computer to directly access memory in another computer's main memory without involving the operating system or CPU of the remote machine. This bypasses the typical network stack, significantly reducing latency and CPU overhead for data transfers.

metadata.title: Access Matrix
metadata.definition: A conceptual model used in operating systems to represent and enforce protection and access rights. It visualizes subjects (like users or processes) as rows and objects (like files, devices, or memory segments) as columns, with each cell defining the specific access rights (e.g., read, write, execute) a subject has to an object.

metadata.title: Access List
metadata.definition: An Access List (often called an Access Control List or ACL) is a list associated with an object (e.g., file, printer) that explicitly specifies which subjects (users or processes) have what type of access (e.g., read, write, execute) to that object. It is a common model for implementing discretionary access control, mediating access requests by checking entries in the list.

metadata.title: Revocation of Access Rights
metadata.definition: Revocation of Access Rights is the process of withdrawing or canceling previously granted permissions or privileges for a subject to access an object. This mechanism is crucial for maintaining security policies dynamically and for responding to changes in user roles, system states, or security incidents.

metadata.title: Security Mechanism
metadata.definition: A Security Mechanism is a tool, technique, or component, often implemented within an operating system, designed to enforce a security policy, protect system resources, or prevent unauthorized access and malicious activity. These mechanisms are the fundamental building blocks used to achieve overall system security goals.

metadata.title: Authentication (OS Context)
metadata.definition: Authentication, in an operating system context, is the process by which the OS verifies the claimed identity of a user or system entity attempting to access its resources. It answers the question 'who are you?' by checking credentials against a stored record.

metadata.title: Authorization (OS Context)
metadata.definition: Authorization, in an operating system context, is the process by which the OS determines what specific actions an already authenticated user or process is permitted to perform on system resources. It answers the question 'what are you allowed to do?' based on predefined policies and granted privileges.

metadata.title: Capability-Based Security
metadata.definition: Capability-Based Security is an access control model where a subject possesses unforgeable tokens, called capabilities, which directly grant specific rights to perform operations on an object. Unlike Access Control Lists (ACLs) that associate permissions with objects, capabilities are held by subjects and presented to objects to prove authorization.

metadata.title: Separation of Privilege
metadata.definition: Separation of Privilege is a security principle stating that a single entity should not be granted all the necessary permissions to complete a sensitive operation; instead, multiple distinct entities or conditions must be met to perform the action. This reduces the impact of a single point of failure or compromise, as an attacker would need to compromise multiple components to achieve their goal.

metadata.title: Security Kernel
metadata.definition: A Security Kernel is a core, highly trusted, and minimal part of an operating system responsible for enforcing the system's security policy. It typically acts as a reference monitor, mediating all access attempts between subjects and objects, and its correctness and integrity are paramount for the overall security of the entire system.

metadata.title: Malware (OS Context)
metadata.definition: Malware, in an operating system context, is malicious software designed to disrupt computer operations, gather sensitive information, or gain unauthorized access to computer systems, often by exploiting or operating within the OS environment. It is a broad category encompassing various types of harmful programs.

metadata.title: Virus (OS Context)
metadata.definition: A Virus, in an operating system context, is a type of malware that attaches itself to legitimate programs or documents and spreads by modifying other computer programs, inserting its own code. It typically requires a host program to execute and often user interaction to spread and infect the system.

metadata.title: Worm (OS Context)
metadata.definition: A Worm is a standalone malware computer program that replicates itself and spreads to other computers over a network without needing to attach to an existing program or typically requiring human intervention. Worms often exploit operating system or network service vulnerabilities to propagate rapidly and autonomously.

metadata.title: Trojan Horse (OS Context)
metadata.definition: A Trojan Horse, in an operating system context, is a type of malware that disguises itself as legitimate or harmless software to trick users into installing or executing it. Once activated, it performs malicious actions in the background, such as creating backdoors, stealing data, or installing other malware, while appearing to be benign or useful.

metadata.title: Buffer Overflow Attack
metadata.definition: A Buffer Overflow Attack exploits a program vulnerability where more data is written to a fixed-size memory buffer than it can hold, causing the excess data to overflow into adjacent memory locations. This uncontrolled overwrite can corrupt critical program data, lead to a system crash, or, most dangerously, enable the execution of arbitrary malicious code.

metadata.title: Stack Smashing Attack
metadata.definition: A Stack Smashing Attack is a specific type of buffer overflow attack that targets the program's call stack, typically by overflowing a local variable buffer to overwrite the function's return address. By manipulating the return address, an attacker can hijack the program's control flow and divert execution to arbitrary malicious code, often referred to as shellcode.

metadata.title: Sandbox (Security)
metadata.definition: A Sandbox is a security mechanism that creates an isolated execution environment for untrusted programs or code, limiting their access to system resources and preventing them from affecting the host operating system or other applications. It acts as a controlled, restricted testing ground, ensuring that potentially malicious actions are contained.

metadata.title: Cryptographic Services (OS Role)
metadata.definition: Cryptographic Services provided by an operating system are a set of functionalities made available to applications and other system components for secure communication, data protection, and integrity verification using cryptographic algorithms. These services abstract away complex cryptographic operations, offering APIs for encryption, decryption, hashing, digital signatures, and key management.

metadata.title: Measured Boot
metadata.definition: Measured Boot is a security process that creates a cryptographically secure and unalterable log of all loaded components during the boot sequence, from the initial firmware to the operating system kernel and its modules. This log, typically stored in a Trusted Platform Module (TPM), allows a remote or local entity to verify the integrity and trustworthiness of the system's entire boot state.

metadata.title: Software Guard Extensions (SGX)
metadata.definition: Software Guard Extensions (SGX) is an Intel CPU technology that allows applications to create private, protected regions of memory called 'enclaves.' Code and data within an enclave are isolated from the rest of the system, including the operating system kernel, hypervisor, and other applications, providing strong confidentiality and integrity guarantees even on a potentially compromised platform.

metadata.title: Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV)
metadata.definition: Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV) is an AMD CPU technology that encrypts virtual machine memory using a dedicated hardware encryption engine. This feature protects the guest VM's confidentiality and integrity from the hypervisor, the host operating system, and other virtual machines, ensuring that only the VM itself can access its unencrypted data.

metadata.title: Kernel Exploitation
metadata.definition: Kernel Exploitation is the act of leveraging a vulnerability within an operating system's kernel to gain unauthorized control or elevate privileges over the system. Since the kernel operates with the highest level of privilege, a successful kernel exploit typically leads to a full system compromise, allowing an attacker to bypass all security mechanisms.

metadata.title: Host Firewall
metadata.definition: A software-based security system running on a specific host machine that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on a defined set of security rules. It protects the individual host from unauthorized access and malicious network activity.

metadata.title: Seccomp (Secure Computing Mode)
metadata.definition: A Linux kernel feature that allows a process to restrict the system calls it can make, effectively limiting its attack surface by preventing access to unnecessary or dangerous kernel functions. It operates by filtering system calls based on a defined whitelist or blacklist using BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) rules.

metadata.title: Hypervisor (VMM)
metadata.definition: A piece of software, firmware, or hardware that creates and runs virtual machines (VMs), allowing multiple operating systems to share a single hardware host. It manages the virtual machines and allocates resources to them, abstracting the underlying physical hardware.

metadata.title: Type-1 Hypervisor (Bare-metal)
metadata.definition: A hypervisor that runs directly on the host hardware, without an underlying host operating system, providing higher performance and security due to direct hardware access. It directly manages hardware resources and provisions them to guest operating systems.

metadata.title: Type-2 Hypervisor (Hosted)
metadata.definition: A hypervisor that runs as a software application on top of a conventional host operating system, providing a virtualized environment for guest operating systems. It relies on the host OS for hardware access and resource management, which can introduce some performance overhead.

metadata.title: Para-virtualization
metadata.definition: A virtualization technique where guest operating systems are modified to be aware they are running in a virtualized environment and collaborate with the hypervisor for better performance. This involves replacing specific privileged instructions with hypervisor calls to optimize interactions.

metadata.title: Hardware-Assisted Virtualization (Intel VT-x, AMD-V)
metadata.definition: A set of CPU extensions (like Intel VT-x and AMD-V) that provide hardware support to facilitate and accelerate virtualization, allowing hypervisors to run unmodified guest operating systems more efficiently. These extensions introduce new CPU operation modes and instructions for virtual machine management.

metadata.title: Virtualization Overhead
metadata.definition: The performance degradation or additional resource consumption incurred when running a virtualized environment compared to running directly on bare metal. This overhead arises from the hypervisor's management tasks, resource abstraction, and translation of privileged instructions.

metadata.title: Docker (Container Platform)
metadata.definition: An open-source platform that automates the deployment, scaling, and management of applications using containerization. It packages an application and its dependencies into a lightweight, portable container that can run consistently across different environments.

metadata.title: Container Runtime
metadata.definition: The software component responsible for running containers, managing their lifecycle (create, start, stop, delete), and ensuring their isolation using underlying OS features like cgroups and namespaces. It typically adheres to standards like the Open Container Initiative (OCI) runtime specification.

metadata.title: Container Image
metadata.definition: A lightweight, standalone, executable package that includes everything needed to run a piece of software, including the code, a runtime, system tools, system libraries, and settings. It is a read-only, versioned template from which containers are created.

metadata.title: Kubernetes (Container Orchestrator)
metadata.definition: An open-source system for automating the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications, often across clusters of hosts. It provides mechanisms for self-healing, load balancing, and rolling updates for distributed applications, ensuring high availability and resilience.

metadata.title: cgroups (Control Groups)
metadata.definition: A Linux kernel feature that allows for the organization of processes into hierarchical groups and the allocation or restriction of system resources (CPU, memory, I/O, network) to these groups. This provides a mechanism for resource isolation and management, crucial for containerization.

metadata.title: Namespaces (Linux Kernel)
metadata.definition: A Linux kernel feature that partitions global system resources such as process IDs, network interfaces, mount points, and user IDs into isolated instances, allowing a group of processes to have its own isolated view of these resources. This is a fundamental building block for container isolation and security.

metadata.title: Chroot Jail
metadata.definition: A security mechanism in Unix-like operating systems that changes the apparent root directory (`/`) for the current running process and its children. It restricts processes to a subset of the filesystem tree, preventing them from accessing files outside the designated 'jailed' directory.

metadata.title: Unikernel
metadata.definition: A specialized, single-address-space machine image constructed by compiling application source code directly with necessary operating system components (drivers, libraries) into a custom, minimal kernel. It runs directly on a hypervisor or hardware, eliminating the need for a general-purpose OS and significantly reducing overhead.

metadata.title: Lightweight Virtual Machine
metadata.definition: A virtual machine designed for extremely fast startup times and minimal resource consumption, often by tightly coupling with the hypervisor or leveraging techniques like para-virtualization or unikernels. They aim to bridge the isolation and security of traditional VMs with the speed and efficiency of containers.

metadata.title: Distributed Shared Memory (DSM)
metadata.definition: A software or hardware abstraction that allows physically separated memories in a distributed system to be accessed as a single, shared address space. It simplifies programming for distributed applications by abstracting explicit message passing into familiar shared memory operations.

metadata.title: Consistency Models (Distributed OS)
metadata.definition: Rules or guarantees that define how memory or data updates are propagated and observed by different nodes in a distributed system, ensuring data integrity and predictable behavior across a shared state. They determine the ordering and visibility of write operations relative to read operations across multiple concurrent access points.

metadata.title: Fault Tolerance (Distributed OS)
metadata.definition: The ability of a distributed system to continue operating correctly and without interruption despite failures of some of its components, preventing service disruption and data loss. It is achieved through redundancy and intelligent failure recovery mechanisms.

metadata.title: Clock Synchronization (Distributed OS)
metadata.definition: The process of ensuring that the clocks of different nodes in a distributed system maintain a consistent and accurate time relative to each other or to a global time source. This consistency is crucial for correctly ordering events, coordinating actions, and maintaining data integrity across the system.

metadata.title: Leader Election (Distributed OS)
metadata.definition: A process in a distributed system where multiple nodes collectively agree on a single node to act as a coordinator or leader, responsible for specific tasks such as managing shared resources, ensuring consistency, or coordinating operations. The elected leader often centralizes certain decisions to simplify system logic and maintain order.

metadata.title: Peer-to-Peer Model
metadata.definition: A decentralized distributed application architecture where each participating node (peer) can act as both a client and a server, directly communicating with other peers to share resources and services without reliance on a central server. This model enhances scalability and resilience by distributing functionality across all nodes.

metadata.title: Middleware (OS Context)
metadata.definition: Software that acts as an intermediary layer between operating systems and applications, providing a common set of services and APIs to facilitate distributed computing and application interoperability. It abstracts away the complexities of heterogeneous systems and network communication.

metadata.title: Hard Real-Time System
metadata.definition: A system where missing a deadline for an operation is considered a catastrophic failure, leading to severe consequences or total system malfunction. These systems require absolute predictability and guaranteed adherence to all timing constraints.

metadata.title: Soft Real-Time System
metadata.definition: A system where occasional missed deadlines are tolerable, leading to degraded performance or reduced quality of service rather than catastrophic failure. These systems prioritize responsiveness and overall throughput, aiming to meet most deadlines but without strict guarantees.

metadata.title: Firm Real-Time System
metadata.definition: A system where missing a deadline means the computed result is useless and effectively discarded, but an occasional missed deadline does not cause catastrophic system failure. It sits between soft and hard real-time systems, balancing the need for timeliness with a tolerance for some failures.

metadata.title: Jitter (Real-time Systems)
metadata.definition: The variation or deviation in the time interval between successive events or the variability in the latency of a real-time task's execution. High jitter indicates a lack of predictability and can severely impact the performance and reliability of real-time applications.

metadata.title: Determinism (Real-time Systems)
metadata.definition: The property of a system where a specific set of inputs always produces the same output within a guaranteed, predictable time frame, regardless of external factors or system load. In real-time systems, it's crucial for ensuring that tasks meet their deadlines consistently.

metadata.title: Priority Inversion
metadata.definition: A problematic scenario in priority-based scheduling where a high-priority task is blocked from executing by a lower-priority task holding a shared resource, and the lower-priority task itself is preempted by an intermediate-priority task. This effectively makes the high-priority task wait for both the low-priority and intermediate-priority tasks, violating priority ordering.

metadata.title: Priority Inheritance Protocol
metadata.definition: A concurrency control mechanism designed to mitigate priority inversion by temporarily elevating the priority of a low-priority task that holds a shared resource needed by a higher-priority task. The low-priority task's priority is boosted to that of the highest-priority task waiting for the resource, ensuring it completes its critical section faster.

metadata.title: Priority Ceiling Protocol
metadata.definition: A concurrency control mechanism that prevents both priority inversion and deadlocks by assigning a 'priority ceiling' to each shared resource, equal to the highest priority of any task that might access it. A task can only acquire a resource if its current priority is strictly higher than the priority ceilings of all resources currently locked by other tasks.

metadata.title: Rate Monotonic Scheduling (RMS)
