It encompasses various technologies, processes, and controls designed to mitigate cyber risks and ensure the confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA) of information.

metadata.title: Information Security
metadata.definition: The practice of protecting information from unauthorized access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification, or destruction. It applies to all forms of information, both digital and physical, and focuses on maintaining the confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA) of data.

metadata.title: Ciphertext
metadata.definition: The result of encrypting plaintext data, rendering it unintelligible without the appropriate decryption key. It is the encrypted form of a message or data, transformed to protect its confidentiality during storage or transmission.

metadata.title: Plaintext
metadata.definition: Unencrypted information or data that is readable and understandable without any special deciphering. It is the original form of a message or data before any encryption is applied.

metadata.title: Certificate Authority
metadata.definition: A trusted third-party entity that issues digital certificates, which verify the identity of individuals, websites, or organizations in cryptographic communications. CAs are crucial for establishing trust in Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) by binding public keys to verified identities.

metadata.title: SSL/TLS (Secure Sockets Layer/Transport Layer Security)
metadata.definition: Cryptographic protocols that provide secure communication over a computer network by ensuring authentication, data encryption, and data integrity between two communicating applications. TLS is the modern successor to SSL, though the term SSL is still commonly used to refer to both.

metadata.title: Firewall (Security)
metadata.definition: A network security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predetermined security rules. It establishes a barrier between a trusted internal network and untrusted external networks, such as the internet, to prevent unauthorized access and protect against cyber threats.

metadata.title: Virus (Malware)
metadata.definition: A type of malicious software that attaches itself to legitimate programs or documents and spreads by modifying other computer programs, often without the user's knowledge or permission. It requires human action (like opening an infected file) to replicate and execute, and typically aims to corrupt data or disrupt system operations.

metadata.title: Worm (Malware)
metadata.definition: A standalone malicious program that replicates itself across computer networks without human interaction, exploiting vulnerabilities to spread from one computer to another. Unlike viruses, worms do not need to attach to a host program or file to propagate.

metadata.title: Trojan Horse (Malware)
metadata.definition: A type of malicious software that disguises itself as legitimate or useful software but, once executed, performs harmful actions without the user's knowledge. Unlike viruses and worms, Trojans do not self-replicate, relying instead on deception to trick users into installing them.

metadata.title: Vulnerability Assessment
metadata.definition: A systematic process of identifying, quantifying, and prioritizing vulnerabilities in a system, network, or application. It aims to discover security weaknesses and potential exploits before they can be leveraged by malicious actors, providing a snapshot of an organization's security posture.

metadata.title: Security Audit
metadata.definition: A systematic evaluation of the security of a company's information system by measuring how well it conforms to a set of established criteria, such as industry standards, regulations, or internal policies. It involves reviewing policies, configurations, controls, and logs to ensure compliance and identify gaps in security posture.

metadata.title: Parallel Computing
metadata.definition: A type of computation where multiple processors or computing units work simultaneously to execute different parts of a program or solve multiple problems concurrently. This approach aims to significantly reduce overall computation time, handle larger datasets, and improve system throughput by leveraging multiple execution streams.

metadata.title: Concurrency (General)
metadata.definition: The ability of different parts of a program, or multiple programs, to execute out of order or in partial order, without affecting the final outcome. It deals with managing multiple tasks that might be executing overlappingly in time, giving the illusion of simultaneous execution, even on a single-core processor.

metadata.title: Thread (General)
metadata.definition: The smallest sequence of programmed instructions that can be managed independently by a scheduler, often as part of a larger process. Threads within the same process share the same memory space, resources, and open files, making inter-thread communication efficient but requiring careful synchronization to avoid race conditions.

metadata.title: Process (General)
metadata.definition: An instance of a computer program that is being executed, including its own separate memory space, registers, program counter, and resources (like open files and network connections). Processes are generally isolated from each other by the operating system, providing robustness and security.

metadata.title: Paxos (Consensus Algorithm)
metadata.definition: A family of protocols for solving the consensus problem in an asynchronous network of unreliable processes, ensuring that all non-faulty processes agree on a single value even if some processes fail. It guarantees safety (never reaching an incorrect decision) and liveness (eventually reaching a decision).

metadata.title: Raft (Consensus Algorithm)
metadata.definition: A consensus algorithm designed to be more understandable than Paxos while providing equivalent fault-tolerance and performance. It achieves consensus by electing a strong leader and managing replicated logs, ensuring all servers agree on the same sequence of state transitions.

metadata.title: Leader Election (Distributed)
metadata.definition: The process in a distributed system where all nodes agree on a single node to act as the coordinator or leader. The elected leader is responsible for managing specific tasks, ensuring consistency, or coordinating operations among the other nodes (followers).

metadata.title: Distributed Ledger
metadata.definition: A decentralized database system that is replicated and shared across multiple sites, countries, or institutions. Each participant in the network maintains a copy of the ledger, and updates are synchronized across the network using a consensus mechanism, ensuring immutability and transparency.

metadata.title: Load Balancing (Distributed)
metadata.definition: The process of distributing incoming network traffic across multiple servers to ensure no single server is overloaded, thereby improving application responsiveness, availability, and resource utilization. It can be implemented at various layers, from DNS to application protocols.

metadata.title: Distributed File System
metadata.definition: A file system that allows multiple users on multiple machines to share files and storage resources across a network. It manages data storage, replication, and access transparently across a cluster of servers, providing high availability and fault tolerance.

metadata.title: Human-Computer Interaction (HCI)
metadata.definition: An interdisciplinary field concerned with the design, evaluation, and implementation of interactive computing systems for human use and with the study of major phenomena surrounding them. It focuses on the interfaces between people and computers, aiming to make technology usable and accessible.

metadata.title: User Interface (UI)
metadata.definition: The space where interactions between humans and machines occur, encompassing all elements a user can see and interact with to operate a software program or device. It includes visual elements like buttons, icons, text fields, and layout, as well as input methods.

metadata.title: User Experience (UX)
metadata.definition: Encompasses all aspects of an end-user's interaction with a company, its services, and its products, focusing on how a user feels about the interaction. Good UX aims to make products useful, usable, desirable, findable, accessible, and credible.

metadata.title: Usability
metadata.definition: A quality attribute that assesses how easy user interfaces are to use, measured by how effectively, efficiently, and satisfactorily users can achieve specific goals. It focuses on learnability, efficiency, memorability, error prevention, and user satisfaction.

metadata.title: Accessibility (HCI)
metadata.definition: The practice of designing and developing products, devices, services, or environments so that they can be used by people with disabilities. It ensures that technology is perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust for all users, regardless of their abilities.

metadata.title: Affordance (HCI)
metadata.definition: A property of an object or an environment that indicates how it can be used, suggesting its possible actions to a user. In HCI, it refers to design cues that signal what action is possible and how to perform it (e.g., a button 'affords' pushing).

metadata.title: User-Centered Design
metadata.definition: An iterative design process in which designers focus on the users and their needs in each phase of the design process. It involves deeply understanding user tasks, goals, and environments, then designing and refining solutions based on continuous user feedback and evaluation.

metadata.title: Interaction Design
metadata.definition: A subset of UX design that focuses on creating engaging interactive systems, considering how users interact with a product or service. It defines the behavior of interactive products, including controls, feedback mechanisms, and how the system responds to user input.

metadata.title: Information Architecture
metadata.definition: The structural design of shared information environments, focusing on organizing, structuring, and labeling content in an effective and sustainable way. It helps users find information and complete tasks by creating clear navigation, labeling, and categorization systems.

metadata.title: Wireframing
metadata.definition: The practice of creating a basic visual guide that represents the skeletal framework of a website or application. Wireframes focus on layout, content prioritization, functionality, and how users will interact with the interface, without concern for visual design details like colors or fonts.

metadata.title: Prototyping (HCI)
metadata.definition: The process of creating preliminary versions or models of a product or system to test ideas, gather feedback, and validate designs before final development. Prototypes can range from low-fidelity sketches to high-fidelity interactive simulations, allowing for iterative refinement.

metadata.title: User Testing
metadata.definition: A research method where real users interact with a product or prototype to identify usability problems, gather qualitative and quantitative data, and determine user satisfaction. It involves observing users as they perform specific tasks and collecting their feedback.

metadata.title: Heuristic Evaluation
metadata.definition: A usability inspection method where expert evaluators assess a user interface against a set of established usability principles, known as heuristics. The goal is to identify common usability problems in the design without involving actual end-users in the evaluation process.

metadata.title: Cognitive Psychology (HCI)
metadata.definition: The application of cognitive psychology principles, theories, and research methods to the design and evaluation of interactive systems. It helps understand how human mental processes like attention, memory, perception, and problem-solving impact user interaction with technology.

metadata.title: Perception (HCI)
metadata.definition: The process by which users receive, interpret, and make sense of information from their environment, including visual, auditory, and haptic feedback from an interface. In HCI, it's crucial for designing interfaces that are easily detectable and understandable by human senses.

metadata.title: Memory (HCI)
metadata.definition: In HCI, memory refers to how users recall information necessary to interact with a system, often divided into short-term (working) memory and long-term memory. Designing interfaces that reduce memory load and aid recall improves usability.

metadata.title: Mental Model (HCI)
metadata.definition: A user's internal representation or understanding of how a system works, its purpose, and how to interact with it. Effective interface design aims to create a mental model in the user that closely matches the actual system's operation.

metadata.title: Fitts's Law
metadata.definition: A predictive model of human movement primarily used in HCI, stating that the time required to move to a target is a function of the distance to the target and its size. It quantifies the speed-accuracy trade-off for pointing tasks.

metadata.title: Hick's Law
metadata.definition: A law in psychometrics describing the time it takes for a person to make a decision as a result of the possible choices he or she has. Decision time increases logarithmically with the number of choices.

metadata.title: Gulf of Execution
metadata.definition: The gap between a user's intentions and the actions that are possible and discoverable within a system. It refers to how well the system's interface supports the user in performing their intended actions.

metadata.title: Gulf of Evaluation
metadata.definition: The gap between the system's current state and presentation, and whether it matches a user's expectations and allows them to understand what has happened. It concerns how well the system provides feedback that is interpretable and congruent with user goals.

metadata.title: Computer Graphics
metadata.definition: The field of computer science that deals with generating images with the aid of computers. It encompasses the creation, manipulation, storage, and display of visual content.

metadata.title: Raster Graphics
metadata.definition: A type of computer graphics where images are represented as a grid of pixels (a bitmap). Each pixel holds color information, and the image quality depends on the resolution; scaling up typically results in pixelation.

metadata.title: Vector Graphics
metadata.definition: A type of computer graphics where images are defined mathematically as paths, points, lines, curves, and shapes, rather than a fixed grid of pixels. They are resolution-independent, meaning they can be scaled indefinitely without loss of quality.

metadata.title: Pixel
metadata.definition: The smallest addressable element in a raster image or on a display screen, short for "picture element." Each pixel typically contains a single color value, forming a larger image when combined with many others.

metadata.title: Resolution (Image)
metadata.definition: The number of pixels (or data points) per unit of physical space or in total that compose an image. Higher resolution means more detail and clarity, often expressed as width x height (e.g., 1920x1080 pixels) or pixels per inch (PPI).

metadata.title: Color Model (RGB)
metadata.definition: An additive color model where red, green, and blue light are added together in various proportions to reproduce a broad array of colors. It is primarily used for displaying images on electronic devices like screens.

metadata.title: Color Model (CMYK)
metadata.definition: A subtractive color model used in color printing, where cyan, magenta, yellow, and key (black) inks are combined on a white background. Colors are created by subtracting light from white, unlike the additive RGB model.

metadata.title: 3D Modeling
metadata.definition: The process of developing a mathematical representation of any three-dimensional surface of an object (either inanimate or living) using specialized software. The output is a 3D model that can be displayed as a two-dimensional image through 3D rendering or used in simulations.

metadata.title: Mesh (3D)
metadata.definition: In 3D computer graphics, a mesh is a collection of vertices, edges, and faces that defines the shape of a 3D object. It forms the skeletal structure upon which textures and other visual properties are applied.

metadata.title: Vertex (3D)
metadata.definition: A fundamental component in 3D computer graphics, a vertex is a point in 3D space defined by its coordinates (x, y, z). Vertices are the building blocks that, when connected by edges, form faces and ultimately a 3D mesh.

metadata.title: Edge (3D)
metadata.definition: In 3D computer graphics, an edge is a straight line segment that connects two vertices, forming the boundary of a face or the intersection of two faces. Edges define the structural lines of a 3D object's mesh.

metadata.title: Face (3D)
metadata.definition: In 3D computer graphics, a face (or polygon) is a flat, enclosed surface formed by connecting three or more vertices with edges. Faces are the visible surfaces of a 3D mesh and determine how light interacts with the object.

metadata.title: Texture Mapping
metadata.definition: A technique in 3D computer graphics for adding fine detail, surface texture, or color to a computer-generated 3D model by mapping a 2D image (a texture map) onto its surface. This avoids the need to model every small detail geometrically.

metadata.title: Shading (Graphics)
metadata.definition: The process in computer graphics of calculating and applying color, texture, and light/shadow effects to a 3D surface to make it appear realistic. It determines how light interacts with the surface and is crucial for visual fidelity.

metadata.title: Rendering Pipeline
metadata.definition: A series of sequential steps that a 3D scene goes through to be converted into a 2D image suitable for display. It typically involves application, geometry, and rasterization stages, processing vertices and pixels sequentially.

metadata.title: Ray Tracing
metadata.definition: A rendering technique that simulates the path of light rays as they interact with objects in a 3D scene. For each pixel, a ray is cast from the camera into the scene, calculating intersections and light contributions from various sources, reflections, and refractions.

metadata.title: Rasterization
metadata.definition: The process of converting vector graphics, such as 3D models and geometric primitives (points, lines, triangles), into a raster image (a grid of pixels) for display on a screen. It determines which pixels are covered by the primitives and assigns colors.

metadata.title: Phong Shading
metadata.definition: An interpolation technique in computer graphics that calculates lighting for each pixel by interpolating surface normals across a polygon and then applying a lighting model at each pixel. This results in smoother-looking surfaces and more accurate highlights compared to Gouraud shading.

metadata.title: Gouraud Shading
metadata.definition: An interpolation technique in computer graphics that calculates lighting at the vertices of a polygon and then interpolates the resulting colors across the polygon's surface to determine the color of each pixel. While faster, it can produce less realistic highlights and faceted appearances on curved surfaces than Phong shading.

metadata.title: Lighting Model (Graphics)
metadata.definition: A mathematical algorithm or set of equations used in computer graphics to simulate how light interacts with surfaces in a 3D scene. It typically accounts for ambient, diffuse, and specular components, determining the final color and brightness of a surface based on light sources, material properties, and camera position.

metadata.title: Transformations (Graphics)
metadata.definition: Mathematical operations applied to geometric objects in a 3D scene to change their position, orientation, or size. Common transformations include translation (moving), rotation (turning), and scaling (resizing), typically represented by matrices.

metadata.title: Perspective Projection
metadata.definition: A projection method used in computer graphics to simulate how objects appear in the real world, where objects further away appear smaller. It projects 3D points onto a 2D viewing plane, incorporating a vanishing point and creating a sense of depth and realism.

metadata.title: Orthographic Projection
metadata.definition: A projection method where 3D objects are projected onto a 2D viewing plane without any sense of depth or perspective; parallel lines remain parallel, and objects do not appear smaller with distance. It is often used for technical drawings or isometric views.

metadata.title: Animation (Computer Graphics)
metadata.definition: The process of creating the illusion of motion and change over time in a static image or model within computer graphics. This is achieved by rapidly displaying a sequence of slightly different images or by parametrically altering properties of objects over frames.

metadata.title: Frame Rate
metadata.definition: The frequency (rate) at which consecutive images (frames) are displayed or generated per second by a graphics system. Measured in frames per second (fps), a higher frame rate generally results in smoother motion and a more responsive visual experience.

metadata.title: Shader (Graphics)
metadata.definition: A small program that runs on the Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) and is responsible for calculating rendering effects like lighting, color, and transformations for each pixel or vertex. Shaders allow for highly customizable and complex visual effects.

metadata.title: Vertex Shader
metadata.definition: A programmable stage in the rendering pipeline that processes individual vertices, typically performing transformations (translation, rotation, scaling), projection, and calculating per-vertex attributes like color or normals. It defines the final position of each vertex on the screen.

metadata.title: Fragment Shader
metadata.definition: A programmable stage in the rendering pipeline that processes individual fragments (potential pixels), typically after vertex processing and rasterization. Its primary role is to calculate the final color of each fragment, often incorporating lighting, textures, and other material properties.

metadata.title: Geometric Modeling
metadata.definition: The process of creating mathematical representations of 3D objects or surfaces suitable for computer processing and display. This involves defining the shape, structure, and topological properties of objects using primitives like points, lines, polygons, or more complex curves and surfaces.

metadata.title: Spline (Computer Graphics)
metadata.definition: A piecewise polynomial curve used in computer graphics for modeling smooth, continuous shapes and paths. Splines are defined by a set of control points, offering flexible and intuitive manipulation of complex curves and surfaces while maintaining smoothness.

metadata.title: B-spline
metadata.definition: A type of spline curve or surface that provides local control over its shape, meaning that moving a single control point only affects a limited portion of the curve. B-splines are widely used in computer-aided design (CAD) and computer graphics due to their flexibility, stability, and ability to represent complex shapes.

metadata.title: Volume Rendering
metadata.definition: A technique for visualizing 3D volumetric data directly, without first converting it into geometric primitives like polygons. It involves casting rays through the volume and integrating color and opacity samples along each ray to produce a 2D image.

metadata.title: Information Visualization
metadata.definition: The study and creation of visual representations of abstract data to amplify human cognition, enabling users to explore, understand, and communicate insights from complex datasets. It focuses on non-spatial data and aims to reveal patterns, trends, and anomalies.

metadata.title: Deontology
metadata.definition: An ethical theory that judges the morality of an action based on whether the action adheres to a rule or rules, rather than on its consequences. It emphasizes duties and rules, asserting that certain actions are inherently right or wrong regardless of their outcomes.

metadata.title: Consequentialism
metadata.definition: An ethical theory that judges the morality of an action based entirely on its outcomes or consequences. Actions are considered morally right if they produce good results, and morally wrong if they produce bad results.

metadata.title: Utilitarianism
metadata.definition: A form of consequentialism that holds the most ethical choice is the one that produces the greatest good for the greatest number of people. It seeks to maximize overall happiness, well-being, or utility across a population.

metadata.title: Virtue Ethics
metadata.definition: An ethical framework that focuses on the character of the moral agent rather than the actions themselves or their consequences. It asks what a virtuous person would do in a given situation, emphasizing the development of moral virtues like honesty, integrity, and compassion.

metadata.title: Rights-based Ethics
metadata.definition: An ethical framework that asserts that individuals have fundamental rights, and morally correct actions are those that respect and uphold these rights. It focuses on the duties of others to respect these entitlements.

metadata.title: Justice as Fairness (Rawls)
metadata.definition: A theory by John Rawls proposing that a just society is one where basic liberties are equally distributed, and social and economic inequalities are arranged to benefit the least advantaged members of society. It uses the concept of the 'veil of ignorance' to determine fair principles.

metadata.title: Ethical Relativism
metadata.definition: The view that moral judgments are true or false only relative to some particular standpoint, such as a culture or historical period, and that no single standard of morality is universally applicable. It suggests there are no objective or absolute moral truths.

metadata.title: Ethical Egoism
metadata.definition: A normative ethical theory that states moral agents ought to do what is in their own self-interest. It differs from psychological egoism (a descriptive theory) by prescribing how people should act, not just describing how they do act.

metadata.title: Moral Absolutism
metadata.definition: The ethical belief that there are absolute standards against which moral questions can be judged, and that certain actions are inherently right or wrong regardless of context or consequences. It stands in opposition to ethical relativism.

metadata.title: Moral Pluralism
metadata.definition: The idea that there are several distinct and sometimes conflicting moral values, principles, or goods that are equally valid and irreducible to one another. It suggests that there can be multiple acceptable ethical frameworks or solutions to moral problems, rather than a single absolute truth.

metadata.title: Ethical Dilemma
metadata.definition: A situation where an individual or organization is faced with making a decision between two or more morally conflicting options, where choosing one option would mean violating another moral principle. There is no clear right or wrong choice, or all choices lead to some negative moral outcome.

metadata.title: Moral Agency
metadata.definition: The capacity of an individual or entity to make ethical judgments based on concepts of right and wrong, and to be held accountable for those actions. For an entity to be a moral agent, it must have the ability to understand consequences, act intentionally, and make choices.

metadata.title: Ethical Reasoning
metadata.definition: The process of thinking through a moral problem, applying ethical principles and frameworks to arrive at a justified decision or conclusion. It involves identifying the ethical issue, considering stakeholders, exploring options, and evaluating their moral implications.

metadata.title: Value Conflict
metadata.definition: A situation where two or more deeply held beliefs, principles, or desired outcomes are incompatible or pull in different directions, making it difficult to choose an action without compromising one value. This often underlies ethical dilemmas.

metadata.title: Principle of Beneficence
metadata.definition: The ethical principle that moral agents should act in a way that benefits others and promotes their well-being. It involves actively doing good, preventing harm, and removing conditions that cause harm.

metadata.title: Principle of Non-maleficence
metadata.definition: The ethical principle to 'do no harm.' It obliges moral agents to avoid causing harm, either intentionally or through negligence, and is often considered a foundational principle in many professional codes of ethics.

metadata.title: Principle of Autonomy
metadata.definition: The ethical principle that respects an individual's right to self-determination and to make informed decisions about their own life and body, free from coercion or manipulation. It requires providing sufficient information for individuals to consent or refuse.

metadata.title: Principle of Justice
metadata.definition: The ethical principle requiring fairness in the distribution of benefits and burdens, and in the treatment of individuals within society. It addresses issues of equity, impartial decision-making, and addressing historical disadvantages.

metadata.title: Principle of Fidelity
metadata.definition: The ethical principle that requires faithfulness to agreements, promises, and professional responsibilities. It entails loyalty, trustworthiness, and honoring commitments made to individuals, clients, or the public.

metadata.title: Principle of Veracity
metadata.definition: The ethical principle that requires truthfulness and accuracy in communication. It obliges moral agents to be honest and avoid deception or misrepresentation in their interactions.

metadata.title: Principle of Privacy (Ethics)
metadata.definition: A fundamental ethical concept asserting an individual's right to control their personal information and interactions, protecting them from unauthorized intrusion or observation. It encompasses the right to be left alone and to determine the extent of information shared about oneself.

metadata.title: Principle of Accountability
metadata.definition: The obligation of an organization or individual to take responsibility for its actions and decisions, particularly concerning the handling of personal data, and to be able to demonstrate compliance with privacy principles and regulations. It often includes mechanisms for enforcement and redress.

metadata.title: Principle of Transparency
metadata.definition: The ethical principle requiring organizations to be open and honest about their data collection, processing, and sharing practices. Individuals should be clearly informed about what data is collected, why it's collected, how it's used, and with whom it's shared.

metadata.title: Informational Privacy
metadata.definition: The right of individuals to control the collection, use, and dissemination of their personal data and information. It pertains to the data about a person and their ability to regulate access to it by others.

metadata.title: Physical Privacy
metadata.definition: The ability of an individual to control access to their physical person, space, and activities. It encompasses freedom from unwarranted physical intrusion, surveillance, and observation in private spaces.

metadata.title: Associational Privacy
metadata.definition: The freedom to choose with whom one associates, forms relationships, or communicates, without unwarranted government or third-party interference, surveillance, or disclosure of those associations. It protects the ability to join groups or form relationships privately.

metadata.title: Proprietary Privacy
metadata.definition: The right of individuals or entities to control the use and access of their personal assets, property, and information related to their economic activities. It often concerns the privacy of one's financial data, intellectual property, or commercial secrets.

metadata.title: Contextual Integrity
metadata.definition: A normative theory of privacy that asserts privacy is maintained when information flows conform to the norms of the context in which they occur. It focuses on the appropriateness of information collection and dissemination based on specific contexts, roles, and expectations.

metadata.title: Privacy by Design (PbD)
metadata.definition: An approach to system engineering that embeds privacy protections into the design and architecture of IT systems, business practices, and networked infrastructures from the outset. It seeks to proactively prevent privacy invasive events rather than reactively addressing them.

metadata.title: Privacy by Default
metadata.definition: A principle stating that, by default, the highest level of privacy settings should be applied without any manual action required from the user. It ensures that personal data is processed with the most privacy-respecting settings as soon as a system or service is deployed.

metadata.title: Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)
metadata.definition: A process designed to help identify and minimize the data protection risks of a project. It is a systematic review of new technologies, programs, or processes that involve the processing of personal data, especially those likely to result in a high risk to individuals' rights and freedoms.

metadata.title: Pseudonymization
metadata.definition: The processing of personal data in such a manner that the personal data can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information, provided that such additional information is kept separately and subject to technical and organizational measures to ensure non-attribution. It's a reversible process.

metadata.title: Anonymization
metadata.definition: The process of transforming personal data into a form where the data subject is no longer identifiable, and it is impossible to re-identify them, even with additional information. This transformation is irreversible and aims to completely strip direct and indirect identifiers.

metadata.title: k-anonymity
metadata.definition: A privacy model used to protect individuals in a dataset by ensuring that each record is indistinguishable from at least k-1 other records concerning certain quasi-identifiers. This makes it difficult to link records back to specific individuals.

metadata.title: l-diversity
metadata.definition: An extension of k-anonymity that addresses its limitations by ensuring that within each group of k identical records (an equivalence class), there are at least l 'well-represented' distinct values for sensitive attributes. This protects against homogeneity and background knowledge attacks.

metadata.title: t-closeness
metadata.definition: A privacy model that further refines k-anonymity and l-diversity by requiring that the distribution of a sensitive attribute within each equivalence class is 'close' to the distribution of the attribute in the overall dataset. This protects against attribute disclosure even if the sensitive values are diverse.

metadata.title: Federated Learning (Privacy Aspect)
metadata.definition: A distributed machine learning approach where models are trained on decentralized datasets located at various client devices (e.g., mobile phones, hospitals) without directly exchanging raw data. Only model updates or gradients are shared with a central server, enhancing data privacy by keeping sensitive data localized.

metadata.title: Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKP)
metadata.definition: A cryptographic method where one party (the prover) can prove to another party (the verifier) that they know a certain piece of information or that a statement is true, without revealing any information about the information itself beyond the fact that they possess it.

metadata.title: Trusted Execution Environments (TEE)
metadata.definition: A secure area of a main processor that guarantees code and data loaded inside are protected with respect to confidentiality and integrity. TEEs provide hardware-enforced isolation, preventing unauthorized access even from privileged software outside the TEE.

metadata.title: Data Minimization Principle
metadata.definition: An ethical and legal principle, central to privacy regulations like GDPR, that mandates organizations should collect and process only the personal data that is absolutely necessary for achieving a specified purpose. It emphasizes collecting less data, storing it for shorter periods, and limiting its accessibility.

metadata.title: Purpose Limitation Principle
metadata.definition: Data collected for a specific, explicit, and legitimate purpose should not be further processed in a manner incompatible with those purposes. It ensures that personal data is only used for the reasons it was initially gathered, preventing scope creep in data usage.

metadata.title: Storage Limitation Principle
metadata.definition: Personal data should not be stored for longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the data was collected or is further processed. Once the purpose is fulfilled and legal obligations met, the data should be deleted or anonymized.

metadata.title: Accuracy Principle (Data Privacy)
metadata.definition: Personal data should be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date. Every reasonable step must be taken to ensure that personal data that is inaccurate, having regard to the purposes for which it is processed, is erased or rectified without delay.

metadata.title: Confidentiality Principle (Data Privacy)
metadata.definition: Personal data should be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction, or damage. This is achieved using appropriate technical or organizational measures.

metadata.title: Integrity Principle (Data Privacy)
metadata.definition: Personal data should be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against alteration or corruption. This involves technical and organizational measures to prevent unauthorized modification or damage to data.

metadata.title: Availability Principle (Data Privacy)
metadata.definition: Personal data should be accessible and usable when needed by authorized entities. This principle ensures that systems and data remain operational and responsive to legitimate requests, preventing denial of service or data loss.

metadata.title: Consent (Data Privacy)
metadata.definition: In data privacy, consent is a legal basis for processing personal data, signifying a freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous indication of the data subject's wishes. This is typically expressed by a statement or a clear affirmative action agreeing to the processing of their data.

metadata.title: Opt-in Consent
metadata.definition: A method of obtaining consent where individuals must explicitly and actively agree to a specific action, such as receiving marketing communications or having their data processed for certain purposes. It requires a clear affirmative action from the user.

metadata.title: Opt-out Consent
metadata.definition: A method of obtaining consent where individuals are assumed to have given their consent unless they actively decline or withdraw it. This often involves pre-checked boxes or a default setting that users must manually change if they do not agree.

metadata.title: Right to be Forgotten
metadata.definition: A data subject's right to request that their personal data be erased and no longer processed, especially when the data is no longer necessary for its original purpose, consent is withdrawn, or there are no legitimate grounds for retention. Also known as the Right to Erasure.

metadata.title: Right to Access Data
metadata.definition: A data subject's right to obtain confirmation as to whether or not personal data concerning them is being processed, and, where that is the case, to access that personal data along with specific information about the processing.

metadata.title: Right to Rectification
metadata.definition: A data subject's right to have inaccurate personal data concerning them rectified without undue delay. This also includes the right to have incomplete personal data completed, including by means of providing a supplementary statement.

metadata.title: Right to Data Portability
metadata.definition: A data subject's right to receive the personal data concerning them, which they have provided to a controller, in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format. They also have the right to transmit those data to another controller without hindrance.

metadata.title: Right to Object to Processing
metadata.definition: A data subject's right to object, on grounds relating to their particular situation, at any time to processing of personal data concerning them. This right is particularly relevant when processing is based on legitimate interests or for direct marketing purposes, including profiling.

metadata.title: Profiling (Data Privacy)
metadata.definition: Any form of automated processing of personal data consisting of using personal data to evaluate certain personal aspects relating to a natural person. This is often done to analyze or predict aspects concerning that natural person's performance at work, economic situation, health, personal preferences, interests, reliability, behavior, location, or movements.

metadata.title: Automated Decision Making (ADM)
metadata.definition: Decisions made solely by automated means without any human intervention, where the decision produces legal effects concerning the individual or similarly significantly affects them. Regulations like GDPR often grant individuals specific rights regarding ADM, including the right to obtain human intervention.

metadata.title: Web Tracking
metadata.definition: The practice of collecting information about a user's activities across websites or over time, often for purposes such as behavioral advertising, analytics, or personalization. This can involve various technologies like cookies, pixels, and device fingerprinting.

metadata.title: Cookie Consent
metadata.definition: The explicit permission given by a user for a website to place cookies on their device and collect data through them. This typically involves a banner or pop-up asking the user to accept, reject, or manage cookie preferences, especially for non-essential cookies.

metadata.title: Device Fingerprinting
metadata.definition: A technique used to uniquely identify a user's device based on the configuration and characteristics of their hardware and software (e.g., browser type, installed fonts, screen resolution, operating system). It allows tracking even without traditional cookies, often raising significant privacy concerns.

metadata.title: Location Privacy
metadata.definition: The ability of an individual to control how their geographical location data is collected, used, and shared. It encompasses concerns about real-time tracking, historical location data, and inference of personal habits or whereabouts from location information.

metadata.title: Facial Recognition Privacy Concerns
metadata.definition: Refers to the privacy implications arising from the collection, storage, analysis, and use of facial recognition data, including potential for mass surveillance, identity theft, and discrimination.

metadata.title: Biometric Privacy
metadata.definition: The protection of personal information derived from unique biological or behavioral characteristics, such as fingerprints, facial features, or voice patterns, from unauthorized access, use, or disclosure.

metadata.title: Genetic Privacy
metadata.definition: The right of individuals to control access to, and the use of, their genetic information, including DNA sequences and related health or ancestry data.

metadata.title: Healthcare Data Privacy (HIPAA)
metadata.definition: The principles and regulations governing the protection of sensitive patient health information (PHI) by healthcare providers, health plans, and related entities, as mandated by laws like HIPAA in the United States.

metadata.title: Educational Data Privacy (FERPA)
metadata.definition: The protection of student education records and the rights of parents (or eligible students) regarding inspection, review, and control over the disclosure of these records, often governed by laws such as FERPA in the US.

metadata.title: Financial Data Privacy (GLBA)
metadata.definition: Regulations safeguarding consumers' nonpublic personal information (NPI) held by financial institutions, requiring them to explain information-sharing practices and protect sensitive data.

metadata.title: Privacy Notice
metadata.definition: A public statement, often legally mandated, explaining how an organization collects, uses, stores, shares, and protects personal information gathered from individuals.

metadata.title: Terms of Service (ToS)
metadata.definition: A legal agreement between a service provider and a user that sets out the rules, guidelines, rights, and responsibilities for using the service or platform.

metadata.title: End-User License Agreement (EULA)
metadata.definition: A legal contract between a software vendor and the purchaser or end-user of the software, specifying the terms under which the software can be used, including restrictions on copying, modification, or distribution.

metadata.title: Privacy Paradox
metadata.definition: The observed discrepancy between individuals' stated concerns about privacy and their actual behavior, often revealing a willingness to share personal data despite expressed reservations.

metadata.title: Re-identification Attack
metadata.definition: A technique used to link anonymized or de-identified data back to specific individuals by combining it with other publicly available or external datasets, thereby compromising privacy.

metadata.title: Linkage Attack
metadata.definition: A privacy attack where multiple datasets, each seemingly harmless in isolation, are combined or correlated to infer sensitive information or potentially re-identify individuals.

metadata.title: Inference Attack
metadata.definition: A privacy attack where an adversary deduces sensitive, private information about individuals or groups from publicly available or seemingly non-sensitive data, even without direct re-identification.

metadata.title: Membership Inference Attack
metadata.definition: An attack against machine learning models where an adversary attempts to determine if a specific data record was part of the model's training dataset by observing its behavior or output.

metadata.title: Attribute Inference Attack
metadata.definition: An attack against machine learning models where an adversary attempts to infer sensitive attributes about an individual whose data was used in the model's training, even if the model doesn't directly output that attribute.

metadata.title: Side-channel Attack (Privacy Context)
metadata.definition: In a privacy context, a side-channel attack exploits information unintentionally leaked from a system's physical implementation (e.g., timing, power consumption, electromagnetic emissions) to infer private data.

metadata.title: Private Information Retrieval (PIR)
metadata.definition: A cryptographic protocol that allows a user to retrieve an item from a database or server without the server learning which item was requested or retrieved by the user.

metadata.title: Private Set Intersection (PSI)
metadata.definition: A cryptographic protocol enabling two parties to compute the intersection of their respective private sets, such that neither party learns any information about the other party's set beyond the elements in the intersection.

metadata.title: California Privacy Rights Act (CPRA)
metadata.definition: A comprehensive state-level data privacy law in California that significantly expands upon the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), granting consumers more control over their personal information and establishing the California Privacy Protection Agency (CPPA).

metadata.title: Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA)
metadata.definition: A U.S. federal law that protects the privacy of student education records, granting parents and eligible students specific rights to access, amend, and control the disclosure of these records.

metadata.title: Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLBA)
metadata.definition: A U.S. federal law requiring financial institutions to explain their information-sharing practices to customers and to safeguard sensitive data. It gives consumers the right to opt-out of some data sharing arrangements.

metadata.title: Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA)
metadata.definition: A U.S. federal law that imposes requirements on operators of online services directed to children under 13, or who have actual knowledge that they are collecting personal information from children under 13. It primarily mandates verifiable parental consent before collecting, using, or disclosing such data.

metadata.title: Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA)
metadata.definition: A U.S. federal law enacted to extend privacy protections for wire and oral communications to include electronic communications and stored electronic information. It restricts government and private entity access to electronic communications content and records without proper legal authorization.

metadata.title: Aadhaar Act (India)
metadata.definition: An Indian law that established the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) and provided for the issuance of unique identification numbers (Aadhaar) to residents, based on their biometric and demographic data. It governs the collection, storage, and use of this sensitive personal information, aiming to prevent its misuse.

metadata.title: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA)
metadata.definition: Canada's federal privacy law that governs how private sector organizations collect, use, and disclose personal information during commercial activities. It balances an individual's right to privacy with the need of organizations to collect, use, or disclose personal information for legitimate business purposes.

metadata.title: Australian Privacy Act 1988
metadata.definition: Australia's primary federal law regulating the handling of personal information by Australian Government agencies and most private sector organizations. It includes 13 Australian Privacy Principles (APPs) that dictate how personal information should be collected, used, stored, and disclosed.

metadata.title: Brazil's Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD)
metadata.definition: Brazil's general data protection law, largely inspired by the GDPR, establishing comprehensive rules for the collection, use, processing, and storage of personal data. It grants individuals extensive rights over their data and imposes strict obligations on data controllers and processors.

metadata.title: Privacy Shield (Defunct)
metadata.definition: A framework for transatlantic data flows, formerly allowing US companies to receive personal data from the EU in compliance with EU data protection requirements. It was invalidated by the Schrems II ruling in 2020 due to concerns over U.S. government surveillance access to transferred data.

metadata.title: Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs)
metadata.definition: Pre-approved, standardized data protection clauses developed by the European Commission that can be embedded into contracts between data exporters and importers. They serve as a legal mechanism to ensure appropriate safeguards for international data transfers, particularly when transferring personal data outside the European Economic Area (EEA) to countries without an adequacy decision.

metadata.title: Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs)
metadata.definition: Internal codes of conduct approved by EU data protection authorities for multinational corporations to legally transfer personal data within their corporate group to countries outside the EEA. BCRs ensure that the entire corporate group adheres to EU data protection standards equivalent to GDPR.

metadata.title: Adequacy Decision (GDPR)
metadata.definition: A formal finding by the European Commission that a non-EEA country or international organization provides an 'adequate' level of data protection. When such a decision is in place, personal data can flow from the EEA to that country without requiring additional safeguards like Standard Contractual Clauses or Binding Corporate Rules.

metadata.title: Schrems II Ruling
metadata.definition: A landmark European Court of Justice (ECJ) ruling in July 2020 that invalidated the EU-US Privacy Shield framework. It also imposed stricter requirements for the use of Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) for data transfers to third countries, emphasizing that data exporters must assess the recipient country's laws and implement supplementary measures where necessary to ensure adequate data protection.

metadata.title: Data Stewardship
metadata.definition: The responsible planning and management of an organization's information assets, including ensuring data quality, security, and privacy, throughout their lifecycle. It involves establishing accountability, policies, and processes to ensure data is used ethically, efficiently, and in compliance with regulations.

metadata.title: Data Quality Ethics
metadata.definition: The ethical considerations and responsibilities associated with ensuring data accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, and validity. It addresses the potential harm, bias, or discriminatory outcomes that can arise from poor data quality, especially when data is used for automated decision-making or to inform critical actions.

metadata.title: Data Collection Ethics
metadata.definition: The moral principles and guidelines governing the methods, transparency, and consent involved in acquiring personal or sensitive information. It emphasizes respecting individuals' autonomy, minimizing intrusion, ensuring fairness, and preventing potential harm or exploitation of data subjects.

metadata.title: Data Sharing Ethics
metadata.definition: The ethical considerations surrounding the disclosure or transfer of data to third parties, focusing on consent, anonymization, purpose limitation, and potential risks to privacy and security. It ensures that data sharing aligns with the expectations of individuals and does not lead to unintended harm or misuse.

metadata.title: Data Retention Ethics
metadata.definition: The ethical principles guiding how long personal or sensitive data should be stored, balancing legal obligations and business needs with privacy concerns and the principle of data minimization. It addresses the potential risks of indefinite data storage, such as increased vulnerability to breaches and re-identification.

metadata.title: Algorithmic Governance
metadata.definition: The framework of rules, policies, and mechanisms designed to manage the development, deployment, and impact of algorithms, particularly those used in automated decision-making. Its primary aim is to ensure fairness, transparency, accountability, and ethical outcomes from algorithmic systems, mitigating risks like bias and discrimination.

metadata.title: Ethical Data Sourcing
metadata.definition: The practice of acquiring data from origins that respect privacy, intellectual property, and consent, avoiding exploitative practices, biases, or illegal means. It emphasizes transparency, fairness, and responsible supply chains for data used in analytics, machine learning, and other applications.

metadata.title: Data Vetting
metadata.definition: The process of critically examining, validating, and assessing data for its quality, integrity, relevance, and ethical implications before use. It involves checking for biases, inaccuracies, privacy risks, and compliance with internal policies and external regulations.

metadata.title: Data Lifecyle Management Ethics
metadata.definition: The ethical considerations and principles that guide the collection, storage, processing, use, sharing, and eventual deletion or archiving of data throughout its entire lifecycle. It emphasizes responsible data stewardship to prevent harm and uphold values such as privacy, fairness, and transparency.

metadata.title: Independent AI Auditing
metadata.definition: The practice of having an external, impartial third party assess an AI system for compliance with ethical guidelines, regulatory requirements, performance standards, and potential biases or risks. Its goal is to provide objective assurance and accountability for AI systems.

metadata.title: Impact Assessment (Ethical)
metadata.definition: A systematic process used to identify, evaluate, and mitigate potential ethical risks and societal consequences of a new technology, project, or policy, especially concerning AI and data systems. It aims to proactively address harms and ensure alignment with societal values.

metadata.title: Transparency (Data and Algorithms)
metadata.definition: The principle that the collection, use, and processing of data, as well as the design, logic, and decision-making processes of algorithms, should be open, understandable, and accessible to relevant stakeholders. It enables scrutiny, accountability, and builds trust.

metadata.title: Explainability (Data and Algorithms)
metadata.definition: The ability to interpret and understand the internal workings, decision-making logic, and rationale behind an AI model's output in a way that is comprehensible to humans. It is crucial for debugging, auditing, ensuring fairness, and building user trust.

metadata.title: Societal Bias
metadata.definition: Pre-existing human prejudices, stereotypes, and systemic inequalities embedded within society that are frequently reflected in the data used to train AI systems and in the problem formulations themselves. This bias can lead to discriminatory or unfair outcomes when perpetuated by algorithms.

metadata.title: Historical Bias
metadata.definition: A form of societal bias that arises from past or present societal inequalities and prejudices being embedded within the data used to train AI models. This can cause models to learn and perpetuate historical discrimination.

metadata.title: Selection Bias (Data)
metadata.definition: Bias introduced into a dataset when the method of data collection or sampling leads to a sample that is not representative of the target population or phenomenon it is intended to model. This can result in distorted conclusions and poor generalization for the AI system.

metadata.title: Measurement Bias (Data)
metadata.definition: Bias that arises from systematic errors or inaccuracies in the way data is collected, recorded, or measured, often due to faulty instruments, inconsistent methodologies, or human error. It results in data that consistently misrepresents the true values.

metadata.title: Omitted Variable Bias
metadata.definition: A type of statistical bias that occurs in regression models when a relevant explanatory variable is left out of the model, and that omitted variable is correlated with both the dependent variable and at least one included independent variable. This leads to biased and inconsistent estimates of the effects of the included variables.

metadata.title: Pre-existing Bias
metadata.definition: Bias that originates from human cognitive shortcuts, social structures, cultural norms, or historical injustices that are independent of the AI system itself. These biases become problematic when they are encoded into data or the problem formulation and subsequently learned and perpetuated by AI.

metadata.title: Technical Bias
metadata.definition: Bias introduced into an AI system due to choices made during its technical design, development, or implementation, rather than solely originating from pre-existing societal biases in the data. This can include algorithmic choices, hardware limitations, or optimization priorities.

metadata.title: Emergent Bias
metadata.definition: Bias that arises or becomes apparent only after an AI system has been deployed and interacts with its real-world environment, users, and broader social contexts. It often results from the complex interplay between the system and its operational environment, leading to unintended and unforeseen consequences.

metadata.title: Group Fairness
metadata.definition: A category of fairness definitions in AI that focuses on achieving equitable outcomes, performance, or treatment across different predefined demographic groups. It aims to ensure that no group is systematically disadvantaged compared to others by an algorithmic system.

metadata.title: Individual Fairness
metadata.definition: The principle that similar individuals should be treated similarly by an AI system, regardless of their group affiliations. It focuses on non-discrimination at the individual level, ensuring consistency for those with comparable relevant attributes.

metadata.title: Subgroup Fairness
metadata.definition: An extension of group fairness that requires fair treatment or outcomes not just for broad demographic groups, but also for their intersections or smaller, more specific subgroups. It addresses the limitations of simple group fairness metrics by considering the unique vulnerabilities of intersecting identities.

metadata.title: Causal Fairness
metadata.definition: A framework for algorithmic fairness that aims to eliminate discrimination by ensuring that sensitive attributes (e.g., race, gender) do not causally influence a decision or outcome, or that an intervention's causal effect is fair across groups. It moves beyond statistical correlations to consider underlying cause-and-effect relationships.

metadata.title: Demographic Parity
metadata.definition: A group fairness metric that requires the proportion of positive outcomes or classifications from an AI system to be statistically equal across different demographic groups. It is also known as 'statistical parity' or 'independence'.

metadata.title: Statistical Parity
metadata.definition: A fairness criterion stating that the probability of an AI system predicting a positive outcome should be statistically independent of an individual's protected attribute. Essentially, it means that the proportion of positive outcomes should be the same across all defined groups.

metadata.title: Equal Opportunity (Fairness Metric)
metadata.definition: A group fairness metric that aims to ensure that individuals who are truly worthy or qualified for a positive outcome (i.e., those with the true positive label) have an equal chance of receiving that positive outcome from an AI system, irrespective of their demographic group. This is often measured by equalizing the true positive rate (TPR) or false negative rate (FNR) across groups.

metadata.title: Equalized Odds
metadata.definition: A fairness metric requiring that a model's true positive rates (TPR) and false positive rates (FPR) are equal across all specified protected groups. This ensures that the model performs equally well for both positive and negative outcomes across these groups.

metadata.title: Predictive Parity
metadata.definition: A fairness metric (also known as 'precision parity') requiring that among individuals predicted to have a positive outcome, the proportion who actually have the positive outcome (precision or positive predictive value) is the same across all protected groups.

metadata.title: Disparate Impact
metadata.definition: Occurs when an algorithm or policy, though neutral on its face and applied uniformly, disproportionately harms or disadvantages individuals belonging to a specific protected group.

metadata.title: Disparate Treatment
metadata.definition: Refers to explicit or intentional discrimination where an algorithm or system treats individuals differently based on their protected characteristics.

metadata.title: Fairness-aware Machine Learning
metadata.definition: An approach to developing machine learning models that explicitly considers, measures, and aims to mitigate various forms of bias and discrimination, ensuring equitable outcomes for different demographic groups.

metadata.title: Bias Detection Techniques
metadata.definition: Methodologies used to identify, quantify, and characterize unfair or discriminatory patterns present in datasets, learned models, or model predictions.

metadata.title: Pre-processing Bias Mitigation
metadata.definition: A category of bias mitigation strategies applied to the training data *before* a machine learning model is trained, aiming to reduce or remove biases present in the input data.

metadata.title: In-processing Bias Mitigation
metadata.definition: A category of bias mitigation strategies that modify the learning algorithm or its objective function *during* the model training process to incorporate fairness constraints directly into the model's learning.

metadata.title: Post-processing Bias Mitigation
metadata.definition: A category of bias mitigation strategies that adjust the final predictions or outputs of a *trained* machine learning model to improve fairness, without modifying the model itself or its training data.

metadata.title: Re-sampling (Bias Mitigation)
metadata.definition: A pre-processing bias mitigation technique that alters the distribution of the training data by over-sampling underrepresented groups or under-sampling overrepresented groups, aiming to balance their representation and reduce bias.

metadata.title: Re-weighting (Bias Mitigation)
metadata.definition: A pre-processing bias mitigation technique that assigns different importance weights to individual data instances in the training set, typically giving higher weights to samples from underrepresented or disadvantaged groups, to influence the model's learning process.

metadata.title: Adversarial Debiasing
metadata.definition: An in-processing bias mitigation technique where a neural network is trained to learn a data representation that is predictive of the target variable but simultaneously impedes an 'adversary' network from accurately predicting protected attributes from this representation, thus promoting fairness.

metadata.title: Counterfactual Fairness
metadata.definition: A strong fairness notion stating that a model's prediction for an individual should remain the same even if their protected attribute were to change, while all other non-protected relevant attributes remained constant or changed consistently with the protected attribute.

metadata.title: Algorithmic Fairness Metrics
metadata.definition: Quantitative statistical measures used to evaluate whether a machine learning model's predictions or performance exhibits bias or discriminatory outcomes across different demographic or protected groups.

metadata.title: Protected Characteristics (Fairness)
metadata.definition: Attributes of an individual or group that are legally recognized and often ethically considered as illegitimate bases for differential treatment or discrimination in various contexts, such as employment, housing, or lending.

metadata.title: Redlining (Algorithmic Discrimination)
metadata.definition: The algorithmic manifestation of the historical discriminatory practice of redlining, where an algorithm or automated system unfairly denies or limits access to services, opportunities, or resources for individuals residing in specific geographic areas, often correlated with race or socioeconomic status.

metadata.title: Algorithmic Stereotyping
metadata.definition: Occurs when an algorithm makes predictions or decisions about an individual by inferring characteristics from the average behavior or perceived traits of a group they belong to, rather than evaluating the individual's unique qualities and merits.

metadata.title: Proxy Discrimination
metadata.definition: Discrimination that occurs when an algorithm or model relies on seemingly neutral features (proxies) that are highly correlated with protected characteristics, leading to indirect discrimination against protected groups.

metadata.title: Algorithmic Affirmative Action
metadata.definition: Refers to intentionally modifying an algorithm or its outcomes to provide preferential treatment or increased opportunities for historically disadvantaged or underrepresented protected groups, aiming to counteract systemic bias and promote equity.

metadata.title: Fairness Through Unawareness
metadata.definition: A naive fairness notion that posits a model is fair if it does not explicitly use protected attributes (like race or gender) as input features, assuming that removing these features will prevent discrimination. This approach often fails due to the existence of proxy features.

metadata.title: Fairness Through Awareness
metadata.definition: A class of fairness definitions in AI where a model's predictions are considered fair if they are similar for individuals who are similar with respect to a set of protected attributes, even if those attributes are explicitly used in the model. This approach often involves directly incorporating protected attributes (like race or gender) during training to achieve equitable outcomes across groups.

metadata.title: Fairness Through Causal Modeling
metadata.definition: A framework for defining and achieving fairness in AI by identifying and mitigating causal pathways that lead to discrimination. It seeks to ensure that decisions are not influenced by protected attributes through unfair causal paths, even if indirect, while allowing for legitimate causal influences.

metadata.title: Algorithmic Collusion
metadata.definition: Occurs when AI algorithms, particularly in competitive markets, independently arrive at and sustain anti-competitive outcomes, such as price fixing or market division, without explicit human intent or communication to collude. This can happen through iterative learning and optimization processes where algorithms learn to coordinate their actions.

metadata.title: Responsible AI Principles
metadata.definition: A set of guidelines and values designed to steer the development, deployment, and use of AI systems in ways that are ethical, beneficial to society, and minimize harm. These principles often include fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, safety, and human oversight.

metadata.title: Autonomous Systems Ethics
metadata.definition: The branch of ethics concerned with the moral implications, responsibilities, and values associated with the design, behavior, and impact of systems that can operate independently without continuous human intervention. It addresses questions of control, safety, responsibility, and the potential for harm or benefit.

metadata.title: Human-AI Teaming Ethics
metadata.definition: Focuses on the ethical challenges and best practices for collaborative systems where humans and AI work together to achieve common goals. It examines issues such as trust, transparency, decision-making authority, accountability, potential for deskilling, and the maintenance of human autonomy and well-being within such partnerships.

metadata.title: Human Oversight of AI
metadata.definition: The practice and ethical imperative of ensuring that humans retain appropriate control, monitoring capabilities, and the ultimate authority over AI systems, particularly in critical decision-making contexts. This aims to prevent unchecked AI errors, biases, and unintended consequences, allowing for human intervention, correction, or override.

metadata.title: Moral Responsibility of AI Systems
metadata.definition: Explores whether, and under what conditions, an AI system itself can be considered morally responsible for its actions, independent of its creators, deployers, or users. This concept delves into questions of AI agency, consciousness, and the capacity for moral reasoning, and is a subject of ongoing philosophical and ethical debate.

metadata.title: Legal Liability for AI Actions
metadata.definition: Concerns who is legally responsible when an AI system causes harm or makes a decision that results in damages. This involves assigning culpability among developers, manufacturers, deployers, operators, and users, often challenging existing legal frameworks designed for human or corporate actors.

metadata.title: AI and Employment Impact
metadata.definition: Refers to the multifaceted effects of AI and automation technologies on the labor market, including job displacement, creation of new job roles, changes in skill requirements, wage impacts, and shifts in work organization. This involves assessing both potential benefits and societal challenges.

metadata.title: AI and Deskilling
metadata.definition: The process by which AI and automation technologies reduce the complexity, skill requirements, or autonomy associated with certain human jobs. This can lead to workers performing more routine, monitored tasks, potentially diminishing their expertise and job satisfaction.

metadata.title: AI and Automation Ethics
metadata.definition: The ethical considerations surrounding the widespread deployment of AI and automation, particularly concerning its societal impact, labor displacement, control over autonomous systems, potential for human alienation, and the equitable distribution of benefits. It overlaps with specific aspects like employment, deskilling, and autonomous systems.

metadata.title: AI and Surveillance Ethics
metadata.definition: Examines the moral and privacy implications of using AI technologies for monitoring, tracking, and data collection, often by governments or corporations. It addresses issues like mass surveillance, privacy invasion, algorithmic bias in surveillance, and the potential for chilling effects on civil liberties.

metadata.title: Algorithmic Manipulation
metadata.definition: The intentional or unintentional influencing of human behavior, decisions, or perceptions by AI algorithms through personalization, recommendation systems, or presentation of information. This can exploit cognitive biases or vulnerabilities, raising ethical concerns about user autonomy and informed consent.

metadata.title: Dark Patterns (Ethical Aspect)
metadata.definition: User interface design choices that intentionally trick or manipulate users into taking actions they might not otherwise choose, often against their own interests, for the benefit of the service provider. Ethically, they raise concerns about user autonomy, transparency, and deceptive design practices.

metadata.title: Filter Bubbles
metadata.definition: A state of intellectual isolation that results from personalized algorithms on the internet selectively guessing what information a user would like to see based on their past online behavior, search history, and demographic data. This can prevent users from encountering diverse viewpoints and challenge their existing beliefs.

metadata.title: Echo Chambers
metadata.definition: A metaphorical space where beliefs are amplified or reinforced by communication and repetition inside a closed system, often online, where differing views are underrepresented or actively excluded. This can lead to increased polarization and a lack of exposure to alternative perspectives.

metadata.title: Misinformation (AI-generated)
metadata.definition: False or inaccurate information that is created or propagated by AI systems, regardless of an intent to deceive. AI tools, especially generative models, can inadvertently produce factually incorrect content, which can then be widely disseminated.

metadata.title: Disinformation (AI-generated)
metadata.definition: Deliberately false or misleading information that is created, amplified, or disseminated by AI systems with the malicious intent to deceive, manipulate, or cause harm. This often involves using AI to craft persuasive narratives, generate realistic fake media, or target specific audiences.

metadata.title: Deepfakes Ethics
metadata.definition: The ethical considerations surrounding the creation and use of deepfakes—synthetic media (video, audio, images) generated by AI, particularly deep learning, that convincingly depict people saying or doing things they never did. Key concerns include consent, reputational harm, privacy violation, misinformation, and their potential use in harassment or fraud.

metadata.title: Synthetic Media Ethics
metadata.definition: Focuses on the moral implications and societal impact of media content generated or modified by AI, particularly concerning issues like authenticity, consent, manipulation, and truth. It addresses the responsible creation, distribution, and consumption of deepfakes and other AI-generated media.

metadata.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Ethics
metadata.definition: Examines the ethical principles and challenges associated with AI systems capable of creating novel content, such as text, images, audio, or code. It addresses concerns like intellectual property, bias amplification, misuse for harmful purposes, and the environmental impact of training these large models.

metadata.title: Large Language Model Ethics
metadata.definition: Specifically investigates the ethical considerations surrounding the development, deployment, and use of Large Language Models (LLMs), which are advanced generative AI systems trained on vast amounts of text data. Key concerns include bias, factual accuracy (hallucinations), intellectual property infringement, data privacy, and the potential for misuse in propaganda or phishing.

metadata.title: Artificial Intelligence Explainability (XAI)
metadata.definition: Refer to the capability of an AI system to provide understandable insights into its decision-making process or predictions, making its internal workings comprehensible to humans. XAI aims to build trust, ensure fairness, comply with regulations, and allow for debugging and improvement of complex AI models.

metadata.title: Artificial Intelligence Interpretability
metadata.definition: Refers to the degree to which a human can understand the cause and effect of an AI model's internal functions, allowing them to comprehend why a specific decision was made. Interpretability is a broader concept than explainability, focusing on the intrinsic understandability of the model itself rather than just generating explanations.

metadata.title: Transparency of AI Models
metadata.definition: Pertains to the ability to understand how an AI system works, including its data sources, algorithms, decision-making logic, and intended purpose. It encompasses making the internal mechanisms and operations of AI systems accessible and comprehensible to relevant stakeholders, fostering trust and accountability.

metadata.title: Reproducibility of AI Research
metadata.definition: The principle that an independent researcher, given the same data, code, and computational environment, should be able to obtain the same results as reported in an original AI study. It is crucial for validating research findings, building cumulative knowledge, and ensuring the trustworthiness and reliability of AI advancements.

metadata.title: Scalable Oversight (AI)
metadata.definition: Refers to the challenge and methodologies involved in effectively monitoring, auditing, and regulating a rapidly growing number and diversity of AI systems across various applications and sectors.
