metadata.definition: In reinforcement learning, the agent is an entity that performs actions within an environment, observes the resulting states and rewards, and learns to choose optimal actions to maximize cumulative reward over time. It is the decision-making component of the RL system, aiming to achieve a specific goal.

metadata.title: Apache Avro
metadata.definition: A data serialization system that provides rich data structures and a compact, fast, binary data format. It relies on a schema (often JSON) to define the data structure, which can evolve over time, making it suitable for data exchange and persistent data storage in Big Data ecosystems.

metadata.title: Apache Cassandra
metadata.definition: An open-source, distributed NoSQL database designed to handle large amounts of data across many commodity servers, providing high availability with no single point of failure. It offers a highly scalable and fault-tolerant architecture, ideal for applications requiring continuous uptime and massive writes.

metadata.title: Apache Flume
metadata.definition: A distributed, reliable, and available service for efficiently collecting, aggregating, and moving large amounts of log data from various sources to a centralized data store like HDFS. It uses an agent-based architecture with sources, channels, and sinks to build data flows.

metadata.title: Apache HBase
metadata.definition: An open-source, non-relational, distributed database modeled after Google's Bigtable, built on top of the Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS). It provides random, real-time read/write access to billions of rows and millions of columns, making it suitable for extremely large datasets.

metadata.title: Apache Oozie
metadata.definition: A workflow scheduler system for managing Hadoop jobs. It allows users to define a series of actions, such as MapReduce, Pig, Hive, or Spark jobs, as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) and run them in a scheduled or event-triggered manner.

metadata.title: Apache ORC
metadata.definition: (Optimized Row Columnar) A free and open-source columnar data storage format designed for Hadoop workloads, offering a highly efficient way to store data for SQL-on-Hadoop engines like Hive and Spark SQL. It provides excellent compression and predicate pushdown, leading to faster query performance.

metadata.title: Apache Parquet
metadata.definition: A free and open-source columnar storage format available to any project in the Hadoop ecosystem, providing efficient data compression and encoding schemes. It is optimized for complex data types and performs well with analytical queries, enabling predicate pushdown and efficient column projection.

metadata.title: Apache Spark Core
metadata.definition: The underlying general-purpose distributed processing engine of Apache Spark, responsible for basic I/O, scheduling, and monitoring tasks. It provides an API for Resilient Distributed Datasets (RDDs), which are fault-tolerant collections of elements that can be operated on in parallel across a cluster.

metadata.title: Apache Spark DataFrame
metadata.definition: A distributed collection of data organized into named columns, conceptually equivalent to a table in a relational database or a data frame in R/Python. It provides a higher-level abstraction over RDDs, offering optimized execution through the Catalyst optimizer and easy integration with SQL.

metadata.title: Apache Spark GraphX
metadata.definition: A component of Apache Spark for graph-parallel computation, which extends the Spark RDD API with a Resilient Distributed Property Graph. It combines the advantages of both ETL and graph processing, allowing users to build and transform graphs and run graph algorithms efficiently.

metadata.title: Apache Spark MLlib
metadata.definition: Spark's scalable machine learning library, built on top of Spark Core, offering a wide range of machine learning algorithms and utilities. It includes tools for classification, regression, clustering, collaborative filtering, dimensionality reduction, and optimization, designed for large-scale data.

metadata.title: Apache Spark SQL
metadata.definition: A Spark module for working with structured data, allowing users to query data using SQL or a DataFrame API. It supports various data sources, integrates seamlessly with Spark programs, and uses the Catalyst optimizer for efficient query execution across distributed datasets.

metadata.title: Apache Spark Streaming
metadata.definition: A component of Apache Spark that enables scalable, high-throughput, fault-tolerant processing of live data streams. It receives live input data streams, such as from Kafka or Flume, and divides them into micro-batches, which are then processed by the Spark engine to generate final results.

metadata.title: Apache Sqoop
metadata.definition: A tool designed for efficiently transferring bulk data between Apache Hadoop and structured datastores such as relational databases. It automates the import of data from RDBMS into HDFS or Hive and the export of data from Hadoop to RDBMS.

metadata.title: Apache YARN
metadata.definition: (Yet Another Resource Negotiator) The resource management layer of Hadoop 2.x+, responsible for managing computing resources and scheduling applications across a cluster. It allows multiple data processing engines (like MapReduce, Spark, Tez) to run concurrently on the same cluster resources.

metadata.title: API Integration
metadata.definition: The process of connecting different applications, systems, or data sources using Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) to enable communication and data exchange. It allows disparate software components to work together seamlessly, facilitating data flow and extending functionality.

metadata.title: Apriori Algorithm
metadata.definition: An algorithm for frequent itemset mining and association rule learning over transactional databases. It identifies frequent individual items in the database and extends them to larger itemsets as long as those itemsets appear sufficiently often in the database.

metadata.title: ARMA Model
metadata.definition: An Autoregressive Moving Average (ARMA) model is a statistical model used for analyzing and forecasting time series data. It combines an Autoregressive (AR) component, which models the linear dependence on its own past values, and a Moving Average (MA) component, which models the linear dependence on past forecast errors.

metadata.title: ARIMA Model
metadata.definition: An Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) model is a generalization of the ARMA model, widely used for time series forecasting. The "Integrated" (I) component indicates that the raw observations have been differenced one or more times to make the time series stationary before applying the ARMA model.

metadata.title: Attention Mechanism (Deep Learning)
metadata.definition: An attention mechanism in deep learning allows a neural network to selectively focus on relevant parts of its input when making predictions. It assigns different weights to different parts of the input sequence, effectively determining how much "attention" each part should receive.

metadata.title: AUC (Area Under the Curve)
metadata.definition: AUC, specifically AUC-ROC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve), is a common performance metric for binary classification models. It measures the ability of a classifier to distinguish between classes, with a value closer to 1 indicating better performance and 0.5 indicating performance equivalent to random guessing.

metadata.title: Autocorrelation
metadata.definition: Autocorrelation measures the linear relationship between a time series's current value and its past values at different lags. It quantifies how correlated a series is with a lagged version of itself, revealing patterns and dependencies within the data over time.

metadata.title: Autoregressive Model (AR)
metadata.definition: An Autoregressive (AR) model is a type of time series model where the output variable's current value linearly depends on its own previous values and a stochastic term. It's denoted as AR(p), where 'p' is the order of the model, indicating the number of past observations used.

metadata.title: Average Precision (AP)
metadata.definition: Average Precision (AP) is a popular metric for evaluating the performance of information retrieval or object detection systems, especially in scenarios with imbalanced classes. It calculates the weighted mean of precisions achieved at each threshold, where the weight is the increase in recall from the previous threshold.

metadata.title: Average Treatment Effect (ATE)
metadata.definition: The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal inference metric that quantifies the average difference in an outcome between individuals who received a treatment and those who did not, across an entire population. It aims to estimate the causal impact of an intervention, assuming all other factors are equal.

metadata.title: AWS EC2
metadata.definition: Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) is a web service that provides resizable compute capacity in the cloud. It allows users to rent virtual servers (instances) to run applications, offering various instance types optimized for different workloads, from general-purpose to memory- or compute-intensive tasks.

metadata.title: AWS Lambda
metadata.definition: AWS Lambda is a serverless, event-driven compute service that lets you run code without provisioning or managing servers. It automatically scales your application by running code only when needed and charging only for the compute time consumed, making it cost-effective for event-driven architectures.

metadata.title: AWS S3
metadata.definition: Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) is an object storage service offering industry-leading scalability, data availability, security, and performance. It provides highly durable and available storage for virtually any type of data, accessible from anywhere on the web.

metadata.title: AWS SageMaker
metadata.definition: AWS SageMaker is a fully managed machine learning service that enables developers and data scientists to build, train, and deploy machine learning models quickly. It provides a comprehensive set of tools for every step of the ML workflow, from data labeling to model monitoring.

metadata.title: Azure Machine Learning
metadata.definition: Azure Machine Learning is a cloud-based service for accelerating and managing the machine learning project lifecycle. It provides a robust platform for training, deploying, and managing ML models, supporting various tools and frameworks for data scientists and developers.

metadata.title: Azure Virtual Machines
metadata.definition: Azure Virtual Machines (VMs) are on-demand, scalable compute resources that provide the flexibility of virtualization without the need to buy and maintain hardware. They allow users to run various operating systems and applications in the cloud, offering control over the operating environment.

metadata.title: Bagging (Ensemble)
metadata.definition: Bagging, short for Bootstrap Aggregating, is an ensemble machine learning technique that improves the stability and accuracy of models and reduces variance. It works by training multiple base models on different bootstrap samples (random samples with replacement) of the original training data and then aggregating their predictions.

metadata.title: Batch Inference
metadata.definition: Batch inference is the process of making predictions on a large collection of data points simultaneously, rather than one by one in real-time. It is typically used for scenarios where predictions are not needed instantly and can be processed periodically, often optimizing for throughput and cost.

metadata.title: Batch Size
metadata.definition: In the context of training neural networks, batch size refers to the number of training examples utilized in one iteration. It is a hyperparameter that determines how many data samples are processed before the model's internal parameters are updated, significantly impacting training speed, memory usage, and convergence stability.

metadata.title: Bayesian Optimization
metadata.definition: Bayesian optimization is a powerful technique for finding the global optimum of objective functions that are expensive to evaluate and often lack a closed-form expression. It uses a probabilistic surrogate model (e.g., Gaussian Process) to approximate the objective function and an acquisition function to determine the next best point to sample.

metadata.title: Bernoulli Naive Bayes
metadata.definition: Bernoulli Naive Bayes is a classification algorithm that applies Bayes' theorem with the "naive" assumption of independence between features, specifically designed for binary or boolean features. It assumes that features are Bernoulli distributed, meaning they represent the presence or absence of a particular feature (e.g., a word in a document).

metadata.title: BERT Embedding
metadata.definition: A numerical representation (vector) of words, subwords, or entire sentences generated by a pre-trained BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) model, capturing rich semantic and contextual information. These embeddings are highly effective for various downstream NLP tasks.

metadata.title: Binning (Data Transformation)
metadata.definition: The process of grouping continuous numerical data into a smaller number of 'bins' or intervals, converting quantitative data into qualitative (ordinal) data. This simplifies data, reduces noise, and can handle outliers.

metadata.title: BLEU Score
metadata.definition: (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) A metric for evaluating the quality of text that has been machine-translated from one natural language to another. It compares the machine-generated output to one or more human-created reference translations, measuring n-gram overlap.

metadata.title: Boosting (Ensemble)
metadata.definition: An ensemble machine learning technique that combines multiple weak learners sequentially to form a strong learner. Each subsequent learner attempts to correct the errors made by the previous ones, focusing more on misclassified instances.

metadata.title: Bootstrap Resampling
metadata.definition: A non-parametric resampling technique where multiple datasets of the same size as the original dataset are created by sampling with replacement from the original data. This method is used to estimate the sampling distribution of a statistic or to assess model stability.

metadata.title: Causal Inference
metadata.definition: The process of drawing conclusions about cause-and-effect relationships from data, identifying whether a change in one variable directly leads to a change in another. It goes beyond mere correlation to establish mechanisms and rule out spurious associations.

metadata.title: Causality
metadata.definition: The relationship between cause and effect, where one event or factor (the cause) directly influences another event or factor (the effect), rather than merely being correlated with it. Establishing causality requires ruling out alternative explanations and often demonstrating a temporal sequence.

metadata.title: CatBoost Classifier
metadata.definition: An open-source gradient boosting on decision trees library, specifically designed to handle categorical features efficiently. It employs a novel ordered boosting scheme and transforms categorical features into numerical ones without requiring extensive preprocessing like one-hot encoding.

metadata.title: Chain Rule (Calculus)
metadata.definition: A fundamental rule in calculus used to compute the derivative of a composite function. It states that the derivative of f(g(x)) is f'(g(x)) multiplied by g'(x), and is crucial for calculating gradients during backpropagation in neural networks.

metadata.title: Chi-Squared Test
metadata.definition: A statistical hypothesis test used to determine if there is a significant association between two categorical variables, or if the observed distribution of a single categorical variable differs significantly from an expected distribution.

metadata.title: CI/CD for Machine Learning
metadata.definition: (Continuous Integration/Continuous Delivery for Machine Learning) An extension of traditional CI/CD pipelines tailored for machine learning workflows. It automates the testing, building, training, deployment, and monitoring of ML models and their associated data and code.

metadata.title: Coaching Loop (MLOps)
metadata.definition: In MLOps, a coaching loop refers to an iterative process where human experts review model predictions, identify errors, provide feedback, and potentially label new data. This feedback is then used to retrain and improve the model, fostering continuous performance enhancement.

metadata.title: Column-Family Model
metadata.definition: A NoSQL database model that stores data in columns rather than rows, where columns are grouped into 'families'. Each row can have different columns, offering high flexibility and scalability for sparse data and analytical workloads, particularly suited for wide tables.

metadata.title: Confidence (Association Rule)
metadata.definition: In association rule mining, confidence is a measure of the reliability of an association rule, defined as the conditional probability that the consequent item(s) appear in a transaction given that the antecedent item(s) are present. It indicates how often the rule is true.

metadata.title: Confounding Variable
metadata.definition: A variable that influences both the independent variable (potential cause) and the dependent variable (effect), creating a spurious association between them. This can mislead researchers into thinking there's a direct causal link when there isn't.

metadata.title: Concept Drift
metadata.definition: A phenomenon in machine learning where the statistical properties of the target variable, or the relationship between input features and the target, change over time in unforeseen ways. This causes the model's performance to degrade, even if the model itself remains unchanged.

metadata.title: Correlation
metadata.definition: A statistical measure that expresses the extent to which two variables are linearly related, meaning they change together at a constant rate. It indicates the strength and direction of a linear relationship but does not imply causation.

metadata.title: Cost Function
metadata.definition: (Also known as Loss Function or Objective Function) A function that quantifies the error or discrepancy between the predicted output of a model and the actual true values. The primary goal of training a machine learning model is to minimize this cost function.

metadata.title: Counterfactual Explanations
metadata.definition: A type of Explainable AI (XAI) that identifies the smallest change to an input that would alter a model's prediction to a predefined, desired outcome. It answers 'What if X had not happened, would Y still have occurred?' or 'What is the minimum change to make the model predict Z?'.

metadata.title: CRISP-DM
metadata.definition: (Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining) A widely used, six-phase methodology that provides a structured approach for planning, executing, and deploying data mining and machine learning projects. It ensures projects are repeatable, manageable, and focused on business understanding.

metadata.title: Cyclicity (Time Series)
metadata.definition: A repeating pattern or fluctuation in a time series data set that occurs at regular intervals, such as daily, weekly, monthly, or yearly. Unlike seasonality, which often refers to calendar-based patterns, cyclicity can occur over irregular or longer periods not tied to fixed calendar components, but still exhibits recurring upward and downward trends.

metadata.title: Data Augmentation (Image)
metadata.definition: Techniques used to artificially increase the size and diversity of a training dataset by creating modified versions of existing images. This helps improve the generalization ability of deep learning models and reduces overfitting, especially when data is scarce.

metadata.title: Data Cleaning
metadata.definition: The process of detecting and correcting (or removing) corrupt, inaccurate, incomplete, or irrelevant records from a dataset. Its goal is to prepare high-quality data for analysis and modeling by ensuring consistency, validity, and accuracy.

metadata.title: Data Drift
metadata.definition: A phenomenon where the statistical properties of the target variable or input features change over time, leading to a degradation in the performance of a deployed machine learning model. It indicates that the data distribution on which the model was trained is no longer representative of the data it encounters in production.

metadata.title: Data Model
metadata.definition: An abstract model that organizes elements of data and standardizes how they relate to one another and to properties of the real world entities. It provides a conceptual framework for data and supports the design of databases and information systems.

metadata.title: Data Observability
metadata.definition: The ability to understand the health and state of data within a system at any given time, providing insights into its quality, freshness, volume, schema, and lineage. It involves monitoring data pipelines and datasets to detect issues early and ensure data reliability and trustworthiness.

metadata.title: Data Pipeline
metadata.definition: A series of automated processes or steps designed to move, transform, and prepare raw data from various sources into a structured format suitable for analysis, reporting, or machine learning models. It ensures data flows efficiently and reliably through different stages.

metadata.title: Data Validation
metadata.definition: The process of ensuring that data conforms to predefined rules, constraints, and formats, and that it is accurate, complete, and consistent. It typically occurs at the point of data entry or ingestion to prevent bad data from entering a system.

metadata.title: Data Versioning
metadata.definition: The practice of tracking and managing changes to datasets over time, allowing for the retrieval of specific data states or versions. This is crucial for reproducibility, auditing, and debugging in data-intensive projects, especially in machine learning.

metadata.title: DBSCAN Clustering
metadata.definition: A density-based clustering algorithm that groups together points that are closely packed together, marking as outliers points that lie alone in low-density regions. It defines clusters as areas of high density separated by areas of lower density.

metadata.title: Decision Tree Classifier
metadata.definition: A supervised machine learning algorithm used for classification tasks that builds a model in the form of a tree structure. It splits the dataset into smaller subsets based on feature values, with each internal node representing a test on an attribute, each branch representing an outcome of the test, and each leaf node representing a class label.

metadata.title: Decision Tree Regressor
metadata.definition: A supervised machine learning algorithm used for regression tasks that builds a tree structure to predict a continuous output value. It partitions the feature space into a set of rectangular regions and predicts the mean or median output value of the training samples within each region.

metadata.title: Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
metadata.definition: A quasi-experimental research design that estimates the causal effect of a treatment or intervention by comparing the changes in outcomes over time between a group that received the treatment (treatment group) and a group that did not (control group). It effectively controls for unobservable time-invariant differences between the groups and common trends over time.

metadata.title: Distributed File System (HDFS)
metadata.definition: A file system designed to store very large files reliably across multiple machines in a cluster, often used in big data processing. HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System) breaks files into blocks and distributes them across nodes, replicating each block for fault tolerance and high availability.

metadata.title: Document Embedding
metadata.definition: A technique to represent entire documents as dense, fixed-size numerical vectors (embeddings) in a high-dimensional space. These embeddings capture the semantic meaning and context of the document, allowing for similarity comparisons and use in machine learning models.

metadata.title: Document Model
metadata.definition: A type of NoSQL database model that stores data in flexible, semi-structured documents, typically JSON or BSON formats. Unlike relational models, documents can have varying structures and nested fields, making them suitable for evolving data and hierarchical data.

metadata.title: Docker Container
metadata.definition: A lightweight, standalone, executable package of software that includes everything needed to run an application: code, runtime, system tools, system libraries, and settings. It virtualizes the operating system level, ensuring consistency across different environments.

metadata.title: Duplicate Removal
metadata.definition: The process of identifying and eliminating redundant or identical records within a dataset. This step is crucial in data cleaning and preprocessing to ensure data accuracy, prevent skewed analysis, and optimize storage.

metadata.title: Eclat Algorithm
metadata.definition: An efficient algorithm for mining frequent itemsets from a transaction database, based on a vertical data format. It uses a depth-first search strategy and intersection of transaction IDs (TIDs) to find frequent itemsets, often outperforming Apriori for certain datasets due to its avoidance of candidate generation.

metadata.title: EfficientNet
metadata.definition: A family of highly efficient and scalable convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that achieve state-of-the-art accuracy with significantly fewer parameters and FLOPs than previous models. It introduces a compound scaling method that uniformly scales network depth, width, and resolution for optimal performance.

metadata.title: ELMo Embedding
metadata.definition: ELMo (Embeddings from Language Models) is a type of contextual word embedding that uses a deep bi-directional LSTM to create embeddings dynamically based on the word's context in a sentence, capturing both word usage and polysemy.

metadata.title: Environment (Reinforcement Learning)
metadata.definition: In Reinforcement Learning, the environment is the external system that an agent interacts with, providing observations (states), receiving actions from the agent, and returning rewards and updated states.

metadata.title: Episode (Reinforcement Learning)
metadata.definition: An episode in Reinforcement Learning refers to a complete sequence of interactions between an agent and its environment, typically starting from an initial state and concluding when a terminal state is reached or a maximum number of steps is exceeded.

metadata.title: ETL (Extract, Transform, Load)
metadata.definition: ETL is a traditional data integration process used to consolidate data from various sources into a data warehouse or other target system. It involves extracting data, transforming it into a clean and consistent format, and then loading it into the destination.

metadata.title: ELT (Extract, Load, Transform)
metadata.definition: ELT is a modern data integration paradigm where data is first extracted from source systems and loaded directly into a data lake or cloud data warehouse in its raw form, with transformations then performed within the target system using its scalable processing capabilities.

metadata.title: Exploration-Exploitation Dilemma
metadata.definition: The exploration-exploitation dilemma is a fundamental problem in decision-making under uncertainty, requiring an agent to balance between trying new actions to discover potentially better outcomes (exploration) and repeatedly choosing the best-known actions (exploitation) to maximize immediate rewards.

metadata.title: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
metadata.definition: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is an initial investigation process on data to summarize its main characteristics, often using statistical graphics and other data visualization methods, to discover patterns, detect outliers, test hypotheses, and uncover insights.

metadata.title: Exponential Linear Unit (ELU) Activation
metadata.definition: The Exponential Linear Unit (ELU) is an activation function for neural networks that outputs the input for positive values and an exponential function for negative values, allowing for negative outputs and helping to alleviate the vanishing gradient problem while often leading to faster convergence.

metadata.title: Exponential Smoothing
metadata.definition: Exponential smoothing is a time series forecasting method that assigns exponentially decreasing weights to past observations, meaning more recent observations contribute more significantly to the forecast than older ones.

metadata.title: F-beta Score
metadata.definition: The F-beta score is an evaluation metric that combines precision and recall into a single score, where the parameter beta allows users to weight recall beta times as much as precision, providing flexibility for different use cases and class imbalances.

metadata.title: Face Recognition
metadata.definition: Face recognition is a computer vision technology capable of identifying or verifying a person from a digital image or video frame by comparing unique facial features against a database of known faces.

metadata.title: Fairness (AI)
metadata.definition: Fairness in AI refers to the principle of ensuring that artificial intelligence systems do not exhibit biases or discriminate against certain demographic groups, promoting equitable treatment and outcomes across different individuals and populations.

metadata.title: FastAPI
metadata.definition: FastAPI is a modern, high-performance web framework for building APIs with Python 3.7+, leveraging standard Python type hints for automatic data validation, serialization, and interactive API documentation generation.

metadata.title: FastText Embedding
metadata.definition: FastText is an efficient, open-source library developed by Facebook AI for learning word embeddings and text classification, notably capable of generating embeddings for out-of-vocabulary words by representing words as sums of their character n-grams.

metadata.title: Feature Creation
metadata.definition: Feature creation, a crucial part of feature engineering, is the process of generating new, more expressive and informative features from existing raw data to enhance the predictive power and performance of machine learning models.

metadata.title: Feature Scaling
metadata.definition: Feature scaling is a data preprocessing technique used to transform numerical features in a dataset to a standard range or distribution, which is essential for many machine learning algorithms that are sensitive to the magnitude of input values.

metadata.title: Feature Store
metadata.definition: A feature store is a centralized data management system designed to standardize, store, and serve machine learning features, ensuring consistency and reusability of features across different models and teams, for both offline training and online inference.

metadata.title: Filter/Kernel (CNN)
metadata.definition: In a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), a filter (also known as a kernel) is a small matrix of weights that slides across the input data (e.g., an image) to perform a convolution operation, detecting specific features or patterns.

metadata.title: Fine-tuning (Transfer Learning)
metadata.definition: Fine-tuning in transfer learning involves taking a pre-trained model (trained on a large dataset for a general task) and further training it on a smaller, specific dataset for a related but distinct task, adjusting its weights to adapt to the new domain.

metadata.title: Flask (Web Framework)
metadata.definition: Flask is a lightweight and extensible Python micro web framework that provides essential tools for building web applications and APIs, allowing developers to choose their own libraries and components to suit specific project needs.

metadata.title: FP-Growth Algorithm
metadata.definition: An efficient algorithm for discovering frequent itemsets in a transactional database without generating candidate sets, employing a frequent pattern tree (FP-tree) to compress the database. It constructs an FP-tree and then mines it recursively to find frequent patterns.

metadata.title: Forward Propagation
metadata.definition: The process in an artificial neural network where input data is passed through the network's layers, applying weights, biases, and activation functions at each neuron, to produce an output prediction. It calculates the output for a given input by moving computations from the input layer through hidden layers to the output layer.

metadata.title: GARCH Model
metadata.definition: Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH) models are statistical models used to model time series data that exhibit time-varying volatility, meaning the variance of the error terms changes over time. They extend ARCH models by allowing the conditional variance to depend on past squared errors and past conditional variances.

metadata.title: Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU) Activation
metadata.definition: GELU is a non-linear activation function used in neural networks, particularly in transformer-based models, that multiplies the input by its cumulative distribution function. It smooths the ReLU activation by incorporating probabilistic descriptions of neuron outputs, performing better in many deep learning tasks.

metadata.title: Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM)
metadata.definition: GMMs are probabilistic models that assume data points are generated from a mixture of a finite number of Gaussian distributions with unknown parameters. They are used for clustering data by assigning a probability that each data point belongs to each cluster, allowing for soft assignments and handling non-spherical clusters.

metadata.title: Gaussian Naive Bayes
metadata.definition: A variant of the Naive Bayes algorithm specifically designed for continuous features, where it assumes that the continuous values associated with each class are distributed according to a Gaussian (Normal) distribution. It calculates the probability of each feature belonging to a class based on this assumption, then applies Bayes' theorem.

metadata.title: Generalization (Machine Learning)
metadata.definition: Generalization in machine learning refers to a model's ability to perform well on new, unseen data, rather than just on the data it was trained on. A model with good generalization has learned the underlying patterns in the data, avoiding overfitting to the training set.

metadata.title: Git Pull Request
metadata.definition: A Git Pull Request (PR) is a feature in version control systems like GitHub or GitLab that allows a developer to notify team members about changes they've pushed to a branch in a repository. It proposes merging their changes into another branch, enabling code review, discussion, and automated checks before integration.

metadata.title: GloVe Embedding
metadata.definition: Global Vectors for Word Representation (GloVe) is an unsupervised learning algorithm for obtaining vector representations (embeddings) of words. It builds on both global matrix factorization and local context window methods, capturing word co-occurrence statistics from a corpus to create meaningful word vectors.

metadata.title: ggplot2 (R Library)
metadata.definition: `ggplot2` is a powerful and versatile data visualization package for the R programming language, based on the grammar of graphics. It allows users to build complex and informative plots layer by layer, starting with data, then adding aesthetics, geometries, facets, and statistical transformations.

metadata.title: Google Cloud AI Platform
metadata.definition: Google Cloud AI Platform is a managed service offered by Google Cloud that provides tools and infrastructure for building, deploying, and managing machine learning models at scale. It offers integrated services for data preparation, model training (e.g., custom code, AutoML), prediction, and MLOps.

metadata.title: GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) Model
metadata.definition: GPT models are a series of large language models developed by OpenAI, characterized by their use of the Transformer architecture and pre-training on vast amounts of text data. They are designed for generative tasks, excelling at understanding context and generating human-like text.

metadata.title: Gradient (Calculus)
metadata.definition: In calculus, the gradient of a scalar-valued multivariable function is a vector containing the partial derivatives of the function with respect to each of its independent variables. It points in the direction of the greatest rate of increase of the function.

metadata.title: Gradient Boosting Classifier
metadata.definition: A Gradient Boosting Classifier is an ensemble machine learning algorithm that builds a strong classifier by sequentially combining many weak base classifiers, typically decision trees. It works by training each new tree to predict the *residuals* or errors of the previous ensemble, minimizing a differentiable loss function through gradient descent.

metadata.title: Gradient Boosting Regressor
metadata.definition: A Gradient Boosting Regressor is an ensemble machine learning algorithm that constructs a strong regressor by combining multiple weak base regressors, typically decision trees, in a sequential manner. Each subsequent tree is trained to correct the errors (residuals) of the preceding ensemble, iteratively reducing the overall prediction error via gradient descent.

metadata.title: Graph Model
metadata.definition: A graph model represents data as a set of nodes (entities) and edges (relationships between entities). It is a flexible data structure suitable for modeling complex relationships, where both nodes and edges can have properties or attributes.

metadata.title: Grayscale Image
metadata.definition: A grayscale image is a digital image in which the value of each pixel represents only an intensity level, typically ranging from black (minimum intensity) to white (maximum intensity), with various shades of gray in between. It contains only lightness information, without any color.

metadata.title: Grid Search (Hyperparameter Tuning)
metadata.definition: Grid Search is a hyperparameter tuning technique that systematically works through multiple combinations of specified hyperparameter values for a given model. It evaluates each combination by training the model and testing its performance (e.g., using cross-validation) to find the set of hyperparameters that yields the best metric.

metadata.title: Heatmap (Data Visualization)
metadata.definition: A heatmap is a graphical representation of data where individual values in a matrix are represented as colors. It is particularly useful for visualizing correlation matrices, showing patterns, or highlighting density and variance within a dataset.

metadata.title: Hinge Loss
metadata.definition: Hinge loss is a loss function primarily used for training classifiers, especially Support Vector Machines (SVMs), for maximum-margin classification. It penalizes misclassifications and correct classifications that are not confident enough, with a loss of zero if the predicted output has the correct sign and exceeds a certain margin.

metadata.title: HOG Features
metadata.definition: Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) is a feature descriptor used in computer vision and image processing for object detection. It works by counting occurrences of gradient orientation in localized portions of an image, providing a robust representation of object shape.

metadata.title: Huber Loss
metadata.definition: Huber Loss is a robust loss function used in regression that is less sensitive to outliers than the traditional squared error loss. It is quadratic for small errors and linear for large errors, combining the benefits of L1 and L2 loss.

metadata.title: Imbalanced Data Handling
metadata.definition: Imbalanced data handling refers to techniques used to address datasets where the number of observations in different classes is significantly unequal, which can lead to biased machine learning models. Common strategies include resampling (oversampling, undersampling) and algorithmic adjustments.

metadata.title: Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
metadata.definition: Independent Component Analysis (ICA) is a computational method used to separate a multivariate signal into additive subcomponents, assuming the subcomponents are statistically independent and non-Gaussian. It is a type of blind source separation.

metadata.title: Integral (Calculus)
metadata.definition: An integral is a fundamental concept in calculus representing the accumulation of quantities and the area under a curve. It is the reverse process of differentiation and can be definite (over a specific interval) or indefinite.

metadata.title: Interpretability (AI)
metadata.definition: Interpretability in AI refers to the degree to which a human can understand the cause of a decision made by a machine learning model. It involves making model predictions and internal mechanisms transparent and comprehensible.

metadata.title: Instrumental Variables
metadata.definition: Instrumental Variables (IV) is a statistical technique used to estimate causal effects when controlled experiments are not feasible or when there is endogeneity, i.e., correlation between a predictor variable and the error term. An instrumental variable affects the predictor but not the outcome directly, except through the predictor.

metadata.title: Jaccard Index
metadata.definition: The Jaccard Index, also known as the Jaccard similarity coefficient, is a statistic used for comparing the similarity and diversity of sample sets. It is calculated as the size of the intersection divided by the size of the union of the two sets.

metadata.title: Joint Probability
metadata.definition: Joint probability is the probability of two or more events occurring simultaneously. For two events A and B, it is typically denoted as P(A and B) or P(A, B).

metadata.title: Jupyter Notebook
metadata.definition: Jupyter Notebook is an open-source web application that allows users to create and share documents containing live code, equations, visualizations, and narrative text. It supports over 40 programming languages and is widely used for data analysis and interactive computing.

metadata.title: JupyterLab
metadata.definition: JupyterLab is the next-generation web-based user interface for Project Jupyter, offering a more flexible, powerful, and extensible development environment than the classic Jupyter Notebook. It integrates notebooks, text editors, terminals, and file viewers into a single, cohesive workspace.

metadata.title: Kaggle
metadata.definition: Kaggle is an online community of data scientists and machine learning practitioners, primarily known for hosting machine learning competitions. It also provides a public data platform, a cloud-based workbench for data science, and educational resources.

metadata.title: Keras
metadata.definition: Keras is an open-source neural network library written in Python, designed to be user-friendly and modular for building and training deep learning models. It provides a high-level API, often running on top of backend engines like TensorFlow, CNTK, or Theano.

metadata.title: Key-Value Model
metadata.definition: A key-value model is a non-relational (NoSQL) database model that stores data as a collection of key-value pairs, where each unique key directly maps to a value. This simple data structure allows for high scalability, fast lookups, and flexible schemas.

metadata.title: Kurtosis
metadata.definition: Kurtosis is a statistical measure that describes the 'tailedness' of the probability distribution of a real-valued random variable. High kurtosis indicates a distribution with more frequent extreme outliers (heavy tails) and a sharper peak compared to a normal distribution.

metadata.title: Label Encoding
metadata.definition: Label Encoding is a data preprocessing technique used to convert categorical labels into numerical values. Each unique categorical value in a feature column is assigned a unique integer, allowing machine learning algorithms to process the data.

metadata.title: Language Model
metadata.definition: A language model is a statistical or neural network model that determines the probability of a sequence of words or characters occurring in a given language. It is fundamental for various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, enabling machines to understand and generate human language.

metadata.title: Lasso Regression
metadata.definition: Lasso (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) Regression is a linear regression method that incorporates L1 regularization. It adds a penalty equal to the absolute value of the magnitude of coefficients to the loss function, which helps in both feature selection and regularization by shrinking some coefficients to exactly zero.

metadata.title: Lasso Regularization (L1)
metadata.definition: Lasso Regularization, also known as L1 regularization, is a technique applied to linear models to prevent overfitting and perform feature selection. It adds a penalty term to the loss function that is proportional to the absolute value of the sum of the magnitudes of the model's coefficients, encouraging some coefficients to become exactly zero.

metadata.title: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA)
metadata.definition: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) is a generative statistical model that explains sets of observations (like documents) by assuming they arise from a mixture of underlying topics. Each topic is characterized by a distribution over words, and each document is characterized by a distribution over topics.

metadata.title: Law of Total Probability
metadata.definition: The Law of Total Probability states that the probability of an event can be found by summing its conditional probabilities over a set of mutually exclusive and exhaustive events. It provides a way to calculate the overall probability of an event when it depends on several intermediate outcomes.

metadata.title: Leaky ReLU Activation
metadata.definition: Leaky ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) is an activation function similar to ReLU, but it allows a small, non-zero gradient when the input is negative. This small slope (typically 0.01) helps to mitigate the 'dying ReLU' problem, where neurons can become inactive and stop learning.

metadata.title: LeNet Architecture
metadata.definition: LeNet is one of the earliest and most influential convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, developed by Yann LeCun in 1998. It typically consists of alternating convolutional and pooling layers followed by fully connected layers, primarily designed for handwritten digit recognition.

metadata.title: Lift (Association Rule)
metadata.definition: In association rule mining, Lift is a metric that measures how much more likely the consequent is given the antecedent, relative to its base probability. A Lift value greater than 1 indicates a positive correlation between the items, less than 1 indicates a negative correlation, and 1 indicates independence.

metadata.title: LightGBM Classifier
metadata.definition: LightGBM Classifier is an open-source gradient boosting framework that uses tree-based learning algorithms for classification tasks. It is designed to be highly efficient and scalable, employing techniques like Gradient-based One-Side Sampling (GOSS) and Exclusive Feature Bundling (EFB) to speed up training while maintaining accuracy.

metadata.title: LightGBM Regressor
metadata.definition: LightGBM Regressor is an open-source gradient boosting framework that utilizes tree-based learning algorithms for regression tasks. It is known for its speed and efficiency in handling large datasets, achieved through optimization techniques like GOSS and EFB.

metadata.title: LIME (Explainable AI)
metadata.definition: LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) is an Explainable AI technique that explains the predictions of any black-box machine learning model by approximating it with a local, interpretable model around the prediction point. It generates explanations by perturbing the input and observing how the model's prediction changes.

metadata.title: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) (Dimensionality Reduction)
metadata.definition: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) is a supervised dimensionality reduction technique used to find a linear combination of features that best separates two or more classes. Unlike PCA, which focuses on maximizing variance, LDA explicitly tries to maximize the separation between classes while minimizing the variance within each class.

metadata.title: Log Loss (Binary Classification)
metadata.definition: Log Loss, also known as cross-entropy loss, is a common evaluation metric for binary classification models that output probabilities. It penalizes incorrect confident predictions more heavily than incorrect uncertain predictions, providing a measure of the uncertainty of the predictions.

metadata.title: Log Transformation
metadata.definition: Log transformation is a data preprocessing technique where the natural logarithm (or any base logarithm) is applied to a variable. This transformation is commonly used to reduce skewness in data, stabilize variance, and improve linearity, making the data more suitable for certain statistical models.

metadata.title: MAE (Mean Absolute Error)
metadata.definition: Mean Absolute Error (MAE) is a common metric used to evaluate the accuracy of regression models. It calculates the average of the absolute differences between the predicted values and the actual values, providing a straightforward measure of prediction error in the same units as the target variable.

metadata.title: Mean
metadata.definition: The mean, also known as the average, is a measure of central tendency calculated by summing all values in a dataset and dividing by the count of those values. It represents the typical or central value of a set of numbers.

metadata.title: Mean-Shift Clustering
metadata.definition: Mean-Shift clustering is a non-parametric clustering algorithm that does not require prior knowledge of the number of clusters. It works by iteratively shifting data points towards the mode (peak density) of their surrounding data, eventually converging to cluster centroids.

metadata.title: Median
metadata.definition: The median is a measure of central tendency that represents the middle value in a dataset when the values are arranged in ascending or descending order. If there is an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle numbers.

metadata.title: Min-Max Scaling
metadata.definition: Min-Max scaling, also known as normalization, is a data preprocessing technique that transforms features to a fixed range, typically between 0 and 1. It rescales the data such that the minimum value of a feature becomes 0 and the maximum value becomes 1, and all other values are scaled linearly within this range.

metadata.title: Missing Value Imputation
metadata.definition: Missing value imputation is the process of replacing missing data in a dataset with substituted values. The goal is to fill in these gaps to allow statistical analysis or machine learning models to proceed, as many algorithms cannot handle missing entries, and to minimize bias introduced by the missingness.

metadata.title: MobileNet
metadata.definition: MobileNet is a family of lightweight, efficient deep convolutional neural networks designed specifically for mobile and embedded vision applications. They achieve efficiency by using depthwise separable convolutions, which significantly reduce the number of parameters and computational cost compared to standard convolutions.

metadata.title: Mode
metadata.definition: The mode is a measure of central tendency that represents the most frequently occurring value in a dataset. A dataset can have one mode (unimodal), multiple modes (multimodal), or no mode if all values appear with the same frequency.

metadata.title: Model Monitoring
metadata.definition: Model monitoring is the continuous process of observing the performance and behavior of deployed machine learning models in production. It involves tracking key metrics, detecting data drift, concept drift, and performance degradation to ensure models remain effective and reliable over time.

metadata.title: Model Serving
metadata.definition: Model serving is the process of deploying a trained machine learning model into a production environment where it can receive new data and make predictions in real-time or batch. It typically involves wrapping the model in an API (e.g., REST API) to enable other applications to consume its predictions.

metadata.title: MongoDB
metadata.definition: A popular open-source NoSQL document database that stores data in flexible, JSON-like documents, allowing for dynamic schemas and horizontal scalability. It is designed for high performance, high availability, and easy scalability.

metadata.title: Moving Average (MA) Model
metadata.definition: A time series model that forecasts future values based on a linear combination of past forecast errors. It is used to smooth out short-term fluctuations and highlight longer-term trends or cycles in data.

metadata.title: Multinomial Naive Bayes
metadata.definition: A variant of the Naive Bayes algorithm primarily used for classification tasks with discrete features, such as text classification where features represent word counts or frequencies. It assumes that features are conditionally independent given the class label, and follows a multinomial distribution.

metadata.title: N-grams
metadata.definition: Contiguous sequences of N items from a given sample of text or speech. They are commonly used in natural language processing to capture local linguistic context and sequential dependencies.

metadata.title: Neo4j
metadata.definition: A leading open-source graph database management system that stores and manages data using nodes, relationships, and properties. It is optimized for connected data, allowing for fast traversal and querying of complex relationships.

metadata.title: Neuron (Perceptron)
metadata.definition: The fundamental building block of an artificial neural network, inspired by biological neurons. A perceptron takes multiple input signals, applies weights to them, sums them up, and then passes the result through an activation function to produce an output.

metadata.title: Norm (L1)
metadata.definition: Also known as Manhattan distance or Taxicab norm, the L1 norm of a vector is the sum of the absolute values of its components. It measures the sum of the magnitudes of the vectors in a space and is often used for regularization to induce sparsity.

metadata.title: Norm (L2)
metadata.definition: Also known as Euclidean norm or magnitude, the L2 norm of a vector is the square root of the sum of the squares of its components. It represents the standard Euclidean distance from the origin to the point defined by the vector and is commonly used for regularization to prevent overfitting.

metadata.title: Normalization (Data)
metadata.definition: The process of scaling numerical data to a standard range, typically between 0 and 1, without distorting the differences in the ranges of values or losing information. It is crucial for algorithms that are sensitive to the magnitude of input features.

metadata.title: NumPy Array
metadata.definition: The fundamental data structure in the NumPy library, representing a multi-dimensional array object. It is a powerful N-dimensional array that supports fast, vectorized mathematical operations, making it essential for numerical computing in Python.

metadata.title: Optimizer (Deep Learning)
metadata.definition: An algorithm or method used to change the attributes of the neural network, such as weights and learning rate, in order to reduce the losses. Optimizers iteratively adjust model parameters to minimize the objective function (loss function).

metadata.title: Outlier Treatment
metadata.definition: The process of identifying and managing data points that significantly deviate from other observations, often due to measurement errors, novel events, or natural variations. Common strategies include removal, transformation, or imputation.

metadata.title: Pandas DataFrame
metadata.definition: A two-dimensional, size-mutable, tabular data structure with labeled axes (rows and columns) from the Pandas library. It is designed to efficiently handle structured data and provides powerful tools for data manipulation and analysis.

metadata.title: Pair Plot
metadata.definition: A grid of scatterplots where each numeric variable in a dataset is plotted against every other numeric variable. It also displays distributions of individual variables on the diagonal, providing a quick way to visualize relationships and distributions within a dataset.

metadata.title: Partial Autocorrelation
metadata.definition: The correlation between a time series and a lagged version of itself, after accounting for the effects of all intermediate lags. It helps in identifying the order of an Autoregressive (AR) model by showing the direct relationship between observations at different time steps.

metadata.title: Perplexity (NLP)
metadata.definition: A common evaluation metric for language models that measures how well a probability distribution or language model predicts a sample. Lower perplexity indicates a better model, as it means the model is less "surprised" by unseen data.

metadata.title: Policy (Reinforcement Learning)
metadata.definition: In Reinforcement Learning, a policy defines the agent's behavior strategy, mapping states of the environment to actions to be taken in those states. It dictates how an agent chooses actions to maximize its cumulative reward.

metadata.title: Potential Outcomes Framework
metadata.definition: A statistical framework for causal inference that conceptualizes causal effects by comparing the outcomes an individual would experience under different treatment conditions. It defines causality as the difference between the potential outcome under treatment and the potential outcome under control for the same individual.

metadata.title: Precision (Classification)
metadata.definition: An evaluation metric in classification, defined as the ratio of true positive predictions to the total number of positive predictions made by the model (true positives + false positives). It measures the accuracy of positive predictions, answering "Of all the instances predicted as positive, how many actually were positive?".

metadata.title: Pre-trained Model
metadata.definition: A model that has already been trained on a large dataset for a similar task, and whose learned weights and biases are then used as a starting point for a new, often related, task. This technique, known as transfer learning, saves training time and can improve performance, especially with limited data.

metadata.title: Primary Key (Database)
metadata.definition: A primary key is a column or a set of columns in a relational database table that uniquely identifies each record. It must contain unique values for each row and cannot contain NULL values, serving as a unique identifier for data integrity and relationships.

metadata.title: Probability Distribution
metadata.definition: A probability distribution is a mathematical function that describes all possible values and the likelihoods that a random variable can take within a given range. It can be discrete, assigning probabilities to distinct values, or continuous, assigning probabilities over intervals.

metadata.title: Probability Space
metadata.definition: A probability space is a formal mathematical construct that provides a model of a real-world experiment or random process. It consists of three components: a sample space (Ω) of all possible outcomes, a set of events (F) which are subsets of Ω, and a probability measure (P) that assigns probabilities to these events.

metadata.title: Propensity Score Matching
metadata.definition: Propensity Score Matching (PSM) is a statistical technique used in observational studies to reduce confounding bias by balancing covariates between treatment and control groups. It involves estimating the probability of treatment assignment (propensity score) given observed covariates, and then matching individuals with similar propensity scores.

metadata.title: Prophet (Time Series Model)
metadata.definition: Prophet is an open-source forecasting procedure developed by Facebook for time series data, designed to be robust to outliers and missing data, and to handle strong seasonal effects. It works by decomposing a time series into trend, seasonality (yearly, weekly, daily), and holiday components.

metadata.title: PyTorch
metadata.definition: PyTorch is an open-source machine learning framework developed by Facebook's AI Research lab (FAIR), widely used for deep learning applications. It is known for its flexibility, Pythonic interface, and dynamic computational graphs, making it popular for research and rapid prototyping.

metadata.title: Q-Value (Reinforcement Learning)
metadata.definition: In reinforcement learning, the Q-value, or action-value function Q(s, a), represents the expected total future reward an agent can obtain by taking a specific action 'a' in a given state 's', and then following an optimal policy thereafter. It is a fundamental concept for value-based reinforcement learning algorithms like Q-learning.

metadata.title: Random Forest Classifier
metadata.definition: A Random Forest Classifier is an ensemble machine learning algorithm for classification tasks that constructs a multitude of decision trees during training. For classification, it outputs the class that is the mode (most frequent) of the classes predicted by individual trees, significantly reducing overfitting and improving accuracy compared to a single decision tree.

metadata.title: Random Forest Regressor
metadata.definition: A Random Forest Regressor is an ensemble machine learning algorithm for regression tasks that operates by building multiple decision trees during training. For regression, it outputs the mean or average prediction of the individual trees, which helps reduce variance and improve the model's overall predictive accuracy.

metadata.title: Random Search (Hyperparameter Tuning)
metadata.definition: Random Search is a hyperparameter optimization technique that involves randomly sampling hyperparameter combinations from a specified distribution for a fixed number of iterations or a fixed time budget. It often outperforms grid search, especially in high-dimensional hyperparameter spaces where many hyperparameters might be uninformative.

metadata.title: Randomized Control Trial (RCT)
metadata.definition: A Randomized Control Trial (RCT) is a type of scientific experiment, commonly used in medicine and social sciences, where participants are randomly assigned to either an experimental group (receiving an intervention) or a control group (receiving a placebo or standard care). This randomization minimizes selection bias and allows for robust causal inference regarding the intervention's effect.

metadata.title: Recall (Classification)
metadata.definition: Recall, also known as Sensitivity or True Positive Rate, is a classification evaluation metric that measures the proportion of actual positive cases that were correctly identified by the model. It is calculated as True Positives divided by the sum of True Positives and False Negatives (TP / (TP + FN)).

metadata.title: Receptive Field (CNN)
metadata.definition: In a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), the receptive field of an output feature (i.e., a neuron in a feature map) is the region in the input image that influences that output feature's value. It determines how much of the original input pixels contribute to a particular feature, growing larger in deeper layers of the network.

metadata.title: Redis
metadata.definition: Redis (Remote Dictionary Server) is an open-source, in-memory data structure store, used as a database, cache, and message broker. It supports various data structures like strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, and streams, making it highly versatile for real-time applications and high-performance caching.

metadata.title: Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
metadata.definition: Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) is a quasi-experimental research design used to estimate causal effects by exploiting an arbitrary cutoff or threshold that assigns individuals to treatment or control conditions. It assumes that individuals just above and just below the cutoff are comparable, allowing for a causal interpretation of the discontinuity in outcomes.

metadata.title: ReLU Activation
metadata.definition: The Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) is a popular activation function in neural networks, defined as f(x) = max(0, x). It introduces non-linearity, which is crucial for deep networks to learn complex patterns, and helps mitigate the vanishing gradient problem by outputting zero for negative inputs and the input value itself for positive inputs.

metadata.title: ResNet Architecture
metadata.definition: Residual Networks (ResNets) are a class of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) characterized by 'skip connections' or 'residual connections' that allow the network to bypass one or more layers. This innovation enables the training of much deeper networks by addressing the vanishing/exploding gradient problem, improving learning efficiency and performance.

metadata.title: REST API
metadata.definition: A REST (Representational State Transfer) API is an architectural style for designing networked applications, defining a set of constraints for how clients and servers communicate. It typically uses standard HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to interact with stateless resources, enabling interoperability between different systems.

metadata.title: Reward (Reinforcement Learning)
metadata.definition: In reinforcement learning, the reward is a scalar feedback signal provided by the environment to the agent, indicating the desirability of its actions. The agent's sole objective is to maximize the cumulative reward it receives over time, guiding its learning process toward optimal behavior.

metadata.title: Reward Shaping (Reinforcement Learning)
metadata.definition: Reward shaping is a technique in reinforcement learning where additional, auxiliary reward signals are provided to the agent, beyond the sparse or delayed true environmental rewards, to guide its learning process more effectively. The goal is to accelerate learning by providing more frequent and informative feedback without altering the optimal policy of the original task.

metadata.title: RGB Channels (Image)
metadata.definition: In digital imaging, RGB refers to the Red, Green, and Blue additive primary colors used to represent a wide spectrum of colors. Each channel is typically an 8-bit integer array representing the intensity of that specific color component at each pixel, ranging from 0 (no intensity) to 255 (full intensity). Combining the three channels creates the final full-color image.

metadata.title: Ridge Regression
metadata.definition: Ridge Regression is a linear regression technique that includes L2 regularization to prevent overfitting by penalizing large coefficients. It adds a penalty equivalent to the squared magnitude of the coefficients to the loss function, shrinking them towards zero but rarely making them exactly zero. This improves model generalization, especially when multicollinearity is present among predictor variables.

metadata.title: Ridge Regularization (L2)
metadata.definition: Ridge Regularization, also known as L2 regularization, is a technique used in machine learning models, primarily linear models, to prevent overfitting by adding a penalty proportional to the sum of the squared magnitudes of the coefficients to the loss function. This penalty encourages coefficients to be small but non-zero, thereby reducing model complexity and improving generalization. It is particularly effective in scenarios with multicollinearity.

metadata.title: RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error)
metadata.definition: RMSE is a frequently used metric to measure the average magnitude of the errors between predicted values and actual values in a regression task. It represents the square root of the average of the squared differences between prediction and actual observation, giving higher weight to larger errors. RMSE is expressed in the same units as the target variable, making it easily interpretable.

metadata.title: ROUGE Score
metadata.definition: ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) is a set of metrics used for evaluating automatic summarization and machine translation software. It works by comparing an automatically produced summary or translation against a set of reference (human-produced) summaries or translations, measuring the overlap of n-grams, word sequences, or word pairs between them. Common variants include ROUGE-N (N-gram overlap) and ROUGE-L (Longest Common Subsequence).

metadata.title: SARIMA Model
metadata.definition: SARIMA (Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average) is a powerful time series forecasting model that extends the ARIMA model to handle time series data with a seasonal component. It incorporates seasonal autoregressive (SAR), seasonal integrated (seasonal differencing), and seasonal moving average (SMA) terms, in addition to the non-seasonal ARIMA components (p, d, q). This model is highly effective for data exhibiting repeating patterns at fixed intervals, such as daily, weekly, or monthly cycles.

metadata.title: SARSA Algorithm
metadata.definition: SARSA (State-Action-Reward-State-Action) is an on-policy temporal difference learning algorithm in reinforcement learning, used to learn an optimal policy for an agent navigating an environment. It updates the Q-value (state-action value) based on the current state, current action, immediate reward, next state, and *next action selected by the current policy*. Because it considers the next action chosen by the current policy, SARSA is considered an "on-policy" control algorithm.

metadata.title: Scikit-learn
metadata.definition: Scikit-learn is a free software machine learning library for the Python programming language, featuring various classification, regression, and clustering algorithms including support vector machines, random forests, gradient boosting, k-means, and DBSCAN. It is designed to interoperate with the Python numerical and scientific libraries NumPy and SciPy, providing a consistent API for many common ML tasks. Scikit-learn is widely used for predictive data analysis due to its ease of use and comprehensive functionalities.

metadata.title: SciPy
metadata.definition: SciPy is an open-source Python library used for scientific computing and technical computing, building on the NumPy array object and providing modules for optimization, linear algebra, integration, interpolation, special functions, FFT, signal and image processing, ODE solvers, and other tasks common in science and engineering. It offers a collection of algorithms and high-level commands for manipulating and visualizing data. SciPy is a fundamental library in the scientific Python ecosystem.

metadata.title: Seasonality (Time Series)
metadata.definition: Seasonality in a time series refers to predictable and recurring patterns or cycles that repeat over a fixed period, such as daily, weekly, monthly, or yearly. These patterns are typically caused by calendar-related factors like time of day, day of the week, or public holidays. Identifying and accounting for seasonality is crucial for accurate forecasting and understanding underlying data trends.

metadata.title: Self-Attention
metadata.definition: Self-Attention, also known as intra-attention, is an attention mechanism that relates different positions of a single sequence to compute a representation of the same sequence. It allows the model to weigh the importance of different words or tokens in an input sequence when encoding a particular word, effectively capturing long-range dependencies and contextual relationships within the data. This mechanism is a key component of Transformer models.

metadata.title: SHAP Values (Explainable AI)
metadata.definition: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values are a game-theoretic approach to explain the output of any machine learning model by computing the contribution of each feature to the prediction for a specific instance. They connect optimal credit allocation with local explanations using Shapley values from cooperative game theory, ensuring fair distribution of the prediction outcome among the features. SHAP values provide consistent and locally accurate explanations, allowing users to understand why a model made a certain prediction.

metadata.title: Sigmoid Activation
metadata.definition: The Sigmoid activation function is a non-linear function used in artificial neural networks that maps any input value to a value between 0 and 1. Defined as `f(x) = 1 / (1 + e^-x)`, it introduces non-linearity, allowing neural networks to learn complex patterns. It is often used in the output layer for binary classification problems, where the output can be interpreted as a probability.

metadata.title: Skewness
metadata.definition: Skewness is a measure of the asymmetry of the probability distribution of a real-valued random variable about its mean. A distribution is skewed if it is not symmetric, meaning one tail is longer than the other. Positive skew (right-skewed) indicates a longer tail on the right and most values concentrated on the left, while negative skew (left-skewed) indicates a longer tail on the left and most values concentrated on the right.

metadata.title: Softmax Activation
metadata.definition: The Softmax activation function is a generalization of the sigmoid function used in the output layer of a neural network for multi-class classification problems. It takes a vector of arbitrary real values as input and squashes it to a vector of probabilities that sum to 1, where each value represents the probability of the input belonging to a particular class. This allows interpretation of the output as a probability distribution over the possible classes.

metadata.title: Spark SQL
metadata.definition: Spark SQL is a module in Apache Spark for structured data processing that provides a SQL interface to query data and integrates relational processing with Spark's functional programming API. It allows users to query data using SQL queries, HiveQL, or Scala, Java, Python, and R APIs, and can read data from various sources like Hive tables, Parquet files, and JSON files. Spark SQL includes a cost-based optimizer to improve query performance and enables seamless integration of SQL queries with complex analytics.

metadata.title: Standard Deviation
metadata.definition: Standard Deviation is a measure of the amount of variation or dispersion of a set of values, quantifying the average amount by which individual data points deviate from the mean of the dataset. A low standard deviation indicates that data points tend to be close to the mean, while a high standard deviation indicates that data points are spread out over a wider range of values. It is the square root of the variance.

metadata.title: Standardization (Z-score Scaling)
metadata.definition: Standardization, or Z-score scaling, is a data preprocessing technique that transforms features to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. For each data point `x`, it is calculated as `(x - mean) / standard deviation`. This process scales features such that they have the properties of a standard normal distribution, making them comparable and improving the performance of many machine learning algorithms that are sensitive to feature scales.

metadata.title: State (Reinforcement Learning)
metadata.definition: In reinforcement learning, a "state" is a complete and sufficient description of the environment at a particular moment in time, providing all the necessary information for an agent to make an informed decision about its next action. The state typically encapsulates observations from the environment and influences the agent's chosen action, the reward received, and the subsequent state transitions. A Markov state has the property that the future is independent of the past given the present state.

metadata.title: Stationarity (Time Series)
metadata.definition: A time series is considered stationary if its statistical properties, such as mean, variance, and autocorrelation, remain constant over time. This implies that the series does not exhibit trends, seasonality, or other systematic changes in its statistical characteristics. Many time series models, like ARIMA, assume stationarity, and non-stationary series often need to be transformed (e.g., through differencing) to achieve stationarity before modeling.

metadata.title: Statistical Significance
metadata.definition: A measure of the likelihood that an observed difference between groups or variables is not due to random chance, typically evaluated using p-values. If the p-value is below a predetermined significance level (e.g., 0.05), the result is considered statistically significant, suggesting a real effect.

metadata.title: Stacking (Ensemble)
metadata.definition: An ensemble learning technique where multiple base models (level-0 models) are trained on the training data, and then a meta-model (level-1 model) is trained on the predictions of these base models. The meta-model learns how to best combine the strengths of the individual base models to make a final, more robust prediction.

metadata.title: Stemming (NLP)
metadata.definition: A text normalization technique in Natural Language Processing that reduces words to their root or base form (stem) by removing suffixes. The resulting stem is often not a valid word itself, but its purpose is to group together words with similar meanings for analysis.

metadata.title: Stop Word Removal
metadata.definition: A common text preprocessing step that removes frequently occurring words (stop words) from text data that are considered to carry little semantic meaning and can hinder analysis. Examples include common words like 'the', 'a', 'is', 'and', which are typically filtered out to focus on more informative terms.

metadata.title: Stratified Sampling
metadata.definition: A sampling technique where the population is divided into distinct, non-overlapping subgroups called strata based on shared characteristics, and then samples are drawn from each stratum. This method ensures that the sample accurately represents the proportions of different subgroups within the population, reducing sampling bias.

metadata.title: Subquery (SQL)
metadata.definition: A query nested inside another SQL query, also known as an inner query or nested query. Subqueries are often used to retrieve data that will be used by the main query as a condition to further restrict the data to be retrieved, or for calculations.

metadata.title: Support (Association Rule)
