metadata.definition: The process by which an LLM learns to learn, meaning it acquires skills to quickly adapt to new tasks or environments with minimal new data or training. This involves learning optimal learning strategies, initialization parameters, or architectural choices, enabling 'learning how to learn' across various tasks.

metadata.title: Continual Learning (LLM)
metadata.definition: The ability of an LLM to continuously learn new information, tasks, or skills from a stream of data over time without catastrophically forgetting previously acquired knowledge. This addresses the problem of 'catastrophic forgetting' common in traditional neural networks by integrating new knowledge while preserving old.

metadata.title: Active Learning (LLM)
metadata.definition: A strategy where an LLM, or an associated system, interactively queries a user or oracle to label new data points that are most informative for its training, aiming to achieve high accuracy with less labeled data. It reduces the cost and effort of manual annotation by prioritizing samples that maximize model improvement.

metadata.title: Self-Supervised Learning (in LLMs)
metadata.definition: A paradigm where an LLM learns robust representations from unlabeled data by generating supervisory signals from the data itself, typically by solving a 'pretext task.' This allows models to leverage vast amounts of readily available unannotated text for pre-training.

metadata.title: AI Agent
metadata.definition: An autonomous entity that perceives its environment, makes decisions, and takes actions to achieve specific goals. In the context of LLMs, it typically refers to an LLM augmented with tools, memory, and planning capabilities to interact with external systems or users.

metadata.title: Autonomous Agent
metadata.definition: An AI agent capable of operating independently for extended periods without continuous human intervention, making its own decisions and adapting to its environment to achieve complex objectives. It typically combines planning, memory, and tool-use to manage tasks from start to finish.

metadata.title: Memory Bank (LLM Agent)
metadata.definition: A component within an LLM agent that stores past interactions, observations, and generated thoughts or actions, enabling the agent to maintain context, learn from experience, and perform long-term reasoning. It often encompasses both short-term (context window) and long-term (e.g., vector database) storage mechanisms.

metadata.title: Retrieval-Augmented Language Model (RALM)
metadata.definition: An LLM architectured to retrieve relevant information from an external knowledge source (e.g., a database, search index) and incorporate it into its generation process. This allows the model to produce more factual, up-to-date, and grounded responses by reducing hallucination and reliance solely on parametric memory.

metadata.title: Symbol Grounding (LLM)
metadata.definition: The challenge of connecting abstract symbols or linguistic representations (words, phrases) used by an LLM to their corresponding real-world referents, sensory experiences, or perceptual features. It addresses whether an LLM truly 'understands' what it's talking about beyond mere statistical correlations between tokens.

metadata.title: Theory of Mind (LLM)
metadata.definition: Refers to an LLM's apparent capacity to attribute mental states (beliefs, intentions, desires, knowledge) to itself and others, and to use this understanding to predict and explain behavior. While LLMs can simulate such understanding through patterns in vast text data, whether they possess genuine internal representation of mental states remains a subject of active debate.

metadata.title: Synthetic Data Generation (LLM)
metadata.definition: The process of creating artificial data, often using LLMs themselves, that mimics the statistical properties and patterns of real-world data. This synthetic data is used for training, testing, or augmenting datasets when real data is scarce, sensitive, or costly to acquire.

metadata.title: Data-centric AI (LLM)
metadata.definition: An approach to AI development that prioritizes improving the quality, consistency, and quantity of the training data over modifying the model architecture. It recognizes that high-quality data is often more impactful for LLM performance, robustness, and fairness than complex model tweaks.

metadata.title: Model-centric AI (LLM)
metadata.definition: A traditional approach to AI development that primarily focuses on iterating and optimizing the model architecture, hyper-parameters, and training algorithms to improve performance. This approach often assumes a fixed or given dataset and emphasizes advances in model design.

metadata.title: Transfer Learning (LLM)
metadata.definition: A machine learning technique where an LLM pre-trained on a large, general-purpose dataset for a broad task (e.g., next-token prediction) is then adapted or fine-tuned on a smaller, specific dataset for a related but different downstream task. This leverages knowledge learned from the source task to improve performance on the target task.

metadata.title: Open-source LLM
metadata.definition: A Large Language Model whose source code, model weights, training data, and often training methodology are publicly accessible, typically under an open license. This allows for inspection, modification, distribution, and commercial use by anyone.

metadata.title: Proprietary LLM
metadata.definition: A Large Language Model developed and owned by a private entity, where the source code, model weights, training data, and often the full API access are not publicly available. These models are typically offered as a service (API) with commercial terms and controlled access.

metadata.title: Large Action Model (LAM)
metadata.definition: An emerging concept describing LLMs that are specifically designed and optimized not just for language generation but for understanding and executing complex sequences of actions in digital environments. LAMs go beyond producing text to perform concrete tasks by interacting with user interfaces, APIs, and software tools.

metadata.title: Authenticity
metadata.definition: Authenticity is the property of being genuine and able to be verified and trusted. In cybersecurity, it ensures that a user, system, or data is who or what it claims to be, preventing impersonation and fraud.

metadata.title: Authorization (Principle)
metadata.definition: Authorization is the process of granting or denying access rights to a resource or system based on a verified identity and predefined policies. It determines what actions an authenticated entity is permitted to perform.

metadata.title: Accountability
metadata.definition: Accountability is the ability to trace all actions and events within a system to a specific entity, ensuring that individuals can be held responsible for their security-related conduct. It relies heavily on comprehensive logging and auditing.

metadata.title: Threat Actor
metadata.definition: A threat actor (or malicious actor/adversary) is an individual, group, or nation-state that poses a risk to an organization's security through malicious intent and capability. They typically seek to exploit vulnerabilities to achieve their objectives.

metadata.title: Risk (Concept)
metadata.definition: In cybersecurity, risk is the potential for loss, damage, or destruction of an asset due to a threat exploiting a vulnerability. It is typically quantified as the combination of the likelihood of an event occurring and the potential impact if it does.

metadata.title: Asset (Security)
metadata.definition: An asset, in a security context, is anything of value to an organization that requires protection. This includes tangible items like hardware and personnel, and intangible items like data, intellectual property, and reputation.

metadata.title: Exposure (Security)
metadata.definition: Exposure in cybersecurity refers to a state where a system, data, or asset is open or susceptible to compromise, often due to a vulnerability or lack of proper controls. It describes the condition of being unprotected or visible to potential threats.

metadata.title: Control (Security)
metadata.definition: A security control is a measure, safeguard, or countermeasure implemented to reduce risk by preventing, detecting, or responding to security incidents. Controls can be technical (e.g., firewalls), administrative (e.g., policies), or physical (e.g., locks).

metadata.title: Least Privilege
metadata.definition: The principle of least privilege dictates that users, programs, or processes should be granted only the minimum necessary permissions or access rights to perform their specific tasks. This minimizes the potential damage if an account or system is compromised.

metadata.title: Security Baseline
metadata.definition: A security baseline is a minimum set of security configurations, policies, and practices that an organization establishes to meet its security requirements. It serves as a standardized, secure starting point for all systems, applications, and networks.

metadata.title: Trust Boundary
metadata.definition: A trust boundary is a logical or physical line in a system's architecture where the level of trust changes, separating assets or systems with different security requirements. All data or communication crossing a trust boundary should be rigorously validated and sanitized.

metadata.title: Security Domain
metadata.definition: A security domain is a collection of systems, networks, or assets that share a common security policy and trust level, and where security controls are uniformly applied. It helps organize and manage security effectively by grouping similar resources.

metadata.title: Security Service
metadata.definition: A security service is a function or capability provided by a system, protocol, or product designed to enforce security policies and protect information and resources. These services typically support the confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA) triad.

metadata.title: Threat Intelligence
metadata.definition: Threat intelligence is evidence-based knowledge, including context, mechanisms, indicators, implications, and actionable advice about an existing or emerging menace or hazard to assets. It helps organizations make informed security decisions and take proactive measures.

metadata.title: Information Security Governance
metadata.definition: Information Security Governance is the system by which an organization directs and controls its information security activities to align with business objectives, manage risk, and ensure compliance. It involves defining roles, responsibilities, policies, and processes.

metadata.title: Compliance Framework
metadata.definition: A compliance framework is a structured set of guidelines, regulations, and best practices that an organization must follow to meet specific legal, industry, or contractual obligations. It helps ensure adherence to mandated security and privacy standards.

metadata.title: Security Awareness Training
metadata.definition: Security awareness training is an educational program designed to inform employees about security best practices, common cyber threats, and their individual roles in protecting organizational assets. Its primary goal is to reduce human error as a potential attack vector.

metadata.title: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard)
metadata.definition: AES is a symmetric-key encryption algorithm adopted as an encryption standard by the U.S. government and widely used worldwide. It is a highly secure and efficient block cipher, supporting key sizes of 128, 192, and 256 bits.

metadata.title: DES (Data Encryption Standard)
metadata.definition: DES is an older symmetric-key encryption algorithm developed in the 1970s and widely adopted as a standard. Due to its relatively short 56-bit key length, it is now considered insecure and vulnerable to brute-force attacks, largely replaced by AES and 3DES.

metadata.title: 3DES (Triple DES)
metadata.definition: 3DES is a symmetric-key encryption algorithm that applies the DES algorithm three times to each data block, providing increased security over plain DES. While more secure than DES, it is significantly slower than AES and is gradually being phased out due to its computational overhead and block size limitations.

metadata.title: Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman
metadata.definition: A variant of the Diffie-Hellman key exchange where a new, temporary private key is generated for each session. This ensures that a compromise of a long-term private key does not compromise past session keys, thereby providing perfect forward secrecy.

metadata.title: Message Digest (MD5)
metadata.definition: A widely-used cryptographic hash function that produces a 128-bit (16-byte) hash value, commonly used for verifying data integrity. While historically popular, it is now considered cryptographically broken due to susceptibility to collision attacks, making it unsuitable for security-critical applications like digital signatures.

metadata.title: SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm 1)
metadata.definition: A cryptographic hash function that produces a 160-bit (20-byte) hash value, designed by the NSA. Like MD5, SHA-1 is now considered cryptographically broken due to the discovery of practical collision attacks, rendering it unsafe for most security applications where collision resistance is critical.

metadata.title: SHA-512
metadata.definition: Part of the SHA-2 family of cryptographic hash functions, SHA-512 produces a 512-bit (64-byte) hash value. It is widely considered secure and is used for various applications requiring strong collision resistance and data integrity, such as digital signatures and password hashing.

metadata.title: Root Certificate
metadata.definition: A digital certificate at the top of a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) hierarchy, issued by a Certificate Authority (CA) to itself. It serves as a trust anchor, implicitly trusted by operating systems and browsers, from which all other certificates in that CA's chain of trust ultimately derive their validity.

metadata.title: Intermediate Certificate
metadata.definition: A digital certificate issued by a root certificate authority (or another intermediate CA) to sign end-entity certificates or other intermediate certificates. Intermediate certificates form a chain of trust between the highly secure root certificate and the more numerous end-entity certificates, allowing the root CA to remain offline and secure.

metadata.title: End-entity Certificate
metadata.definition: A digital certificate issued by an intermediate certificate authority (or directly by a root CA) to an individual, server, or device. This certificate identifies the subject and contains its public key, enabling secure communications and proving identity in applications like web browsing (HTTPS) or email signing.

metadata.title: Key Management (Cryptography)
metadata.definition: The comprehensive set of practices, policies, and procedures for generating, exchanging, storing, using, revoking, and destroying cryptographic keys throughout their lifecycle. Effective key management is crucial for the security of any cryptographic system, as even the strongest algorithms are vulnerable if keys are compromised.

metadata.title: Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS)
metadata.definition: A property of a key agreement protocol that ensures that a compromise of a long-term private key does not compromise past session keys. Even if an adversary records encrypted communications and later obtains the server's private key, they cannot decrypt the previously recorded sessions because the session keys were ephemeral.

metadata.title: Side-channel Attack (Cryptographic)
metadata.definition: An attack that extracts sensitive information from a cryptographic system by observing its physical implementation, rather than by targeting cryptographic weaknesses directly. Attack vectors include timing variations, power consumption, electromagnetic radiation, acoustic emissions, or cache hits during cryptographic operations.

metadata.title: Cryptographic Random Number Generator
metadata.definition: An algorithm designed to produce sequences of numbers that appear random and are unpredictable, even to an attacker who knows the generator's internal state (but not the seed). Unlike general-purpose PRNGs, CRNGs (also known as CSPRNGs) are suitable for cryptographic applications such as key generation, nonces, and salts, where unpredictability is paramount.

metadata.title: Nonce
metadata.definition: An acronym for "number used once," a nonce is a random or pseudo-random value that is used only a single time within a cryptographic communication or operation. Its primary purpose is to prevent replay attacks and to ensure uniqueness for cryptographic parameters, such as initialization vectors (IVs) or parts of a key exchange.

metadata.title: Salt (Cryptographic)
metadata.definition: A unique, random string of data added to an input, such as a password, before it is hashed. Salting prevents dictionary attacks and precomputed rainbow table attacks by ensuring that identical passwords produce different hash values, making each password hash unique and requiring a brute-force attacker to compute hashes for each salt.

metadata.title: Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP)
metadata.definition: A cryptographic protocol where one party (the prover) can prove to another party (the verifier) that they know a secret value without revealing any information about the secret itself. ZKP ensures that the verifier learns nothing beyond the fact that the statement is true.

metadata.title: Firewall (Network)
metadata.definition: A network security device or software that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predetermined security rules. Firewalls establish a barrier between a trusted internal network and untrusted external networks (like the internet), preventing unauthorized access and filtering malicious traffic.

metadata.title: IPsec (Internet Protocol Security)
metadata.definition: A suite of protocols used to secure Internet Protocol (IP) communications by authenticating and encrypting each IP packet. IPsec operates at the network layer and provides data confidentiality, integrity, and authentication, commonly used for VPNs and secure routing.

metadata.title: SSL/TLS VPN
metadata.definition: A Virtual Private Network (VPN) technology that uses the Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) or its successor, Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocols, to create a secure, encrypted tunnel for remote access. Unlike IPsec VPNs, SSL/TLS VPNs often operate at the application layer, allowing browser-based access or client software to establish secure connections over standard web ports.

metadata.title: TLS (Transport Layer Security) Protocol
metadata.definition: A cryptographic protocol designed to provide secure communication over a computer network, widely used for web browsing (HTTPS), email, and instant messaging. TLS ensures data confidentiality, integrity, and authentication between a client and a server, succeeding the now-deprecated SSL protocol.

metadata.title: SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) Protocol
metadata.definition: A deprecated cryptographic protocol that provided secure communication over a computer network, historically used for web browsing and other applications. SSL has been superseded by TLS due to various security vulnerabilities found in its earlier versions, and its use is now strongly discouraged.

metadata.title: SSH (Secure Shell) Protocol
metadata.definition: A cryptographic network protocol for operating network services securely over an unsecured network. SSH provides a secure channel over an untrusted network by using strong encryption and authentication, commonly used for remote command-line access, remote execution, and secure file transfer (SFTP).

metadata.title: Domain Name System (DNS) Cache Poisoning
metadata.definition: An attack where an attacker injects fraudulent DNS data into a DNS resolver's cache, causing the resolver to return incorrect IP addresses for domain names. This redirects users attempting to access a legitimate website to a malicious server controlled by the attacker.

metadata.title: DHCP Snooping
metadata.definition: A security feature on network switches that acts as a firewall between untrusted hosts and trusted DHCP servers. It validates DHCP messages, allowing legitimate DHCP traffic while dropping malicious or malformed packets, preventing rogue DHCP servers and client spoofing.

metadata.title: Port Security
metadata.definition: A Layer 2 security feature on network switches that restricts input to an interface by limiting and identifying the MAC addresses allowed to send traffic through that port. It prevents unauthorized devices from connecting to a switch port.

metadata.title: VLAN Hopping
metadata.definition: A network attack where an attacker on one Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) gains unauthorized access to resources on a different VLAN. This typically involves tricking a switch into believing the attacker's system is a trunk port or by double-tagging frames.

metadata.title: BGP Security
metadata.definition: Refers to the measures and best practices implemented to secure the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), which is crucial for routing traffic across the internet. It aims to prevent attacks like route hijacking, IP prefix spoofing, and BGP session hijacking.

metadata.title: SYN Flood
metadata.definition: A type of Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attack where an attacker sends a high volume of SYN packets to a target server, initiating a TCP handshake but never completing it. This overwhelms the server's connection table (SYN queue), preventing legitimate clients from establishing connections.

metadata.title: Amplification Attack
metadata.definition: A type of Denial-of-Service (DoS) attack where an attacker leverages publicly accessible services to magnify a small request into a much larger response, directing the amplified response to a target victim. This consumes the victim's bandwidth and resources.

metadata.title: WEP Security
metadata.definition: Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP) is an old and highly insecure security algorithm for 802.11 wireless networks, designed to provide data confidentiality comparable to a wired network. It uses a static pre-shared key and the RC4 stream cipher, making it vulnerable to various attacks due to fundamental design flaws.

metadata.title: WPA Security
metadata.definition: Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA) is a security standard for wireless networks, introduced as an interim solution to address the critical vulnerabilities of WEP. It uses TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol) for encryption and message integrity, and generally includes 802.1X for authentication, offering improved but still imperfect security.

metadata.title: WPA2 Security
metadata.definition: Wi-Fi Protected Access II (WPA2) is a robust security standard for wireless networks, providing strong encryption using AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) and CCMP (Counter Mode with Cipher Block Chaining Message Authentication Code Protocol). It significantly improves upon WPA and WEP by fixing known cryptographic weaknesses.

metadata.title: WPA3 Security
metadata.definition: Wi-Fi Protected Access 3 (WPA3) is the latest and most secure standard for wireless networks, building on WPA2 with enhanced features like SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) for stronger handshake protection against offline dictionary attacks, and individualized data encryption in public Wi-Fi hotspots.

metadata.title: EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol)
metadata.definition: A universal authentication framework frequently used in wireless networks (802.1X) and Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) connections. EAP provides a general mechanism for authentication and supports multiple authentication methods (EAP types), allowing for flexible and extensible authentication systems.

metadata.title: RADIUS Protocol
metadata.definition: Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) is a networking protocol that provides centralized Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) management for users connecting to a network service. It is widely used in 802.1X, VPNs, and wireless networks.

metadata.title: TACACS+ Protocol
metadata.definition: Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+) is a proprietary Cisco protocol providing centralized Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) services, often used for device administration (e.g., routers, switches, firewalls). Unlike RADIUS, it separates AAA functions and encrypts the entire packet body.

metadata.title: 802.1X Authentication
metadata.definition: An IEEE standard for Port-Based Network Access Control (PNAC) that provides an authentication mechanism to devices attempting to attach to a LAN or WLAN. It prevents unauthorized devices from gaining access to the network by requiring authentication before granting full network access.

metadata.title: Network Segmentation Gateway
metadata.definition: A device or system that enforces security policies and controls traffic flow between different network segments (e.g., VLANs, subnets, zones). It acts as a barrier, preventing unauthorized communication and limiting the blast radius of security incidents.

metadata.title: Broken Authentication (Web App)
metadata.definition: A security vulnerability in web applications where authentication mechanisms are incorrectly implemented, allowing attackers to bypass authentication, impersonate legitimate users, or compromise user accounts. This often stems from weak credential management, insecure session handling, or flawed multi-factor authentication.

metadata.title: Sensitive Data Exposure (Web App)
metadata.definition: A web application security vulnerability where applications fail to properly protect sensitive data at rest or in transit, leading to unauthorized disclosure. This includes personal information, financial data, or credentials that are stored, processed, or transmitted without adequate encryption or other security controls.

metadata.title: XML External Entities (XXE)
metadata.definition: A web application vulnerability that occurs when an XML parser processes XML input containing references to external entities, which can be exploited to read local files, execute commands, conduct SSRF attacks, or perform denial-of-service.

metadata.title: Broken Access Control (Web App)
metadata.definition: A web application security vulnerability where restrictions on what authenticated users are allowed to do are not properly enforced, allowing users to access or perform actions outside their intended permissions. This can lead to unauthorized information disclosure, data modification, or privilege escalation.

metadata.title: Security Misconfiguration (Web App)
metadata.definition: Occurs when security settings are improperly configured, default settings are left unchanged, unnecessary features are enabled, or unpatched systems are deployed, creating exploitable vulnerabilities. This broad category includes issues from server misconfigurations to application-specific settings.

metadata.title: Insecure Deserialization
metadata.definition: A vulnerability where an application deserializes untrusted data without proper validation, allowing an attacker to manipulate serialized objects or data structures to execute arbitrary code, bypass authentication, or perform other malicious actions.

metadata.title: Insufficient Logging & Monitoring (Web App)
metadata.definition: Refers to a lack of adequate logging and active monitoring of security-relevant events, making it difficult to detect, investigate, and respond to security incidents in a timely manner. Without proper visibility, breaches can go unnoticed for extended periods.

metadata.title: Command Injection (Web App)
metadata.definition: An attack where an attacker injects operating system commands into an application input field that is then executed by the system, typically through a shell. This allows the attacker to execute arbitrary commands on the server hosting the application.

metadata.title: Integer Overflow
metadata.definition: A condition that occurs when an arithmetic operation attempts to create a numeric value that is larger than the maximum value that can be stored in the available memory space (e.g., a 32-bit integer). This can lead to unexpected behavior, buffer overflows, or security vulnerabilities if not handled gracefully.

metadata.title: Format String Vulnerability
metadata.definition: A vulnerability arising when an application processes user-supplied input as a format string in functions like `printf()` or `sprintf()` without proper sanitization. This can allow attackers to read from or write to arbitrary memory locations, crash the program, or execute arbitrary code.

metadata.title: Race Condition (Software)
metadata.definition: A flaw that occurs when the output or result of a program is unexpectedly dependent on the sequence or timing of other uncontrollable events, such as multiple threads or processes accessing and modifying shared resources concurrently. In security, this can lead to privilege escalation, data corruption, or bypasses.

metadata.title: Directory Traversal
metadata.definition: An attack that aims to access unauthorized files and directories stored outside the web root folder by manipulating file paths using sequences like `../` (dot-dot-slash) or similar encoding. This vulnerability can lead to information disclosure or, in some cases, remote code execution.

metadata.title: File Inclusion (Local/Remote)
metadata.definition: A vulnerability where an application builds a path to an executable file using user-supplied input without proper validation, leading to either Local File Inclusion (LFI) for files on the server or Remote File Inclusion (RFI) for files on a remote server. This can result in arbitrary code execution or sensitive data exposure.

metadata.title: Security Headers (HSTS, CSP, X-Frame-Options)
metadata.definition: HTTP response headers that provide client-side security policies to web browsers, mitigating common web vulnerabilities such as cross-site scripting (XSS), clickjacking, and protocol downgrade attacks by enforcing specific browser behaviors and content loading rules.

metadata.title: Parameterized Queries
metadata.definition: A method of constructing database queries where placeholders are used for user-supplied data, and the data is then passed separately to the database engine. This approach inherently prevents SQL injection by ensuring user input is treated as data, not executable code.

metadata.title: Prepared Statements
metadata.definition: A feature used by database systems to execute the same or similar database statements repeatedly with high efficiency and enhanced security. The statement structure is compiled once, and then varying parameters are bound for each execution, inherently preventing SQL injection attacks by separating code from data.

metadata.title: Secure Coding Guidelines
metadata.definition: A set of best practices and rules for developers to follow during software development to minimize the introduction of security vulnerabilities. These guidelines cover areas such as input validation, error handling, authentication, authorization, and cryptographic practices, aiming to build security into the code from the start.

metadata.title: Secure Development Life Cycle (SDLC)
metadata.definition: An extension of the traditional Software Development Life Cycle that integrates security activities and considerations into every phase, from requirements gathering and design to testing, deployment, and maintenance. Its goal is to build security in from the start, rather than bolting it on later, thereby reducing vulnerabilities and cost.

metadata.title: OpenID Connect (OIDC)
metadata.definition: An identity layer built on top of the OAuth 2.0 protocol, enabling clients to verify the identity of the end-user based on the authentication performed by an authorization server, as well as to obtain basic profile information about the end-user in an interoperable and REST-like manner.

metadata.title: JSON Web Token (JWT)
metadata.definition: A compact, URL-safe means of representing claims to be transferred between two parties. JWTs are often used for authentication and authorization, allowing a server to verify the authenticity and integrity of data without needing to query a database for every request, and can be optionally encrypted.

metadata.title: Mobile Application Security
metadata.definition: The practice of securing applications developed for mobile devices (smartphones, tablets) against various threats, including insecure data storage, insufficient transport layer protection, insecure authentication, side-channel attacks, and reverse engineering. It involves applying security principles throughout the app's lifecycle.

metadata.title: OWASP ASVS (Application Security Verification Standard)
metadata.definition: A comprehensive framework and standard for verifying the security of web applications and services. It provides a list of security requirements and tests that can be used to establish a level of confidence in the security of an application, serving as a guide for architects, developers, testers, and security consumers.

metadata.title: Dependency Confusion
metadata.definition: A supply chain attack where an attacker registers a malicious package with the same name as an internal, private package in a public package repository. Build systems configured to prefer public repositories then download and use the malicious public version instead of the intended private one.

metadata.title: File Permissions
metadata.definition: Controls that define who can access a file or directory and what operations (read, write, execute) they can perform. Improper file permissions are a common source of security vulnerabilities, leading to unauthorized data access, modification, or execution.

metadata.title: User Account Management (OS)
metadata.definition: User Account Management in an Operating System involves the creation, modification, and deletion of user accounts, along with defining their access rights and permissions to system resources. This process is crucial for enforcing the principle of least privilege, ensuring accountability, and isolating user activities.

metadata.title: Group Account Management (OS)
metadata.definition: Group Account Management in an Operating System organizes multiple user accounts into logical groups to simplify the assignment and management of shared permissions and access rights. This method streamlines administration and reinforces security by applying policies to collections of users rather than individual accounts.

metadata.title: Password Policy (OS)
metadata.definition: A Password Policy is a set of rules enforced by an Operating System or application regarding the creation, complexity, and lifecycle of passwords. Its primary goal is to enhance security by making passwords harder to guess or crack, thereby protecting user accounts from unauthorized access.

metadata.title: Account Lockout Policy (OS)
metadata.definition: An Account Lockout Policy defines conditions under which a user account will be temporarily or permanently locked after a specified number of consecutive failed login attempts. This security measure is designed to protect against brute-force attacks and automated password-guessing tools.

metadata.title: Security Patches
metadata.definition: Security Patches are updates released by software vendors to fix vulnerabilities, bugs, or weaknesses discovered in their software or operating systems. Applying these patches promptly is critical for preventing exploitation by attackers and maintaining system integrity and confidentiality.

metadata.title: Memory Protection (DEP, ASLR, NX Bit)
metadata.definition: Memory Protection mechanisms like Data Execution Prevention (DEP), Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), and the NX (No-Execute) bit are operating system features designed to prevent common memory-based attacks such as buffer overflows. They achieve this by controlling which memory regions can execute code and by randomizing memory locations of key processes, making exploits harder to predict and execute.

metadata.title: System Calls Security
metadata.definition: System Calls Security focuses on ensuring that interactions between user-mode applications and the operating system kernel, performed via system calls, are properly controlled and secured. This involves validating system call parameters, enforcing access controls, and limiting the scope of what applications can request from the kernel to prevent privilege escalation or system compromise.

metadata.title: Sandbox (OS)
metadata.definition: An OS Sandbox is a security mechanism that isolates running programs or processes from the rest of the system, limiting their access to system resources, memory, and network. This containment strategy prevents potentially malicious or vulnerable applications from damaging the host system or accessing sensitive data outside their designated boundaries.

metadata.title: Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) Security
metadata.definition: UEFI Security encompasses measures taken within the Unified Extensible Firmware Interface to ensure the integrity and authenticity of the boot process and firmware itself. Key features like Secure Boot prevent unauthorized operating systems or malware from loading during startup by verifying digital signatures.

metadata.title: IaaS Security
metadata.definition: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) Security involves securing the foundational computing resources provided by a cloud provider, such as virtual machines, networks, and storage. Under the shared responsibility model, the customer is primarily responsible for securing the operating systems, applications, data, and network configurations *within* their deployed infrastructure, while the provider secures the underlying physical infrastructure.

metadata.title: PaaS Security
metadata.definition: PaaS (Platform as a Service) Security focuses on securing the application development and deployment platform provided by a cloud vendor. In this shared responsibility model, the cloud provider manages the underlying infrastructure, operating systems, and middleware, while the customer is responsible for the security of their applications, data, and configuration of platform services.

metadata.title: SaaS Security
metadata.definition: SaaS (Software as a Service) Security pertains to the security of ready-to-use applications delivered over the internet by a cloud provider. Under the shared responsibility model, the provider is typically responsible for nearly all aspects of security, including infrastructure, platform, and application layers, while the customer is primarily responsible for data they input, user access management, and secure configuration of application features.

metadata.title: Community Cloud Security
metadata.definition: Community Cloud Security involves protecting cloud infrastructure and services shared by multiple organizations with common security, compliance, or mission-related concerns. This model presents unique security challenges due to the need to balance resource sharing and collaboration with strict data isolation and adherence to specific regulatory frameworks for all participating entities.

metadata.title: Serverless Function Security (Lambda Security)
metadata.definition: Serverless Function Security, exemplified by AWS Lambda Security, involves securing stateless, event-driven compute functions in the cloud. Key concerns include managing function permissions (least privilege), securing input/output, protecting secrets, and ensuring dependencies are free from vulnerabilities, as the underlying infrastructure management is entirely handled by the cloud provider.

metadata.title: Identity and Access Management (IAM) in Cloud
metadata.definition: Identity and Access Management (IAM) in the cloud is a framework of policies and technologies that enables organizations to manage digital identities and control user access to cloud resources. It ensures that only authenticated and authorized users and services can perform specific actions on specific cloud assets, enforcing the principle of least privilege.

metadata.title: Data Encryption in Cloud
metadata.definition: Data Encryption in Cloud involves transforming sensitive data into an unreadable format to protect its confidentiality both at rest (when stored) and in transit (when being transmitted). Cloud providers offer various encryption services, often integrated with key management systems, to help customers meet compliance requirements and secure their information.

metadata.title: Cloud Storage Security
metadata.definition: Cloud Storage Security encompasses the practices and controls used to protect data stored in cloud-based object, file, or block storage services. This includes managing access permissions, enforcing encryption, ensuring data integrity, implementing proper backup and disaster recovery, and protecting against accidental deletion or unauthorized access.

metadata.title: Network Security Groups (Cloud)
metadata.definition: Network Security Groups (NSGs) in cloud environments are virtual firewalls that control inbound and outbound network traffic to virtual machines, subnets, and other network interfaces. They operate at the network layer, allowing or denying connections based on source/destination IP addresses, ports, and protocols, thus providing granular network segmentation and access control.

metadata.title: Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) Security
metadata.definition: Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) Security involves configuring and protecting an isolated, private network within a public cloud environment, providing control over its IP address range, subnets, route tables, and network gateways. This ensures network isolation for cloud resources and allows for secure connectivity, traffic filtering, and robust segmentation.

metadata.title: Secrets Management (Cloud)
metadata.definition: Secrets Management in the cloud is the process of securely storing, accessing, and lifecycle managing sensitive authentication credentials and cryptographic keys required by applications, services, and users. It aims to eliminate hardcoded secrets, centralize secret storage, and provide granular access control and auditing for these critical assets.

metadata.title: DevSecOps Principles
metadata.definition: Integrating security practices throughout the entire software development lifecycle (SDLC), from design to deployment and operations, ensuring security is a shared responsibility. It aims to automate security tasks and embed them into the CI/CD pipeline, shifting left to identify and remediate vulnerabilities early.

metadata.title: Cloud Logging and Monitoring
metadata.definition: The continuous collection, storage, analysis, and alerting on log data and operational metrics from cloud infrastructure and applications. It is critical for identifying security incidents, troubleshooting performance issues, and ensuring compliance.

metadata.title: Cloud Data Loss Prevention (DLP)
metadata.definition: A set of tools and processes designed to prevent sensitive data from leaving an organization's control, whether accidentally or maliciously, within cloud environments. It identifies, monitors, and protects data in motion, at rest, and in use.

metadata.title: Cloud API Security
metadata.definition: The practice of securing the Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) that enable communication between cloud services, applications, and users. It involves authentication, authorization, encryption, rate limiting, and input validation to protect against common API threats.

metadata.title: Multi-Cloud Security
metadata.definition: The strategies and technologies used to manage security risks and ensure consistent protection across multiple distinct cloud service providers (CSPs) simultaneously. It addresses challenges like differing security models, identity management, and compliance across various cloud platforms.

metadata.title: Data at Rest Encryption
metadata.definition: The cryptographic protection of data when it is stored on persistent storage devices, such as hard drives, SSDs, databases, or cloud storage. This ensures that even if unauthorized access to the storage medium occurs, the data remains unreadable without the decryption key.

metadata.title: Data in Transit Encryption
metadata.definition: The cryptographic protection of data as it moves across networks, such as between two systems, over the internet, or within a private network. This prevents eavesdropping and tampering during data transfer.

metadata.title: Data in Use Encryption
metadata.definition: The cryptographic protection of data while it is being actively processed by a computer system, such as in CPU registers, RAM, or CPU caches. This is the most challenging form of encryption due to the need for data to be decrypted for computation and then re-encrypted.

metadata.title: Tokenization (Data Security)
metadata.definition: The process of replacing sensitive data with a non-sensitive substitute, called a token, that has no intrinsic meaning or value. The original sensitive data is stored securely in a separate token vault, and the token can be used in place of the original data in less secure environments.

metadata.title: GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation)
metadata.definition: A comprehensive data privacy and security law enacted by the European Union, granting individuals control over their personal data and imposing strict requirements on organizations that collect, store, and process it. It applies to any organization handling data of EU citizens, regardless of the organization's location.

metadata.title: CCPA (California Consumer Privacy Act)
metadata.definition: A state statute in California that enhances privacy rights and consumer protection for residents of California. It grants consumers the right to know what personal information is collected about them, the right to delete it, and the right to opt-out of its sale.

metadata.title: HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act)
metadata.definition: A U.S. federal law establishing national standards to protect sensitive patient health information (PHI) from being disclosed without the patient's consent or knowledge. It sets requirements for the security, privacy, and integrity of PHI.

metadata.title: PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard)
metadata.definition: A set of security standards designed to ensure that all companies that process, store, or transmit credit card information maintain a secure environment. It is mandated by the major credit card brands for entities handling cardholder data.

metadata.title: Data Disposal Policy
metadata.definition: A documented set of rules and procedures outlining how an organization securely and permanently removes data from storage media when it is no longer needed. This prevents unauthorized access to sensitive information after its useful life.

metadata.title: Information Rights Management (IRM)
metadata.definition: A technology that allows organizations to control and protect digital information by applying usage policies directly to the content itself, regardless of where the data resides. It enforces access restrictions, preventing unauthorized viewing, printing, forwarding, or copying.

metadata.title: Penetration Testing (Pen Test)
metadata.definition: A simulated cyberattack against a computer system, network, or web application to identify exploitable vulnerabilities before malicious actors can find and exploit them. It involves ethically hacking the system to discover weaknesses and assess the security posture.

metadata.title: Red Team Operations
metadata.definition: A full-scope, multi-layered attack simulation designed to test an organization's overall security posture, including technology, people, and processes, from an adversary's perspective. The goal is to bypass security controls, achieve specific objectives (e.g., exfiltrate data), and identify gaps in detection and response capabilities.

metadata.title: Blue Team Operations
metadata.definition: The defensive security functions within an organization responsible for protecting assets, detecting threats, and responding to security incidents. Blue teams implement security controls, monitor systems, analyze alerts, and conduct forensics.

metadata.title: Purple Team Operations
metadata.definition: A collaborative approach where red and blue teams work together to improve an organization's security posture by sharing knowledge and insights. The red team performs attacks, and the blue team actively observes, defends, and provides feedback, leading to more effective security improvements.

metadata.title: Bug Bounty Programs
metadata.definition: Programs offered by organizations where individuals (often independent security researchers) are invited to discover and report software vulnerabilities in exchange for recognition and/or financial compensation. They leverage the global security community to enhance product security.

metadata.title: Metasploit Framework
metadata.definition: A powerful open-source penetration testing framework that provides a wide array of tools for developing, testing, and executing exploits against remote target systems. It helps security professionals identify vulnerabilities, verify mitigations, and conduct security assessments.

metadata.title: Nessus Scanner
metadata.definition: A widely used proprietary vulnerability scanner developed by Tenable, designed to identify security vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and compliance issues across various network devices, servers, and applications. It provides detailed reports on potential security risks.

metadata.title: Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS)
metadata.definition: An open industry standard for assessing the severity of computer system security vulnerabilities, providing a numerical score and qualitative severity ratings (e.g., Low, Medium, High, Critical). It helps organizations prioritize vulnerability remediation efforts based on a standardized calculation.

metadata.title: Vulnerability Remediation
metadata.definition: The process of identifying, prioritizing, and eliminating or mitigating security vulnerabilities in systems, applications, and networks. This typically involves applying patches, reconfiguring systems, implementing security controls, or rewriting insecure code.

metadata.title: Asset Inventory (for VM)
metadata.definition: A comprehensive and up-to-date record of all virtual machines (VMs) and associated virtual infrastructure components within an organization's environment. This inventory includes details such as VM name, operating system, applications, owner, purpose, network configuration, and security posture.

metadata.title: Incident Response Life Cycle
metadata.definition: A structured, multi-stage process that organizations follow to prepare for, detect, analyze, contain, eradicate, recover from, and learn from security incidents. Common models include the NIST Incident Response Life Cycle (Preparation, Detection & Analysis, Containment, Eradication & Recovery, Post-Incident Activity).

metadata.title: Incident Detection
metadata.definition: The process of identifying and recognizing suspicious activities or events that indicate a potential security breach or policy violation. This involves monitoring logs, network traffic, security alerts, and user behavior for anomalies or known malicious patterns.

metadata.title: Incident Analysis
metadata.definition: The phase of incident response where security analysts thoroughly investigate a detected security event to understand its scope, root cause, impact, and the adversary's techniques. This involves correlating data from various sources, forensic examination, and intelligence gathering.

metadata.title: Post-Incident Activity
metadata.definition: The final phase of the incident response life cycle focused on learning from a security incident to improve future response capabilities and prevent recurrence. This includes conducting a post-mortem review, documenting lessons learned, updating policies, and implementing new security controls.

metadata.title: Playbook (Incident Response)
metadata.definition: A detailed, step-by-step guide that outlines the specific actions, procedures, and responsibilities for responding to a particular type of security incident. Playbooks standardize response efforts, ensuring consistency and efficiency.

metadata.title: Runbook (Incident Response)
metadata.definition: A more granular, technical document often part of or referenced by a playbook, providing specific instructions for executing individual tasks or procedures within an incident response workflow. Runbooks focus on 'how to' accomplish specific technical operations.

metadata.title: Business Continuity Plan (BCP)
metadata.definition: A comprehensive strategy outlining how an organization will maintain essential business functions during and after a significant disruption, such as a natural disaster, cyberattack, or critical system failure. It focuses on keeping the business operational, minimizing downtime, and protecting assets.

metadata.title: Disaster Recovery Plan (DRP)
metadata.definition: A specific component of a Business Continuity Plan that focuses on the processes, policies, and procedures for restoring IT infrastructure and services following a disaster or major disruption. The DRP aims to recover critical systems to an operational state within defined recovery time objectives (RTOs) and recovery point objectives (RPOs).

metadata.title: Forensic Readiness
metadata.definition: The state of an organization's systems, processes, and personnel being prepared to effectively collect, preserve, analyze, and present digital evidence in a legally admissible manner following a security incident. This involves proactive planning and implementation of forensic capabilities.

metadata.title: Computer Security Incident Response Team (CSIRT)
metadata.definition: A dedicated team within an organization responsible for coordinating and managing responses to computer security incidents. A CSIRT typically handles incident detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, and post-incident review.

metadata.title: Security Monitoring
metadata.definition: The continuous process of observing and analyzing an organization's systems, networks, and data for security-related events and potential threats. It involves collecting logs, network traffic, and other data sources to detect anomalies, suspicious activities, and indicators of compromise.

metadata.title: Log Management
metadata.definition: The comprehensive process of collecting, centralizing, storing, retaining, and managing log data generated by various systems, applications, and network devices. Effective log management is crucial for security monitoring, incident response, compliance, and forensic analysis.

metadata.title: Alert Management
metadata.definition: The systematic process of handling, prioritizing, investigating, and responding to security alerts generated by various monitoring systems. Effective alert management aims to reduce alert fatigue, minimize false positives, and ensure timely response to genuine threats.

metadata.title: Threat Hunting
metadata.definition: A proactive and iterative cybersecurity activity where security analysts actively search for undetected threats, anomalies, or malicious activities within a network or dataset that have bypassed existing security controls. It relies on hypotheses and deep understanding of adversary tactics.

metadata.title: Indicators of Compromise (IoC)
metadata.definition: Forensic artifacts or pieces of data found on a network or operating system that indicate a high probability of a computer intrusion or security breach. IoCs serve as evidence of an attack and can be used for detection, threat hunting, and incident response.

metadata.title: MITRE ATT&CK Framework
metadata.definition: A globally accessible knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world observations, used as a foundation for developing specific threat models and methodologies. It helps organizations understand adversary behavior, assess defensive capabilities, and improve threat detection and response.

metadata.title: Cyber Kill Chain
metadata.definition: A framework developed by Lockheed Martin that describes the seven stages of a cyberattack, from reconnaissance to actions on objectives, helping organizations understand and disrupt adversary operations at various points. By breaking down attacks into discrete phases, it enables better defense planning and incident response.

metadata.title: Security Playbook (SecOps)
metadata.definition: A documented, step-by-step guide detailing how security teams should respond to specific types of cybersecurity incidents or alerts, ensuring consistent, efficient, and effective handling of threats. Playbooks automate or semi-automate responses, reducing human error and improving reaction times.

metadata.title: Security Runbook (SecOps)
metadata.definition: A detailed guide for performing routine, repetitive operational tasks in a security environment, often used for automating standard procedures or for junior analysts to execute common activities. Runbooks focus on predictable, operational workflows rather than incident-specific responses.

metadata.title: User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA)
metadata.definition: A cybersecurity solution that monitors and analyzes user and entity (e.g., applications, devices) behavior patterns to detect anomalies and identify potential insider threats, compromised accounts, or sophisticated external attacks. UEBA leverages machine learning to establish baselines and spot deviations from normal activity.

metadata.title: Managed Security Service Provider (MSSP)
metadata.definition: A third-party company that provides outsourced cybersecurity monitoring and management services to organizations, helping them protect their data and systems without maintaining an extensive in-house security team. MSSPs offer services like 24/7 monitoring, incident response, vulnerability management, and compliance support.

metadata.title: Risk Identification
metadata.definition: The process of discovering, recognizing, and describing risks that could potentially impact an organization's assets, operations, or objectives. This foundational step in risk management involves identifying sources of risk, potential events, their causes, and potential consequences.

metadata.title: Risk Analysis (Qualitative)
metadata.definition: A method of risk analysis that uses descriptive language, expert judgment, and scales (e.g., high, medium, low) to assess the likelihood and impact of risks, without assigning specific monetary values. It is often used for initial screening or when precise data is unavailable, providing a relative prioritization of risks.

metadata.title: Risk Analysis (Quantitative)
metadata.definition: A method of risk analysis that assigns specific numerical or monetary values to the likelihood and impact of risks, allowing for precise calculation of potential financial losses and the cost-benefit of security controls. This approach provides objective data for risk prioritization and investment decisions.

metadata.title: Risk Treatment (Avoid, Mitigate, Transfer, Accept)
metadata.definition: The process of selecting and implementing measures to modify risk, typically categorized into four main strategies. These strategies aim to manage risks down to an acceptable level consistent with the organization's risk appetite.

metadata.title: Inherent Risk
metadata.definition: The level of risk that exists in the absence of any controls or other mitigating factors, representing the raw or intrinsic risk associated with an activity, system, or asset. It is the risk before any security measures have been applied.

metadata.title: Risk Appetite
metadata.definition: The amount and type of risk that an organization is willing to seek or accept in the pursuit of its strategic objectives, reflecting its overall risk posture and culture. It sets the high-level boundaries for risk-taking, often defined by the board of directors or senior management.

metadata.title: Risk Tolerance
metadata.definition: The acceptable deviation around a risk appetite or the specific maximum amount of risk an organization is willing to endure for a particular risk, often expressed as thresholds or limits. It provides more granular, operational boundaries than risk appetite.

metadata.title: Acceptable Risk
metadata.definition: The level of residual risk that an organization is willing to live with after applying controls, because the cost of further mitigation outweighs the potential benefit, or the risk is deemed sufficiently low. This is the risk remaining after all chosen treatments have been implemented.

metadata.title: Compliance Audit
metadata.definition: A formal, independent examination to determine whether an organization's operations, processes, and controls adhere to specific regulatory requirements, industry standards, or internal policies. Its purpose is to provide assurance that an organization is meeting its legal and contractual obligations.

metadata.title: Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC)
metadata.definition: A strategic discipline encompassing the entire framework of processes, policies, and technologies an organization uses to manage its overall governance, achieve business objectives while managing risks, and ensure adherence to relevant laws and regulations. GRC aims to align IT and business objectives with security and regulatory demands.

metadata.title: NIST RMF (Risk Management Framework)
metadata.definition: A structured, six-step process developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) that guides federal agencies and other organizations in managing cybersecurity and privacy risks to information systems and organizations. It provides a comprehensive, systematic, and repeatable approach to integrating security and privacy into the system development life cycle.

metadata.title: ISO 27005 (Information Security Risk Management)
metadata.definition: An international standard that provides guidelines for information security risk management, supporting the general concepts specified in ISO/IEC 27001 and detailing the steps for identifying, analyzing, evaluating, treating, and monitoring information security risks. It offers a structured approach to managing information security risks within an organization.

metadata.title: Cost-Benefit Analysis (Security Controls)
metadata.definition: A systematic process of comparing the estimated financial benefits of implementing a security control (e.g., reduced losses from breaches, avoided fines) against its estimated costs (e.g., purchase, implementation, maintenance). This analysis helps justify security investments and prioritize controls based on their return on investment (ROI).

metadata.title: Business Impact Analysis (BIA)
metadata.definition: A systematic process to determine and evaluate the potential effects of an interruption to critical business operations as a result of a disaster, accident, or emergency. It identifies critical business functions, their interdependencies, and establishes recovery time objectives (RTO) and recovery point objectives (RPO) essential for business continuity and disaster recovery planning.

metadata.title: Malware Signature
metadata.definition: A distinctive pattern or characteristic sequence of bytes, code, or behaviors that uniquely identifies a known piece of malware. Antivirus software uses these signatures to detect and block malicious files by matching them against a database of known threats.

metadata.title: Heuristic Analysis (Malware)
metadata.definition: A malware detection technique that identifies suspicious characteristics, behaviors, or anomalies in code or system activity rather than relying on exact signatures. It attempts to infer malicious intent based on a set of rules, algorithms, or machine learning models.

metadata.title: Static Malware Analysis
metadata.definition: The process of examining malware without executing it, typically involving the inspection of its code, structure, and metadata. This method helps understand the malware's potential functionality, dependencies, and indicators of compromise (IOCs) before execution.

metadata.title: Dynamic Malware Analysis
metadata.definition: The process of executing malware in a controlled and isolated environment, such as a sandbox, to observe its runtime behavior, system interactions, and network communications. This method reveals the actual impact and functionality of the malware under specific conditions.

metadata.title: Sandbox (Malware Analysis)
metadata.definition: An isolated virtual environment designed to safely execute and observe suspicious programs or files without risking harm to the host system. It allows analysts to perform dynamic analysis, recording all activities of the malware for detailed inspection.

metadata.title: Obfuscation (Malware)
metadata.definition: The act of intentionally making malware code difficult to understand or analyze by humans and automated tools, without changing its core functionality. This technique aims to evade detection by security software and hinder reverse engineering efforts.

metadata.title: Packing (Malware)
metadata.definition: A specific form of obfuscation where malware executables are compressed and/or encrypted to hide their original code and make static analysis more challenging. The packed malware usually contains a small 'stub' or 'loader' that unpacks and executes the original payload in memory at runtime.

metadata.title: Dropper (Malware)
metadata.definition: A type of malware whose primary function is to install or 'drop' other malicious files onto a target system. The dropper often contains the final payload fully within its own executable, meaning it does not require an active internet connection after initial execution to deploy its components.

metadata.title: Downloader (Malware)
metadata.definition: A type of malware whose main purpose is to connect to a remote server, download additional malicious components or payloads, and then execute them on the compromised system. Unlike a dropper, it relies on network connectivity to fetch its final payload, often as a smaller initial stage of an attack.

metadata.title: Backdoor (Malware)
metadata.definition: A hidden method or vulnerability intentionally created or exploited in a system, application, or network to bypass normal authentication and security controls, granting unauthorized remote access. Backdoors allow attackers to maintain persistent and covert access to a compromised system.

metadata.title: Bootkit
metadata.definition: A type of rootkit that infects the boot sector or Master Boot Record (MBR) of a hard drive, or the UEFI firmware, allowing it to load before the operating system starts. This grants the malware very high privileges and makes it extremely difficult to detect and remove, often persisting across OS reinstallation.

metadata.title: Command and Control (C2) Server
metadata.definition: A central server used by attackers to communicate with and remotely manage compromised systems (bots) within a botnet. It sends commands to the infected machines, receives exfiltrated data, and allows the attacker to orchestrate malicious activities.

metadata.title: Polymorphic Malware
metadata.definition: Malware that changes its identifiable code or signature with each infection or instance while retaining its original functionality. It achieves this by using a mutation engine to alter its appearance (e.g., encryption keys, instruction reordering), making it harder for signature-based antivirus software to detect.

metadata.title: Metamorphic Malware
metadata.definition: Malware that completely rewrites its own code with each iteration, creating a new, functionally equivalent but syntactically different version of itself. Unlike polymorphic malware, it doesn't just encrypt its payload; it changes its entire structure, including its transformation engine, making it extremely challenging for signature-based detection and heuristic analysis.

metadata.title: Malicious Document (Macro)
metadata.definition: A document, typically a Microsoft Office file (e.g., Word, Excel, PowerPoint), that contains embedded malicious code (macros) designed to execute when the document is opened, often prompting the user to enable macros. These macros can download further malware, exfiltrate data, or execute system commands.

metadata.title: Chain of Custody
metadata.definition: A documented, unbroken trail of evidence that shows the chronological sequence of handling, collection, preservation, transfer, and analysis of physical or digital evidence. It is crucial in digital forensics to maintain the integrity and ensure the admissibility of evidence in legal proceedings.

metadata.title: Network Forensics (Digital)
metadata.definition: The process of capturing, recording, and analyzing network traffic to identify intrusions, understand attack methodologies, and gather evidence of malicious activity. It involves examining network packets, logs from various network devices, and configurations to reconstruct events.

metadata.title: Mobile Forensics
metadata.definition: The scientific process of recovering digital evidence and data from mobile devices like smartphones and tablets. This includes extracting data from the device's file system, memory, SIM cards, and associated cloud backups, analyzing app data, communications, and location history.

metadata.title: Email Forensics
metadata.definition: The examination of email communications, including headers, content, attachments, and server logs, to investigate cybercrimes, identify the origin of malicious emails, and recover evidence. It helps trace sender identities, delivery paths, and identify malicious payloads or phishing attempts.

metadata.title: Registry Analysis (Windows Forensics)
metadata.definition: The process of examining the Windows Registry, a hierarchical database storing system and application configurations, user preferences, and security settings, to uncover evidence of malicious activity, user actions, or system changes. It's a critical component of Windows digital forensics.

metadata.title: Event Log Analysis (Forensics)
metadata.definition: Examination of system-generated records (logs) to identify security incidents, system anomalies, and user activities. Critical for understanding the sequence of events leading to a compromise or system failure.

metadata.title: NTFS Forensics
metadata.definition: The process of analyzing data and metadata stored on a New Technology File System (NTFS) partition, commonly found in Windows environments, to uncover forensic evidence. This includes examining MFT, journal files, and deleted file remnants.

metadata.title: EXT4 Forensics
metadata.definition: The specialized forensic examination of the Fourth Extended Filesystem (EXT4), prevalent in Linux and Unix-like operating systems, to extract and analyze digital evidence. This involves understanding inode structures, journaling, and block allocation.

metadata.title: Metadata Analysis (Forensics)
metadata.definition: The examination of data about data (metadata) associated with files, documents, or digital artifacts to gain insights into their origin, history, and usage. This can reveal creation times, authors, modification dates, and geo-locations.

metadata.title: Data Recovery (Forensics)
metadata.definition: The process of salvaging inaccessible, lost, corrupted, or deleted data from digital storage media during a forensic investigation. This often involves specialized software and techniques to reconstruct file fragments or restore entire partitions.

metadata.title: Evidence Acquisition (Forensics)
metadata.definition: The systematic process of identifying, collecting, and preserving digital evidence from various sources in a forensically sound manner. This ensures the integrity and admissibility of evidence in legal proceedings.

metadata.title: Evidence Preservation (Forensics)
metadata.definition: The measures taken to protect and maintain the integrity, authenticity, and legal admissibility of digital evidence once acquired. This includes establishing a chain of custody and preventing any alteration or contamination of the evidence.

metadata.title: Forensic Workstation
metadata.definition: A dedicated, isolated computer system configured with specialized hardware and software tools optimized for performing digital forensic investigations. It typically includes write-blockers, ample storage, and various forensic analysis suites.

metadata.title: Hashing (Forensic)
metadata.definition: The process of generating a unique fixed-size digital fingerprint (hash value) for a file, drive, or data set, used to verify data integrity and authenticity in forensic investigations. Any change to the data, even a single bit, will result in a different hash value.

metadata.title: Write Blocker
metadata.definition: A hardware or software device that prevents any modifications from being made to a connected storage device, thereby preserving the integrity of potential digital evidence. This is crucial during forensic acquisition to ensure data is not inadvertently altered.

metadata.title: Stenography Detection (Forensics)
metadata.definition: The forensic technique of identifying hidden information embedded within seemingly innocent files (e.g., images, audio, video) using steganography. This often involves statistical analysis, anomaly detection, or specialized software tools.

metadata.title: Authentication (IAM)
metadata.definition: The process of verifying the identity of a user, system, or application attempting to access a resource. It answers the question, 'Are you who you claim to be?'

metadata.title: Authorization (IAM)
metadata.definition: The process of determining what actions an authenticated user or system is permitted to perform on a resource. It answers the question, 'What are you allowed to do?'

metadata.title: Accounting (AAA)
metadata.definition: The process of tracking user activities and resource consumption, logging what an authenticated and authorized user does while accessing a system. This data is used for auditing, billing, and incident investigation.

metadata.title: Single Factor Authentication (SFA)
metadata.definition: An authentication method that relies on only one type of credential to verify a user's identity. This typically involves using something the user knows, such as a password or PIN.

metadata.title: Passwordless Authentication
metadata.definition: An authentication method that allows users to verify their identity without needing to enter a traditional password. This typically leverages biometrics, cryptographic keys, or magic links.

metadata.title: Knowledge Factor (Authentication)
metadata.definition: An authentication factor based on something the user *knows*, such as a password, PIN, or a secret question's answer. It relies on the user's memory for verification.

metadata.title: Possession Factor (Authentication)
metadata.definition: An authentication factor based on something the user *has*, such as a physical token, a smart card, or a mobile phone receiving a one-time password (OTP). It verifies ownership of an item.

metadata.title: Inherence Factor (Authentication)
metadata.definition: An authentication factor based on something the user *is*, typically relying on unique biological characteristics. This includes biometrics like fingerprints, facial recognition, or iris scans.

metadata.title: Password Hash (IAM)
metadata.definition: A one-way cryptographic function applied to a user's password, storing the resulting hash value instead of the plaintext password. This protects passwords from direct exposure even if a database is compromised, as the original password cannot be easily derived from the hash.

metadata.title: Rainbow Table Attack
metadata.definition: A Rainbow Table Attack is a precomputed attack designed to reverse cryptographic hash functions, commonly used to crack passwords. It involves comparing a target hash against a pre-generated table of hashes and their corresponding plaintext values, significantly speeding up password cracking compared to brute-force methods.

metadata.title: Brute-force Attack (IAM)
metadata.definition: A Brute-force Attack in Identity and Access Management (IAM) is a trial-and-error method used to discover credentials by systematically trying every possible combination of characters until the correct one is found. This attack is often automated and can target passwords, PINs, or encryption keys.

metadata.title: Dictionary Attack (IAM)
metadata.definition: A Dictionary Attack in IAM is a specific type of brute-force attack that attempts to guess credentials by trying a large list of common words, phrases, and previously compromised passwords. It leverages the tendency of users to choose simple, easily memorable, or default passwords.

metadata.title: Pass-the-Hash Attack
metadata.definition: A Pass-the-Hash (PtH) attack is an exploitation technique where an attacker authenticates to a remote server or service by using the underlying cryptographic hash of a user's password, rather than the plaintext password itself. This attack is common in Windows environments where NTLM hashes are often used for authentication without ever exposing the actual password.

metadata.title: Kerberos Protocol
metadata.definition: Kerberos is a network authentication protocol that provides strong authentication for client/server applications by using secret-key cryptography. It allows nodes to prove their identity to one another across a non-secure network connection, primarily used for Single Sign-On (SSO) within Active Directory domains.

metadata.title: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol)
metadata.definition: LDAP is an open, vendor-neutral, industry-standard application protocol for accessing and maintaining distributed directory information services. It is commonly used to store and retrieve information about users, groups, devices, and other network resources, acting as a central directory for authentication and authorization.

metadata.title: Federated Identity Management
metadata.definition: Federated Identity Management is an arrangement between multiple organizations or domains that allows a user's single digital identity to be used across independent systems. It enables Single Sign-On (SSO), where a user authenticates once with an identity provider and gains access to multiple service providers without re-authentication.

metadata.title: User Provisioning
metadata.definition: User provisioning is the process of creating, updating, and managing user accounts and their associated access rights across various IT systems and applications. It ensures that new users have the necessary access to resources from day one and that their permissions are correctly aligned with their roles.

metadata.title: Deprovisioning
metadata.definition: Deprovisioning is the process of systematically revoking user access rights and removing or disabling their accounts from IT systems and applications.
