It works by dividing the array into 'runs' (monotonically increasing or decreasing sequences), sorting these runs using insertion sort, and then merging them using a modified merge sort.

metadata.title: Comparison Sort Lower Bound
metadata.definition: States that any comparison-based sorting algorithm requires at least O(n log n) comparisons in the worst case to sort n items. This fundamental lower bound is derived from the decision tree model, which shows that a tree with n! leaves (representing all possible permutations) must have a height of at least log(n!).

metadata.title: Quadratic Probing
metadata.definition: A specific form of open addressing where, upon a collision at an index `h(k)`, subsequent probe locations are determined by `(h(k) + i^2) % M`, for `i = 1, 2, 3, ...`, where `M` is the table size. This method helps to reduce primary clustering compared to linear probing by spreading out probes more aggressively.

metadata.title: Topological Sort (Kahn's Algorithm)
metadata.definition: An algorithm for topological sorting that works by iteratively finding nodes with no incoming edges (in-degree 0), adding them to the sorted list, and then removing their outgoing edges. This process updates the in-degrees of subsequent nodes, continuing until all nodes are processed or a cycle is detected.

metadata.title: Strongly Connected Components (Tarjan's)
metadata.definition: An efficient algorithm for finding the strongly connected components (SCCs) of a directed graph using a single Depth-First Search (DFS) traversal. It uses Breadth-First Search (BFS) to find augmenting paths in the residual graph, specifically focusing on paths with the fewest edges, which guarantees polynomial time complexity, typically O(VE²).

metadata.title: Dinic's Algorithm
metadata.definition: A more efficient algorithm for computing the maximum flow in a flow network, improving upon Edmonds-Karp. It operates in phases, where each phase constructs a level graph using BFS and then finds a 'blocking flow' by performing multiple DFS traversals on this level graph, leading to a complexity of O(V²E) for general graphs and O(VE) for unit capacity networks.

metadata.title: Eulerian Path/Circuit
metadata.definition: An Eulerian path is a path in a graph that visits every edge exactly once. An Eulerian circuit is an Eulerian path that starts and ends at the same vertex. Such paths or circuits exist if and only if the graph is connected and all (for a circuit) or all but two (for a path) vertices have even degrees.

metadata.title: Naive String Matching
metadata.definition: Naive String Matching is a straightforward algorithm that searches for a pattern within a text by sliding the pattern one character at a time across the text and comparing characters at each possible alignment. It has a worst-case time complexity of O(M*N), where M is pattern length and N is text length.

metadata.title: Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) Algorithm
metadata.definition: The Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) algorithm is an efficient string matching algorithm that avoids re-checking characters that have already been matched. It achieves linear time complexity by pre-processing the pattern to construct a 'Longest Proper Prefix which is also a Suffix' (LPS) array, which guides shifts in case of a mismatch.

It uses a cycle-finding algorithm (Floyd's cycle-finding algorithm) to detect collisions in a sequence generated by a pseudo-random function modulo 'n', leveraging the birthday paradox.

metadata.title: Sieve of Eratosthenes
metadata.definition: An ancient, highly efficient algorithm for finding all prime numbers up to a specified integer 'n'. It works by iteratively marking as composite (i.e., not prime) the multiples of each prime, starting with 2, until only prime numbers remain unmarked.

metadata.title: Modular Inverse Algorithm
metadata.definition: This algorithm computes the modular multiplicative inverse of an integer 'a' modulo 'm', which is an integer 'x' such that `(a * x) % m = 1`. It typically relies on the Extended Euclidean Algorithm or, if 'm' is prime, Fermat's Little Theorem.

metadata.title: Chinese Remainder Theorem (Algorithm)
metadata.definition: The Chinese Remainder Theorem provides a unique solution to a system of linear congruences with distinct, pairwise coprime moduli. The associated algorithms construct an integer 'x' that satisfies all given congruences simultaneously.

metadata.title: RSA Algorithm (Basic Steps)
metadata.definition: RSA is a public-key cryptosystem widely used for secure data transmission, based on the difficulty of factoring the product of two large prime numbers. Its basic steps involve key generation (public and private keys), encryption using the public key, and decryption using the private key, all leveraging modular exponentiation.

metadata.title: Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange (Basic Steps)
metadata.definition: Diffie-Hellman is a method of securely exchanging cryptographic keys over a public channel, allowing two parties to establish a shared secret key without any prior shared secret. It relies on the mathematical difficulty of the discrete logarithm problem in modular arithmetic.

metadata.title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (Basic Concept)
metadata.definition: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) is an approach to public-key cryptography based on the algebraic structure of elliptic curves over finite fields. It offers equivalent security to non-ECC cryptography with smaller key sizes, leveraging the computational difficulty of the Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem (ECDLP).

metadata.title: Linear Programming (Simplex Method)
metadata.definition: The Simplex Method is an iterative algorithm for solving linear programming problems, which involve optimizing a linear objective function subject to linear equality and inequality constraints. It systematically moves from one vertex of the feasible region to an adjacent one, always improving the objective function value until an optimal solution is reached.

metadata.title: Integer Linear Programming (Concept)
metadata.definition: Integer Linear Programming (ILP) is a type of linear programming where some or all of the decision variables are restricted to be integers. Unlike standard linear programming, which can be solved in polynomial time, ILP problems are generally NP-hard, making them significantly more complex to solve.

metadata.title: Gradient Descent Algorithm
metadata.definition: Gradient Descent is a first-order iterative optimization algorithm used for finding the local minimum of a differentiable function. It works by repeatedly taking steps proportional to the negative of the gradient of the function at the current point, effectively moving in the direction of steepest descent.

metadata.title: Genetic Algorithm (Concept)
metadata.definition: A Genetic Algorithm (GA) is a metaheuristic search algorithm inspired by the process of natural selection and evolution. It operates on a population of candidate solutions, applying genetic operators like mutation, crossover, and selection over generations to evolve progressively better solutions to optimization and search problems.

metadata.title: Ant Colony Optimization (Concept)
metadata.definition: Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) is a probabilistic metaheuristic technique for solving computational problems which can be reduced to finding good paths through graphs. It is inspired by the foraging behavior of real ants, where ants collectively find shortest paths between their colony and food sources by depositing pheromone trails. The algorithm simulates this process, with artificial ants constructing solutions based on heuristic information and pheromone levels, which are then updated to reflect the quality of the solutions.

metadata.title: Parallel Computing Model (PRAM)
metadata.definition: The Parallel Random Access Machine (PRAM) is a theoretical shared-memory model for parallel computation, where multiple processors can access a common global memory in unit time. It abstracts away communication costs and synchronization overheads, focusing on the inherent parallelism of an algorithm. PRAM models are categorized by how they handle concurrent read/write operations to the same memory location (e.g., EREW, CREW, CRCW).

metadata.title: Work-Depth Model
metadata.definition: The Work-Depth model is a theoretical framework for analyzing the efficiency of parallel algorithms, independent of the number of available processors. It characterizes an algorithm by two main metrics: 'work' (the total number of operations performed by all processors) and 'depth' (the length of the longest chain of dependencies, also known as span or critical path length). This model helps determine the maximum speedup achievable and the minimum possible execution time on an infinite number of processors.

metadata.title: MapReduce Paradigm
metadata.definition: MapReduce is a programming model and an associated distributed framework for processing large datasets in parallel across a cluster of computers. It simplifies distributed data processing by breaking down tasks into two main phases: a 'Map' phase, which processes input key-value pairs independently to generate intermediate key-value pairs, and a 'Reduce' phase, which aggregates these intermediate values based on their keys to produce the final output.

metadata.title: Distributed Consensus (Paxos Concept)
metadata.definition: Paxos is a family of protocols for solving the distributed consensus problem, enabling a set of processes to agree on a single value, even if some processes fail or messages are lost. It guarantees safety (all agreed-upon values are valid and consistent) and liveness (eventually, a value will be agreed upon) in an asynchronous network with crash failures, making it fundamental for building fault-tolerant distributed systems.

metadata.title: Distributed Consensus (Raft Concept)
metadata.definition: Raft is a distributed consensus algorithm designed for understandability and proven to be equivalent to Paxos in fault tolerance and performance. It achieves consensus by electing a single strong leader who is responsible for managing a replicated log, ensuring that all state changes are consistently applied across all servers in a cluster. The protocol simplifies the problem into three subproblems: leader election, log replication, and safety.

metadata.title: Load Balancing Algorithm
metadata.definition: A load balancing algorithm distributes computing workloads across multiple resources, such as servers, network links, or CPUs, to optimize resource utilization, maximize throughput, minimize response time, and prevent any single resource from becoming overloaded. Its primary goal is to improve the overall performance, scalability, and reliability of a system by efficiently sharing the computational demand.

metadata.title: Parallel Sorting (Odd-Even Transposition)
metadata.definition: Odd-Even Transposition Sort is a simple parallel sorting algorithm particularly well-suited for a linear array of processors. It works in alternating phases: 'odd' phases where odd-indexed elements compare and swap with their right neighbors, and 'even' phases where even-indexed elements compare and swap with their right neighbors. This process repeats `N` times for an array of `N` elements, ensuring that the array is sorted.

metadata.title: Las Vegas Algorithm
metadata.definition: A Las Vegas algorithm is a randomized algorithm that always produces the correct output (or finds a correct solution), but its running time is probabilistic and may vary on different executions. While it is guaranteed to produce a correct result upon termination, there is no deterministic upper bound on its execution time, and it might occasionally take an extremely long time or fail to terminate within practical limits.

metadata.title: Monte Carlo Algorithm
metadata.definition: A Monte Carlo algorithm is a randomized algorithm that has a deterministic running time, but its output may be incorrect with a certain (usually small and controllable) probability. These algorithms are useful when a correct answer is too expensive to compute deterministically, and an approximate or possibly incorrect answer within a fixed time budget is acceptable. They typically offer either a 'yes-biased' (false positives) or 'no-biased' (false negatives) error probability.

metadata.title: Randomized Quick Sort
metadata.definition: Randomized Quick Sort is a variant of the Quick Sort algorithm where the pivot element is chosen randomly from the array elements at each step. This randomization helps to ensure that the algorithm's worst-case time complexity of O(n^2), which typically occurs with consistently bad pivot choices, becomes extremely unlikely. The expected time complexity of Randomized Quick Sort remains O(n log n) for any input distribution, making it robust in practice.

metadata.title: Randomized Primality Test (Miller-Rabin)
metadata.definition: The Miller-Rabin primality test is a probabilistic (Monte Carlo) algorithm used to efficiently determine if a given large number is prime. It works by testing a number against several randomly chosen 'witnesses' for properties that all prime numbers satisfy. If the number fails any test, it is definitively composite; if it passes all tests, it is declared 'probably prime' with a high probability, which increases with the number of witnesses used.

metadata.title: Min-Cut Algorithm (Karger's)
metadata.definition: Karger's algorithm is a randomized algorithm for finding a minimum cut in an undirected graph. It repeatedly selects a random edge and contracts its two endpoints into a single new vertex, preserving multiedges. This process continues until only two vertices remain, at which point the edges between these two super-vertices form a cut. By repeating the algorithm multiple times, one can find the minimum cut with a high probability.

metadata.title: Approximation Ratio
metadata.definition: The approximation ratio (or approximation factor) is a performance metric for approximation algorithms that quantifies how close the algorithm's solution is to the optimal solution for an optimization problem. For a minimization problem, it's defined as the ratio of the algorithm's solution value to the optimal solution value (always ≥ 1). For a maximization problem, it's the ratio of the optimal value to the algorithm's solution value (also always ≥ 1).

metadata.title: Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (PTAS)
metadata.definition: A Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (PTAS) is a family of approximation algorithms for an optimization problem that can achieve an approximation ratio arbitrarily close to optimal. For any desired constant `ε > 0`, there exists an algorithm within the scheme that produces a solution with an approximation ratio of `(1+ε)` for minimization problems or `(1-ε)` for maximization problems. The running time of a PTAS is polynomial in the input size `n`, but may be exponential in `1/ε`.

metadata.title: Fully Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (FPTAS)
metadata.definition: A Fully Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (FPTAS) is a more powerful type of approximation scheme than a PTAS. For an FPTAS, not only is its running time polynomial in the input size `n`, but it is also polynomial in `1/ε`, where `ε` is the error parameter determining the approximation ratio. This means an FPTAS is practical even when a very high degree of accuracy (small `ε`) is required, as its exponential dependence on `1/ε` is removed.

This means an FPTAS is practical even when a very high degree of accuracy (small `ε`) is required, as its exponential dependence on `1/ε` is removed.

metadata.title: Vertex Cover Approximation
metadata.definition: The Vertex Cover problem is NP-hard, requiring finding the smallest set of vertices in a graph such that every edge has at least one endpoint in the set. A simple and widely known 2-approximation algorithm for Vertex Cover works by repeatedly picking an arbitrary edge, adding both of its endpoints to the vertex cover set, and then removing all edges incident to these two vertices, continuing until no edges remain. This greedy strategy guarantees that the size of the found vertex cover is at most twice the size of the minimum vertex cover.

metadata.title: Set Cover Approximation
metadata.definition: The Set Cover problem is NP-hard, involving finding the minimum number of sets from a given collection whose union contains all elements of a universal set. A standard greedy approximation algorithm for Set Cover repeatedly selects the set that covers the maximum number of currently uncovered elements until all elements are covered. This algorithm achieves an approximation ratio of `ln(max_set_size) + 1` (where `max_set_size` is the maximum number of elements in any set), which is also denoted as `H(max_set_size)` where `H` is the harmonic number.

metadata.title: TSP Approximation (Triangle Inequality)
metadata.definition: For the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP), which is NP-hard, when the edge weights satisfy the triangle inequality (direct path is always shortest or equal to indirect paths), there exist effective approximation algorithms. A well-known 2-approximation algorithm involves first computing a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) of the graph, then performing a depth-first traversal of the MST, and finally constructing a tour by visiting vertices in the order they are first encountered in the DFS. This tour's length is guaranteed to be at most twice the length of the optimal TSP tour.

metadata.title: Knapsack Problem Approximation
metadata.definition: The Knapsack Problem is an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem where the goal is to choose a subset of items, each with a weight and a value, to maximize the total value while not exceeding a given weight capacity. While the 0/1 Knapsack problem is NP-hard, it admits a Fully Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (FPTAS). This FPTAS can produce a solution whose total value is within a `(1-ε)` factor of the optimal value, with a running time that is polynomial in both the number of items (`n`) and `1/ε`.

metadata.title: Turing Machine (Deterministic)
metadata.definition: A deterministic Turing Machine (DTM) is a mathematical model of computation consisting of a finite state control, an infinite tape divided into cells, and a read/write head. At each step, based on its current state and the symbol under the head, it deterministically writes a symbol, moves the head, and transitions to a new state.

metadata.title: Complexity Class NP
metadata.definition: The complexity class NP (Non-deterministic Polynomial time) comprises decision problems for which a 'yes' instance's solution can be verified in polynomial time by a deterministic Turing machine. Equivalently, problems in NP can be solved by a non-deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time.

metadata.title: Complexity Class NP-Complete
metadata.definition: A problem is NP-Complete if it is in NP and is also NP-Hard. This means it is among the 'hardest' problems in NP, as any other problem in NP can be polynomially reduced to it, implying that an efficient solution for one NP-Complete problem would lead to efficient solutions for all problems in NP.

metadata.title: Polynomial-Time Reduction
metadata.definition: A polynomial-time reduction is a transformation from an instance of problem A to an instance of problem B such that A has a 'yes' answer if and only if B has a 'yes' answer, and the transformation process itself can be computed in polynomial time. It demonstrates that problem A is no harder than problem B, denoted A ≤p B.

metadata.title: P vs NP Problem
metadata.definition: The P vs NP problem is a major unsolved question in theoretical computer science asking whether every problem whose solution can be quickly verified (NP) can also be quickly solved (P). Formally, it asks if the complexity classes P and NP are equivalent (P = NP) or if P is a proper subset of NP (P ⊂ NP).

metadata.title: Hierarchy Theorem (Time)
metadata.definition: The Time Hierarchy Theorem states that for any 'well-behaved' (constructible) function f(n), there exist decision problems solvable in time O(f(n) log f(n)) that cannot be solved in time O(f(n)). This formally proves that providing more time strictly increases the class of problems that can be solved.

metadata.title: Interactive Proof System (Concept)
metadata.definition: An interactive proof system is a computational model involving two parties: a computationally powerful but untrusted Prover (P) and a polynomial-time Verifier (V). The Prover attempts to convince the Verifier of the truth of a statement through a series of messages, with the Verifier accepting true statements with high probability and rejecting false ones with high probability.

metadata.title: Probabilistically Checkable Proofs (PCP)
metadata.definition: A Probabilistically Checkable Proof (PCP) is a type of interactive proof where a Verifier, using randomization, checks a proof of a mathematical statement by querying only a small, constant number of bits from the proof. The PCP Theorem states that every language in NP has a probabilistically checkable proof that can be checked in polynomial time using a logarithmic number of random bits and querying only a constant number of bits.

metadata.title: Fixed-Parameter Tractability (FPT)
metadata.definition: A problem is fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) if it can be solved by an algorithm whose running time is f(k) * poly(n), where n is the input size, k is a parameter of the input, f is an arbitrary computable function, and poly is a polynomial function. This means the exponential growth in runtime is confined to the parameter k, making the problem tractable for small k, even if it is NP-hard in general.

metadata.definition: Parameterized Complexity is a framework for analyzing the computational difficulty of problems by considering their input size 'n' and one or more additional 'parameters' 'k' that describe structural properties of the input. It seeks to classify problems as fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) if they admit algorithms with running times f(k) * poly(n), allowing for efficient solutions when the parameter k is small, even if the problem is NP-hard in general.

metadata.definition: Undecidability refers to the property of a decision problem for which no algorithm can be constructed that always produces a correct 'yes' or 'no' answer in a finite amount of time, regardless of the input. Such problems are inherently impossible to solve algorithmically.

metadata.title: Halting Problem
metadata.definition: The Halting Problem is a famous undecidable decision problem asking whether, given a description of an arbitrary computer program and an arbitrary input, one can determine if the program will finish running or continue to run forever. Alan Turing proved in 1936 that no general algorithm can solve the Halting Problem for all possible program-input pairs.

metadata.title: Reduction (Computability)

If Problem A can be reduced to Problem B, then solving Problem B can be used to solve Problem A, implying that Problem B is 'at least as hard' as Problem A.

metadata.title: Online Algorithms (General Concept)
metadata.definition: Online algorithms are algorithms that process their input piece-by-piece in a serial fashion, without having the entire input available at the start. They must make decisions locally at each step, based only on the information processed so far, without knowledge of future input.

metadata.title: Competitive Analysis (Online Algorithms)
metadata.definition: Competitive analysis is a method for evaluating the performance of online algorithms by comparing their output to that of an optimal offline algorithm, which has full knowledge of the entire input in advance. The competitive ratio is defined as the worst-case ratio of the online algorithm's cost to the optimal offline algorithm's cost.

metadata.title: External Memory Algorithm
metadata.definition: External memory algorithms (or out-of-core algorithms) are designed to process data that is too large to fit into a computer's main memory (RAM). These algorithms optimize for minimizing accesses to slower external storage devices, such as hard drives or SSDs, often by exploiting principles like locality and sequential access.

metadata.title: Streaming Algorithm

metadata.title: Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH)
metadata.definition: Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) is a randomized technique used for efficiently finding approximate nearest neighbors in high-dimensional spaces. It works by hashing similar items to the same 'buckets' with high probability, while dissimilar items are hashed to different buckets with high probability, thereby speeding up similarity searches.

metadata.title: Bloom Filter (Algorithm)
metadata.definition: A Bloom filter is a space-efficient probabilistic data structure used to test whether an element is a member of a set. It can yield false positives (reporting an element is in the set when it's not) but never false negatives (never failing to report an element that is in the set), and offers constant time insertion and query operations.

metadata.title: Fast Walsh-Hadamard Transform (FWHT)

metadata.title: Matrix Multiplication Algorithm (Strassen's)
metadata.definition: A divide-and-conquer algorithm for matrix multiplication that is asymptotically faster than the standard algorithm. It recursively splits matrices into smaller sub-matrices and performs 7 multiplications instead of 8 for each block, reducing the computational complexity from O(N^3) to O(N^log2(7)), approximately O(N^2.807).

metadata.title: Blockchain Consensus Algorithms (Proof of Work Concept)

metadata.title: Homomorphic Encryption (Algorithmic Concept)
metadata.definition: A form of encryption that permits computations to be performed directly on encrypted data without prior decryption, yielding an encrypted result that, when decrypted, is identical to the result of performing the same operations on the unencrypted data. This capability enables secure data processing in untrusted environments, such as cloud servers, while maintaining data privacy.

metadata.title: Inheritance (OOP)

metadata.title: Static Method
metadata.definition: A method that belongs to the class itself, rather than to any specific instance (object) of the class. It can be called directly on the class name without creating an object, and it cannot access instance-specific data (non-static fields or methods) because it doesn't operate on a particular object.

metadata.title: Functional Programming Paradigm
metadata.definition: A programming paradigm that treats computation as the evaluation of mathematical functions and emphasizes immutability, pure functions, and higher-order functions. It seeks to avoid changing state and mutable data, leading to more predictable, testable, and concurrent-friendly code.

metadata.title: Pure Function
metadata.definition: A function that adheres to two main properties: given the same inputs, it will always return the same output (deterministic), and it produces no observable side effects. It relies only on its input parameters for computation and does not modify any external state or perform I/O that affects anything outside its scope.

metadata.title: Immutability (Programming)
metadata.definition: The principle that once an object or data structure is created, its internal state cannot be changed. Any operation that appears to modify an immutable object will instead return a new object with the desired changes, leaving the original object untouched. This enhances predictability, thread safety, and simplifies reasoning about program state.

metadata.title: Side Effect (Programming)
metadata.definition: Any observable change to the system's state or behavior that occurs outside the local scope of a function, beyond returning a value. Common side effects include modifying a global variable, writing to a file, performing I/O operations, or mutating an object passed as an argument, making code harder to reason about and test.

metadata.title: Closure (Programming)
metadata.definition: A function that "remembers" its lexical environment (the scope in which it was declared) even after that environment has finished executing. This allows the function to access and manipulate variables from its outer scope, even when called from a different, unrelated scope, effectively 'closing over' those variables.

metadata.definition: Chaining is a collision resolution technique used in hash tables where each slot (or 'bucket') in the hash table array points to a linked list of all key-value pairs that hash to that same index. metadata.title: NP-Completeness
metadata.definition: A property of decision problems that are both in NP and are NP-hard. This means they are among the 'hardest' problems in NP; if any NP-complete problem can be solved in polynomial time, then all problems in NP can be solved in polynomial time (implying P=NP).

metadata.title: NP-Hardness
metadata.definition: A property of problems that are at least as hard as any problem in NP. A problem H is NP-hard if every problem L in NP can be reduced to H in polynomial time, meaning H is at least as computationally challenging as all NP problems. NP-hard problems do not necessarily have to be in NP themselves.

Definition: The ability of different parts of a program or system to execute independently and seemingly simultaneously, often by interleaving their execution over a single processor. It deals with managing multiple tasks that are in progress at the same time, giving the illusion of parallelism.

metadata.title: Parallelism (OS)
metadata.definition: The ability to execute multiple tasks or parts of a task at the exact same physical time, typically on multiple CPU cores or processors. It is about actually doing many things at once, requiring hardware support for simultaneous execution.

metadata.title: Race Condition
metadata.definition: A condition where the outcome of multiple threads or processes accessing and modifying shared data depends on the unpredictable relative timing of their execution. It occurs when multiple operations try to affect the same state without proper synchronization, potentially leading to data corruption or unexpected results.

metadata.title: Critical Section
metadata.definition: A segment of code within a concurrent program that accesses shared resources or data that must not be concurrently accessed by more than one thread or process. Entry to and exit from a critical section must be guarded by synchronization mechanisms to prevent race conditions.

metadata.title: Lock (Synchronization)
metadata.definition: A synchronization primitive that restricts access to a shared resource or critical section to only one thread or process at a time. A thread acquires the lock before entering the critical section and releases it upon exiting, thereby ensuring mutual exclusion.

metadata.title: Mutex (Synchronization)
metadata.definition: A synchronization primitive specifically designed for mutual exclusion, ensuring that only one thread can acquire the lock (or 'own the mutex') at any given time. It is essentially a binary semaphore (value 0 or 1) often used to protect critical sections.

metadata.title: Deadlock (OS)
metadata.definition: A situation in a multi-process or multi-thread system where two or more processes are permanently blocked because each is waiting for the other to release a resource. Deadlocks occur when four conditions are simultaneously met: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

metadata.title: Deadlock Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm)
metadata.definition: A strategy for preventing deadlocks by dynamically analyzing resource-allocation requests to ensure that the system always remains in a 'safe state.' The Banker's Algorithm, a prominent example, checks if granting a resource request would lead to an unsafe state where a deadlock could eventually occur, and only grants the request if the state remains safe.

metadata.title: Deadlock Detection
metadata.definition: A strategy for handling deadlocks by allowing the system to enter a deadlocked state, then periodically running an algorithm to identify deadlocked processes and resolve the situation. Once detected, the system typically recovers by preempting resources or terminating one or more processes involved in the deadlock.

metadata.title: CPU Scheduling
metadata.definition: The process of determining which process or thread will execute on the CPU next, and for how long, from the set of ready-to-run processes. Its primary goal is to maximize CPU utilization, throughput, and minimize turnaround time, waiting time, and response time.

metadata.title: First-Come, First-Served Scheduling
metadata.definition: A non-preemptive CPU scheduling algorithm where processes are executed strictly in the order they arrive in the ready queue. It is simple to implement but can lead to long waiting times if a long process arrives before several short ones, a phenomenon known as the convoy effect.

metadata.title: First Normal Form (1NF)

metadata.title: Second Normal Form (2NF)

metadata.title: Atomicity (ACID)
metadata.definition: The 'A' in ACID properties, Atomicity ensures that a database transaction is treated as a single, indivisible unit of work. metadata.title: Locking (Database)
metadata.definition: A concurrency control mechanism where a database object (like a row, table, or page) is marked as 'in-use' by a transaction, preventing other transactions from accessing or modifying it until the lock is released. Locks can be shared (allowing multiple reads) or exclusive (allowing only one write or read).

The resulting relation will have a schema that is the concatenation of the schemas of R and S, and its number of tuples will be the product of the number of tuples in R and S.

metadata.title: Division Operation (Relational Algebra)
metadata.definition: The Division operation (R ÷ S) in relational algebra is a powerful operation used to find tuples in one relation (R) that are associated with *all* tuples in another relation (S). It is defined for relations R(A, B) and S(B) where A and B are sets of attributes; the result is a relation containing attributes A, with tuples (a) such that for all tuples (b) in S, the tuple (a, b) exists in R.

It comes in two main forms: Tuple Relational Calculus and Domain Relational Calculus, both based on mathematical logic and predicate calculus.

metadata.title: Tuple Relational Calculus
metadata.definition: Tuple Relational Calculus (TRC) is a form of relational calculus where variables range over tuples. A query in TRC specifies a predicate that the desired tuples must satisfy. It uses quantifiers (∃ for 'there exists' and ∀ for 'for all') to formulate queries.

metadata.title: Functional Dependency
metadata.definition: A Functional Dependency (FD) is a constraint between two sets of attributes in a relation, typically expressed as X → Y. It states that if two tuples have the same values for attributes in set X, then they must also have the same values for attributes in set Y; essentially, X uniquely determines Y.

metadata.title: Trivial Functional Dependency
metadata.definition: A Trivial Functional Dependency (TFD) is a functional dependency X → Y where Y is a subset of X (Y ⊆ X). These dependencies are always true and provide no additional information about the relationships between attributes, as the values for Y are inherently determined by X if Y is part of X.

Once a transaction is committed, its changes are saved and cannot be undone by a ROLLBACK statement, ensuring the 'D' (Durability) in ACID properties.

metadata.title: ROLLBACK Statement
metadata.definition: The ROLLBACK statement is a Transaction Control Language (TCL) command that undoes all changes performed during the current transaction since its beginning or since the last SAVEPOINT, restoring the database to a previous consistent state. This ensures the 'A' (Atomicity) in ACID properties, preventing partial updates from being permanently saved.

Each distinct value in the indexed column has a bitmap, where a '1' bit indicates that the corresponding row has that value, making it highly efficient for low-cardinality columns and complex WHERE clauses with multiple conditions.

It allows for advanced text queries such as keyword searches, phrase matching, and proximity searches, often involving linguistic analysis like stemming and stop-word removal.

This means the actual data rows are stored within the leaf nodes of the index structure, allowing for very fast retrieval of data based on the indexed column.

This significantly improves query performance by avoiding costly table lookups.

metadata.title: Columnar Storage

This organization is highly optimized for analytical queries that often aggregate data across many rows but only require a subset of columns, leading to better compression and I/O efficiency.

metadata.title: RAID 0
metadata.definition: RAID 0 (Striping) is a RAID level that stripes data across multiple disks, distributing data blocks sequentially. It provides improved performance by allowing simultaneous read/write operations but offers no data redundancy or fault tolerance; the failure of any single disk results in complete data loss.

metadata.title: RAID 1
metadata.definition: RAID 1 (Mirroring) is a RAID level that mirrors data identically across two or more disks, creating an exact copy of the data on each drive. It offers excellent fault tolerance and read performance, as data can be read from any disk, but at the cost of storage capacity (50% efficiency for two disks).

metadata.title: RAID 5

metadata.title: Lost Update Problem
metadata.definition: The Lost Update Problem is a concurrency anomaly where an update made by one transaction is overwritten and effectively disappears due to another concurrent transaction updating the same data item. This leads to data inconsistency, as one of the updates is permanently lost.

metadata.title: Conflict Serializability
metadata.definition: Conflict serializability is a property of a schedule of concurrent transactions where its effect is equivalent to some serial schedule (where transactions execute one after another in some order) by preserving the order of all conflicting operations. Conflicting operations involve at least one write operation and refer to the same data item (e.g., read-write, write-read, write-write).

metadata.title: View Serializability
metadata.definition: View serializability is a property of a schedule of concurrent transactions where its effect is equivalent to some serial schedule. It ensures that for every transaction in the schedule, it reads the same initial values, sees the same sequence of updates, and produces the same final write values as it would in some serial execution, making it a weaker condition than conflict serializability.

metadata.title: Strict Two-Phase Locking (2PL)
metadata.definition: A concurrency control protocol that requires transactions to acquire all locks before releasing any, and holds all exclusive (write) locks until after the transaction commits or aborts, ensuring both serializability and strict recoverability. This prevents cascading rollbacks and guarantees that only committed changes are visible.

Definition: A type of lock placed on a data item that grants exclusive access to a single transaction, preventing any other transaction from both reading or writing to that item. It is also known as a write lock and is essential for ensuring data integrity during modifications.

metadata.title: Timestamp Ordering Concurrency Control
metadata.definition: A concurrency control protocol that assigns a unique timestamp to each transaction and orders operations based on these timestamps to ensure serializability. Transactions are allowed to proceed only if their operations maintain the timestamp order of conflicting operations, potentially aborting transactions that violate this order.

metadata.title: Timestamp Ordering Concurrency Control

Transactions are allowed to proceed only if their operations maintain the timestamp order of conflicting operations, potentially aborting transactions that violate this order.

metadata.title: Multiversion Concurrency Control (MVCC)
metadata.definition: A concurrency control method that maintains multiple versions of data items, allowing read operations to access older, consistent versions without blocking write operations, and write operations to create new versions. This minimizes read-write conflicts, improves concurrency, and often enables snapshot isolation.

metadata.title: Pessimistic Concurrency Control
metadata.definition: A concurrency control approach that assumes conflicts between concurrent transactions are highly likely, and therefore prevents conflicts by acquiring locks on data items before operations are performed. This strategy prioritizes data consistency and integrity by blocking transactions until locks are released.

metadata.title: Livelock
metadata.definition: A state in concurrent systems where two or more transactions or processes continuously change their state in response to each other without making any progress towards completion. Unlike deadlock, processes are not blocked but are actively executing operations that prevent useful work, often due to overly polite or conflict-avoiding algorithms.

metadata.title: Isolation Level (Database)
metadata.definition: A property of database transactions that defines how and when changes made by one transaction become visible to other concurrent transactions. It specifies the degree to which a transaction must be isolated from the effects of other concurrent transactions, thereby controlling various concurrency phenomena like dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads.

metadata.title: Read Uncommitted Isolation Level
metadata.definition: The lowest isolation level where a transaction can read data that has been modified by other concurrent transactions but not yet committed. This allows 'dirty reads,' meaning a transaction might read data that is later rolled back, potentially leading to inconsistent results, but offers the highest concurrency.

metadata.title: Read Committed Isolation Level
metadata.definition: An isolation level where a transaction can only read data that has been committed by other transactions, thereby preventing dirty reads. metadata.title: Repeatable Read Isolation Level
metadata.definition: An isolation level that guarantees that if a transaction reads a specific row multiple times, it will always see the same data, preventing non-repeatable reads. metadata.title: Serializable Isolation Level

metadata.title: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)
metadata.definition: A standard technique for ensuring atomicity and durability in database systems, where all changes to the database are first recorded in a persistent log file before being applied to the actual data files. This ensures that in case of a crash, changes can be recovered (redo) or undone (undo) based on the log, maintaining data integrity.

metadata.title: Checkpoint (Database)
metadata.definition: A mechanism in database recovery that periodically flushes all dirty (modified) data pages from memory to disk and records the current state in the transaction log. Checkpoints reduce the amount of work required during recovery by limiting the portion of the log that needs to be scanned for redo and undo operations after a system crash.

metadata.title: Undo Log
metadata.definition: A component of a transaction log that records the old values of data items before they are modified by a transaction. In case a transaction aborts or the system crashes, the undo log is used to restore the database to its state prior to the start of the uncommitted transaction, ensuring atomicity.

metadata.title: Redo Log

This involves loading the backup data and then optionally applying transaction logs to roll forward to a more recent point in time.

metadata.title: Shadow Paging
metadata.definition: A database recovery technique that creates a shadow copy of the database's page directory during a transaction. All updates are applied to new physical pages, and only upon commit is the shadow page directory atomically swapped to become the current directory, ensuring atomicity and durability without explicit undo/redo logging.

metadata.title: Mark-Sweep Garbage Collection
metadata.definition: A two-phase garbage collection algorithm. In the 'mark' phase, the collector traverses the object graph starting from root references to identify all reachable (live) objects. In the 'sweep' phase, it then iterates through the entire heap, reclaiming memory from all unmarked (unreachable) objects and making it available for future allocations.

metadata.title: Copying Garbage Collection
metadata.definition: A garbage collection algorithm that divides the heap into two or more regions, typically called 'from-space' and 'to-space'. During collection, it copies all live objects from the 'from-space' to the 'to-space', compacting them contiguously, and then the entire 'from-space' is discarded. This method naturally prevents fragmentation.

metadata.title: Generational Garbage Collection
metadata.definition: An optimization strategy for garbage collection based on the 'weak generational hypothesis', which states that most objects die young, and old objects are likely to stay alive longer. The heap is divided into different generations (e.g., young, old), with young generations collected more frequently using faster algorithms, while older generations are collected less often using more robust but slower algorithms.

This method is relatively simple but cannot collect cyclic data structures unless augmented with other techniques.

metadata.title: Concurrency (Concept)
metadata.definition: The ability of different parts of a program or multiple programs to make progress independently, often by interleaving their execution over time on a single processor or by running truly simultaneously on multiple processors. It deals with managing multiple tasks that *appear* to run at the same time to achieve better responsiveness or throughput.

metadata.title: Process (Operating System)

metadata.title: Thread (Operating System)
metadata.definition: A lightweight unit of execution within a process, sharing the same virtual memory space, open files, and other resources as other threads in that same process. Each thread, however, has its own program counter, stack, and register set, enabling finer-grained concurrency and parallelism within a single program.

metadata.title: Green Thread
metadata.definition: A type of thread managed entirely by the user-level runtime system or library, rather than by the operating system kernel. They are often cheaper to create and context-switch than OS threads, but their scheduling is typically cooperative, and they usually cannot utilize multiple CPU cores simultaneously without explicit runtime support, mapping multiple green threads to fewer OS threads.

metadata.title: Fiber (Programming)

metadata.title: Starvation (Concurrency)
metadata.definition: A condition in concurrent programming where a particular process or thread repeatedly loses the race for a shared resource or CPU time, indefinitely preventing it from making progress. This can happen due to unfair scheduling policies, persistent contention, or biased resource allocation, effectively blocking the starved entity from ever executing.

metadata.definition: A synchronization primitive used in concurrent programming to prevent multiple threads or processes from simultaneously accessing a shared resource or critical section. Only one thread can acquire the mutex (short for mutual exclusion) at a time, ensuring exclusive access and preventing data races and inconsistent states.

Definition: A class of top-down parsers that scan the input from Left to right, producing a Leftmost derivation. An LL(k) parser uses 'k' tokens of lookahead to make parsing decisions without backtracking, suitable for grammars that are unambiguous with limited lookahead.

metadata.title: LR Parser
metadata.definition: A powerful class of bottom-up parsers that scan the input from Left to right and produce a Rightmost derivation in reverse. LR parsers can handle nearly all context-free grammars, making them widely used in practice, with variants including SLR, LALR, and GLR.

metadata.title: LALR Parser
metadata.definition: A type of bottom-up LR parser (Look-Ahead LR) that is less powerful than canonical LR but more powerful than SLR, and generates significantly smaller parsing tables than canonical LR. metadata.title: SLR Parser

metadata.title: Orthogonality (Language Design)
metadata.definition: Orthogonality in language design refers to the principle that a small set of primitive constructs can be combined in a relatively small number of ways to form the language's features, with each combination having a clear, predictable meaning. metadata.title: Linear Type
metadata.definition: A linear type is a feature in a type system that ensures a resource or value typed as 'linear' is used exactly once: it must be consumed and neither discarded nor duplicated. This property is primarily used to manage unique resources safely, prevent unwanted side effects from uncontrolled aliasing, and enable more precise control over memory or I/O operations.

metadata.title: Isomorphism (Type Theory)
metadata.definition: In type theory, two types A and B are isomorphic if there exist two functions, f: A → B and g: B → A, such that composing them in either direction yields the identity function (g(f(x)) = x and f(g(y)) = y). This signifies that the types are structurally equivalent and can be converted into each other without any loss of information.

metadata.title: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (CSMA/CD)
metadata.definition: A media access control method used in early Ethernet networks and half-duplex connections where a device first listens (carrier sense) to see if the medium is free before transmitting. If a collision is detected during transmission, the device stops, waits a random backoff time, and retries the transmission.

metadata.title: Spanning Tree Protocol (STP)
metadata.definition: An IEEE 802.1D network protocol that prevents loop formation in a switched Ethernet network by selectively blocking redundant paths. It ensures a single, loop-free logical path between all network devices, preventing broadcast storms, MAC table instability, and multiple frame copies.

metadata.title: Classful Addressing (IPv4)
metadata.definition: An outdated IPv4 addressing scheme where IP addresses were divided into predefined classes (A, B, C, D, E) based on the first few bits of the address, explicitly defining the network and host portions. This system led to inefficient address allocation and is superseded by Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR).

It addresses IPv4 address exhaustion by mapping many private customer IP addresses to a smaller pool of public addresses, often resulting in customers being behind 'double NAT'.

It helps devices on a segment reach devices on another segment without needing to know about routing or having a default gateway configured.

metadata.title: Distance-Vector Routing
metadata.definition: Distance-vector routing is a class of dynamic routing protocols where each router periodically exchanges its entire routing table with its directly connected neighbors. The best path to a destination is determined by its 'distance' (metric) and the 'vector' (next-hop router) provided by a neighbor.

metadata.title: Link-State Routing
metadata.definition: Link-state routing is a class of dynamic routing protocols where each router builds a complete topological map of the entire network. This is achieved by exchanging small 'link-state advertisements' (LSAs) with all other routers within its area, and then running Dijkstra's algorithm to calculate the shortest path to every destination.

metadata.title: OSPF Designated Router (DR)
metadata.definition: The OSPF Designated Router (DR) is a router elected on a multi-access network segment (like Ethernet) to reduce the number of adjacencies and LSA flooding. It serves as a central point for all routers on that segment to exchange link-state information, minimizing overhead.

metadata.title: EIGRP DUAL Algorithm
metadata.definition: DUAL (Diffusing Update Algorithm) is the core algorithm used by EIGRP to calculate the shortest, loop-free paths to all destinations. It maintains a topology table that includes both successor (best) routes and feasible successor (backup) routes, allowing for extremely fast convergence in the event of a primary path failure.

metadata.title: Round Trip Time (RTT)
metadata.definition: The total time it takes for a data packet to travel from a source to a destination and for an acknowledgment packet to be sent back to the source. RTT is a fundamental measure of network latency, impacting the perceived responsiveness of network applications.

metadata.title: Congestion Collapse
metadata.definition: A severe degradation of network performance that occurs when network congestion becomes so extreme that effective network throughput drops drastically, often approaching zero. It is characterized by excessive packet retransmissions, increased queueing delays, and routers dropping most incoming packets.

metadata.definition: A mechanism that allows network routers to signal impending congestion to end hosts by marking packets, rather than dropping them. This proactive notification enables ECN-aware senders to reduce their transmission rate before actual packet loss occurs, thus improving network efficiency and reducing retransmissions.

metadata.title: Random Early Detection (RED)
metadata.definition: An active queue management algorithm used in network routers to prevent congestion collapse by proactively dropping packets or marking them for Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) before queues become full. RED randomly drops packets based on a calculated average queue length and configured thresholds, aiming to signal congestion to senders early.

metadata.title: IPSec Tunnel Mode
metadata.definition: An IPSec mode where the entire original IP packet (header and payload) is encrypted and authenticated, then encapsulated within a new IP packet with a new header. This mode is typically used for connecting networks (e.g., site-to-site VPNs) or connecting remote users to a private network, as it hides the internal network topology.

metadata.title: Site-to-Site VPN
metadata.definition: A type of Virtual Private Network (VPN) that establishes a secure, encrypted connection between two or more fixed networks, such as two branch offices of an organization. Unlike remote access VPNs, individual clients do not connect directly, but rather entire networks communicate securely through VPN gateways (e.g., routers or firewalls).

metadata.title: Stateful Firewall

It remembers outgoing requests and automatically permits corresponding incoming responses, significantly enhancing security and efficiency.

metadata.definition: Quality of Service (QoS) refers to mechanisms and technologies that manage network traffic to minimize packet loss, latency, and jitter, ensuring predictable and desired performance levels for critical applications. It allows prioritizing certain types of traffic over others.

metadata.title: Traffic Shaping
metadata.definition: Traffic Shaping is a QoS mechanism that delays packets exceeding a configured rate, buffering them to smooth out traffic bursts and prevent network congestion. It aims to reduce the variability of packet arrivals and ensure traffic conforms to a specific rate.

metadata.title: Weighted Fair Queuing (WFQ)
metadata.definition: Weighted Fair Queuing (WFQ) is a flow-based queuing algorithm that provides fairness by ensuring each active traffic flow receives a proportional share of available bandwidth. It dynamically allocates bandwidth based on assigned weights or flow characteristics, preventing a single flow from monopolizing resources.

metadata.title: Class-Based Weighted Fair Queuing (CBWFQ)
metadata.definition: Class-Based Weighted Fair Queuing (CBWFQ) is an enhanced queuing mechanism that allows administrators to define custom traffic classes based on various criteria (e.g., protocol, port, IP address). Each class is then assigned a guaranteed minimum bandwidth, and excess bandwidth is shared fairly.

metadata.definition: Strict Priority Queuing (SPQ) is a basic QoS queuing algorithm where packets in a higher-priority queue are always transmitted before any packets in lower-priority queues. While ensuring immediate processing for high-priority traffic, it risks starving lower-priority traffic.

metadata.title: Label Switched Path (LSP)

metadata.title: Network Topology (Bus, Star, Ring, Mesh, Tree)

metadata.title: MPLS Traffic Engineering

metadata.title: Jitter Buffer
metadata.definition: A jitter buffer (or playout buffer) is a temporary storage area used in real-time communication systems, such as VoIP or video conferencing, to compensate for variations in packet arrival times (jitter). It collects incoming packets, holds them briefly, and then releases them at a steady rate to ensure smooth playback and prevent audio/video dropouts.

metadata.definition: Echo cancellation is a signal processing technique used in telecommunications to remove unwanted echoes from a communication path, particularly in voice calls. It identifies and subtracts the echo signal that originates from the speaker's own voice being picked up by their microphone after being played through the far-end speaker.

metadata.title: IP Multicast
metadata.definition: IP Multicast is a method of sending network traffic from a single source to multiple selected receivers simultaneously, efficiently utilizing network bandwidth. Instead of sending separate copies to each receiver (unicast) or to all devices (broadcast), multicast sends one copy to a specific group address, and network routers duplicate it only when necessary to reach all group members.

metadata.title: Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP)
metadata.definition: The Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) is a communication protocol used by hosts and adjacent routers on IPv4 networks to establish and maintain IP multicast group memberships. Hosts use IGMP to inform local routers that they want to receive multicast traffic for a particular group, and routers use IGMP to discover which groups have active members on their directly attached networks.

metadata.title: Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF)
metadata.definition: Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF) is a security and loop-prevention mechanism used in IP routing, primarily for multicast and unicast source validation. An RPF check ensures that an incoming packet arrived on the interface that would be used to send a unicast packet back to the source of that incoming packet, preventing spoofing and forwarding loops.

This spectrum enables extremely high bandwidth and data rates, crucial for enhanced mobile broadband, but is characterized by shorter range and susceptibility to physical obstructions.

metadata.title: Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC) (5G)
metadata.definition: URLLC is one of the three primary 5G service categories, focusing on providing extremely high reliability (e.g., 99.999%) and very low end-to-end latency (e.g., <1ms) for mission-critical applications. It addresses use cases where even tiny delays or failures can have severe consequences.

metadata.title: Enhanced Mobile Broadband (eMBB) (5G)
metadata.definition: eMBB is one of the three primary 5G service categories, designed to deliver significantly higher data rates, increased network capacity, and improved coverage compared to 4G technologies. Its main objective is to provide a superior mobile internet experience for consumers and enterprises.

metadata.title: Massive Machine Type Communications (mMTC) (5G)
metadata.definition: mMTC is one of the three primary 5G service categories, focused on enabling connectivity for an extremely large number of low-cost, low-power devices over a wide geographical area. These devices typically transmit small amounts of data infrequently, making power efficiency and scalability paramount.

metadata.title: Open Radio Access Network (Open RAN)
metadata.definition: Open RAN is an industry movement towards open, disaggregated, and virtualized radio access network (RAN) architectures. It advocates for open interfaces between RAN components (e.g., radio unit, distributed unit, centralized unit) to foster multi-vendor interoperability, innovation, and competition.

metadata.title: Virtual RAN (vRAN)
metadata.definition: Virtual RAN (vRAN) is a Radio Access Network (RAN) architecture that centralizes and virtualizes baseband processing functions, moving them from proprietary hardware appliances to software running on commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) servers. This allows for greater flexibility, scalability, and resource pooling compared to traditional RANs.

metadata.title: Cloud RAN (CRAN)
metadata.definition: Cloud RAN (CRAN) is an advanced architectural evolution of vRAN that centralizes baseband processing units (BBUs) into cloud-based data centers, connecting them to remote radio units (RRUs) via high-bandwidth fronthaul links. This centralization enables advanced coordination, dynamic resource allocation, and reduced operational costs.

metadata.title: Dynamic Spectrum Sharing (DSS)
metadata.definition: A technology that enables 4G (LTE) and 5G New Radio (NR) to operate simultaneously within the same frequency band by dynamically allocating spectrum resources between the two technologies based on real-time demand. DSS facilitates a smoother and faster transition to 5G coverage using existing spectrum assets.

metadata.title: Deterministic Networking (DetNet)
metadata.definition: An IETF-defined architecture that provides bounded latency, low packet loss, and high reliability over Layer 2 and Layer 3 networks, enabling time-sensitive applications to operate predictably over IP networks. DetNet often leverages TSN capabilities at Layer 2 to achieve end-to-end determinism.

metadata.title: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD)
metadata.definition: A communication method that uses principles of quantum mechanics to establish a shared, secret cryptographic key between two parties. QKD's unique property is that any attempt by an eavesdropper to intercept the key is physically detectable, thereby guaranteeing the key's security.

metadata.definition: Cryptographic algorithms designed to be secure against attacks by quantum computers, which are capable of breaking many current public-key cryptosystems like RSA and ECC. PQC aims to future-proof digital communications and data security against the advent of large-scale quantum computing.

metadata.definition: A security framework that operates on the principle 'never trust, always verify,' requiring strict identity verification and device posture assessment for every user and device attempting to access network resources. Access is granted based on the least privilege needed, irrespective of the user's location.

metadata.title: SmartNIC (Smart Network Interface Card)
metadata.definition: A SmartNIC is a Network Interface Card (NIC) with integrated programmable processing capabilities, typically incorporating an FPGA or ARM CPU, which offloads network functions from the host CPU. This acceleration frees up host resources, improves performance, and enables advanced network services directly at the server's edge.

metadata.title: Programmable Data Plane
metadata.definition: The programmable data plane refers to the ability to define and dynamically modify how network devices (like switches and routers) process and forward packets. This allows network engineers to customize forwarding logic, implement new protocols, and adapt network behavior in real-time, contrasting with traditional fixed-function hardware.

metadata.title: Internet Exchange Point (IXP)
metadata.definition: An Internet Exchange Point is a physical infrastructure where Internet service providers (ISPs), content delivery networks (CDNs), and other network operators exchange Internet traffic between their networks directly. IXPs facilitate peering relationships, reducing latency and transit costs by localizing traffic exchange.

metadata.title: Peering (Networking)
metadata.definition: Peering is a voluntary and direct interconnection between two administratively separate Internet networks for the purpose of exchanging traffic between their respective users without paying a third party. This arrangement typically reduces transit costs and often improves performance and redundancy by shortening traffic paths.

metadata.title: Transit (Networking)
metadata.definition: Transit is the service where one network pays another network (typically a larger, Tier 1 or Tier 2 ISP) to carry its traffic to the entire global Internet. Unlike peering, transit provides full access to the global routing table, allowing the buying network to reach any destination on the Internet through the selling network.

metadata.title: Anycast DNS
metadata.definition: Anycast DNS is a networking technique where multiple DNS servers, located in different geographic locations, are configured with the same IP address. Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) routing then directs client DNS requests to the topologically nearest available server, improving performance, redundancy, and DDoS mitigation.

metadata.definition: Zero-Touch Provisioning is a method that allows network devices, such as switches and routers, to automatically configure themselves upon initial power-up without requiring manual intervention. This process typically involves discovering a configuration server and downloading its operational configuration and software images.

metadata.title: Chaos Engineering (Networking)
metadata.definition: Chaos Engineering is the practice of intentionally injecting failures into a network system to proactively identify weaknesses and improve its resilience and fault tolerance. By simulating real-world issues like packet loss, latency, or link failures in a controlled environment, engineers can discover and fix problems before they impact users.

metadata.title: Network Emulation
metadata.definition: Network emulation is a technique that reproduces the behavior of a real network or specific network conditions (e.g., latency, packet loss, bandwidth limitations) within a controlled test environment. It allows applications and protocols to be tested as if they were running on the actual network, enabling realistic evaluation without needing the full physical infrastructure.

metadata.title: Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) Communication
metadata.definition: V2X Communication is a comprehensive communication system that allows vehicles to exchange information with various entities, including other vehicles (V2V), infrastructure (V2I), pedestrians (V2P), and the network (V2N). Its primary goal is to enhance road safety, improve traffic efficiency, and support autonomous driving functionalities.

metadata.title: Dedicated Short Range Communications (DSRC)

metadata.title: Cache Hit
metadata.definition: An event where the CPU requests data, and that data is found in a higher-speed cache memory level (e.g., L1, L2, L3). This results in fast access to the data, significantly improving system performance by avoiding slower main memory access.

metadata.title: Write-Through Cache
metadata.definition: A cache writing policy where data is written simultaneously to both the cache and main memory. While simpler to implement and ensuring immediate data consistency, it can be slower due to waiting for main memory write operations and increased bus traffic.

metadata.title: Write-Back Cache
metadata.definition: A cache writing policy where data is initially written only to the cache. The updated cache line is marked as "dirty," and the changes are written back to main memory only when the dirty cache line is evicted from the cache. This policy generally offers better performance by reducing main memory traffic but introduces complexity in maintaining data consistency.

metadata.title: RISC Architecture

RISC processors emphasize hardware simplicity and rely on compilers to translate high-level language code into these simple instructions, often utilizing many registers and pipelining.

metadata.title: CISC Architecture

CISC processors aim to achieve tasks in fewer lines of assembly code, but instructions can have variable lengths and take multiple clock cycles.

metadata.title: Von Neumann Architecture
metadata.definition: A computer architecture where program instructions and data are stored together in the same memory space, and share a common bus for fetching. This design simplifies memory management but can lead to the "Von Neumann bottleneck" as the CPU must alternately fetch instructions and data, potentially limiting throughput.

Instructions are broken down into stages (e.g., Fetch, Decode, Execute, Write-back), and a new instruction begins a stage as soon as the previous instruction completes that stage, much like an assembly line.

metadata.definition: A single oscillation or period of a processor's clock signal, representing the smallest unit of time in which a CPU can perform an operation. All operations within a CPU are synchronized to these cycles.

metadata.title: Cycles Per Instruction (CPI)
metadata.definition: The average number of clock cycles required to execute a single instruction on a particular processor architecture. A lower CPI indicates greater efficiency, meaning fewer clock cycles are wasted per instruction.

metadata.title: Big-endian
metadata.definition: A byte order convention in which the most significant byte (MSB) of a multi-byte data type is stored at the lowest memory address, and the least significant byte (LSB) at the highest address. This is analogous to how numbers are written from left to right.

metadata.definition: The process by which multiple devices or masters connected to a shared computer bus compete for control of the bus to perform data transfers. An arbitration mechanism ensures that only one device has exclusive access at any given time to prevent conflicts.

metadata.definition: The mechanism by which the CPU switches from executing one process or thread to another. It involves saving the current state (context) of the running task and loading the saved state of the next task to be executed.

metadata.title: Preemptive Scheduling
metadata.definition: A CPU scheduling approach where the currently executing process can be interrupted and moved to the ready state by the operating system, often due to a higher-priority process becoming ready or a time slice expiring. This ensures fairness and responsiveness by preventing a single process from monopolizing the CPU.

metadata.definition: A non-preemptive CPU scheduling algorithm where processes are executed in the order they arrive in the ready queue. Once a process starts, it runs to completion without interruption.

metadata.title: Shortest Job First (SJF) Scheduling
metadata.definition: A CPU scheduling algorithm that associates with each process the length of its next CPU burst and schedules the process with the shortest estimated burst first. SJF can be either non-preemptive or preemptive (known as Shortest Remaining Time First, SRTF), aiming to minimize average waiting time and turnaround time.

Processes are permanently assigned to a specific queue based on characteristics like process type (e.g., interactive, batch, system processes) or priority.

These systems are categorized as hard real-time (missing a deadline is catastrophic) or soft real-time (missing a deadline is undesirable but tolerable).

It involves mechanisms to control the order of execution and ensure mutual exclusion for critical sections.

metadata.title: Semaphore (Counting)
metadata.definition: A synchronization primitive that is an integer variable accessed only through two atomic operations: `wait()` (decrements the semaphore, blocking if value is zero) and `signal()` (increments the semaphore). A counting semaphore's value can range over an unrestricted domain, typically used to control access to a resource that has multiple instances.

metadata.title: Semaphore (Binary)
metadata.definition: A special case of a counting semaphore that can only take on the values 0 or 1, often used to implement mutual exclusion. It functions similarly to a mutex lock, where `wait()` decrements the semaphore (if > 0) and `signal()` increments it (if < 1), allowing only one process into a critical section at a time.

metadata.definition: Strategies employed by an operating system to resolve a deadlock situation once it has occurred, typically involving either process termination or resource preemption. The goal is to break one or more of the four necessary conditions for deadlock, allowing the system to continue operation.

metadata.definition: A fixed-size block of physical memory (RAM). Physical memory is divided into these frames, which serve as containers for pages—fixed-size blocks of a process's logical address space—when they are loaded from disk.

metadata.title: Page Table Entry (PTE)
metadata.definition: An entry within a page table that contains information about a specific page in a process's logical address space. Each PTE typically includes the physical page frame number where the page is stored, along with control bits such as valid/invalid, read/write, and dirty/referenced flags.

metadata.title: Swapping
metadata.definition: A memory management technique where an entire process or parts of it can be temporarily moved from main memory (RAM) to secondary storage (disk) and then brought back into memory later. This allows more processes to run than can fit in physical RAM simultaneously, improving multiprogramming at the cost of disk I/O.

metadata.title: Segmentation (Memory Management)
metadata.definition: A memory management scheme that views a program's logical address space as a collection of variable-sized segments, rather than a single contiguous space. Each segment corresponds to a logical unit of the program, such as code, data, stack, or a subroutine, and is mapped independently to physical memory.

metadata.title: Page Replacement Algorithm (FIFO)
metadata.definition: The First-In, First-Out (FIFO) page replacement algorithm replaces the page that has been in memory for the longest duration, irrespective of how frequently it has been accessed. It is simple to implement but can suffer from Belady's anomaly, where increasing the number of available page frames can sometimes lead to more page faults.

metadata.title: Page Replacement Algorithm (LRU)
metadata.definition: The Least Recently Used (LRU) page replacement algorithm replaces the page that has not been used for the longest period of time. It operates on the assumption that pages used recently are more likely to be used again soon, making it a good practical approximation of the optimal algorithm.

metadata.title: Page Replacement Algorithm (Optimal)
metadata.definition: The Optimal page replacement algorithm replaces the page that will not be used for the longest period of time in the future. It guarantees the lowest possible page-fault rate and serves as a theoretical benchmark, but it is impossible to implement in practice because it requires perfect foreknowledge of future page access patterns.

metadata.definition: The Least Frequently Used (LFU) page replacement algorithm replaces the page that has been used the least number of times. It maintains a count of how often each page in memory has been accessed, assuming that pages accessed less often are less likely to be needed in the future, although it may retain pages heavily used in the distant past.

metadata.definition: First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) disk scheduling services I/O requests in the exact order they arrive in the disk queue. While simple to implement, it often leads to suboptimal performance due to potentially high and erratic head movement.

metadata.title: Disk Scheduling (SCAN)
metadata.definition: The SCAN (Elevator) disk scheduling algorithm moves the disk head in one direction, servicing all requests in its path, until it reaches the end of the disk or the last request in that direction. It then reverses direction and repeats the process, resembling an elevator's movement.

metadata.title: Disk Scheduling (C-SCAN)
metadata.definition: Circular-SCAN (C-SCAN) disk scheduling is a variation of SCAN where the disk head moves in only one direction, servicing requests, and once it reaches the end, it immediately jumps back to the beginning of the disk without servicing requests on the return trip. This ensures a more uniform wait time for requests across the disk.

metadata.title: Buffering (I/O)
metadata.definition: A technique in I/O management where a temporary storage area (buffer) in memory is used to hold data during I/O transfers, effectively decoupling the producer and consumer of data. It helps to smooth out data transfer rates between devices with different speeds and reduces the number of direct I/O operations.

metadata.title: Spooling (I/O)
metadata.definition: Spooling (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line) is a technique where data from various I/O jobs are temporarily stored on a fast access storage device (like a disk) before being processed by a slower peripheral device. It allows multiple applications to 'write' to the same slow device concurrently without waiting for each other.

metadata.title: Strong Consistency
metadata.definition: Strong consistency is a consistency model where any read operation is guaranteed to return the most recently written value, and all processes observe operations in the same global order. It implies immediate visibility of updates across the entire system, ensuring that once a write is completed, all subsequent reads reflect that write.

metadata.title: Sequential Consistency
metadata.definition: Sequential consistency is a consistency model that guarantees that the result of any execution is the same as if all operations by all processors were executed in some sequential order, and the operations of each individual processor appear in that sequence in the order specified by its program. It's weaker than strong consistency but ensures all nodes see operations in the same relative order, even if not immediately after a write.

metadata.title: Mutual Exclusion (Concurrency)

metadata.title: Lock (Synchronization Primitive)
metadata.definition: A synchronization mechanism used to enforce mutual exclusion, allowing only one thread at a time to access a shared resource or critical section of code. A thread must acquire the lock before entering the critical section and release it afterward, preventing other threads from accessing the resource concurrently and ensuring data integrity.

metadata.title: Spinlock
metadata.definition: A type of lock that causes a thread trying to acquire it to simply wait in a tight loop ('spin') repeatedly checking if the lock is available. It is efficient when threads wait for very short periods, as it avoids the overhead of context switching, but can waste CPU cycles if held for longer durations due to busy-waiting.
