metadata.title: Gustafson's Law
metadata.definition: An equation that states that the speedup achieved by parallelizing a program is limited by the fraction of the program that must be executed serially, and crucially, by the scaling of the problem size with the number of processors. It suggests that if the problem size scales with the number of processors, then the speedup can be nearly linear, overcoming limitations of Amdahl's Law.

metadata.title: Producer-Consumer Problem
metadata.definition: A classic synchronization problem in concurrency where one or more 'producer' threads generate data and put it into a shared buffer, while one or more 'consumer' threads take data from the buffer and process it. The problem requires robust synchronization mechanisms to prevent buffer overflow, underflow, and race conditions, ensuring safe data exchange.

metadata.definition: An undesirable state of a system caused by the activation of a fault, where the system's internal state deviates from its specified correct behavior. An error is the manifestation of a fault, representing an incorrect value or state within the system's boundaries.

Failure is the observable outcome of an error impacting the system's external behavior and violating its service contract.

metadata.definition: The practice of duplicating critical components or functions within a system to ensure that if one component fails, there is a backup available to take over, preventing system failure. Redundancy is a core principle of fault tolerance and high availability, enhancing overall system reliability.

The primary goal is to prevent the propagation of erroneous data or states, thus ensuring data integrity and system safety, even if it means sacrificing availability.

metadata.title: Checkpointing
metadata.definition: A fault tolerance technique where the entire state of a running application or system is periodically saved to stable storage (a checkpoint) so that, in case of a failure, the system can be restored to the last valid checkpoint instead of restarting from the beginning. This reduces the amount of work lost due to a crash.

This approach ensures data consistency and limits the amount of computation lost due to the failure.

metadata.title: Heartbeat (System Monitoring)
metadata.definition: A periodic signal generated by a system or component to indicate that it is operational and responsive. Other systems or monitoring agents listen for these heartbeats; if a heartbeat is not received within a predefined interval, the sender is presumed to have failed or become unresponsive, triggering an alert or corrective action.

metadata.title: Watchdog Timer
metadata.definition: A hardware or software timer used to monitor the operation of a computer program or electronic device. It must be periodically reset (fed) by the monitored system; if the system fails to reset the timer before it expires, the watchdog triggers a predefined corrective action, such as a system reset or an interrupt, to recover from unresponsiveness.

metadata.definition: A race condition vulnerability that occurs when a system checks the state of a resource (Time-of-Check) and then uses that state later (Time-of-Use), but the state of the resource changes between these two operations. An attacker can exploit this window to create an inconsistent or malicious state, leading to unauthorized access or privilege escalation.

metadata.title: Rowhammer (Attack)
metadata.definition: A hardware-level side-channel attack that exploits a physical vulnerability in modern DRAM (Dynamic Random-Access Memory) chips, where repeatedly accessing (hammering) a row of memory can cause electrical interference that induces bit flips in physically adjacent, unaccessed 'victim' rows. Attackers can leverage these uncontrolled bit flips to gain unauthorized access or elevate privileges within a system.

metadata.title: Meltdown (Vulnerability)
metadata.definition: A hardware vulnerability affecting modern out-of-order execution CPUs, allowing unprivileged programs to read data from arbitrary kernel memory locations, including sensitive data. It exploits a race condition where speculative execution can leave traces in the CPU cache even if the instruction is later aborted due to privilege violations.

metadata.definition: A class of hardware vulnerabilities that exploit speculative execution in modern CPUs, allowing an attacker to trick a program into accessing arbitrary memory locations and leak their contents via side channels. metadata.title: RAID Level 0 (Striping)
metadata.definition: A RAID configuration that splits (stripes) data across multiple hard drives without parity or mirroring. It offers improved performance (read/write speeds) as data can be accessed simultaneously from multiple disks, but provides no data redundancy, meaning the failure of any single drive results in complete data loss.

metadata.title: RAID Level 0 (Striping)
metadata.definition: A RAID configuration that splits (stripes) data across multiple hard drives without parity or mirroring. It offers improved performance (read/write speeds) as data can be accessed simultaneously from multiple disks, but provides no data redundancy, meaning the failure of any single drive results in complete data loss.

metadata.title: RAID Level 1 (Mirroring)
metadata.definition: A RAID configuration that duplicates (mirrors) data across two or more hard drives. It provides excellent data redundancy, as the system can continue operating if one drive fails, but its usable capacity is halved (or more, depending on the number of mirrors).

metadata.title: RAID Level 5 (Striping with Parity)
metadata.definition: A RAID configuration that stripes data blocks across multiple drives and distributes parity information among all drives. It offers a good balance of performance, capacity, and data redundancy, allowing for the failure of any single drive without data loss. Recovery is performed using the distributed parity.

metadata.title: RAID Level 10 (Striping and Mirroring)
metadata.definition: Also known as RAID 1+0, this configuration combines RAID 1 (mirroring) and RAID 0 (striping). Data is first mirrored in sets, and then these mirrored sets are striped together. It offers excellent performance and high data redundancy, tolerating multiple drive failures as long as no two failed drives are from the same mirrored set.

metadata.title: Symmetric Relation
metadata.definition: A binary relation R on a set A is symmetric if, whenever an element 'a' is related to an element 'b', then 'b' is also related to 'a'. Formally, for all a, b ∈ A, if (a, b) ∈ R, then (b, a) ∈ R.

metadata.title: Transitive Relation
metadata.definition: A binary relation R on a set A is transitive if, whenever 'a' is related to 'b' and 'b' is related to 'c', then 'a' is also related to 'c'. Formally, for all a, b, c ∈ A, if (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R, then (a, c) ∈ R.

metadata.title: Equivalence Relation
metadata.definition: A binary relation R on a set A is an equivalence relation if it is simultaneously reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Equivalence relations partition a set into disjoint equivalence classes, where all elements within a class are related to each other.

metadata.title: Partial Order Relation
metadata.definition: A binary relation R on a set A is a partial order relation if it is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive. Antisymmetric means that if (a, b) ∈ R and (b, a) ∈ R, then a must equal b.

metadata.title: Total Order Relation
metadata.definition: A partial order relation R on a set A is a total order relation (or linear order) if for every pair of elements a, b ∈ A, either (a, b) ∈ R or (b, a) ∈ R. This means that every pair of elements in the set is comparable.

metadata.title: Chinese Remainder Theorem
metadata.definition: The Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) provides a unique solution to a system of linear congruences if the moduli are pairwise coprime. It states that for given integers a1, ..., ak and pairwise coprime integers n1, ..., nk, there exists a unique integer x modulo N = n1*...*nk that satisfies x ≡ ai (mod ni) for all i.

metadata.title: Group Axioms
metadata.definition: The four fundamental axioms that define a mathematical group (G, *): 1) Closure: For all a, b in G, a * b is in G. 2) Associativity: For all a, b, c in G, (a * b) * c = a * (b * c). 3) Identity Element: There exists an element e in G such that for every a in G, a * e = e * a = a. 4) Inverse Element: For every a in G, there exists an element a⁻¹ in G such that a * a⁻¹ = a⁻¹ * a = e.

metadata.title: Ring Axioms
metadata.definition: The axioms defining a mathematical ring (R, +, *): 1) (R, +) is an abelian group. 2) Multiplication is associative: (a * b) * c = a * (b * c). 3) Multiplication distributes over addition: a * (b + c) = (a * b) + (a * c) and (a + b) * c = (a * c) + (b * c).

metadata.title: Field Axioms
metadata.definition: The axioms defining a mathematical field (F, +, *): 1) (F, +, *) is a commutative ring. 2) The multiplicative identity (1) is not equal to the additive identity (0). 3) Every non-zero element 'a' in F has a multiplicative inverse a⁻¹ such that a * a⁻¹ = 1. These axioms ensure all standard arithmetic operations are well-defined.

metadata.title: Row Echelon Form
metadata.definition: Row Echelon Form (REF) is a specific structure for a matrix obtained through Gaussian elimination, where: 1) All non-zero rows are above any rows of all zeros. 2) The leading entry (pivot) of each non-zero row is 1. 3) Each leading entry is to the right of the leading entry in the row above it.

metadata.title: Reduced Row Echelon Form
metadata.definition: A matrix is in reduced row echelon form (RREF) if it satisfies four conditions: (1) all zero rows are at the bottom, (2) the leading entry (pivot) of each non-zero row is 1, (3) each pivot is to the right of the pivot in the row above it, and (4) each pivot is the only non-zero entry in its column. RREF is unique for any given matrix and is used to solve systems of linear equations and find matrix inverses.

metadata.title: Subspace (Linear Algebra)

metadata.title: Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality
metadata.definition: A fundamental inequality stating that for any two vectors x and y in an inner product space, the absolute value of their inner product is less than or equal to the product of their magnitudes (norms), i.e., |<x, y>| ≤ ||x|| ||y||. Equality holds if and only if x and y are linearly dependent.

metadata.title: Multivariable Integral (Double, Triple)
metadata.definition: A multivariable integral extends the concept of a definite integral to functions of multiple variables, typically used to compute volumes, masses, or other quantities over multi-dimensional regions. A double integral calculates volume under a surface over a 2D region, while a triple integral calculates hypervolume or mass over a 3D region.

metadata.title: Line Integral
metadata.definition: A line integral is an integral where the function to be integrated is evaluated along a curve or path in space, rather than over a region. It is commonly used to calculate work done by a force field, fluid flow circulation, or the mass of a wire with varying density.

metadata.title: Surface Integral
metadata.definition: A surface integral is an integral of a function over a surface in three-dimensional space, generalizing double integrals to curved surfaces. It is used to compute flux through a surface, total mass/charge distributed over a surface, or the total area of a parameterized surface.

metadata.title: Maclaurin Series
metadata.definition: A Maclaurin series is a special case of a Taylor series expansion of a function f(x) about x=0, representing the function as an infinite sum of terms calculated from the function's derivatives evaluated at zero. It provides a polynomial approximation of a function near the origin.

metadata.title: Lagrange Multiplier
metadata.definition: The method of Lagrange multipliers is a strategy for finding the local maxima and minima of a function subject to equality constraints. It introduces a new scalar variable (the Lagrange multiplier) for each constraint, transforming the constrained optimization problem into an unconstrained one solvable by finding critical points of an auxiliary Lagrangian function.

metadata.title: Convex Function
metadata.definition: A function `f` is convex if, for any two points `x₁` and `x₂` in its domain, the line segment connecting `(x₁, f(x₁))` and `(x₂, f(x₂))` lies entirely above or on the graph of `f`. Mathematically, `f(tx₁ + (1-t)x₂) ≤ tf(x₁) + (1-t)f(x₂)` for all `t ∈ [0, 1]`.

metadata.title: Concave Function
metadata.definition: A function `f` is concave if, for any two points `x₁` and `x₂` in its domain, the line segment connecting `(x₁, f(x₁))` and `(x₂, f(x₂))` lies entirely below or on the graph of `f`. Equivalently, `f` is concave if `-f` is convex, meaning `f(tx₁ + (1-t)x₂) ≥ tf(x₁) + (1-t)f(x₂)` for all `t ∈ [0, 1]`.

metadata.title: Strictly Convex Function
metadata.definition: A function `f` is strictly convex if it is convex and the line segment connecting any two distinct points `(x₁, f(x₁))` and `(x₂, f(x₂))` lies strictly above the graph of `f` for all interior points of the segment. Mathematically, `f(tx₁ + (1-t)x₂) < tf(x₁) + (1-t)f(x₂)` for all `t ∈ (0, 1)` and `x₁ ≠ x₂`.

metadata.title: Convex Hull
metadata.definition: The convex hull of a given set of points or objects is the smallest convex set that contains all those points or objects. Geometrically, it can be visualized as the shape formed by a rubber band stretched tightly around all the given points.

metadata.title: Jensen's Inequality
metadata.definition: Jensen's inequality is a fundamental result in convex analysis stating that for a convex function `f`, the value of the function at the average (or expected value) of a variable is less than or equal to the average of the function's values. For a concave function, the inequality is reversed: `f(E[X]) ≥ E[f(X)]`.

metadata.title: Mean Value Theorem
metadata.definition: The Mean Value Theorem states that for a function `f(x)` that is continuous on a closed interval `[a, b]` and differentiable on the open interval `(a, b)`, there exists at least one point `c` in `(a, b)` such that the instantaneous rate of change at `c` (`f'(c)`) is equal to the average rate of change over the entire interval (`(f(b) - f(a)) / (b - a)`).

metadata.title: Rolle's Theorem
metadata.definition: Rolle's Theorem is a special case of the Mean Value Theorem, stating that if a function `f(x)` is continuous on a closed interval `[a, b]`, differentiable on the open interval `(a, b)`, and `f(a) = f(b)`, then there must exist at least one point `c` in `(a, b)` where the derivative `f'(c)` is zero.

metadata.title: L'Hôpital's Rule
metadata.definition: L'Hôpital's Rule is a powerful method used to evaluate limits of indeterminate forms, specifically `0/0` or `∞/∞`. It states that if `lim (x→c) f(x) = 0` and `lim (x→c) g(x) = 0` (or both are `±∞`), then `lim (x→c) f(x)/g(x) = lim (x→c) f'(x)/g'(x)`, provided the latter limit exists.

metadata.title: Event (Probability)
metadata.definition: In probability theory, an event is a specific set of one or more outcomes from a random experiment's sample space. It is a subset of the sample space, representing a particular result or collection of results of interest.

metadata.title: Probability Measure
metadata.definition: A probability measure is a function that assigns a probability (a real number between 0 and 1, inclusive) to each event in a sample space, satisfying three axioms: non-negativity (P(A) ≥ 0), normalization (P(S) = 1 for the sample space S), and countable additivity for disjoint events.

metadata.title: Union of Events

metadata.title: Complement of an Event
metadata.definition: The complement of an event E, denoted Eᶜ or E', is the set of all outcomes in the sample space S that are not in E. The probability of the complement of an event is 1 minus the probability of the event itself (P(Eᶜ) = 1 - P(E)).

It involves using bitwise operators to set, clear, toggle, or test specific bits, often for optimization, space efficiency, or low-level control.

metadata.title: Prefix Sum Array
metadata.definition: A Prefix Sum Array (also known as a cumulative sum array) is an auxiliary data structure where each element `P[i]` stores the sum of all elements from the beginning of the original array up to index `i`. This enables efficient O(1) calculation of the sum of any subarray.

metadata.title: Difference Array
metadata.definition: A Difference Array is an auxiliary array where `D[i]` stores the difference between `A[i]` and `A[i-1]` (with `D[0] = A[0]`), allowing for range updates to the original array `A` in O(1) time. The original array can then be reconstructed by taking prefix sums of the difference array.

metadata.title: Huffman Coding
metadata.definition: Huffman Coding is a greedy algorithm for lossless data compression that builds a prefix-free binary code for a set of characters based on their frequencies of occurrence. It assigns shorter codes to more frequent characters and longer codes to less frequent ones, minimizing the total encoded length.

metadata.title: Lempel-Ziv-Welch (LZW) Compression
metadata.definition: LZW compression is a universal lossless data compression algorithm that replaces repeating sequences of data (strings) with fixed-length codes. It builds a dictionary of these sequences dynamically from the input data, making it adaptive and effective for various data types.

metadata.title: Run-Length Encoding (RLE)
metadata.definition: Run-Length Encoding (RLE) is a simple, lossless data compression technique that reduces the size of a data stream by replacing consecutive occurrences of the same data value ('runs') with a single instance of the value and a count. It is most effective for data with long sequences of identical values.

metadata.title: Garbage Collection Algorithm
metadata.definition: A Garbage Collection (GC) algorithm is an automatic memory management process that frees up memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable or used by a program. Its primary goals are to prevent memory leaks, reduce programmer burden, and improve memory efficiency.

metadata.title: Mark and Sweep (GC)
metadata.definition: Mark and Sweep is a foundational garbage collection algorithm that operates in two phases: first, it 'marks' all objects in memory that are reachable from a set of root references. Second, it 'sweeps' through the entire memory heap, reclaiming all unmarked (unreachable) objects as free space.

metadata.title: Memory Pool
metadata.definition: A memory pool is a memory management technique where a block of pre-allocated contiguous memory is set aside to fulfill allocation requests for objects of a specific type or size. This approach reduces allocation/deallocation overhead and external fragmentation, improving performance.

metadata.title: Modular Inverse
metadata.definition: For an integer 'a' and a modulus 'm', the modular inverse of 'a' (denoted a⁻¹) is an integer 'x' such that (a * x) % m = 1. It exists if and only if 'a' and 'm' are coprime (i.e., gcd(a, m) = 1). It is essential for division in modular arithmetic.

metadata.title: Tarjan's Algorithm (SCC)
metadata.definition: An efficient graph algorithm that finds the strongly connected components (SCCs) of a directed graph in linear time, O(V + E). It uses a single depth-first search (DFS) and maintains discovery times and low-link values for each node to identify SCCs.

metadata.definition: A path in a graph that visits every edge exactly once and starts and ends at the same vertex. A connected graph has an Eulerian circuit if and only if every vertex has an even degree.

metadata.title: Hamiltonian Cycle
metadata.definition: A cycle in a graph that visits every vertex exactly once, without repeating any vertex (except the start/end vertex). Unlike Eulerian circuits, there's no simple condition to determine if a graph has a Hamiltonian cycle, making it an NP-complete problem.

metadata.title: Square Root Decomposition

metadata.title: Mo's Algorithm (Offline Queries)
metadata.definition: Mo's Algorithm is an offline query processing technique that efficiently answers multiple range queries on an array by sorting them in a specific order based on square root decomposition of their ranges. This sorting minimizes the total movement of range endpoints, allowing for fast updates (typically O(1)) as the window slides.

metadata.title: Heavy-Light Decomposition (Tree)
metadata.definition: Heavy-Light Decomposition (HLD) is a technique that decomposes a tree into a set of 'heavy paths' and 'light edges', such that any path from the root to a leaf, or between any two nodes, traverses at most O(log N) heavy paths. This allows path queries and updates on trees to be processed using data structures like segment trees on linear paths.

metadata.title: Centroid Decomposition (Tree)
metadata.definition: Centroid Decomposition is a recursive tree decomposition technique where, in each step, a 'centroid' (a node whose removal divides the tree into subtrees of size at most N/2) is chosen, processed, and then the algorithm is recursively applied to the resulting smaller subtrees. This creates a centroid tree structure with logarithmic depth.

metadata.title: Li Chao Tree (Convex Hull Trick)
metadata.definition: A Li Chao Tree is a specialized data structure, often implemented as a segment tree or implicit binary search tree, used to maintain a set of lines and efficiently query for the minimum (or maximum) y-coordinate among all lines at a given x-coordinate. It's particularly useful for dynamic Convex Hull Trick problems where lines can be added online.

metadata.title: Suffix Automaton
metadata.definition: A Suffix Automaton is a powerful directed acyclic graph (DAG) that represents all distinct substrings of a given string in a compact and efficient manner. It contains N states and at most 3N-4 edges for a string of length N, allowing for fast substring-related queries.

metadata.definition: Segment Tree Lazy Propagation is an optimization technique for segment trees that allows range updates (e.g., adding a value to all elements in a range or setting them to a new value) to be performed efficiently in O(log N) time. It works by deferring the application of updates to child nodes until those nodes are actually visited for a query or another update.

It is commonly used to solve linear recurrence relations or count paths in graphs.

metadata.definition: Probabilistic Counting refers to a class of algorithms that estimate the number of distinct elements (cardinality) in a large multiset or data stream using probabilistic methods. These algorithms typically involve hashing and tracking properties of hash values (like leading zeros or minimums) to provide approximate counts with high accuracy and low memory footprint.

It works by converting large sets into small, fixed-size 'signatures' (min-hash values) such that the similarity of these signatures approximates the Jaccard similarity of the original sets.

metadata.title: Residual Graph (Max Flow)
metadata.definition: For a given flow network and a current flow, the residual graph represents the 'remaining capacity' in the network, indicating how much more flow can be sent and how much flow can be 'returned'. For every edge (u,v) with capacity c and flow f, it contains a forward edge (u,v) with capacity c-f and a backward edge (v,u) with capacity f.

metadata.title: Adversary Argument (Lower Bound)
metadata.definition: An Adversary Argument is a technique used to establish theoretical lower bounds on the computational complexity of problems. It posits an 'adversary' who makes choices during an algorithm's execution that always force the algorithm to perform the maximum possible number of operations, thus proving a minimum complexity for any algorithm solving that problem.

metadata.definition: CPU cache effects describe how an algorithm's memory access patterns influence its performance due to the CPU's hierarchical cache system. Algorithms that exhibit good data locality, meaning they access data that is already in cache or near recently accessed data, typically perform much faster by reducing cache misses.

metadata.title: False Sharing (Concurrency)
metadata.definition: False sharing is a performance degradation issue in concurrent programming where independent data items, accessed by different CPUs, happen to reside within the same cache line. When one CPU modifies its data, the entire shared cache line is invalidated for other CPUs, causing unnecessary cache coherence traffic and reloads, even though the data items themselves are unrelated.

metadata.title: Lock-Free Data Structure
metadata.definition: A lock-free data structure is a concurrent data structure that guarantees system-wide progress: at least one thread attempting an operation will complete it in a finite number of steps, even if other threads are arbitrarily delayed or crash. It achieves concurrency without using traditional locks, typically relying on atomic operations like Compare-and-Swap (CAS).

This holds true regardless of the execution speed or even failures of other threads, thus preventing starvation and ensuring maximum robustness.

metadata.title: Read-Copy-Update (RCU)
metadata.definition: Read-Copy-Update (RCU) is a synchronization mechanism optimized for data structures that are frequently read but rarely updated. It allows concurrent reads without locking, while updates are performed by creating a new copy of the data, modifying the copy, atomically swapping pointers to the new version, and then deferring the reclamation of the old version until all active readers have completed.

metadata.title: Transactional Memory
metadata.definition: Transactional Memory (TM) is a concurrency control mechanism that allows a sequence of memory operations to be executed atomically as a single transaction. If a conflict occurs with another transaction (e.g., read-write conflicts), the transaction is rolled back and retried, simplifying concurrent programming by abstracting explicit locking.

metadata.title: MapReduce (Big Data)

It involves two main phases: a 'Map' phase that processes input data into intermediate key-value pairs, and a 'Reduce' phase that aggregates these intermediate values based on their keys to produce the final output.

metadata.definition: The Hilbert curve is a continuous fractal space-filling curve that maps a multi-dimensional space into a one-dimensional space while attempting to preserve locality. Points that are close in the original multi-dimensional space tend to remain close along the one-dimensional Hilbert curve, making it highly effective for spatial indexing and optimizing data access patterns.

metadata.title: Radix Tree (Patricia Trie)
metadata.definition: A Radix Tree, also known as a Patricia Trie or compact prefix tree, is an optimized trie data structure where nodes with only one child are merged with their child. This compression strategy reduces the number of nodes in sparse tries by representing common prefixes as single edges, making it highly efficient for storing and searching strings with shared prefixes.

metadata.title: X-Fast Trie
metadata.definition: An X-Fast Trie is a dictionary data structure that combines a Patricia trie with hash tables to achieve O(log log U) worst-case time for search, insert, and delete operations, where U is the size of the universe of possible keys. It is particularly efficient when the universe of keys is very large, but the number of actual stored elements is much smaller.

metadata.title: Scapegoat Tree
metadata.definition: A Scapegoat Tree is a self-balancing binary search tree that maintains balance by rebuilding entire subtrees when an imbalance factor exceeds a predefined threshold, rather than using rotations. It offers amortized O(log N) time for insertions and deletions, distinguishing itself by its 'lazy' balancing approach and potentially simpler implementation compared to rotation-based trees.

metadata.title: Karatsuba Algorithm (Multiplication)
metadata.definition: A fast multiplication algorithm that reduces the number of single-digit products required to multiply two n-digit numbers by using a divide-and-conquer approach. It achieves an asymptotic complexity of O(n^log2(3)) ≈ O(n^1.58), which is faster than the traditional O(n^2) long multiplication for sufficiently large numbers.

metadata.title: Strassen's Algorithm (Matrix Multiplication)
metadata.definition: A recursive algorithm for matrix multiplication that achieves a lower asymptotic complexity than the standard O(N^3) algorithm. By performing 7 multiplications instead of 8 for 2x2 matrices and then applying this recursively, it achieves a complexity of O(N^log2(7)) ≈ O(N^2.807) for N x N matrices.

metadata.title: Pollard's Rho Algorithm (Factorization)
metadata.definition: A probabilistic integer factorization algorithm designed to find small prime factors of a composite number. It works by finding cycles in a sequence generated by a pseudo-random function modulo the number to be factored, exploiting the Birthday Paradox to efficiently find factors.

metadata.title: Mutex (Concurrency)
metadata.definition: A synchronization primitive that provides mutual exclusion, ensuring that only one thread can access a critical section of code or a shared resource at any given time. It acts as a lock that a thread acquires before entering the critical section and releases upon exiting, preventing race conditions.

metadata.title: Semaphore (Concurrency)
metadata.definition: A synchronization primitive that controls access to a limited pool of resources, allowing a specified number of threads to access a resource concurrently. It maintains an internal counter, which is decremented when a thread acquires a resource (P operation) and incremented when released (V operation), blocking threads if the count reaches zero.

metadata.title: Livelock (Concurrency)
metadata.definition: A concurrency problem where two or more threads repeatedly change their state in response to each other, but without making any progress towards completing their respective tasks. Unlike deadlock, threads are not blocked but are actively 'busy-waiting' and reacting to each other in a loop, preventing useful work.

metadata.title: Linearizability (Concurrency)
metadata.definition: A strong correctness condition for concurrent objects, guaranteeing that operations appear to take effect instantaneously at some point between their invocation and response times. It ensures that concurrent operations behave as if they were executed sequentially, respecting the real-time ordering of non-overlapping operations.

metadata.title: Tree Decomposition (Graph)
metadata.definition: A representation of a graph as a tree structure, where each node of the tree (called a bag) corresponds to a subset of the original graph's vertices. It satisfies properties that relate the connectivity of the original graph to paths in the tree, allowing many NP-hard problems on graphs to be solved in polynomial time on graphs with small treewidth.

metadata.title: Kuratowski's Theorem (Planar Graphs)
metadata.definition: A fundamental theorem in graph theory that provides a necessary and sufficient condition for a graph to be planar. It states that a finite graph is planar if and only if it does not contain a subgraph that is a subdivision of K5 (the complete graph on 5 vertices) or K3,3 (the complete bipartite graph on 3 + 3 vertices).

metadata.definition: Risk Acceptance is a risk treatment strategy where an organization consciously decides to tolerate the potential consequences of a specific risk without implementing additional controls. This decision is typically made when the cost of mitigation outweighs the potential impact, or the likelihood of the risk is deemed acceptably low.

metadata.title: Bell-LaPadula Model
metadata.definition: The Bell-LaPadula Model is a formal state machine model for enforcing confidentiality in multi-level security systems. It operates under two primary rules: the 'Simple Security Property' (no read up) preventing subjects from reading objects at a higher security level, and the '*-property' (no write down) preventing subjects from writing to objects at a lower security level.

metadata.title: Block Cipher
metadata.definition: A Block Cipher is a symmetric-key encryption algorithm that operates on fixed-size blocks of plaintext, transforming them into ciphertext blocks of the same size using a secret key. Each block is processed as a whole, either independently or in a chained manner, making it suitable for encrypting large amounts of data.

metadata.title: Stream Cipher
metadata.definition: A Stream Cipher is a symmetric-key encryption algorithm that encrypts plaintext one bit or one byte at a time, continuously generating a pseudo-random keystream. This keystream is then combined with the plaintext, typically using an XOR operation, to produce ciphertext, making it efficient for real-time communication.

metadata.title: RC4
metadata.definition: RC4 (Rivest Cipher 4) is a widely-used and fast stream cipher designed by Ron Rivest. It generates a pseudo-random keystream based on a secret key, which is then XORed with the plaintext to create ciphertext; however, due to several identified vulnerabilities, particularly with weak keys and non-random nonces, it is now considered cryptographically insecure for most applications and has been deprecated.

It allows secure communication over an insecure channel but typically results in ciphertext that is twice the size of the plaintext.

metadata.title: Cryptographic Hash Function
metadata.definition: A Cryptographic Hash Function is a mathematical algorithm that takes an input of arbitrary size (message) and returns a fixed-size bit string, called a hash value or message digest. It possesses properties like collision resistance, pre-image resistance, and second pre-image resistance, making it computationally infeasible to reverse or find two different inputs that produce the same hash, thereby ensuring data integrity and authenticity.

metadata.title: MD5

While historically popular for verifying data integrity, it is now considered cryptographically broken due to known and exploitable collision vulnerabilities, making it unsuitable for security-critical applications like digital signatures or SSL certificates.

It provides the same output sizes as SHA-2 (224, 256, 384, 512 bits) but uses a different internal sponge construction, offering a distinct and potentially more secure alternative to SHA-2, particularly as a defense against future cryptanalytic breaks.

metadata.title: HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code)
metadata.definition: HMAC is a specific type of Message Authentication Code (MAC) constructed using a cryptographic hash function and a secret cryptographic key. It is used to simultaneously verify both the data integrity and the authenticity of a message, protecting against both accidental alteration and malicious tampering, provided the key is known only to the sender and intended receiver.

metadata.title: Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA)
metadata.definition: The Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) is a Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) for digital signatures, based on the mathematical properties of discrete logarithms. It allows for the authentication of the sender's identity and the integrity of a message, providing non-repudiation, but unlike RSA, it is used exclusively for signing and cannot be used for encryption.

metadata.title: RSA Digital Signatures
metadata.definition: RSA Digital Signatures are a digital signature scheme based on the RSA cryptosystem, leveraging the computational difficulty of factoring large numbers. A sender signs a message using their private key, and anyone with the corresponding public key can verify the signature, thus providing authenticity, integrity, and non-repudiation for the message.

metadata.title: Perfect Forward Secrecy
metadata.definition: Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS), also known as forward secrecy, is a property of a key agreement protocol that ensures compromise of long-term secret keys does not compromise past session keys. Each session key is ephemeral and generated independently, preventing decryption of previously recorded traffic.

metadata.title: Zero-Knowledge Proof
metadata.definition: A Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) is a method by which one party (the prover) can prove to another party (the verifier) that they know a certain piece of information, without revealing any details about that information itself. It ensures the verifier learns nothing beyond the fact that the prover possesses the knowledge.

Its most prominent application, Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), allows for information-theoretically secure key exchange, where eavesdropping is physically detectable.

metadata.title: Cipher Block Chaining (CBC)
metadata.definition: Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) is a mode of operation for block ciphers where each block of plaintext is XORed with the previous ciphertext block before being encrypted. This chaining mechanism makes the ciphertext dependent on all preceding plaintext blocks, enhancing security compared to ECB, and requires an Initialization Vector (IV).

metadata.title: Counter Mode (CTR)
metadata.definition: Counter Mode (CTR) is a block cipher mode of operation that effectively turns a block cipher into a stream cipher. It encrypts a sequential counter value, which is then XORed with the plaintext to produce ciphertext, allowing for parallel encryption/decryption and direct access to any block.

metadata.title: Electronic Codebook (ECB)
metadata.definition: Electronic Codebook (ECB) is the simplest mode of operation for block ciphers, where each block of plaintext is encrypted independently using the same cryptographic key. This mode is generally insecure for data larger than one block because identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks, revealing patterns and making it unsuitable for most applications.

metadata.title: Output Feedback Mode (OFB)
metadata.definition: Output Feedback Mode (OFB) is a block cipher mode of operation that turns a block cipher into a synchronous stream cipher. It generates a keystream by repeatedly encrypting an Initialization Vector (IV), and this keystream is then XORed with the plaintext to produce ciphertext. OFB's keystream generation is independent of the plaintext or ciphertext, making it susceptible to certain types of attacks if the IV is reused.

metadata.title: Stored XSS

metadata.definition: An attack that tricks a web browser into sending an authenticated request to a vulnerable web application, which the user is currently logged into. The attacker crafts a malicious request (e.g., a money transfer) and embeds it on a site they control, relying on the victim's browser automatically sending session cookies.

This technique is crucial for understanding the state of a system at a specific point in time, especially in live system analysis or post-mortem investigations.

metadata.definition: Process isolation is a security principle and mechanism that ensures processes running on a system operate independently of each other, preventing one process from accessing or interfering with the memory, resources, or execution of another without explicit permission. This containment limits the potential impact or 'blast radius' of a compromised process.

metadata.definition: A Secure Enclave is a hardware-based secure subsystem within a System-on-Chip (SoC) that provides a separate, isolated execution environment for processing sensitive data, even if the main processor or operating system is compromised. It ensures the confidentiality and integrity of code and data running within its protected memory regions.

metadata.title: Trusted Execution Environment (TEE)
metadata.definition: A Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) is a secure area inside a main processor that guarantees code and data loaded inside it are protected with respect to confidentiality and integrity. It provides a level of security above the richness of the OS but below the fully fledged isolation of a hypervisor, typically by leveraging hardware features to isolate a small trusted OS and its applications.

metadata.title: Intel SGX
metadata.definition: Intel Software Guard Extensions (SGX) is a set of security features built into some Intel CPUs that allows user-level code to allocate private regions of memory, called enclaves, that are protected from other processes, including the OS, hypervisor, and even BIOS. It aims to protect selected code and data from disclosure or modification, even on a compromised platform.

metadata.title: ARM TrustZone
metadata.definition: ARM TrustZone is a security extension for ARM processors that creates two separate execution environments, a 'Secure World' and a 'Normal World', sharing the same processor core. The Secure World hosts a small trusted OS and applications, providing a hardware-isolated environment for critical computations and data, while the Normal World runs the main operating system.

metadata.title: Shared Responsibility Model (Cloud)
metadata.definition: The Shared Responsibility Model is a framework that delineates the security responsibilities between a cloud service provider (CSP) and its customers. The CSP is generally responsible for the security *of* the cloud (infrastructure, physical facilities, etc.), while the customer is responsible for security *in* the cloud (data, applications, network configuration, etc.), with the exact division varying by service model (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS).

Under the shared responsibility model, customers are largely responsible for securing operating systems, applications, network configurations, and data within their provisioned resources.

It implies that data stored in a particular nation's jurisdiction is exclusively governed by that nation's legal framework, even if accessed from elsewhere.

metadata.title: Cloud Data Encryption
metadata.definition: Cloud data encryption is the process of transforming data stored or transmitted in cloud environments into an unreadable format to protect its confidentiality. This typically includes encryption at rest for stored data and encryption in transit for data moving across networks.

metadata.title: Container Registry Security
metadata.definition: Container registry security involves protecting the integrity and confidentiality of container images stored in a registry, as well as controlling access to these images. Key aspects include scanning images for vulnerabilities, signing images to ensure authenticity, and managing permissions for image push/pull operations.

metadata.title: Kubernetes Security

metadata.title: Data Encryption in Use
metadata.definition: Data encryption in use protects data while it is being actively processed or computed by an application or system. This is traditionally the most challenging state of data to protect, as the data must often be unencrypted for computation, but new techniques like homomorphic encryption or confidential computing aim to address this.

metadata.title: Data Minimization
metadata.definition: Data minimization is the principle of collecting, processing, and storing only the absolute minimum amount of personal data necessary to achieve a specified purpose. It reduces the scope of potential data breaches and enhances privacy by limiting the exposure of sensitive information.

metadata.definition: Secure data destruction is the process of permanently and irretrievably eliminating data from storage media to prevent unauthorized recovery and access. This goes beyond simple deletion, employing methods like overwriting, degaussing, or physical destruction to ensure data cannot be reconstructed.

metadata.title: Watermarking (Digital)
metadata.definition: Digital watermarking involves embedding hidden information, often copyright or ownership details, directly into a digital medium such as an image, audio, or video file. This embedded data is robust to common transformations and undetectable without a specific decoder, primarily used for copyright protection, source tracking, and tamper detection.

metadata.title: Steganography
metadata.definition: Steganography is the practice of concealing a message within another message or a physical object, in such a way that the presence or contents of the hidden message are not readily apparent. Its goal is to achieve covert communication by making the secret message indistinguishable from ordinary data.

metadata.title: Authentication Factor
metadata.definition: An authentication factor is a distinct category of information or characteristic used to verify an individual's identity during an authentication process. These factors typically fall into three main types: something you know (knowledge), something you have (possession), or something you are (inherence).

metadata.title: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
metadata.definition: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) is a security system that requires users to provide two or more distinct authentication factors from different categories to verify their identity. By combining knowledge, possession, or inherence factors, MFA significantly enhances security, making it much harder for unauthorized users to gain access.

metadata.title: Two-Factor Authentication (2FA)
metadata.definition: Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) is a specific type of Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) that requires exactly two distinct authentication factors to verify a user's identity. It commonly combines a knowledge factor, like a password, with a possession factor, such as a smartphone or security token, to provide enhanced security.

metadata.title: Single Sign-On (SSO)
metadata.definition: Single Sign-On (SSO) is an authentication scheme that enables a user to log in with a single set of credentials to multiple independent software systems within a given session. SSO streamlines the user experience by eliminating the need to re-enter credentials for each application and simplifies identity management for administrators.

metadata.definition: Biometric authentication is a security process that verifies a user's identity by analyzing unique biological or behavioral characteristics. This method relies on 'something you are' to provide a highly secure and often convenient way to authenticate users, reducing reliance on passwords.

metadata.title: Password Authentication
metadata.definition: Password authentication is a widely used method where a user proves their identity by providing a secret string of characters (password) that only they should know. This process relies on the 'something you know' authentication factor, comparing the entered password against a stored, usually hashed, version.

metadata.title: Certificate-based Authentication
metadata.definition: Certificate-based authentication is an authentication method where a user or device proves their identity by presenting a digital certificate, which is cryptographically signed by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA). This method leverages asymmetric cryptography to establish trust and verify authenticity, often as a strong alternative to traditional passwords.

It is primarily used to enable web-based Single Sign-On (SSO) in federated identity environments, allowing users to authenticate once and access multiple services.

metadata.definition: OAuth (Open Authorization) is an open standard for access delegation, widely used as a way for users to grant third-party websites or applications access to their information on other websites without sharing their passwords. metadata.title: OpenID Connect Protocol
metadata.definition: OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an authentication layer built on top of the OAuth 2.0 framework, enabling clients to verify the identity of the end-user based on authentication performed by an authorization server. It provides a simple, identity layer that allows clients to obtain basic profile information about the end-user, often used for Single Sign-On (SSO).

metadata.definition: FIDO U2F is an open authentication standard that strengthens and simplifies two-factor authentication (2FA) using specialized USB, NFC, or Bluetooth security devices. It promotes strong password hygiene by allowing users to create complex, unique passwords for every online account and securely retrieve them when needed, often via browser extensions or desktop applications.

metadata.title: Identity Governance and Administration (IGA)
metadata.definition: Identity Governance and Administration (IGA) is a comprehensive framework that manages digital identities and access rights across an organization's IT landscape. IGA solutions streamline identity lifecycle management, automate access provisioning, enforce policy, and facilitate access certification to ensure compliance, reduce risk, and improve operational efficiency.

metadata.title: Privileged Access Management (PAM)
metadata.definition: Privileged Access Management (PAM) is a security strategy and set of technologies designed to manage, control, and monitor highly sensitive accounts and access rights within an IT environment. PAM focuses on accounts with elevated permissions, such as administrator or root accounts, to prevent insider threats, mitigate the impact of external attacks, and achieve regulatory compliance.

metadata.title: Active Directory Security
metadata.definition: Active Directory (AD) Security encompasses the practices, configurations, and tools used to protect Microsoft Active Directory from unauthorized access, compromise, and abuse. Securing AD is critical because it serves as the primary identity store and authentication service for most Windows-based enterprise networks, controlling access to critical resources and applications.

metadata.title: Identity Federation
metadata.definition: Identity Federation is a system or agreement that allows a user's digital identity and attributes to be shared across multiple, independent security domains or organizations. This enables seamless Single Sign-On (SSO) and simplified access to resources hosted by different services, establishing trust relationships between identity providers and service providers without redundant credential management.

metadata.title: Identity Deprovisioning
metadata.definition: Identity deprovisioning is the systematic process of revoking and removing a user's access rights and accounts across all organizational systems when their role changes, they leave the organization, or their access is no longer required. This critical security measure prevents unauthorized access by former personnel or those whose privileges have changed.

metadata.title: Credential Stuffing
metadata.definition: Credential stuffing is a cyberattack where threat actors use lists of stolen usernames and passwords (often obtained from data breaches) to gain unauthorized access to other unrelated online services. It exploits the common practice of users reusing the same credentials across multiple websites.

metadata.title: Brute Force Attack (Passwords)
metadata.definition: A brute force attack is a trial-and-error method used by attackers to guess credentials, cryptographic keys, or encrypted data by systematically trying every possible combination of characters. These attacks are typically automated and can be very time-consuming but effective against weak or short passwords.

metadata.title: Dictionary Attack (Passwords)
metadata.definition: A dictionary attack is a type of brute force attack that attempts to guess a password by trying a pre-compiled list of common words, phrases, and previously compromised passwords. This method exploits the human tendency to choose easily memorable and weak passwords.

metadata.title: Rainbow Table Attack (Passwords)
metadata.definition: A rainbow table attack is an attack technique used to crack hashed passwords more efficiently than a traditional brute-force attack by employing precomputed tables of hashes for a large number of potential passwords. It sacrifices storage space for computation time, enabling rapid reversal of hashes to their original plaintext passwords without having to recompute each hash individually.

metadata.title: Incident Containment
metadata.definition: Incident containment is the phase of incident response focused on limiting the scope and impact of a security incident to prevent further damage, unauthorized access, or spread of the attack. This often involves isolating affected systems, networks, or accounts.

metadata.definition: Incident eradication is the phase of incident response focused on removing the root cause of the incident and any remnants of the attack from affected systems and networks. metadata.title: Disk Forensics
metadata.definition: Disk forensics is a specialized branch of digital forensics focused on the acquisition, preservation, and analysis of data stored on computer hard drives, solid-state drives, and other storage media. Its goal is to uncover hidden, deleted, or otherwise unobservable information relevant to an investigation without altering the original evidence.

metadata.title: Chain of Custody (Forensics)
metadata.definition: The Chain of Custody in forensics refers to a documented, unbroken chronological record of the possession, handling, transfer, analysis, and disposition of physical or electronic evidence. Maintaining a strict chain of custody is crucial to ensure the integrity, authenticity, and legal admissibility of evidence in legal proceedings.

metadata.title: Indicators of Attack (IoA)
metadata.definition: Indicators of Attack (IoAs) are forensic artifacts or patterns of behavior that reveal an ongoing malicious attempt to compromise a system or network, focusing on the attacker's tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) rather than just known bad files or IPs. Unlike Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) which are reactive, IoAs are proactive signals that indicate an attack is in progress, allowing for early detection and intervention. They are typically behavioral and context-rich, providing insights into the attacker's objectives and methods.

metadata.title: Adversary Emulation
metadata.definition: Adversary emulation is a cybersecurity testing methodology that simulates the actions of a specific, known threat actor or group by replicating their tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). This approach aims to provide a realistic assessment of an organization's security posture and its ability to detect, prevent, and respond to sophisticated real-world attacks. It goes beyond generic vulnerability scanning or penetration testing by focusing on how a specific adversary would operate.

metadata.title: Incident Playbook
metadata.definition: An incident playbook is a documented, step-by-step guide outlining predefined procedures and actions to be taken by an organization in response to specific types of cybersecurity incidents. Playbooks help minimize damage, reduce recovery time, and improve overall incident management maturity.

metadata.title: Digital Forensics Readiness

metadata.title: Spyware
metadata.definition: Spyware is a type of malicious software designed to secretly gather information about a person or organization and relay it to an unauthorized third party, without the user's knowledge or consent. It typically monitors user activities, collects personal data, and can install additional harmful software. The collected information can include browsing history, personal files, credentials, and keystrokes.

metadata.title: Adware
metadata.definition: Adware is software that automatically displays or downloads unwanted advertisements, often in the form of pop-ups, banners, or redirecting browser traffic to specific websites. While some adware may be benign, many forms are considered malicious as they can track user browsing habits, slow down system performance, and sometimes act as a conduit for installing other malware. It typically arrives bundled with legitimate software or via drive-by downloads.

metadata.title: Botnet
metadata.definition: A botnet is a network of compromised computer systems, often referred to as 'bots' or 'zombies,' that are controlled by a single attacker or 'bot-herder' without the knowledge of their owners. These compromised devices, which can include PCs, servers, and IoT devices, are typically used to perform coordinated malicious tasks on a large scale, such as launching Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks, sending spam, or distributing malware. The bot-herder uses a command-and-control (C2) server to direct the botnet.

metadata.title: Keylogger
metadata.definition: A keylogger is a type of surveillance technology used to record every keystroke made on a specific computer or mobile device. These can be implemented as hardware devices, software programs, or even within web browsers, operating covertly to capture sensitive information like usernames, passwords, credit card numbers, and other personal data. Keyloggers are often used by attackers to steal credentials or spy on users.

metadata.title: Backdoor
metadata.definition: A backdoor is a covert method of bypassing normal authentication or encryption to gain unauthorized, remote access to a computer system, application, or network. It is often created intentionally by developers for maintenance purposes but can also be inserted maliciously by attackers or malware to maintain persistent access. Backdoors allow attackers to control or access a system without being detected by standard security protocols.

metadata.title: Fileless Malware
metadata.definition: Fileless malware is a sophisticated type of malicious software that operates entirely in computer memory, without writing any files to disk, making it extremely difficult to detect by traditional signature-based antivirus solutions. Instead, it leverages legitimate system tools, built-in operating system processes, and memory-resident techniques to execute its payload and persist across reboots. This technique significantly reduces the attack's footprint and improves stealth.

metadata.title: Exploit Kit
metadata.definition: An exploit kit is a software package designed to automate the process of exploiting known vulnerabilities in client-side software, typically web browsers and their plugins (like Adobe Flash, Java, or Acrobat Reader). Attackers use exploit kits by driving traffic to malicious web pages hosting the kit, which then probes the visitor's system for vulnerable software. If a vulnerability is found, the kit delivers a payload, often malware, to compromise the system without user interaction.

metadata.title: Zero-Day Exploit
metadata.definition: A zero-day exploit is a cyberattack that takes advantage of a software vulnerability that is unknown to the software vendor or public, meaning there is no existing patch or workaround available. The term 'zero-day' refers to the fact that the vendor has had zero days to fix the vulnerability once it's discovered and exploited. These exploits are highly prized by attackers due to their effectiveness and difficulty of detection, often used in targeted attacks by sophisticated adversaries.

metadata.title: Denial of Service (DoS)
metadata.definition: A Denial of Service (DoS) attack is a cyberattack designed to make a machine or network resource unavailable to its intended users by temporarily or indefinitely disrupting services of a host connected to the Internet. DoS attacks typically overwhelm the target with a flood of traffic or requests, or by exploiting a vulnerability that causes the system to crash. The goal is to deny legitimate users access to information or services.

metadata.title: Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS)
metadata.definition: A Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack is a more powerful and complex form of DoS attack that uses multiple compromised computer systems as sources of attack traffic. These 'botnet' devices simultaneously target a single victim, overwhelming the target's network, server, or application with a massive flood of legitimate-looking requests or malicious data. DDoS attacks are harder to mitigate due to their distributed nature and high volume, making it difficult to distinguish malicious traffic from legitimate user requests.

metadata.title: Social Engineering
metadata.definition: Social engineering is a manipulation technique that exploits human psychology and trust to trick individuals into divulging confidential information or performing actions that benefit an attacker. It relies on psychological tactics rather than technical hacking, leveraging deception, persuasion, and impersonation to bypass security measures. Common motives include gaining unauthorized access, stealing data, or financial fraud.

metadata.title: Spear Phishing
metadata.definition: Spear phishing is a highly targeted form of phishing attack where an attacker sends a fraudulent email or electronic message to a specific individual, organization, or business, often appearing to be from a trusted sender. Unlike generic phishing, spear phishing messages are meticulously crafted using specific information about the target, gleaned from public or stolen sources, to make the communication seem legitimate and increase the likelihood of success. The goal is typically to steal sensitive data, deploy malware, or gain unauthorized access.

metadata.title: Whaling (Phishing)
metadata.definition: Whaling is a highly specific type of spear phishing attack that targets high-profile individuals within an organization, such as senior executives, CEOs, or high-level managers. The attackers often pose as a superior or another trusted authority to trick the victim into performing critical actions like authorizing large financial transfers, revealing sensitive company information, or granting access to critical systems. Due to the victim's position, the potential impact of a successful whaling attack can be severe.

metadata.title: Vishing
metadata.definition: Vishing, a portmanteau of 'voice' and 'phishing,' is a form of social engineering attack that uses voice communication, typically over the phone, to trick individuals into revealing personal information or performing actions. Attackers often impersonate trusted entities like banks, government agencies, or tech support to gain the victim's trust and manipulate them. The goal is usually to steal credentials, financial data, or induce monetary transfers.

metadata.title: Smishing
metadata.definition: Smishing, a portmanteau of 'SMS' and 'phishing,' is a social engineering attack that uses text messages (SMS) to trick victims into clicking malicious links, downloading malware, or divulging sensitive personal information. Attackers typically send messages that appear to be from legitimate sources like banks, delivery services, or government agencies, often creating a sense of urgency or offering an enticing reward to prompt immediate action. The goal is usually to steal credentials, financial information, or install malicious software.

metadata.title: Baiting (Social Engineering)
metadata.definition: Baiting is a social engineering technique where an attacker offers something enticing, a 'bait,' to lure a victim into compromising their security or disclosing information. The bait often appeals to curiosity or greed and typically involves physical media infected with malware or a deceptive online offer. Once the victim takes the bait, their system may be compromised, or their credentials stolen.

metadata.definition: Pretexting is a form of social engineering where an attacker creates a fabricated scenario or false identity (a 'pretext') to manipulate a victim into divulging sensitive information or performing an action beneficial to the attacker. The attacker uses this deception to build trust and bypass security protocols.

metadata.title: Tailgating
metadata.definition: Tailgating, also known as piggybacking, is a physical security breach where an unauthorized individual gains access to a restricted area by closely following an authorized person through a controlled entry point, often without the authorized person's explicit consent or knowledge.

metadata.title: Shoulder Surfing
metadata.definition: Shoulder surfing is the act of obtaining sensitive information by visually observing a victim's private actions, such as their screen, keyboard, or physical documents, often from an advantageous position in public or semi-public spaces.

metadata.title: Watering Hole Attack
metadata.definition: A watering hole attack is a type of cyberattack where an attacker identifies and infects a website frequently visited by a specific target group, such as employees of a particular company or members of an industry, with the goal of compromising members of that group when they visit the site.

metadata.title: Man-in-the-Middle Attack (MITM)
metadata.definition: A Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attack is a form of cyberattack where an attacker secretly intercepts, relays, and potentially alters communication between two parties who believe they are communicating directly. The attacker positions themselves in the communication path, gaining full control over the information exchanged.

metadata.title: Man-in-the-Browser Attack (MITB)
metadata.definition: A Man-in-the-Browser (MITB) attack is a type of Man-in-the-Middle attack specifically targeting a web browser, typically through a Trojan horse or malicious browser extension. The malware infects the browser, allowing the attacker to intercept, modify, or insert data directly within the victim's browser session before it is sent to the web server or displayed to the user.

metadata.title: Supply Chain Attack
metadata.definition: A supply chain attack is a cyberattack that targets less secure elements in an organization's supply chain to gain unauthorized access to the main target. This typically involves tampering with legitimate software, hardware, or third-party services before they reach the end user, introducing vulnerabilities or backdoors.

metadata.title: Insider Threat
metadata.definition: An insider threat is a security risk that originates from within the targeted organization, typically from current or former employees, contractors, or business partners who have legitimate access to systems, data, or physical premises. These threats can be malicious (intentional harm) or unintentional (negligence or error).

metadata.title: Covert Channels (Timing)
metadata.definition: A timing covert channel is a communication path that transmits information by modulating the time at which events occur, or the order of events, in a system where such communication is not intended. Information is encoded in the temporal characteristics of system operations, such as delays or execution times.

metadata.definition: A storage covert channel is a communication path that transmits information by directly or indirectly writing to and reading from a shared storage location or resource, where the existence of this communication is unintended by the system's security policy. Data is encoded by modifying attributes or contents of shared storage elements.

metadata.title: Side-Channel Attack (Power Analysis)
metadata.definition: A power analysis side-channel attack exploits information leaked through the fluctuating power consumption of an electronic device, particularly during cryptographic operations. By measuring and analyzing these power traces, an attacker can infer sensitive data like secret keys or internal states of an algorithm.

metadata.definition: A cache timing side-channel attack infers sensitive information by observing the timing differences in memory access patterns due to the behavior of processor caches during program execution. metadata.definition: Memory corruption is a class of software bugs where a program inadvertently writes to or reads from an unintended memory location, often leading to unpredictable behavior, program crashes, or critical security vulnerabilities. These vulnerabilities can be exploited for privilege escalation, data leakage, or arbitrary code execution.

This typically occurs due to biased scheduling or continuous competition from other processes with higher priority or more favorable timing.

metadata.title: Deterministic Parallelism

metadata.title: Universal Scalability Law
metadata.definition: A model proposed by Neil J. Gunther that extends Amdahl's Law by introducing two additional factors: contention (delay caused by shared resources) and coherency (delay caused by maintaining consistent shared data). It predicts how the performance of a system scales with increasing workload, showing that contention and coherency costs can eventually cause performance to decrease (super-linear scaling is rare and often an artifact).

metadata.title: Speedup (Parallel Computing)
metadata.definition: A measure of the performance gain achieved by executing a program in parallel compared to its best sequential execution. It is calculated as the ratio of the execution time of the best sequential program (T_1) to the execution time of the parallel program using P processors (T_P), expressed as S_P = T_1 / T_P.

metadata.title: Parallel Efficiency
metadata.definition: A metric that quantifies how well the processors in a parallel system are utilized. It is calculated as the speedup divided by the number of processors (E_P = S_P / P), representing the average fraction of time processors are productively working. An efficiency of 1 (or 100%) indicates perfect utilization.

metadata.title: Memory Wall

This gap means that CPU performance is often limited by how quickly it can retrieve data from memory, rather than by its computational power, creating a bottleneck.

To circumvent this, processor manufacturers have largely shifted towards multi-core architectures rather than increasing single-core clock speeds, allowing for more computation within a practical power envelope.

metadata.title: Flynn's Taxonomy
metadata.definition: A classification scheme for computer architectures based on the number of instruction streams and data streams they can simultaneously process. It categorizes architectures into four main types: Single Instruction, Single Data (SISD); Single Instruction, Multiple Data (SIMD); Multiple Instruction, Single Data (MISD); and Multiple Instruction, Multiple Data (MIMD).

metadata.title: SIMD Architecture (Single Instruction, Multiple Data)
metadata.definition: A type of parallel computer architecture where a single control unit fetches and executes a single instruction at a time, but that instruction operates simultaneously on multiple distinct data streams. This is highly effective for data-parallel tasks that involve applying the same operation to many data elements.

metadata.title: SIMD Architecture (Single Instruction, Multiple Data)
metadata.definition: A type of parallel computer architecture where a single control unit fetches and executes a single instruction at a time, but that instruction operates simultaneously on multiple distinct data streams. This is highly effective for data-parallel tasks that involve applying the same operation to many data elements.

metadata.title: MIMD Architecture (Multiple Instruction, Multiple Data)
metadata.definition: A type of parallel computer architecture where multiple independent processors simultaneously execute different instruction streams on different data streams. This offers the most general form of parallelism, allowing for both task parallelism and data parallelism, and is the basis for most modern multi-core processors and distributed computing systems.

metadata.title: MIMD Architecture (Multiple Instruction, Multiple Data)
metadata.definition: A type of parallel computer architecture where multiple independent processors simultaneously execute different instruction streams on different data streams. This offers the most general form of parallelism, allowing for both task parallelism and data parallelism, and is the basis for most modern multi-core processors and distributed computing systems.

metadata.title: SISD Architecture (Single Instruction, Single Data)
metadata.definition: A type of computer architecture where a single processor executes a single instruction stream on a single data stream sequentially. This is the traditional uniprocessor architecture, common in early computers and still forms the basis of individual cores in modern processors when executing a sequential portion of code.

metadata.title: MISD Architecture (Multiple Instruction, Single Data)
metadata.definition: MISD is a parallel computing architecture in Flynn's Taxonomy where multiple processing units operate on the same data stream but execute different instruction streams. This model is rarely implemented in practice due to its limited practical applications compared to other paradigms.

metadata.title: Distributed Memory Architecture
metadata.definition: A distributed memory architecture consists of multiple processing units, each with its own private memory, where processors communicate explicitly by sending messages over an interconnection network. There is no global shared address space.

metadata.title: Hybrid Memory Architecture
metadata.definition: A hybrid memory architecture combines both shared memory and distributed memory components, often found in large-scale parallel systems. Nodes typically use shared memory within themselves (e.g., multi-core CPUs) and distributed memory for communication between nodes (e.g., across a cluster).

metadata.title: Uniform Memory Access (UMA)
metadata.definition: UMA is a type of shared memory architecture where all processors can access any memory location with the same latency and bandwidth. This simplifies programming as all memory is equally accessible, but limits scalability.

metadata.title: Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA)
metadata.definition: NUMA is a shared memory architecture where processors can access local memory (connected directly to them) faster than remote memory (connected to other processors). This design improves scalability by reducing contention on a single memory bus but introduces varying memory access latencies.

metadata.title: Cache Coherent NUMA (CC-NUMA)
metadata.definition: CC-NUMA is a NUMA architecture that adds a hardware-based cache coherence mechanism to ensure data consistency across all processor caches. It combines the scalability of NUMA with the programming ease of a coherent shared memory model, albeit with increased hardware complexity.

metadata.title: Symmetric Multiprocessing (SMP)
metadata.definition: SMP is a shared memory architecture where multiple identical processors share a common main memory and I/O bus, accessing all memory locations uniformly. All processors are treated equally by the operating system and can execute any task.

metadata.title: Massively Parallel Processor (MPP)
metadata.definition: An MPP system is a distributed memory architecture composed of many independent processing nodes, each with its own processor and memory, interconnected by a high-speed network. They are designed for extreme scalability and often utilize message passing for inter-node communication.

metadata.definition: A manycore processor is an integrated circuit containing a large number of independent processing cores (tens to hundreds), designed for highly parallel workloads. These cores typically share a common chip, sometimes with shared caches, but often have local memory access.

metadata.definition: A CUDA Core is a fundamental processing unit within NVIDIA GPUs, capable of executing a single thread of instructions. GPUs contain hundreds to thousands of these cores, enabling massive parallel execution, particularly for SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Thread) workloads.

metadata.definition: A Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) is a key building block of NVIDIA GPU architecture, comprising multiple CUDA Cores, Tensor Cores (in newer generations), special function units, shared memory, and registers. The SM manages the execution of warps (groups of threads) and schedules instructions.

It excels at highly data-parallel tasks where the same operation is applied to large arrays or vectors of data.

metadata.definition: An interconnection network is the communication infrastructure that allows different components (processors, memory modules, I/O devices) within a parallel or distributed system to exchange data. Its topology, latency, and bandwidth are critical for system performance.

metadata.title: Network-on-Chip (NoC)
metadata.definition: A Network-on-Chip (NoC) is a paradigm for communication subsystems in integrated circuits, replacing traditional shared buses with a packet-switched network. NoCs are used to connect cores, memory blocks, and other IP blocks on a single chip, offering better scalability, performance, and power efficiency.

metadata.definition: A bus interconnect is a shared communication pathway consisting of parallel wires that allows multiple devices to transmit and receive data. It is simple to implement but suffers from contention and limited scalability as more devices are added.

metadata.title: Crossbar Switch
metadata.definition: A crossbar switch is a non-blocking interconnection network where any input can be connected to any available output simultaneously without contention. It provides high bandwidth and low latency but requires a large number of switches, making it expensive and complex for large systems.

metadata.title: Mesh Network
metadata.definition: A mesh network is an interconnection network topology where processors are arranged in a 2D or 3D grid, and each processor is connected directly to its immediate neighbors. It offers good scalability and path diversity but communication latency can increase with distance between nodes.

metadata.definition: A network topology where nodes are arranged in an n-dimensional grid, with each node connected to its neighbors in all dimensions. It includes wrap-around connections (toroidal links) from the last node to the first in each dimension, creating a highly interconnected and scalable structure.

metadata.definition: A network topology where 2^N nodes are interconnected, with each node representing a vertex in an N-dimensional cube and connected to its N nearest neighbors along the edges. This topology offers excellent connectivity and low diameter, making it efficient for various parallel algorithms.

metadata.title: Fat Tree Network
metadata.definition: A hierarchical network topology designed to provide uniform bisection bandwidth at all levels, ensuring that communication capacity between any two halves of the network remains constant. It achieves this by increasing the number of links (making them 'fatter') at higher levels of the hierarchy, preventing bottlenecks.

metadata.definition: A technology that enables one computer to directly access memory from another computer without involving the CPU or operating system on the target machine. This kernel bypass mechanism significantly reduces latency and increases throughput for data transfers, making it ideal for high-performance computing.

metadata.title: Shared Memory Programming Model
metadata.definition: A programming model where multiple processing units (e.g., CPU cores or threads) can access a common memory address space. Programmers utilize synchronization primitives like locks and semaphores to manage concurrent access and prevent data corruption due to race conditions.
