metadata.title: 3DES (Triple DES)
metadata.definition: 3DES is a symmetric-key encryption algorithm that applies the DES algorithm three times to each data block, providing increased security over plain DES. metadata.definition: A variant of the Diffie-Hellman key exchange where a new, temporary private key is generated for each session. This ensures that a compromise of a long-term private key does not compromise past session keys, thereby providing perfect forward secrecy.

metadata.title: Root Certificate
metadata.definition: A digital certificate at the top of a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) hierarchy, issued by a Certificate Authority (CA) to itself. It serves as a trust anchor, implicitly trusted by operating systems and browsers, from which all other certificates in that CA's chain of trust ultimately derive their validity.

metadata.definition: A digital certificate issued by a root certificate authority (or another intermediate CA) to sign end-entity certificates or other intermediate certificates. Intermediate certificates form a chain of trust between the highly secure root certificate and the more numerous end-entity certificates, allowing the root CA to remain offline and secure.

metadata.definition: The comprehensive set of practices, policies, and procedures for generating, exchanging, storing, using, revoking, and destroying cryptographic keys throughout their lifecycle. metadata.title: Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS)
metadata.definition: A property of a key agreement protocol that ensures that a compromise of a long-term private key does not compromise past session keys. Even if an adversary records encrypted communications and later obtains the server's private key, they cannot decrypt the previously recorded sessions because the session keys were ephemeral.

metadata.title: Side-channel Attack (Cryptographic)
metadata.definition: An attack that extracts sensitive information from a cryptographic system by observing its physical implementation, rather than by targeting cryptographic weaknesses directly. Attack vectors include timing variations, power consumption, electromagnetic radiation, acoustic emissions, or cache hits during cryptographic operations.

metadata.title: Cryptographic Random Number Generator
metadata.definition: An algorithm designed to produce sequences of numbers that appear random and are unpredictable, even to an attacker who knows the generator's internal state (but not the seed). Unlike general-purpose PRNGs, CRNGs (also known as CSPRNGs) are suitable for cryptographic applications such as key generation, nonces, and salts, where unpredictability is paramount.

metadata.title: Nonce
metadata.definition: An acronym for "number used once," a nonce is a random or pseudo-random value that is used only a single time within a cryptographic communication or operation. Its primary purpose is to prevent replay attacks and to ensure uniqueness for cryptographic parameters, such as initialization vectors (IVs) or parts of a key exchange.

metadata.title: Salt (Cryptographic)
metadata.definition: A unique, random string of data added to an input, such as a password, before it is hashed. Salting prevents dictionary attacks and precomputed rainbow table attacks by ensuring that identical passwords produce different hash values, making each password hash unique and requiring a brute-force attacker to compute hashes for each salt.

metadata.title: Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP)
metadata.definition: A cryptographic protocol where one party (the prover) can prove to another party (the verifier) that they know a secret value without revealing any information about the secret itself. ZKP ensures that the verifier learns nothing beyond the fact that the statement is true.

metadata.title: WPA3 Security

They achieve this by controlling which memory regions can execute code and by randomizing memory locations of key processes, making exploits harder to predict and execute.

metadata.title: System Calls Security
metadata.definition: System Calls Security focuses on ensuring that interactions between user-mode applications and the operating system kernel, performed via system calls, are properly controlled and secured. This involves validating system call parameters, enforcing access controls, and limiting the scope of what applications can request from the kernel to prevent privilege escalation or system compromise.

metadata.title: Sandbox (OS)
metadata.definition: An OS Sandbox is a security mechanism that isolates running programs or processes from the rest of the system, limiting their access to system resources, memory, and network. This containment strategy prevents potentially malicious or vulnerable applications from damaging the host system or accessing sensitive data outside their designated boundaries.

metadata.title: Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) Security

metadata.title: IaaS Security
metadata.definition: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) Security involves securing the foundational computing resources provided by a cloud provider, such as virtual machines, networks, and storage. metadata.title: Network Security Groups (Cloud)

metadata.definition: A one-way cryptographic function applied to a user's password, storing the resulting hash value instead of the plaintext password. This protects passwords from direct exposure even if a database is compromised, as the original password cannot be easily derived from the hash.

metadata.title: Rainbow Table Attack
metadata.definition: A Rainbow Table Attack is a precomputed attack designed to reverse cryptographic hash functions, commonly used to crack passwords. It involves comparing a target hash against a pre-generated table of hashes and their corresponding plaintext values, significantly speeding up password cracking compared to brute-force methods.

This phase includes various testing types like penetration testing, vulnerability scanning, static application security testing (SAST), and dynamic application security testing (DAST) to ensure the system meets its security requirements.

metadata.title: Security Deployment Phase (SSDLC)
metadata.definition: The phase in the Secure Software Development Life Cycle (SSDLC) where the securely developed and tested software is prepared for and moved into production environments. Key activities include hardening infrastructure, configuring security controls, managing secrets, and ensuring proper logging and monitoring are in place.

metadata.definition: A side-channel attack is a non-invasive physical attack that exploits unintended information leakage from a cryptographic system's physical implementation rather than its theoretical algorithm. Attackers analyze physical parameters like power consumption, electromagnetic emanations, or execution time to infer secret keys or other sensitive data.

metadata.definition: A cryptographic primitive that allows a party (the committer) to commit to a value at one point in time, revealing it later. The scheme ensures that the committer cannot change the committed value (binding property) and that the verifier learns nothing about the value before it's revealed (hiding property).

metadata.title: Threshold Signature Scheme (TSS)
metadata.definition: A type of multi-party computation (MPC) that distributes the signing capability for a single cryptographic key among multiple participants, such that a valid signature can only be produced if a predefined threshold number of participants cooperate. No single participant ever holds the full private key, enhancing security and fault tolerance.

metadata.title: Verifiable Random Function (VRF)
metadata.definition: A cryptographic primitive that provides a 'provably fair' way to generate random numbers, allowing anyone to verify that the random output was correctly generated by a specific party using a secret key, without revealing the secret key itself. It produces a verifiable, pseudo-random output along with a proof.

metadata.title: Block (Blockchain)
metadata.definition: A fundamental data structure in a blockchain, comprising a collection of validated transactions and other relevant information. Each block is cryptographically linked to the previous one through hashing, forming a secure, immutable, and append-only chain of records.

metadata.title: Block Header
metadata.definition: The metadata section of a blockchain block, typically containing information like the hash of the previous block, the Merkle root of the transactions within the block, a timestamp, a nonce, and the difficulty target. The block header is often hashed itself to create the block's unique identifier and prove work in PoW systems.

metadata.title: Genesis Block
metadata.definition: The very first block ever mined and validated on a blockchain network. It has no preceding block and serves as the foundational block from which all subsequent blocks are chained, establishing the initial state, parameters, and rules of the entire ledger.

metadata.title: UTXO Model
metadata.definition: Stands for 'Unspent Transaction Output' model, primarily used by Bitcoin and similar cryptocurrencies. In this model, every transaction consumes a set of existing unspent outputs as inputs and produces a new set of unspent outputs, which can then be spent in future transactions, effectively tracking discrete units of value.

metadata.definition: A blockchain node that downloads and verifies every transaction and every block from the genesis block onwards, maintaining a complete, up-to-date copy of the entire blockchain ledger. This allows it to independently verify the network's state and security without relying on third parties.

metadata.title: Miner (Blockchain)
metadata.definition: A node in a Proof-of-Work (PoW) blockchain network responsible for creating new blocks by solving a computationally intensive cryptographic puzzle. The first miner to solve the puzzle broadcasts the new block, and if accepted by the network, is rewarded with newly minted cryptocurrency and transaction fees.

metadata.title: Decentralization
metadata.definition: The principle in blockchain where control and decision-making power are distributed among many participants rather than being concentrated in a single entity or small group. This eliminates single points of failure, reduces censorship risk, and fosters network resilience.

metadata.definition: A divergence in the blockchain's history, typically occurring when the network splits into two separate paths due to conflicting blocks, protocol changes, or different versions of client software. Forks can be temporary, resolved by the network's consensus, or permanent, leading to a new, distinct blockchain.

metadata.title: Hard Fork
metadata.definition: A permanent and backward-incompatible change to the blockchain protocol, requiring all participants to upgrade their software to the new rules. Nodes that do not upgrade will operate on the old chain, effectively creating two separate and independent blockchains.

While compatible, an upgrade is recommended for full functionality and security.

metadata.title: Double-Spending
metadata.definition: The malicious act of spending the same unit of digital currency more than once. In traditional digital systems, this is prevented by a central authority, but in blockchain, it's mitigated by robust consensus mechanisms, transaction verification, and the immutability of the confirmed ledger.

metadata.title: 51% Attack
metadata.definition: A scenario where a single entity or coordinated group gains control of more than 50% of the network's total mining (Proof-of-Work) or staking power (Proof-of-Stake). With this majority control, they could potentially manipulate the blockchain, such as reversing transactions, censoring new ones, or producing empty blocks.

metadata.definition: A waiting area or 'memory pool' maintained independently by each blockchain node for unconfirmed transactions that have been broadcast to the network but have not yet been included in a block. Transactions remain in the mempool until a miner or validator picks them for inclusion in a new block, typically prioritizing those with higher fees.

metadata.title: Nonce (Blockchain)
metadata.definition: In Proof-of-Work, it's an arbitrary number miners adjust to find a valid block hash that meets the network's difficulty target. For accounts in chains like Ethereum, it's an incrementing counter for each transaction sent from an address, preventing replay attacks and ensuring transaction order.

metadata.title: EIP-1559 (London Hard Fork)
metadata.definition: An Ethereum Improvement Proposal implemented in the London hard fork that reformed Ethereum's transaction fee mechanism. It introduced a 'base fee' that is burned and a 'priority fee' (tip) that goes to the miner/validator, making fees more predictable and adding deflationary pressure to ETH.

The exchange handles the token sale process, often vetts the project, and typically lists the token on its platform immediately after the sale.

metadata.title: Token Vesting Schedule
metadata.definition: A token vesting schedule is a pre-defined timeline that dictates when and how newly issued cryptocurrency tokens will be released and become transferable. It is commonly applied to tokens allocated to founders, team members, advisors, and early investors to ensure long-term commitment and prevent immediate large-scale selling.

metadata.title: Tokenomics
metadata.definition: Tokenomics is the study of a cryptocurrency project's economic model, encompassing its token's supply, distribution, utility, and incentive mechanisms. It analyzes how these factors influence the token's value, user behavior, and the overall health and sustainability of the ecosystem.

metadata.title: ERC-20 Token Standard
metadata.definition: The ERC-20 token standard is a technical specification for creating and issuing fungible tokens on the Ethereum blockchain. It defines a common set of rules and functions that all ERC-20 compliant tokens must implement, ensuring interoperability within the Ethereum ecosystem.

metadata.title: ERC-721 Token Standard
metadata.definition: The ERC-721 token standard is a technical specification for creating unique, non-fungible tokens (NFTs) on the Ethereum blockchain. Each ERC-721 token has a distinct identifier, ensuring that it cannot be replaced by another token, making it suitable for representing digital collectibles or unique assets.

metadata.title: ERC-1155 Token Standard
metadata.definition: The ERC-1155 token standard is a multi-token standard on the Ethereum blockchain that allows a single smart contract to manage both fungible (like ERC-20) and non-fungible (like ERC-721) tokens, and even semi-fungible tokens. This standard significantly improves efficiency for projects dealing with diverse token types, such as in gaming.

metadata.title: Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)

metadata.title: Reentrancy Attack
metadata.definition: A critical smart contract vulnerability where an external contract call recursively calls back into the original contract before the initial call's state updates are fully completed. This allows an attacker to repeatedly drain funds or manipulate the contract's state by exploiting the incomplete state transition logic.

metadata.title: Flash Loan Attack
metadata.definition: An exploit where an attacker takes out an uncollateralized 'flash loan' (a loan that must be repaid within the same transaction block) and uses the massive borrowed capital to manipulate market prices or exploit vulnerabilities in other DeFi protocols. The attacker profits from the temporary market imbalance or exploit before repaying the loan within the single atomic transaction.

metadata.title: Front-Running (Blockchain)
metadata.definition: A predatory practice where a miner, validator, or sophisticated actor observes a pending transaction in the public mempool and then submits their own transaction with a higher gas fee to ensure it gets processed before the original transaction. This allows the front-runner to profit from information asymmetry, commonly seen in decentralized exchange (DEX) trading.

Miners compete to solve a cryptographic puzzle, and the chain with the most cumulative proof of work is considered the valid one.

metadata.title: Mining (PoW)
metadata.definition: In Proof of Work (PoW) blockchains, mining is the process by which participants (miners) use computational power to repeatedly guess a cryptographic nonce until they find a valid hash for a new block. This puzzle-solving effort validates transactions, secures the network, and results in rewards (newly minted currency and transaction fees) for successful miners.

metadata.definition: A cooperative arrangement where multiple cryptocurrency miners combine their computational resources (hash rate) to increase their collective probability of solving a block and earning rewards. metadata.definition: In Proof of Stake (PoS) networks, a staking pool allows multiple token holders to combine their assets to meet the minimum staking requirements for operating a validator node. This enables individuals with smaller amounts of cryptocurrency to collectively participate in staking, earn rewards, and contribute to network security.

metadata.definition: The dynamic group of participants in a Proof of Stake (PoS) blockchain who are responsible for proposing, validating, and finalizing new blocks. metadata.title: Slashing (PoS)
metadata.definition: A critical punitive mechanism in Proof of Stake (PoS) blockchains where a portion of a validator's staked cryptocurrency is confiscated. This penalty is imposed for malicious behavior (e.g., double-signing blocks), prolonged inactivity, or other violations of network rules, serving to maintain network security and honest participation.

metadata.title: Delegated Proof of Stake (DPoS)
metadata.definition: A variant of Proof of Stake where token holders vote to elect a limited number of 'delegates' or 'witnesses' who are then responsible for validating transactions and producing blocks. This system aims to achieve higher transaction throughput and faster block finality by having a smaller, more efficient set of validators.

metadata.title: Proof of Authority (PoA)
metadata.definition: A consensus mechanism where blocks are validated by a limited and pre-selected set of trustworthy authorities, rather than through energy-intensive competition (PoW) or economic stake (PoS). PoA networks offer high transaction throughput and are often favored for private, consortium, or sidechain applications where identity and reputation are paramount.

metadata.title: Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT)
metadata.definition: A characteristic of distributed computer systems that allows them to reach consensus and operate correctly even if some of their components (nodes) fail or act maliciously by sending incorrect or contradictory information. BFT algorithms are crucial for maintaining consistency and reliability in decentralized environments, including many blockchain networks.

metadata.title: Federated Byzantine Agreement (FBA)
metadata.definition: A class of consensus mechanisms designed for distributed systems where participants establish trust relationships with specific subsets of other nodes (quorum slices), rather than relying on a global, fixed set of validators. This allows for flexible and overlapping trust networks, enabling open membership and resilience against Byzantine failures.

metadata.title: Proof of Elapsed Time (PoET)
metadata.definition: A consensus mechanism primarily used in permissioned blockchains, where participants are chosen to create new blocks based on a fair lottery system using secure, verifiable timers. It leverages Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) like Intel SGX to ensure that each participant waits a randomly chosen, verifiable period of time, and the first to complete their wait wins the right to propose a block.

metadata.title: Proof of History (PoH)
metadata.definition: A novel cryptographic clock within the Solana blockchain, which is not a consensus mechanism itself but a key component that generates a verifiable, sequential record of events. By embedding timestamps into the blockchain, PoH allows validators to process transactions in parallel and establish a verifiable order of events without requiring real-time communication between all nodes, greatly enhancing throughput.

metadata.title: Finality (Blockchain)
metadata.definition: The guarantee that once a transaction has been recorded on a blockchain, it cannot be reversed, altered, or removed. It ensures the immutability and permanence of confirmed transactions, preventing double-spending.

metadata.definition: A type of finality where a transaction is considered final with a high, but not absolute, certainty. The probability of a transaction being reversed decreases exponentially as more blocks are added on top of it, making a chain reorganization extremely difficult but theoretically possible.

metadata.title: Economic Finality
metadata.definition: A state where reverting a transaction or block would incur a financial cost so prohibitively high (e.g., through slashing of staked assets or immense energy expenditure) that it becomes economically irrational or infeasible for any attacker. It provides a practical guarantee against reversal based on adverse economic incentives.

metadata.title: Long-Range Attack (PoS)
metadata.definition: A specific type of attack in Proof-of-Stake (PoS) blockchains where an attacker attempts to create an alternative, longer chain starting from genesis or a very old block using keys of validators who have long exited the network or whose stake has since been moved. The 'nothing-at-stake' problem exacerbates this, as there's no inherent cost for validators to participate in multiple conflicting chains from the past.

metadata.title: Nothing-at-Stake Problem (PoS)
metadata.definition: A fundamental challenge in early Proof-of-Stake (PoS) designs where validators incur no significant cost for validating blocks on multiple competing forks. This incentivizes validators to vote on every possible chain split, making it difficult for the network to converge on a single canonical chain and enabling attackers to create long, conflicting forks without penalty.

metadata.title: Sharding (Blockchain)
metadata.definition: A database partitioning technique applied to blockchains, where the entire network is divided into smaller, interconnected partitions called 'shards.' Each shard processes a subset of transactions and maintains its own state, allowing for parallel transaction processing and significantly increasing the overall network's throughput and scalability.

metadata.title: Rollups (Blockchain)
metadata.definition: A Layer 2 scaling solution that executes transactions off-chain, bundles hundreds of these transactions into a single batch, and then submits a compressed representation (or a cryptographic proof) of this batch to the Layer 1 blockchain. This significantly reduces the data footprint on the main chain while inheriting its robust security guarantees.

metadata.title: Optimistic Rollup
metadata.definition: A type of Rollup that 'optimistically' assumes all transactions processed off-chain are valid by default. It allows a 'challenge period' (typically 7 days) during which anyone can submit a 'fraud proof' to the Layer 1 if they detect an invalid state transition. If a fraud is proven, the invalid transaction is reverted, and the responsible party (sequencer) is penalized.

metadata.title: ZK-Rollup
metadata.definition: A type of Rollup that uses zero-knowledge cryptography (specifically ZK-SNARKs or ZK-STARKs) to generate a compact cryptographic 'validity proof' for off-chain transaction batches. This proof is then submitted to the Layer 1, immediately and cryptographically verifying the correctness of all transactions within the batch without requiring a challenge period.

metadata.title: Validium
metadata.definition: A Layer 2 scaling solution similar to a ZK-Rollup in that it uses zero-knowledge proofs for validity, but differs significantly in its data availability model. While computation is verified with ZK proofs on Layer 1, the transaction data itself is stored off-chain and managed by a committee of data availability operators, rather than being posted to Layer 1. This offers higher scalability but introduces a trust assumption regarding data availability.

metadata.title: Plasma (Blockchain)
metadata.definition: An early Layer 2 scaling framework that allows for the creation of 'child chains' nested on top of a main Layer 1 blockchain. These child chains process transactions off-chain, with the Layer 1 used only for dispute resolution and the periodic commitment of Merkelized roots representing the child chain's state. Users can exit funds back to Layer 1 if the child chain misbehaves, though the exit process can be complex.

metadata.definition: An independent blockchain that runs parallel to a main Layer 1 blockchain and is connected to it via a two-way peg, allowing assets to be transferred between the two chains. Sidechains have their own consensus mechanisms and block producers, offering increased scalability and customizability for specific applications, but typically do not inherit the full security of the main chain.

metadata.title: State Channel
metadata.definition: A Layer 2 scaling solution that allows two or more participants to conduct multiple transactions off-chain directly with each other without immediately broadcasting them to the Layer 1 blockchain. Only the initial opening and final closing states of the channel (or disputes) are recorded on the main chain, significantly reducing transaction fees and latency.

metadata.title: Payment Channel (e.g., Lightning Network)

metadata.title: Data Availability Problem
metadata.definition: In blockchain scaling solutions, particularly rollups, the Data Availability Problem refers to ensuring that all transaction data, especially for off-chain processed transactions, is published and accessible to all participants so they can reconstruct the chain state and verify its validity. Without data availability, a malicious sequencer could withhold data, preventing users from exiting or verifying the chain.

metadata.title: Interaction (Smart Contract)
metadata.definition: Interaction with a smart contract involves calling its functions or reading its state variables on a blockchain. This can be done via transactions, which modify the contract's state and incur gas fees, or via calls, which are read-only operations that do not alter state and are typically free.

metadata.title: Event-driven Architecture (Blockchain)
metadata.definition: Event-driven architecture in blockchain refers to a design pattern where components communicate by emitting and reacting to events, rather than direct calls. In blockchain, smart contracts emit 'events' to log changes on-chain, which can then be listened to by off-chain services or DApp frontends for asynchronous processing and real-time updates.

metadata.title: Nash Equilibrium
metadata.definition: Nash Equilibrium is a concept in game theory where each player's chosen strategy is the best response to the strategies chosen by all other players. In this state, no player can improve their outcome by unilaterally changing their strategy, assuming others' strategies remain constant.

metadata.title: Tragedy of the Commons
metadata.definition: The Tragedy of the Commons is an economic problem where individuals, acting independently and rationally according to their own self-interest, ultimately deplete a shared limited resource, even when it is clear that doing so is contrary to the group's long-term best interest. This concept is relevant in designing resource management within blockchain systems.

metadata.title: Quantum Computing (Threat to Crypto)
metadata.definition: Refers to the potential of powerful quantum computers to break currently utilized public-key cryptography algorithms, such as RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC), which underpin the security of most blockchain networks and cryptocurrencies. Shor's algorithm, for example, can efficiently factor large numbers and solve discrete logarithms, compromising key generation and digital signatures.

metadata.title: Lattice-based Cryptography
metadata.definition: A family of public-key cryptographic algorithms whose security relies on the computational difficulty of solving certain problems in high-dimensional lattices. It is considered one of the most promising approaches for post-quantum cryptography, offering strong resistance against attacks from quantum computers.

metadata.title: Code-based Cryptography
metadata.definition: A branch of post-quantum cryptography that bases its security on the computational hardness of decoding general linear codes, such as the syndrome decoding problem. These schemes typically offer large key sizes but are considered highly resistant to attacks by quantum computers.

metadata.title: Hash-based Signatures
metadata.definition: A class of digital signature schemes that derive their security solely from cryptographic hash functions, rather than number-theoretic problems. These schemes are inherently quantum-resistant because collision resistance and pre-image resistance of hash functions are believed to be difficult even for quantum computers, making them a viable post-quantum solution.

metadata.title: Statelessness (HTTP)
metadata.definition: HTTP is a stateless protocol, meaning each request from a client to a server is treated as an independent transaction without knowledge of previous requests. The server does not store any session information about the client between requests, necessitating other mechanisms for state management.

metadata.title: Multi-Page Applications (MPAs)
metadata.definition: Multi-Page Applications (MPAs) are traditional web applications where each distinct user interaction, such as clicking a link or submitting a form, typically triggers a full page reload. This means the browser fetches and renders an entirely new HTML document for most navigation events, with each page usually having its own dedicated URL.

metadata.title: Database Transactions (ACID)
metadata.definition: A sequence of one or more database operations that are treated as a single logical unit of work, which either all succeed (commit) or all fail (rollback) together, ensuring data consistency and integrity. ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability, which are the properties guaranteed by transactions.

metadata.title: Database Normalization (1NF)
metadata.definition: The first normal form (1NF) is a foundational rule in relational database design stating that each column in a table must contain only atomic (indivisible) values, and there should be no repeating groups of columns or rows. This ensures that each cell holds a single piece of data.

metadata.title: Database Normalization (2NF)
metadata.definition: The second normal form (2NF) builds on 1NF and requires that all non-key attributes in a table be fully functionally dependent on the *entire* primary key. If the primary key is composite, no non-key attribute should depend only on a part of it.

This is a browser-enforced security mechanism designed to prevent malicious cross-origin requests, as by default, browsers block such interactions.

metadata.title: Secure Cookie Flags (HttpOnly)
metadata.definition: The `HttpOnly` cookie flag instructs web browsers to prevent client-side scripts, such as JavaScript, from accessing the cookie's value. This measure significantly mitigates the risk of Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks, as an attacker exploiting an XSS vulnerability cannot easily steal session cookies containing sensitive information.

metadata.title: Secure Cookie Flags (Secure)
metadata.definition: The `Secure` cookie flag ensures that a cookie is only sent by the browser over encrypted HTTPS connections. This prevents the cookie from being transmitted over unencrypted HTTP, protecting its contents from being intercepted and read by attackers during transit, especially over public Wi-Fi networks.

metadata.title: Secure Cookie Flags (SameSite)
metadata.definition: The `SameSite` cookie flag is a security measure that tells browsers whether to send cookies with cross-site requests, primarily to mitigate Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks and unwanted cross-site information leakage. It has three modes: `Strict`, `Lax`, and `None`, each providing different levels of protection and functionality.

metadata.title: Page Load Time
metadata.definition: Page Load Time refers to the total duration it takes for a web page to fully render and become interactive in a user's browser, starting from the moment the initial request is made until all resources (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, etc.) are downloaded and processed. It is a critical metric for user experience and website performance.

metadata.title: Time To First Byte (TTFB)
metadata.definition: Time To First Byte (TTFB) is a foundational web performance metric that measures the time taken from the initial request for a resource until the first byte of that resource's response is received by the browser. It indicates how quickly the server responds to a request and is influenced by server processing time, network latency, and routing.

metadata.title: First Contentful Paint (FCP)
metadata.definition: First Contentful Paint (FCP) measures the time from when the page starts loading until any part of the page's content, such as text, images, or non-white background canvas, is rendered on the screen. It provides the first visual feedback to the user, indicating that the page is actually loading and not just a blank screen.

metadata.title: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)
metadata.definition: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) is a Core Web Vital metric that reports the render time of the largest image or text block visible within the viewport. LCP is considered a key indicator of a page's perceived loading speed, as it typically marks the point when the page's main content has likely loaded and become useful to the user.

metadata.title: Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)
metadata.definition: Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) is a Core Web Vital metric that quantifies the unexpected shifting of visual page content during loading, which can be disorienting and frustrating for users. It measures the sum of all individual layout shift scores for every unexpected layout shift that occurs during the entire lifespan of the page.

metadata.title: First Input Delay (FID)
metadata.definition: First Input Delay (FID) is a Core Web Vital metric that measures the time from when a user first interacts with a page (e.g., clicks a button, taps a link, types into a text field) to the time when the browser is actually able to begin processing that interaction. It quantifies the responsiveness of a page during its load phase.

metadata.title: Core Web Vitals
metadata.definition: Core Web Vitals are a set of specific, real-world user experience metrics from Google that evaluate the loading performance, interactivity, and visual stability of web pages. They include Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), First Input Delay (FID), and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), and are significant factors in search engine ranking.

metadata.title: Cross-Browser Testing
metadata.definition: Cross-browser testing is the practice of testing a website or web application across different browsers, operating systems, and devices to ensure a consistent user experience and functional compatibility. It addresses variations in rendering engines, JavaScript implementations, and CSS interpretations to guarantee the application works as expected for all users.

metadata.title: Browser Rendering Engine
metadata.definition: A browser rendering engine is a core software component of a web browser responsible for interpreting and displaying web content (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) on a user's screen. It parses the document, constructs a Document Object Model (DOM), calculates styles, performs layout, and ultimately paints the pixels that form the visible webpage.

metadata.title: Cross-Origin Isolation
metadata.definition: A security feature that allows web pages to opt-in to a more secure and powerful environment by requiring specific HTTP headers (`Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy`). This isolation prevents other origins from synchronously accessing the document's state, enabling features like `SharedArrayBuffer` and high-resolution performance timers.

metadata.title: GraphQL Subscriptions
metadata.definition: A feature within GraphQL that allows clients to receive real-time updates from a server whenever specific data changes or events occur. Unlike queries (fetch once) or mutations (change once), subscriptions maintain a persistent connection, typically via WebSockets, to push updates to clients.

metadata.title: WebSockets API
metadata.definition: A communication protocol and API that provides full-duplex, low-latency, and persistent communication channels over a single TCP connection between a client (e.g., web browser) and a server. It enables real-time, bidirectional data exchange, unlike traditional HTTP request-response cycles.
